Seldom does a game come around that challenges our perception of a genre. A game that makes one questions the established definition of what "entertainment" really is. A game so
that it transcends our wildest expectations  and leaves us begging for more. Such a game has not graced this earth since Quest 64 - that is -
paves the way for the true Golden Age of gaming. Take on the role of Blake Drake, fabled older brother of Nathan Drake from the Tomb Raider series, as he works to stop the new face of terrorism headed by 3:16 Stone Cold Steven Austin and his group of highly trained robot soldiers. Along the way, Blake, only armed with the power of friendship and his own style of mixed martial arts (and also guns), is as modest as he is kind and decides to collect the missing treasures for his closest friend Ibne Batoota who is very sad. Meanwhile, Blake's sister is kidnapped by Stone Cold's robo-thugs and she might died, but I don't know I haven't finished the game yet.
controls like a dream. From the stiff movement to the camera that knows what you want better than you do, controlling Blake is as natural as breathing. Coupled with truly next generation MoCap technology and animations that feel more realistic than real life - if it were any more real, it would be real. Often times I found myself pausing the game and looking around the room to double check I was not actually there in the lush deserts of France. Developer Sememaphone really let their innovation show in the games special effects, notably with the motion controlled fire and
particle effects on the castable spells. The robot guards in-game cloaking devices were so impressive
.
Peter Moneylox has really outdone himself this time, and I for one cannot wait until the next installment in the
series. Truly
has set the bar for what games can achieve, and it may take years to dethrone this behemoth of a video game. While I am normally against funding terrorism, I cannot suggest enough that you buy this masterpiece.

Okay, so maybe in the future I'll write a game for Operation Arrowhead but for now this is a review on Arma 2. Honestly, don't buy this game. This is a great game with dozens of hours to play and a lot of *fun* hours, something a lot of games don't do. There are an unbelievable amount of choices in singleplayer gameplay this game has, and all are really enjoyable. LOOK AT LAST PARAGRAPH FOR WHY TO NOT BUY IT.
For Arma 2's campaign, it isn't amazing, but it can be pretty fun. I really think the RPG elements they added were pretty cool, especially making this game's campaign less linear and more about random events, since that gives this game a lot of replayablility, along with like 4 different endings. The more short-term missions felt like a good scenario, but sometimes the long missions drag on a lot, adding unnecessary hours of just driving that isn't really fun. A good example is the mission "Razor Two", an unbelievably boring missions that takes like 3 extra hours (without a walkthrough) to get every piece of evidence and do everything. Too many of these missions have the evidence thing, and it's definitely rewarding at the end game, but when I realized what it did, I was really, really disappointed. It plays it out to be a huge thing that really affects the game, because I mean, collecting evidence of terrible war-crimes is a pretty big deal; unfortunately, it literally just gives you strong reinforcements so the last mission is easier, and that really made me feel like spending maybe an extra 5 hours on the campaign (and this campaign is short, the campaign is probably 15 hours if you don't search for evidence). Overall, this campaign isn't bad, but I don't think I'd recommend getting the game for it; it just isn't memorable.
Scenarios are an entirely different story. These are pretty fun, and there are a lot of them (I think 7 of them). They are essentially a short term burst of action and fun while including some decisions that aren't necessarily long term, but rewarding. They all vary in gameplay a good amount too, giving lots of choices for gameplay style and pace. There are even some that feel like a one-man first person RTS, which is really interesting, especially since it still maintains the feeling of a sim. Overall, I strongly recommend at least trying every scenario, they are really well made and fun to play, and just feel good.
Armory and Editor are shorter in descriptions, but much more in content than Scenarios and the Harvest Red Campaign so I'll group them together. The interesting thing about Armory is it really feels more like just a thing to mess around with, experiment, and get a feel for the weapons, but it can be much more than that. There are little side missiosn that you get to do that put your weapon into actual realistic situations so you can imagine its usefulness on the battlefield, which is a pretty neat thing to add. I don't personally like editor, but for anyone who has fun making levels, this is really well done. It's pretty simple to use, and it doesn't take too long to make a detailed, fun, and good mission to try yourself. Also, you can download other people's missions to judge them yourself, which can be really fun. While I don't think these are as good as the main stuff for singleplayer, but these are just fun little things to tinker with while you're bored.
This doesn't really sound like I dislike this game, and I don't, I think it's amazing, but it isn't worth buying, which is really unfortunate. Despite all the angry reviews going about these days, DCU is still a plenty enjoyable MMO, and has a blend of action gameplay and comic book flair that makes it uniquely addicting. Just know that the "free" component, like most MMOs these days, is more or less a trial zone. You need to subscribe up to get the full experience, which includes finding the gear to push your overal level higher by doing the episodal content. Kind of like Destiny, only DCU did it first.
General gist of things is, you enter the game as one of a wave of new heroes or villains brought about by an alternate timeline Lex releasing a swarm of nanomachines that he stole from Braniac, containing information from all the superhumans he'd digitized in the process of conquering Earth, into the atmosphere. Lots of customization avaliable that doesn't have to be directly tied to your loadout, all in that very distinct modern DC style. If that's your speed, you'll feel plenty of home.
Game plays like a third-person brawler in most cases, with your primary weapon determining your general combat style and effective range, while your power set determines your secondary combat role: tank, controller, or healer. You can readily swap between damage and secondary roles at any time, which makes transitioning from running solo in the overworld and running dungeons as your chosen sub-class more painless. Tank and healer is obvious, but controller is a bit different; they operate as debuffers and have a secondary effect on many of their abilities to restore the energy pool (mana, basically) of group members. Powers can be chosen from two trees that often have unique synergies with each other depending on the power set, and the powers themselves remain the same regardless of role. Switching role simply activates a different secondary effect, depending on the power in question.
The initial 30 levels, where you hit the points needed to fully load out your power sets, are fairly straightforward and largely involve a heroes vs villains plotline with both big and small figures in the DC universe. Some of the voice acting is...questionable, at times, but the sheer breadth of DC references and the fact that you can have Mark Hamill's Joker mentoring you make it all worth it. Trust me.
Short of it is, try it out in free mode, decide of the combat and atmosphere clicks with you, then subscribe up to get access to all the episodic content as well as a slew of other stuff. Plus, the subscription works across Planetside and both Everquests too, so there's that.

ONLY BECAUSE ITS FREE, BUT EVEN THIS REQUIRES ELABORATION
To start with the gameplay: They don't try to hide the fact that most of the side missions are fetch quests. The only thing that breaks up the monotony are the massive invasions and major arkfall events which bring huge amounts of players to certain areas. If it weren't for these this game would be an open-world third person shooter and not an MMO. There really isn't a point to doing the main story line, most of your exp, earnable weapons, and time is better spent on invasions and arkfalls. The main story line is also very boring. Your main storyline objective from the stratocarrier crash to San Francisco is to hold off waves of enemies while 'x' character does something until the time runs out, or enter the same bunker 8000 times and grind through waves of enemies to achieve 'x' objective. The bosses are easy and lame, none requires any real skill. Most of the weapons are useful, but there are a few contrived weapons classes that serve no useful purpose whatsoever: Pump Action Shotgun=Good close range weapon, while Sawed off Shotguns=Useless filler weapons tier. I killed the last boss in fewer than 10 minutes, using only a shotgun. *Yawn* (Stick to invasions, that's where the players are when the game doesn't crash) When you do get a massive amount of players in an area for an arkfall the server has a habit of lagging and crashing. It will happen, expect it!
The PVP is almost non-existant outside of duels (friends-only) and "Shadow War" which is a  team-based cooperative PVP objective area. This area is voluntary by clicking on the Shadow War icon in the map screen. There are no exclusive PVP servers.
Graphics: So, the graphics are straight out of 2006. This is not an exageration, but a matter of fact. The famous San Francisco row houses are entirely the same 2 dodads. They just copy-pasted them around the map. It gets annoying looking at the same dodad replicated around the entire map. Alot of the terrain until you hit San Francisco is Copy-Pasted. I had the feeling the developers didn't even try to mix it up in alot of places. San Francisco downtown utilizes only one major landmark from the city, the rest are imported dodads that are replicated in other places in the map, which is greatly disappointing. The Skinning is also limited and the NPCs are stock farmer, stock mercenary, stock alien to a disappointing extent. I think there are only 3 or 4 skins in total for one of the faction mercenaries.
Sound: Do you like the sound of "I'm pinned down goddamnit!" Every time you do a mission with the sheriff you'll hear it...at least 50 times. Learning the character names is not even remotely important to any part of the story, because they're not, and you won't. Some weapons have different sounds, like the machine gun, shotguns, and pistols, but subcartegory weapons don't sound any different. BMGs and LMGs both make the same noise when firing, Sawed off shotguns, pump-action shotguns, and combat shotguns also sound the same etc. The NPCs all make the same grunting noises, depending on faction; the enemies, depending on the faction, make the same noises as well. When you talk to certain characters their lips don't move outside of cut-scenes. Annoying
AI: Like any MMO AI it's pitiful. Any mission involving AI allies will have you doing all of the work, while they yell the same 3 lines at random points and occasionally get shot up requiring you to assist them. The enemy AI isn't any better and the AI is mostly annoying because of it.
Bonus factors: The game tries to force you to do faction grinding missions to buy gear from their mercs. The more of these you do, the better your reputation with that faction. While on the surface this is a pretty neat idea, it's not a new one. It's been effected better in other MMOs, and comes across as 'last minute added in' here. Having a good rep with a faction doesn't really grant you anything outside of the vendor areas, also vendor missions are usually enemy grind areas. These aren't bad when you have alot of players, because you can clear the areas quickly, but many players don't do these missions because the loot and exp from them aren't as good as arkfalls and invasions. You will need to clear some of these areas eventually to get the more interesting 'mount' style vehicles, like, the black Dodge Challenger.
Summary: I actually enjoy the invasions and the major arkfall events. When you have alot of people moving around an area in vehicles and on foot in the scenario the game really is nice, both aesthetically and from a cooperative standpoint it's fun. The Graphics are poor, the story-line useless and boring with forgetable characters, and the dialogue is velveeta-level cheesy. If you have a few regular devoted players the game could be fun, but compared to others its nothing to write home about.

Outland is a beautiful, stylish platformer succesfully exploiting a twist mechanic to the fullest. The artwork and character designs are really nice and the main reason for me to keep coming back at this game. Storywise there's not a lot going on, but it's presented in a nice way anyway. The meat of the game is at the level design and mechanics.
The levels can be hard as nails at times, but never are they impossible. If you die a lot it's your own fault, so count to ten and try again. I haven't felt the need to throw my controller against the wall as yet, but I can't promise that won't change for the rest of the game. And still it is fun. There are multiple ways of using your color shift and other abilities to make your way, which give a sense of freedom and satisfaction once you manage to get through.
The way the map works reminds me of the mazelike map Knytt uses but more lineair; you won't get lost as long as you follow the guide (but feel free to digress or come back at an earlier point to get some bonus loot).
Yes, I recommend this game, either on sale or at full price. It's challenging, beautiful and addictive, so give it a go. I wouldn't know how it plays without a controller though, didn't have a reason to  try that. Same goes for co-op.

Outland is a great platformer with tight controls and a pleasing aesthetic, that goes well with the underlying gameplay mechanic. You switch your alignment from light/blue to dark/red at the press of a button. In red mode, red projectiles or energy beams can't hurt you, only blue ones, whereas you can only deal damage to blue enemies, and vice versa in blue mode. Once you have multiple projectile sources and enemies of different color (or even switching colors in intervals) on a screen, things start to get tough, but never frustrating.
One thing this game is missing is a proper story. Every now and then you get some text, but nothing exactly groundbreaking. The focus of this game is definitely art and gameplay.
I played the game originally on PS3 a few years ago, now again on Steam (finally). You can finish it in around 8 hours. You can then search for all the collectibles and try Arcade mode or some special Online Coop challenges. I'd say you can easily get another 8 hours out of this (or depending on how far you want to get on the leaderboards even more).
Conclusion: Great game, great controls, great art style. Story irrelevant. If you're into Metroidvania platformers you should definitely give this one a try.

Outland is a great game. I had not recommended this game initially due to the lack of rebindable keys, but the devs have fixed it and so a proper review is in order.
I had heard many great things about Outland, and this game really was on the top of the list of games I wished would come to PC so that I could play it. Overall, after playing it and beating the final boss, I must say it has lived up to expectations.
The visuals and settings is amazing, there is a good score accompanying the action, and the challenge (especially the boss fights) is well-done. I loved the tight and responsive movement controls...really one of the best-controlling platformers in that respect I've played.
Gameplay is composed mainly of platforming, combat and polarity switching, often times combining two or all three of the gameplay mechanics. The regular level sections aren't necessarily difficult. They pose a challenge, and you may die, but compared to the boss fights they are pretty do-able.
As for the boss fights, they increase in difficulty from one to the other. I found the 4th boss rather difficult, and the final boss is about learning and applying everything you have learned. It is not easy, and took me more than 2 hours to complete the final one. But still I found the challenge fair and kept going at it until I was done. Only 3% have completed the game...so you get an idea.
Alongside all that, there is a decent amount of exploring to do. Some exploring can be done linearly (meaning as you progress), while others are done while backtracking. I did as much linear exploration as I could, and it took me slightly more than 10 hours to complete the game.
All in all, Outland is as great as I expected it to be. I enjoyed the challenge and setting of the game. As such, naturally the game gets a thumbs up from me.

I bought this game when it first came out on the PlayStation Network in 2011. It was delayed because of the infamous April 2011 PlayStation hack, but I didn't know about it until the day it released. I played the demo to see what it was about; immediately after finishing the demo, I ran to my dad and begged him to help me buy the game.
Outland is an action platformer implementing a system that lots of gamers seem to have fond memories of whereas Outland is still the first instance of it to me: "color" switching. When you change to red energy, you can absorb red energy from the world and attack blue enemies. Vice versa, when you change to blue energy, you can absorb blue energy and attack red enemies. This comes together in a non-puzzle game to give you some challenges that you'll have to think for a moment about how to solve. That being said, there's nothing challenging about the "puzzles" you come across, and the solution is fairly simple. Easier said than done, as the saying goes!
: Outland's gameplay is very much based off of this one mechanic. You'll be color-switching a lot. Thankfully, it's done instantaneously through the push of a button, so you'll be back to hack-and-slashing as if nothing happened. Hack-and-slash is very expertly done here, and the color system is often used but never to a point where you get sick of it. It feels completely natural. Jumping and moving around feels fluid, and seems to work better than most other platformers. This is especially so with the wall-jumping, which, as other reviews have stated, works better here than anywhere else. Boss fights are given major importance, and the game does well at making them feel large and epic even when they don't have to be. It works brilliantly.
: The story is so intriguing. This is a case of "the story is minimal and doesn't matter much" and "it's good enough to make you want to keep going and enjoy it" at the same time. You play a man who has been experiencing visions of the past due to your spirit being a reincarnation of a hero from 30,000 years ago. You're tasked with the same quest that he was: defeat the Sisters of Chaos who aim to destroy the world that they created. The enemies you meet were once good, but they have been corrupted by Chaos, and you must defeat them to restore balance to the Earth along the way. The only voice actor is the narrator, and while his lines and acting are not as iconic as Bastion's, he gives a solid performance that has stuck with me.
: I want to keep this short and sweet: Buy the Outland - Special Edition pack. I did so as soon as I could. You won't regret owning the soundtrack, composed by Ari Pulkkinen (Super Stardust HD, Trine, Angry Birds, Resogun). The music fits perfectly with the settings they were composed for, and the boss fight tracks have been on loop on my computer since 2011. As for the sound design, it's absolutely solid. That sound when your blade hits an enemy is one of my favorite, and there's a lot of subtle cues like running through the grass, sliding down a wall, that just make this feel like a living world. For an Earth corrupted by Chaos, it still sounds beautiful.
: And I thought the graphics were beautiful on the PS3! Holy crap! The game looks absolutely gorgeous at 1920x1080. I can't tell you if a game is running at 30fps or 60fps because I really don't care either way, but the game definitely runs smoothly on my computers with no issues.
: For an indie game at $10, you are not going to go wrong here. The replayability is definitely limited, but the experience is one that may stick with you for three years like it has for me. There are few minor issues with the PC port specifically (I don't want to see two control schemes at once), but those absolutely pale in comparison to the rest of the game. I have recommended Outland to all of my friends since 2011, and that has not changed.
EDIT Oct 21 2014: I have now played co-op since writing the review, which works just as well as on the PS3 version. Unfortunately, that also means the game is just as dead, so if you want to play the campaign in full co-op or do the co-op challenges for the achievement, I'd suggest getting a friend.
Additionally, Housemarque and the devs at Knockout Games who ported Outland to PC are continously updating the game! My review previously mentioned a bug with the intro video glitching out, and this has since been fixed along with other updates such as better GPU handling and smoother co-op experiences.

I am reading the reviews below and can't believe all of these train engineer wannabes who can't recommend this game.  First of all, yes, believe it or not it is a game.  Secondly, if you want to be a real engineer then get up from your computer and drive a real train. Otherwise, graphics are great!  you can make you own routes, etc.  At the price I bought it for $9.49 on Steam how could one complain? Just have fun with it and chill the hell out!

- Convincing simulation: In cab controls (lots of dials/switches/buttons), conducting each train feels different and unique enough to be a new experience
- Built-in scenario/map creator
- Difficulty scalable from practical free roam to very strict failure
- Trains are modeled nicely, pretty to look at
- Variety of camera controls
- Tutorials (can even learn a lot about how trains function IRL)
- Tons of DLC to add variety (this is a PRO assuming that money is not an obstacle)
- Base game feels bare and stripped of content, DLC almost required to keep interest
- Sound is unpolished/unfinished: trains virtually silent, very little ambient/cabin sound (no immersion via audio at all)
- Graphics specifically pertaining to scenery are awful (trains look great, but you're going to spend hours staring at fugly low quality scenery)
- Performance: even on a high end machine, you can count on regular FPS drops and chattering of all sorts
- Game play (almost by nature) is very repetitive, with long periods of do-nothing.  After ~20 hours, I'm done with it.
- Technical difficulty galore... occasionally patches will break the game and leave it unplayable for months on end.
- Very little to no developer/community relationship and communication
I regret buying this game even at the sale price at the time.  If you absolutely love trains, I would still wait for a deep deep sale.
I can't recommend because the cons outweigh the pros by a fairly large margin.  The core of the game is great fun, but where the idea is nice, the execution and details completely fall through.  Adding salt to the wound:  terrible community relations, technical support (most of my emails/tweets/communication went completely unanswered - still have pending support request unresolved from a half year ago).  Even though the game has its fun moments, it's fraught with holes, and is not good value.

*Update 11/2016 - Nominated for Steam Awards; 'I'm not crying, there is something in my eye'* | A wonderful tale with a unique and refreshing gameplay control experience.  The dual character control from one controller is easy to pick up, and the various puzzles and gameplay elements introduced throughout the game keep the control style from getting stale.
Many aspects of the journey of the brothers involve helping others, and in return, they help the brothers to advance through the various areas and puzzles, which is delivered wonderfully and seamlessly (no fetch quests).  With a more peaceful overtone to the game, when you do encounter the few “violent” pieces of the game they have that much greater impact and dig a bit deeper into your emotions.
The graphics, environment/set design, and audio are all very well done.  On your journey you pass through many beautiful landscapes with perfectly matched gentle music scores and ambience, dark and dreary battlefields with ominous overtones, and magical places with quite a unique and mystical feel.
“Brothers” is a wonderful experience, and I would recommend it to anyone who wants to fill 3 hours with a memorable, fun, and sometimes ‘heart-string pulling’, time.

I just don't think that full price of 14 euros is right for 3-4 hour game.

There's a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥moves where the entire time enemies only spawn on one side of your ship so you beef up your weapons, armour, etc entirely on that side. . . then a big wave comes at the other side all at once. Since you just spent all your money on engines to get 5 stars you now can't build any guns on that side, so you just have to take it like a ♥♥♥♥♥ and deal with only getting 3/4 stars from having half your ship blown up, or just restart the mission.
Still, it's a fun reverse TD/strategy game. There's a metagame that involves upgrading your parts/perks that make it almost laughably easy when you revist the early levels after beating the full game. The last few missions of each line are still legitimately challenging though.

An objectively solid game. Decent voice acting, nice graphics, and so on.
What the game description doesn't mention is that Space Run is the most irritating type of puzzle game; the player must build exactly the right type of turret in exactly the right spot at the right time, or fail the mission. After about 4 hours of play time, you'll just be restarting missions until you figure out the sequence the level designers want you to follow, or looking up the solutions on YouTube; this is where it stops being fun and starts feeling like work.

It was fun in the beginning, but at some point the difficulty ramps up quite high. Eventually I was advancing only through torturous trial and error, memorizing the incoming vectors of every ship and asteroid (which never change btw) and optimizing construction accordingly. Maybe that's what some people want, but not me. Oh well, it was fun while it lasted I guess.
Tentative recommendation, if you want a space-y twist on a tower defense game.

The only thing that seems to need work is the progression. Everything is fun and smooth until 53 stars. (Level 53?) It's not the end yet,  but it's now almost impossible to get new stars. Furthermore, the currency is so worthless at this point that it's really hard to buy further upgrades. How about allowing unused nuts to become currency at the end of each map? I don't want to keep running the same maps grinding out money to update something insignificant. Without doing so, you'll never get to the true upgrades that will help you progress.
Games don't have to last forever. Artificially preventing me from completing a game by forcing me to grind is not the same as actually building in more hours worth of content. I stopped playing Final Fantasy for just this reason. Let's not pretend this is a good idea.
The game is fun and worth the money I paid for it. The only thing lacking is my sense of accomplishment from finishing the game. Unfortunately, at this point I'm tired of running the same maps over and over....

I agree fully with an earlier reviewer who said the game needs a pause button to let you build and adjust things when things get really tense.
I think the difficulty level progresses smoothly and trying to get "5 star" runs on some of the later levels is definitely a challenge that extends the play time for those looking for more.
One thing that bugs me is that once you've built all of the upgrades, there is nothing to do with your money.  You hit the fully upgraded point with a few missions left and then the money just keeps piling on (hitting the $99,999 limit fairly quickly).  Even if there was some dumb achievment for getting to $1 million, it would give something to do with that excess cash.
7.5/10

Unearthed: Trail of Ibn Battuta is a bad game.  The physics are bad, the AI is bad, the combat is terrible, the graphics are mediocre, the first vehicle sequence is probably one of the worst things I've ever tried to play, characters constantly clip into themselves, the story is laughable, the voice-acting is workmanlike, and the camera is jerky and unfriendly.
However, it is a very charming game with some interesting ideas buried under its terribleness.  Firstly, any game set in the middle east where you aren't a white guy blowing half of it up is uncommon, and fewer games still feature a badass Muslim woman in a hijab blowing away mummies and evil corporate goons with an AK-47.  It's an Uncharted knockoff, and it's terrible, but it seems like it's more a lack of experience and technical expertise that makes it terrible than a lack of passion or effort by the dev team.  Yes, it's bad, but they poured their souls into this damnit.

This game is an MMO, and that means there are a lot of people in the server with you, and they can help you complete missions because they have the missions too, which is awesome and its a mechanic that makes this game sometimes. You are not just running around killing stuff by yourself you are running around killing stuff with a random person, it makes an otherwise empty world feel alive, which is awesome. There is also something cool about seeing someone fly down the road in the opposite direction while driving alone, its a little thing, but I love it.
The theme mainly has to do with Mutants to start with, and it is fun shooting and looting alone, but with a friend it is even better. This game does take a while to download though, but I think it is worth the wait. You are a Ark Hunter, who was implanted with an EGO device, which is sort of like Cortana. And you are on a ship, and it crashes. And you have to help with everything. Not going into anymore detail as not to spoil it.
I think this game succeeded in making it feel like a single player game if you want it to be, but still being an MMO, which is rare, because you don't have to be in a huge party to do anything, which is great for someone with major social anxiety like me ;)

Ingredients
+1 cup white sugar
+1/2 cup butter
+2 eggs
+2 teaspoons vanilla extract
+1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
+1 3/4 teaspoons baking powder
+1/2 cup milk
Directions
1.Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Grease and flour a 9x9 inch pan or line a muffin pan with paper liners.
2.In a medium bowl, cream together the sugar and butter. Beat in the eggs, one at a time, then stir in the vanilla. Combine flour and baking powder, add to the creamed mixture and mix well. Finally stir in the milk until batter is smooth. Pour or spoon batter into the prepared pan.
3
Bake for 30 to 40 minutes in the preheated oven. For Warband White cupcakes, bake 20 to 25 minutes. Cake is done when it springs back to the touch.
4.Enjoy my wonderful Warband White cake.

A review for those who actually want to know a little about the gameplay. Before we go any further: This game does actually feature full on nudity, this is something that I thought would be eluded to but never shown.  I was wrong.
I originally bought HuniePop during a Steam sale for £1.74 as both a joke to myself and out of sheer curiosity, I didn't expect to be sucked in to the game as much as I was.
Boiled down to the bare minimum, HuniePop is a mixture of the Visual Novel and Match Three genres, two genre's that I have never been particularly fond of.  I have never been truly gripped by adventure games nor have I been compelled to play Candy Crush Saga for more than 10 minutes, to my surprise this did not stop me from getting several hours of enjoyment out of the game.
In HuniePop, the player has to muster up enough courage to chat with girls, go on dates and woo them.  This will be done by talking to the girls, asking questions and remembering any information that they have previously told you about theirself (something I find difficulty doing in real life - Google might be a good wingman here). The dating component is where the match three puzzling comes in to play - Each icon within the grid acts as a trait, different girls like different traits.  For example, one girl may love Romance and hate Sexuality while another enjoys Talent and hates Flirtation.  Matching 3 or more of a trait that any girl likes, will provide a Passion (Score) boost.
It is also possible to buy the girls gifts, unique gifts, food and drinks which will in turn, give you Hunie, which is used to increase your skills.  Higher skills will result in receiving higher scores during the match three element of the game.
I imagine a lot of people out there are similar to me; not super in to adventure games, match three puzzlers or even anime and are looking to have a quick laugh with HuniePop, however I have genuinely enjoyed the casual nature and ridiculousness of the game.
That being said, if you are in to big-titted anime waifu's, this game is also for you.

+Fun skill based combat

CONS
_______________________
+Players attitudes (No more or no less than any other online games)
Free-to-Play Limitations
____________________
-Currency capped at $2000
-Limited Power selection for character creation
-Limited access to content (affects gearing vs subscribed players)
-Limited Access to certain weapons (Shield is the only one at present time)
-Limited inventory and Bank slots
-Limited Character creation slots
All-in-all it's fun and it has had some bad views and reviews in the past, (myself included), but customer service will work with you as long as you provide proof for the issues that come up and talk maturely with them. If something goes wrong, don't assume the worst, First, take the time to contact the customer support and make sure you post your issue under the right category for effective help.

Warning: Spoilers.
Red Faction: Guerilla is one of the most understated games of its generation. On reception it received mixed reviews upon release due to what was deemed, a overly simplistic storyline with little imagination, mission repetitiveness and clumsy AI. While I do not deny that these claims have some validity, they do little to tarnish what is in my view a great experience and well worth the £15 price tag.
Where to begin? The physics engine is amazing. It puts even some modern sandbox games to shame. Tired of those ridiculous moments in GTA or like, where an impenetrable tree somehow halts a lorry travelling at full speed? Not to worry. Everything in Red Faction: Guerilla is destructible – from small buildings, industrial complexes to large scale bridges. Furthermore how you proceed to do this totally up to you. You could plant charges in key locations, drive a truck through supports, or simply go to town with a sledge hammer; all of which are immensely satisfying when that 1000 ton structure comes flying down, often on top of your enemy. In fact the game encourages destruction, as salvage is produced from destroyed buildings and vehicles – which you can pick up and trade in for upgrades. The setting in which this occurs is highly realistic; Mars being in the process of terraforming is beautifully captured. Some areas such as Oasis are beginning to show numerous signs of localised life, while areas such as the Badlands – bandito domain, remain an inhospitable wasteland.
The combat follows on from the physics engine. By using the environment to your advantage, combined with your knowledge of explosives, you can send buildings toppling on your enemy – or you could just shoot them, or pretty much whatever else you want to do. Often when fighting the enemy, dubbed EDF (more on this later), guerillas fighters will join you and semi-large scale battles can ensue. This can turn into insanity when bandits, who are favourable to no side in your struggle, also join in -  effectively causing a three-way conflict. The purpose of your missions are to extensively reclaim territory from the enemy. You can do this in a variety of ways. Destroying buildings, rescuing hostages, attacking conveys, supporting your fellow guerilla combatants, stealing vehicles in a time limit, or just following the mainstream quests. There are also a series of fun mini-games which give you a challenge to destroy certain buildings with limited equipment, rewarding you with extra salvage. Sadly, the problem with this – as I alluded to above, is that the AI is slightly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Often your fellow guerillas will walk in front of you whilst you are firing a weapon, or the enemy in a car chase will go 'banzai' – sending 10s of vehicles after you, which often clash into each other and end up impeding themselves. They also seem incapable of breaking and sometimes go flying off cliffs to their impending doom. I have seen enemy flyers drive into bridges because I happen to be under one (and so on).
However this is not a huge issue (its often very amusing!), and later in the game you will be thankful for the AI's stupidity as combat becomes increasingly difficult – perhaps to the point of insanity. The game is called Red Faction: Guerilla for a reason. You are out gunned and out manned in every respect; the organised enemy will come down on you like a ton of bricks meaning that combat, even with the AI's deficiency, is never dull. The EDF always have more to throw at you.
Speaking of which, this is probably a good time to discuss the plot. You are tasked with liberating Mars from the EDF (Earth Defence Force), an organisation that terrorises the local Martian population and uses them like slave labour. You yourself are effectively forced to join the resistance group 'Red Faction' after your brother, who later is revealed to be an insurgent, is killed by the EDF. That's pretty much the premise of the plot, and not a lot else develops past that. Is it simplistic? Yes, and certainly because of the limited character development I found myself displaying a certain apathy towards supposedly key characters. I simply did not care about the humans I was  meant to be protecting, which is slightly flawed given the whole focus of the game.
Nevertheless I feel that the combat more than makes up for this. Red Faction: Guerilla achieves what it set out to achieve, namely to entertain. It does this in bucket loads, providing hours of destructive joy (don't be fooled by playtime, I originally bought this on the PS3). However a word of caution, you will need to download the 'Games for Windows Life' client to be able to play it and save in game. This is an outdated inconvenience which will hopefully be removed in the future.

Tastee: Lethal Tactics is a simultaneous squad based tactics game finally out of early access on PC.  Following a very similar path as Frozen Synapses the premise is simple, each game is broken down into 2 phases the planning stage where you direct the movement, vision and attacks of your 4-5 mercenaries and in the action phases you watch the results of your actions unfold.
Obviously to be good at Tastee this means not only being precise with your tactics but also predicting what the enemy is going to do next. So many times I thought I had a perfect strategy only to wrongly predict where the enemy was and get sniped as I walked past a window or suddenly have a grenade land at my feet.
Your team is made up of a bunch of misfits each with a key ability such as long range sniping skills, the ability to throw a flashbang, the ability to conceal or simply put “has the biggest explosions”. Each character has a unique feel but sometimes visually they can be hard to differentiate when zoomed out and lets not even discuss the issue with having 2 characters standing on the same spot and being unable to click on one.
Single player is as you would expect a selection of missions loosely tied together with a story but in actual fact it acts as one long tutorial for multiplayer slowly drip feeding you a new character and a new ability as you go. It is however pretty tough and only a few missions in I started to feel my rustiness at strategy game starting to shine through.
Multiplayer however is where this game is strong… but only if you know what to expect. See the first time I played this the other player took forever to take his turn and I ended up quitting. But then I realised this game is similar to all those multiplayer mobile games you have played where someone can have many games going on at once and you merely wait until the other player has made their turn… and that could take ages… days in fact. It’s an interesting take on multiplayer but personally I found this choice bizarre and would have preferred time-outs after 5 mins of no activity in order to speed things up a bit.
When things go well however the game is immensely satisfying. Each time you watch the action unfold with no idea of what is actually going to happen, you will either be met with crushing disappointment as 2 team mates die, victory as you kill an enemy or gleeful surprise as you kill 2 by accident.
In general this is a good game and there is a lot of depth here on offer but the UI is very fiddly and cumbersome. The different actions are controller by a ring display and this includes things such as sprint, crouch look and wait, but the annoying thing is you also have to cancel everything. This means I can somehow have sprinting and crouching selected or my look direction that is totally inappropriate now has to be deselected before I can select a new one. A minor thing on the surface but when a turn in TASTEE takes so many clicks this can drag. Equally movement often doesn’t go the way you and sometimes the maps are not clear where you can and can’t go.
Overall TASTEE is a decent strategy game that bares a strong resemblance to Frozen Synapse so if you enjoyed that you will enjoy this. There is a good game in here but I can’t help but feel that a few tweaks could have made it great… I would give it a thumb to the side if I could.

Outland, the action-platformer by Housemarque, originally came out on the Xbox 360 and Playstation 3 over three years ago. It was a good game then, it's still a good game today.
First off let's discuss the port. It's decent, but could be better. For whatever reason the vsync locks at 30 fps, which causes frame-rate judders. The alternative is to turn off in-game vsync and then force it on via your videocard's control panel. I tried this but somehow I still got screen-tearing. Maybe I just suck at computers. Also there's no option to turn off vibration if you're using a 360 pad. Never been a fan of force feedback, so needless to say I didn't like this. The image-quality is a bit too soft as well. It supports resolutions at and above 1920x1080 but I dunno, it feels like it could use some AA, that would make the art-direction really stand out.
Usually when people talk about this game they mention a shump called
Oh right. Kid Icarus. Yep that old Nintendo game about Greek Mythology and Eggplant Wizards. Seriously though, the world the hero explores is governed by light and dark(or blue bullets and red bullets). Early on you're given a sword and not long after that, the ability to switch between light & dark(blue & red). When you want to absorb bullets or lasers you should be the same color, when you want to attack enemies you have to be the opposite color. Your color can also affect objects such as floating platforms or spikes. Expect numerous situations to crop up where you have to switch between colors constantly to proceed. This isn't a puzzle game but you will have to think every now and then, at least for a moment.
Switching colors isn't always an option. For example, you might run into a red enemy while area is filled with red bullets. The trick here is to use one of your special attacks. These can include a power strike, a laser, and flashy explosion. Next up are the exploratory powers. Certain powers can be attained to make getting around easier. In typical fashion, previous areas can be explored to find more cash, life/energy upgrades, and concept art unlocks. Fair warning, this is the full extent of the exploration in this game.
Main reason I enjoy this game is it's just so fluid. Back when it came out in 2011 I started the demo thinking "Well...whatever..I guess I gotta try it." I immediately fell in love with its smooth controls, responsive moves, and that wall-jump. There's nothing better than a good wall-jump. So many games these days have them, but they rarely get it right. Outland's wall-jump is smooth, clean, and tight. Just running, jumping, and slashing also feel real good. Exploration is solid as well, though as I mentioned this game is mostly linear, so it's not like you'll miss any huge optional areas if you don't check around. On the other hand, at least you don't have to slash every wall in the hopes of finding a secret. Most of these areas are clearly marked by a cracked wall, a hole big enough to slide through, etc.
There are also a handful of boss-fights. There is a slight puzzle element involved with each fight, and constant slashing won't get you anywhere. One of the minor additions to the PC version is that there are checkpoints during boss-battles. It's a nice gesture, though I figure most people will get stuck at the final boss. The finale doesn't really have any checkpoints either, so you'll definitely want to have all the life upgrades.
Content-wise you should get your money's worth. The first play-through is likely going to take about 5 hours, 6-7 depending on how fast you can collect everything. While there isn't a hard difficulty or anything, there is an arcade mode. Basically this cuts the world up into stages, and your goal is to shoot for the high score. Housemarque did a fine job designing this game with an arcade mindset. There's a time limit to account for and a multiplier bonus that continually rises, just as long as you don't take any damage. The arcade mode is definitely worth checking out. There's also online co-op. Story & Arcade mode are available as well as special co-op challenges. The real challenge however is finding somebody to play this game with. Hopefully you'll have better luck than I.
To sum it all up, Outland's strengths are in its controls, its audiovisual direction, and its focused arcade-like game design. If you go in expecting some Metroidvania you're gonna be severely disappointed. This isn't a exploration-heavy game, and there definitely aren't any sweet rare drops. Outland does well in most everything it sets out to do, so it deserves my every recommendation.

Platformers are fun, and so is exploration. Both of those go together like peanut butter and jelly. Outland is no exception. Developed my Housemarque, Outland originally was released for Xbox Live Arcade and the PlayStation Network back in 2011, but the game is just now making its way to PC. Now before going any further, it is crucial to point out that while it’s published by Ubisoft on the Xbox 360, Housemarque is self-publishing on Steam and as a result
The game starts with the nameless hero having strange dreams and visions of the past. Thinking it may be illness, the hero turns to medicine which proves to be ineffective. He turns to a shaman who told him stories of a huge battle that took place 30,000 years ago between a Great Hero and Two sisters of Chaos, who control Light from the sun and the other controls the darkness of the moon. The battle imprisoned the sisters, but it also took the life of the Great Hero. The shamantells him how the hero is the reincarnation of that Great Hero, and only he can stop the event from reoccurring.
The player controls a nameless hero throughout numerous stages and areas. Completing these areas involves running through the level once to hit a level or switch followed by navigating back through the level to advance, but that makes it sound simple. I can assure you that you will be in for a surprise. Outland is difficult and sometimes infuriating. While the first area may seem easy to begin with, difficulty increases the further you progress. Oh but it’s not just using melee attacks to kill the various enemies and endless amount of spiders, Outland quickly throws you in to the Bullet-Hell and puzzle genres. One of Outlands key features is the ability to switch colors, or ‘spirits’ as they are referred to.
Switching from red to blue is crucial to navigating your way through the beautifully designed levels. You will find yourself wondering “how?” several times throughout the game. Rapid spirit switching, wall jumps, slides, the works. It is a tough game. Enemies will kill you, opposite spirit projectiles will kill you, and spiders WILL kill you. Outland is tough, but it is very fun. Now we should probably talk about how the game actually runs. It’s safe to say the port is a very good one. I’ve had a few issues where the game crashes after tabbing out for a short period, but so far that has been a very rare occurrence. Since the game originally released on consoles, using a controller is recommended here. The keyboard controls feel very cramped for the many abilities you can unlock.
All the keys are just grouped together in a very non user friendly way, sadly those keys cannot be rebound outside of switching to the only other layout, which isn’t much better. Control issues aside, performance is very good. It’s a 2D Platformer so most anything will be able to run the game. I haven’t noticed any major issues outside of some very rare tiny glitches, for the most part though the game performs and feels fantastic.
Simply put, the game is gorgeous. Amazing backgrounds mix so well with the contrasting Blue and Red spirit colors. Outland presents itself perfectly. The moment you start playing the game, you can see all of the artistic talent that went into the game. 2D Platformers tend to always have a very unique art style, and Outland is just another example of that. The silhouette of the player and the various enemies is reminiscent of Limbo, but are highlighted by vivid shades of Red and Blue, and occasionally yellow.
Campaign Only, Metroidvania Style Story.
Campaign Modified Co-Op, Arcade Style Challenges, Co-Op Challenge Rooms
Specialized Tasks Awarding Honor Stamps
Ability To Back Up & Load Saves From The Cloud
Full Controller Support for Xinput Enabled Devices.
Tradable & Marketable Digital Cards Related To Medium Awarded Base On Playtime.
Outlands scores are composed by Ari Pulkkinen who is known for such games as the Trine franchise and most recently Resogun. As well as composing the scores, he also contributed to the general sound design. The game sounds good, sword slashes provide a satisfying sense of contact when you attack an enemy and everything else mixes perfectly with the setting to help immerse the player into the game.
The multiplayer component of the game becomes more and more fleshed out as you go farther in the single campaign. There are certain elements that unlock as you encounter them throughout the game, the first of these modes is to do the campaign cooperatively, the changes from single player are mostly to switches or any specific advancement article is made to be needed to be activated by both parties. You are given complete free roam from your partner and not required to stay on screen, this helps with exploration as you cover more ground. The only gripe about the multiplayer was that it has this rubber banding issue where the game kept trying to sync what we both would be doing constantly. This led to some lag as it always appeared that animations were a frame or so behind then correct before going behind again.
Outland is a fun game. Exploration feels fun and it feels good when you are rewarded for going off the beaten path. The music and sound ties perfectly with the gorgeous stages and background to create some very nice eye and ear candy. Combat plays a key role in the game. You have a basic melee attack as well as unlockable abilities such as the slide. Combos are very possible, and probably the most satisfying element of the combat system. A simple slide will throw the enemy in the air allowing you to set up for juggle combos that feel straight out Street Fighter or Marvel vs Capcom. Unfortunately, that novelty wears off fairly quickly.
Once you figure out the best combos to use, combat feels more like a routine and a choir, then something you might look forward too. Where the combat fails, the exploration makes up for those shortcomings. Wall jumping and spirit switching around the stages can be rewarding. It’s not always best to follow the straight and narrow, you are rewarded for exploring. Whether you find some of the 40+ collectable masks which can be used for unlocking concept art or upgrading abilities, or finding a totem which allows you to pay your collect coins for a very helpful health upgrade.
Combat becomes repetitive and feels like a choir that sometimes can be avoided, with the exception of boss battle which honestly are fun. The game shines in its tough and thought provoking puzzles and landscapes. Feeling that great relief once you get past that one puzzle you finally beat is something that some games today fail to even provide, but Outland does. I feel good about recommending Outland. Only being held back by the games length and the dull combat, Outland proves to be a very fun and satisfying mix of Metroidvania and Puzzle games.

Outland is one of my favorite downloadable games from the last console generation, and I'm extremely happy that it was ported to PC.
(Edit: this has been addressed in patches)
Outland is something of a simple metroidvania with an Ikaruga color-changing mechanic. Players can change between light and dark after an early section of the game and use these forms to attack opposite aligned enemies, harmlessly absorb same-colored bullets and beams, and interact with the environment. There's a somewhat large world to explore and plenty of bosses to take down. The game features an arcade mode with leaderboards, and a coop mode that has a few specific levels. There is also some cooperative stuff in the game - some specific coop challenges and the main campaign allows coop (though due to the nature of the game, only the host progresses).
The player's main weapon is a sword, and combat is very quick and simple. There are some upgrades to the player's abilities, but no alternate weapons, armor, etc (the game doesn't really need them).
The game is absolutely gorgeous, especially at high resolutions and it's pretty to see in motion. The story is very much something of an origin/creation story for a different world, and it's kind of neat, but don't expect a ton of character development, spoken dialog, etc. If there's a reason to buy this game, it's delicious eye-candy and solid gameplay.
Yeah, good. Get it!

What I've experienced (purely the single player) so far is a beautiful game, with interesting mechanics and engaging boss fights. I guess what I would sum it up as would be "Old school platformers meet Metroid meet Ikaruga." It doesn't really bring anything new and innovative to the table mechanic wise, but it does mesh them well against a unique art style.
Unfortunately the keys are not rebindable, a pretty basic feature that I would have expected, especially in a game where response needs to be fast and intuitive. I struggled with the default keyboard keys - switching to gamepad made it a lot easier. The settings are minimalistic. Resolution & Vsync, that's your lot.
I'm struggling a little with the combat; I'm not sure if enemies vary widely in difficulty, or if I'm just incredibly slow sometimes. I often find myself repeating segments and suffering trial-by-patience but I imagine a large part of that is my inexperience with platformers. The puzzle parts for me far exceed the action. I've found them very engaging and well designed.
It's far from perfect; but in my humble opinion it's a pretty high quality game and excellent value entertainment for a full price of £5. Sadly I can't comment on the co-op until one of my friends goes ahead and buys it... hint hint.

This is an amazing, and a depressing, game.
The control mechanic, a single-player co-op experience, works wonderfully well.  And while it says it's designed for a controller, and you'll see people saying it cannot be played via keyboard, I got along just fine.  I found the keyboard controls to work well.  The puzzles are terrific, and mostly stem from having two characters cooperate to perform a task.
There's nothing particularly difficult about the game.  It's a casual game, but it's a terrific experience.
The theme also deals with loss and death, which makes chapters 3 and 4 entirely unsuitable for a younger audience.  Up until then, if you discount the opening cut scene, I could play this game with my daughter, and we'd have a blast.  But chapters 3 and 4 lay on the theme with a heavy hand.
I do highly recommend the game, but could wish that they'd made it less of a message about coping with death and loss.  A more light-hearted game with the same control mechanic would be an awesome father-daughter playing experience for us.

This game combines turn based combat mechanics with a deep and rich tactical system for both PvE and PvP game play.
Full Review:
Textual:
As always, a video conveys the best impression of the game many times over that what a few words can do.
TASTEE is all about slow, planned, tactical and premeditated combat. Every turn is planned out to the last move, position and view angle and the game stands strongest when you take the time to do so.
Now, it needs to be noted that this is a Niche title for sure and that unless you enjoy a slow paced & tactical game play, that it might not be the thing for you. But if you do... boy is this a treat!
A well put together story mode, coupled with a great tutorial set the stage for what you'll learn is some of the most chess-like mind-melding and enjoyable turn based action I've played in ages. With a great variety of maps, an interesting (and mostly balanced) mix of characters to choose form and great use of the environment to obstruct, empower and employ player interaction allows for this game to shine.
Using the games "preview" mode for turns, you can fine tune every action to your hearts content and coupling that with the A-Sync PvP game play (you can do a turn and log out, and then do your next turn when you log back in) means that you'll have multiple matches going on at any time and that you are not bound by a timer or ticker to force you to take your next action. Very cool.
What i'll say as well is that the games controls are quite fiddly. Making you sometimes waste time to get an action "just right". Also the PC Options and performance are bare bones and "acceptable" at best. .
Not perfect, but a damn good turn based tactical action game none the less.

I enjoyed the game a lot, I love being able to play as,well, any of the characters in the game that you own (of a certain faction) I loved switching between being a pilot to a tanker simutaniously in-game. Being able to switch when something ran out, or simply got boring kept the game going for me and my fellow teammates
BUT UNFORTUNATELY they changed this system, only allowing you to be only one type of character in a game, so your either stuck as a tanker (boring after a time and repetitive), pilot (ok in terms of gameplay) a paratrooper (pretty fun for the time being, but runs out quickly)  recon (get ready to camp) or infantry (pretty basic, they mainly do the objectives) and you have to use that character for the entire match. Keep in mind that you can't quit a game once you are in it, you can head back to the loadouts and even quit the game and come back and you will be forced into playing that game as long as it is still going, once it is over or you run out of respawns you can find another game. This just leads gameplay to a dead end most of the time, just doing attempting something over and over and dying over and over until you run out of respawns
Despite the bugs and glitches, which are actually funny and don't even effect the game, the game does run smoothly, and does have a very wide range of weapons and vehicles (which need to be unlocked, which involves grinding, with the best weapons needing the most grinding to get) and can be fun and pretty intense
Heroes and Generals has a ways to go, with many problems that do need to be solved, since it is free2play I can't bash it too harshly, and the in-game payments aren't really forced upon you, and are just there to assist in skipping some grinding. I can't recommend this to hardcore fps players or anyone who has played Battlefield, as for more average players, and maybe even noobs, go at it.
Since it is in development we will be seeing a lot of changes in the game, hopefully for the better, as for now I can recommend it since there isn't much harm in playing the game, since it is free, but if this changes or the game gets worse I simply will not be able to recommend this to anyone, as for now, I do recommend it

Passtech Games pushes out a rather unique tower-defense game that draws upon all new features. Space Run offers a unique combination of space tactics, tower defense, and arcade combat systems.
You play a rather cocky captain Buck Mann, a space runner, whose mission is to deliver goods across the universe. He normally doesn’t chase the credits, but some debits with the notorious gangsters has caused a change of heart. Buck is given a chance to by Big Cargo executive Susan to delivery some highly important cargo. This first mission unlocks the opportunity to prove himself as a reputable Space Runner. As the deliveries continue Buck Mann gains new clients Nuclear Star, VIP Travel, Out of This World, and AI Squared. Can he make all the deliveries and become the best Space Running in the Galaxy?
The campaign is composed of 30-missions, each company offers Buck Mann six missions each. Throughout each of your clients you’ll face ever stronger foes and have to fight off fearsome pirate lords: Captain Black and Brownbeard the Pirate. Not only do you have to fight off meddlesome pirates, but you need to protect your ship through asteroid belts and ever more deadly cargo. The campaign is ever changing as every mission new enemies and challenges are introduced keeping the game fresh and entertaining.
Space Run plays like a traditional tower defense, in that you place turrets in your base and they target enemies without your control. Each tower has special abilities you can unlock with can give you a higher degree of control over them. Every tower has its usage and you’ll notice as you play you will be switching out between them continuously. A mixture of anti-ballistic missile systems, machine gun turrets, mass rocket launchers, super shields, engines that can control the space-time-continuum, and much more. This game has a fantastic difficulty curve from Easy to Hard offering gaming for all player-types. Hard is more difficult and will require repeat plays to get 5-star while on the other hand easy is so simple you can gun through it on one run and get a perfect game.
Space Run is an incredibly interesting new take onto Tower Defense games that puts high speed micro-managing with unique map concepts to provide a fantastic gaming experience. Each map requires speed as well as a protecting cargo which requires proper management of the player’s resources. The unique bosses pose new threats not just on the players cargo, but they also stop the player meaning if he/she is not far enough ahead of the timer they may get pulled back and lose the 5-star delivery. If you like Tower Defense Games, like micromanaging, enjoy space combat, or want a unique gaming experience then Space Run is the game for you. I definitely recommend this game and based on how you play it you can easily get 10-20 hours of gameplay out of it before repeating yourself.
Pros:
+Unique enemies that keep the game interesting.
+Interesting ship dynamics and management.
+Loads of engineering upgrades and abilities.
+Awesome boss battles and strategies.
+Clean graphics and smooth user interface.
+Fast paced space simulator with highly diversified playing methods.
+Smooth difficulty curve – made for all players.
+Cargo dynamics that require the player to have to play in unique ways.
Cons:
-Sadly no survival mode.
-Turrets almost always annoyingly target enemy ship engines rather than their weaponry. Seeing as Engines do nothing for enemy ships it almost always results in your turrets getting beat up a lot more than they need to.
-Enemy EMP weapon seem to always seem to switch targets while your EMP weapons shoot the same thing over and over. Result is all your systems are down and the enemy only has an engine down.

Brothers really is fantastic and one of the stand out games of 2013.

It’s an adventure set in a fairy tale world that flows evocatively between moments of whimsy and tragedy.   It’s a coming of age tale, it’s about bonds and friendship and loss, it is a modern Ico, conceptually simple yet beautifully crafted.

You control two brothers simultaneously, each half of the controller moving one of the siblings. Interaction with the world is simple, there’s only one interaction button for each boy and there are no menus or magic or combat. Controlling each individual character is simple, but coordinating their actions in order to transverse their world is somewhat akin to trying to pat your head while rubbing your stomach.
That’s not to say the game is difficult. While there are puzzles to solve, there’s little in the way of real challenge. But the game isn’t about that, it’s not about getting a high score or finding collectable items. It’s a story waiting to be told and every interaction tells part of the story.
The game is essentially wordless, with a simlish like language used. Instead the story is told through the animation. As the two brothers interact with the same object their personality comes through, the care free nature of the youngest brother and the older one trying to be strong and responsible while still being a teenager.
The game is only a couple of hours longs, but it’s very lean and takes you on quite a journey in in that time. It’s also a remarkably pretty game with a lovely soundtrack. There’s plenty more that can be told about Brothers but it’s really a game that deserves to be experienced.

This game is a triumph.  It is an art piece that I have never seen the likes of.  Its what games like Gone Home, and Dear Esther dream they could be, but fail to understand what makes the medium of video games so incredible, and unlike any other form of entertainment.  Those games try and tell you a story, they tell it to you through heavy dialogue, and little to no interactivity.  What makes this game such a masterpiece is that it is the complete opposite of those games.  It has absolutely no dialogue whatsoever, and the story is told through the controls, and masterful directing.  That is...incredible.  I have never played a game that made me feel like I meant something, that I was part of the story, and that I wasn't just an observer.  This game perfectly demonstrates how gaming as a medium can be the most unique, and amazing form of entertainment.  Interactivity.
The world is gorgeous.  You can go through any point in that game and take a screenshot, and it will look amazing.  Whether the scene is filled with hope, and wonder.. or darkness, and despair.  Every second of this game is jaw dropping.  And to top it all off, the directing is flawless.  I never had the camera go into the wall, or any awkward position, and every time the camera panned to a different location you could see the beautiful world in the background.  And the world is complete.  This is something that most games lack, and is one of the most underappreciated, yet most important parts of making an immersive game.  Every point of the game you go through, you can look back and see what you just went through.  You just scaled a mountain, and the camera pans to the side to show you what you just went through, and you see the entire level you just completed, and its beautiful, and you feel accomplished.
The story is simple, yet what makes the game shine so much is how it tells it.  There is no dialogue, there is no narration, the story is told through the controls, and through the directing.  You are your characters, and you push through every challenge, and every puzzle not by pushing buttons to make characters on a screen do what you want, but by being completely immersed, and facing everything as part of the story, not just the hand of god.
This game made me weep.  Few games can make me feel such intense emotions, but this one hit hard.  I expected everything that happens, and I think everyone who has played this game new what happens too.  its a simple story. but because of how mind blowingly amazing this game is created the story doesn't matter, its how the story is presented that makes this game a masterpiece.  Its short, about 2:30-3:00 hours.  But any longer would seem too long, and any shorter would seem to short.  it was a good length for what the game had to offer.
No other genre can do what gaming can do.  And its about high time more game developers start taking it seriously.  Take a book or movie for example, its impossible to get that much interactivity from any other artform, to immerse yourself and not just watch, and observe the story, but to become a part of it.  This game is the perfect example of what story driven games should be.  Not listening to a voice while you walk in a straight line like Dear Esther.  Not a movie with small segments of QTE's like Heavy Rain.  Not like every other game that is just shooting people/etc with a small cutscene here and there.  No.  This game tells the story through what you do, with a small cutscene here and there to transition what you will do next.
This game is a straight 10/10.  Not a doubt in my mind.

After spending a small amount of time with this game I feel confident enough to write a short review.
I grabbed the game during the summer sale expecting it to be refunded because I didn't like how the demo felt to me. The game was ugly, the animations were stiff, and the combat was a little clunky. I stopped playing the demo and asked a well trsuted friend about the main game and what it's like. He kept recommending it to me and eventually I broke down and dropped the money for it thinking I would have made a mistake. But I was very wrong.
At first, this is not a game for you visual junkies out there. This is a prime example of a game that's looks like crap but it's all backed up with great depth, and gameplay. It's pretty much a Total War style game with Elder Scrolls like combat, a standard RPG system, total war like map exploration, army size, and morale system. I haven't really played much into the ecomonic system but I bet it's just as cool as the rest of the game. After you mold your custom Male or Female character's destiny, you'll spend a lot of your time recruiting volunteers and performing tasks for Guild Masters, or named familes and or people to build up your reputation and get towns, cities, and castles to like you.
Visually this game is gross looking and it still uses old Direct X 9 which was Windows XP's graphics library. Animation could still use some work.
The Gameplay is where this game really shines. Multiplayer is Chivalry based arena style combat where you choose a warrior to fight with and help your team carry out a series of objectives or just simply whipe out the opposition completely to win. Singleplayer is basically you, and a vast open world full of opportunities. You march with an army to locate deserters, bandits, caravans, farmers, merchants, other friendly and or hostile armies. Once you get into actual combat you are given a field to battle in where you help your men destroy the enemy. You can charge at the enemy with your men, or opt to stand back and watch them fight from a spectator camera but where's the fun in that? Once an enemy character falls, you may choose to equip their weapons and shields for the duration of combat. After that though, you can loot everything and sell it for Denar.
It took some getting used to but I've enjoyed my current time with it so far.

Overall Experience: 9/10

As a former part-time developer on the project, I spent a lot of time with TASTEE. However, as a UI programmer, I didn't play any role in developing the core gameplay. This left me able to look at the game critically as it evolved over time.
If TASTEE wasn't as engaging of a multiplayer experience, my playtime would be much lower. I actually went home and played matches after a day of working on the game. TASTEE takes the cerebral gameplay formula of Frozen Synapse then adds more depth and wraps it all in a polished presentation. There is an impressive amount of strategy required to master this game, and it all looks and feels great.
The single-player aspect of TASTEE is a fully realized feature that may be worth the asking price alone for turn-based tactics fans. The presentation is just as polished as the rest of the game and it's a great way to practice the basic mechanics before going online. Unlocking new mercs is a nice carrot-on-a-stick to push you to the end of the story and a gentle way to learn the units.
TASTEE is a must-play for turn-based tactics fans and Frozen Synapse fans. Even after ~315 hours of playing and working on this game I'll still be coming back!

I've never played a Tactics game in my life, I must say I I'll be playing them from now on. Tastee must be noob friendly, because my experience with the first few hours has been smooth and forgiving. Anyone whom is not a tactical fan, or hasn't ever thought about them, should give this a try. :) (The development team has also stated that they will continue to support the game after launch, so that's a bonus.)
Positive:
- Smooth first experience.
- Really intuitive controls.
- The MOMENTS. I was told that the game was a game of moments, but I didn't really get it. Since the game is based around the concept of time start/stop, you often get .1 seconds away from epic moments like sniper shots or bomb explosions, only to have it freeze for the next planning phase.
Negative:
- I experienced a few tiny glitches which fixed themselves with no user intervention, mostly attributed to lag.
- Some controls are prone to user error that one might not notice, but that's my fault for not paying 100% attention when issuing commands.

There's a niche audience here, and that's the audience that liked Frozen Synapse. If you like planning out moves down to the step trying to mess with your opponent, then Tastee will be a game up your alley, especially if you can find friends and human opponents to play against. For me, it's way too slow: I find myself getting way to impatient for what the game wants from me, and end up walking into a hail of bullets. But if you have patience and really have a tactical mind, the game will reward you as you can play mind games with your opponent and try to lure them into your trap, or bum rush them unexpectedly. Just don't expect the AI to give you a fair fight, as it seems to really screw with you (at least in my experience) by knowing what you're going to do before hand, unless you take things REALLY slow. Trying to find an online game was a problem due to not a lot of people playing, but it may have not been during the core hours (in the evening) when people were on. All in all, there's no much improvement on the Synapse formula here, but it's got a fresh coat of paint that some will appreciate, and maybe a more active fan base (because of the age of that game). It's just not for me, that's for sure.

In TASTEE, you need to be very methodical and carful with every tiny move you make.  Once you get the hang of it and pick up the pace, it's even more fun.
My biggest gripe is that there doesn't currently seem to be anything to spend your earnings on.  It'd be nice if you could spend your cash on upgrades of some kind.
Also, like I said, it's pretty dang hard.  The AI always seems to know where your characters are, and critically, where your characters are looking.  This might not be the case, but the AI sure seems to have an unfair advantage.  But you might be into that! Multiplayer, of course, would be a different story.  But waiting for another player to finish their planning can take AGES.  So grab a beer.
Overall, it feels like the game is ALMOST done.  Interesting and fun take on turn-based tactics.  Add the ability to upgrade, strip the AI of its advantage, and you've got yourself a solid game.
If you're really into tactical games like this, I'd say it's a buy.  Otherwise, maybe wait a bit and see if the devs tweak it a little more.

What a treat!
This is an exceptionally fun amusement.
It's a tower defense game ... in  space!  :-)
What it does with gameplay
and audio/visual presentation is especially satisfying.
The way the music and sound FX
are coordinated to the player's actions
reminds me of a similar feeling I get
from playing the arcade game, Raiden,
if that makes any sense.
Let's just say,
it feels solid and fun.
Another feature I appreciate,
is being able to change which direction
the turrets are aimed.
In fact,
with all ship components being hex-shaped spaces,
I was pleasantly reminded
of all those hex-based tabletop starship games
that I got to play in the 1970's and 80's.
In the later stages of the game,
you'll know if you haven't quite conquered a mission.
It can be rather overwhelming,
particularly trying to micromanage
when many things are happening at once.
However, if you figure out a mission
and get your module placement and timing correct,
then you are rewarded with an entertaining Space Run.
A few final notes:
There are at least a few references to other sci-fi shows
which was great.  There's probably more.  :-)
The game has only glitched a few times
that I've noticed
in the hours I've played it.
Seems stable to me.
And ... this game can be addictive.
It can easily suck hours of your life away,
before you know it.  Buyer beware!
BOTTOMLINE:
Should you buy it?
