NOTE: The following review was written for TS2014 ... I can not yet review TS2015 because the compulsory re-branding (free upgrade) has broken my installation completely, I'm not sure I can be bothered to re-install TS from scratch, but If I do I will review TS2015 then.
ALSO NOTE: (for the hard of intellect) The ingame hours listed above are from TS2013 a version of this simulator I would reccommend, unfortuantely later versions of TS are compulsory and cannot be avoided. which is the main reason I dont reccommend TS and why the following review is still relevant.
TS is a hybrid, existing somewhere between game and simulator, because this gamulator lives in this middle ground anyone interested in casually driving trains for XP or serious rail simulation fans looking for the experience of driving a train like real driver in a simulated environment or those like myself with an interest in creating scenarios and routes may be frustrated in equal measure, however for very different reasons.
TS2014 is not a new product, its a compulsory upgrade from TS2013 which was a compulsory upgrade from TS2012 and so on.
TS2013 can be used off the shelf as a ready to play product, in this form it works adquately but its very limited in scope, to get any meaningful use from TS2014 requires a serious financial investment in some of the DLC (depending on your area of interest) and an investment in time in making your own content in the form of scenarios and routes. For anyone interested in simulating reality making your own scenarios using the editor is essential, this is probably TSs strongest aspect  however if you undertake this you will come up against many of the software’s myriad bugs and design limitations, the process can be encapsulated in one word: "Frustrating” however it can be rewarding when you do discover a work-around for any of the problems you will encounter.
TS also suffers from (in my experience):
*Poor unhelpful patronising support with less than a rudimentary understanding of the product.
*Falling value for money in packs that come with less skins than previous releases and routes released without the common stock that use them, Ubiquitous stock is conspicuous in its absence while the developers release rare and one-off locos.
*A complexity of incompatible assets, and cut down incompatible replacements for withdrawn DLC making the sharing of scenarios impractical. (for instance there are 5! different versions of the class 66, all incompatible with each other!)
*Variable quality in DLC from “outstanding” to “not-fit-for-purpose”, some DLC cannot be driven without using the driver interface, because of little omissions like the sounds of doors closing not being included, this is bad news if you want full immersion. The sounds on some of the DLC are diabolical others less so.
*A game menu UI that is a temple to style over functionality.
*Long standing unresolved bugs including, benign graphical bugs such as floating passengers and more serious CTD session ending bugs such as the corrupted asset in the scenery folder of London to Brighton that crashes the editor.
*Aggressive marketing, in-your-face advertising and the monetisation of almost every aspect, you are spammed with advertising when waiting for scenarios to load and you cannot even work towards achievements without investing in DLC
*Widespread censorship of genuine concerns on official channels, giving other users advice on workarounds or patches for bugs is prohibited.
*Design limitations, such as its impossible to create “late running” scenarios because the software wont allow the pick-up of passengers from a stop you arrive late at and a save and resume system that can cause AI to be mistimed, collide, derail and off-path in scenarios.
*Unless you have a powerful set up you will have to chose between graphical quality or performance, if you take the performance route TS is ugly but it can be pretty if you don’t mind some stuttering.
All of these things you should not expect from a premium priced product but can be overlooked or worked around if you are a serious rail simulator buff, I would still recommend this product even with these (and other) Shortcomings.
However:
The reason I cannot recommend TS2014 is confidence. Every autumn there is a compulsory relaunch of the product, Its called a “Free update” and in general it carries new ways to monetise the software, some new bugs and a few “bread and circuses” changes, the important part of this is the software changes and unless you want to isolate yourself from ever using the product again you have no choice in accepting it. [EDIT: On the 6th Jan my last working copy of TS2013 was automaticly upgraded bypassing Steam disabled automatic updates, It appears its not actually possible to prevent the update at all, only delay it by a few months. the updates are fully compulsory, as a customer you have no choice]
Because things change every year it has completely smashed my confidence in the product, how long before it becomes intentionally or accidentally unusable? There is no way of knowing if all the hours that may have spent on scenario creation or weeks of gaining achievements or months on route building or the considerable amount of money spent on DLC will just be wasted or unusable a few years down the line.
I find this single aspect utterly demoralising, I simply can no longer be motivated to spend time creating something that may in future be taken away from me without my consent, in this sense its a self fulfilling prophesy.
The release of TS2014 has turned a flawed but enjoyable entertainment (TS2013) into my biggest ever regret, I feel like I have been conned. All the hours I spent making scenarios and routebuilding in TS2013 have been wasted because I have been forced to "upgrade" to TS2014.
Not recommended, unless you are a masochist.
EDIT: 4/12/2013, I think the fact that Railsimulator marked this and many other reviews as "off topic" says more than I could ever say about TS. Actions speak louder than words.
EDIT: 6/12/2013 Steam moderators overturned DTGs off topic flagging and made this review visable again.

I've have given this game many chances. I play it for a bit, than uninstall it, and then I reinstall it, thinking I may have missed something, seeing as a huge portion of people love this game.
However, the more I try to play this game, the more I am mindblown this game is so popular. Let me elaborate a little.
First off, I'm not knocking the games aesthetic appeal. It's a very good looking game for the most part. There are a few textures that look like they were made for a 90s PC mystery game, but overall, I am pretty impressed with the games looks, and how fast it runs.
That's not my complaint though. That little feature right there, is the ONLY thing this game has going for it. Once you get past the looks of the game, get ready for a mind bogglingly BAD control scheme, unusable menus, and possibly the worst voice acting and music you've ever heard in a game.
Let's start with the music and voice acting. Good lord are these bad. The score sounds like it's from an old 80's Segal movie. It's trying SO hard to be badass, and it falls so short. I'm not saying it's BAD music in itself, but with scenarios they play it in, like WALKING ACROSS A DECK, they've decided that blaring rock solos so loud, to the point where you can't even hear character dialogue, is appropriate. Really? Why is that an issue? The music should never drown out dialogue in a game, especially when it's ambient background music. This should only happen if the music is LITERALLY happening from something in the environment, like a concert or something. Now along with audio, lets look at voice acting. Now, not ALL of it is bad, but the majority is pretty much something out of vampire diaries. I know most marines and soldiers are normal guys who all want to have a good time as much as anyone else, and use phrases like "bro" and "dude" like anyone else, but when those phrases are used in this game... Oh my god. It legitimately sounds like that ONE kid from school that tried way too hard to fit in. They emphasize "BRO" way too much. "Tell me about that new sweet house of yours, BRO." And if you read that with a 90's surfer accent, you'd be spot on.
Let's move onto menus. This SHOULD have been something simple. However, I made an online game over LAN (so no one would join) and was simply trying to get the hang of the controls. First off, just trying to make the game, was a task in itself. WHY IS THERE NO SIMPLE MODE SELECT?! Instead, we get this rediculous list of unspecified random words. 1. FIRST OF WAR. WHAT IS THAT??? Is that a mode? Is that the campaign? What is that? A little description would be nice, but no, there's nothing else. Just a huge list of things like that. So I selected a random one, and I get the campaign. That's fine in itself, but I'll get back to this later. Let's move on for now.
So let's talk about controls. I have never, in my life played a game, that has the most backwards, rediculous, most roundabout way ever, to make controls for a shooter. Now, I'm no huge CoD fan at all. I've played a few, but I've never lost my crap over them or anything. They're mainly just "meh" games. But I'll tell you one thing; NEVER have I EVER complained about controls in a CoD game, or a BF game, or a Halo game, or just about ANY other shooter ever. Why change this scheme? I've looked at the controls, there's no reason to have them that way. Why can't MMB be the button for zooming with the scope? Guess what you use instead? THE "+" key! So NOW you're juggling between your mouse and your keys, and switching hands and WHY NOT JUST USE THE SAME CONTROLS THAT HAVE ALWAYS WORKED? So why not use the MMB to zoom the scope? Oh, I see why! Because it's being used to scroll the "ACTION WHEEL" so I can open a ♥♥♥♥ING door. No, you can't just click to open a door. You scroll to select the action, and THEN click to open. Mind you, this is how ANY action in the game works. If there's multiple things going on, like say, you're near a door, and a gun, and a person to talk to, you have to scroll through all this♥♥♥♥♥♥ and pick the one you want AMIDST all the action going on. So have fun juggling with your scroll wheel on your mouse, while trying not to get shot. Why isn't "F" the action key you ask? Because THAT'S being used to switch weapons! WHY NOT THE NUMBER KEYS?? BECAUSE THOSE ARE BEING USED FOR RANDOM SQUAD DIALOGUE! ... "C" is crouch, which is fine, but for SOME reason this isn't a toggled crouch. You have to hit "X" to stand, and "z" to prone. WHY? Why get rid of these instincts that have been ingrained in our brain since the first Halo game? Why change something that works perfectly well? Why not HOLD "C" for a couple of seconds to prone, and just hit it again to stand?
So as the tutorial is teaching me this, and I think I'm getting the hang of it, and I continue to hear more robot people try to voice act, I finish the tutorial. Well you know how I'd selected the mission from the "create a game" menu before? Well instead of acting like a normal ♥♥♥♥ing game, and continuing to the next mission, it just repeats. WHAT? Why would I want to do that? Why not go to the next one? That's literally the most irritating and pointless system possible. This isn't Gallaga. I don't want to try and replay to get a higher score. I WANT TO PLAY THE GAME. So I try to quit the game, but hitting quit JUST RESTARTS THE ♥♥♥♥ING LEVEL. I had to ALT+TAB to minimize and then task manager that son of a ♥♥♥♥♥. Then I figured since I'm doing all this crap, might as well uninstall it!
I can't recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a game that plays well. If you can see past the broken controls, bad dialouge, a mediocre score, and unworkable menus, and truly enjoy what Arma is trying to be, then go right ahead, and game on. But for me, some one who is probably overly critical, I can't enjoy, or recommend this game.

Red Faction: Guerrilla is a somewhat open-world FPS with RPG elements. While you have freedom to move about, you cannot access the next area until you've completed certain objectives. Overall, the graphics are great, and the game-play, handling and general game progression is good. You play a character who leads a rebellion, but the planets governing body is too large and your resources are too little. The only way to put a dent in their regime, is to use guerrilla tactics. You infiltrate an area, do as much damage as you can, and then retreat to either another location, or come back to the same place, but only once the guards disperse. You cannot take on a whole encampment or patrol detachment and stay fighting for prolonged periods of time, so for all the fan-boys who like to rampage unchecked, this is not the game for you. A 18 yo student is constantly bullied at school and starts finding solace in a fantastical world that slowly mixes with reality.
Don't get fooled by this premise though, sadly the actual game is as mind-numbing as an actual dose of morphine due to its amateurish narrative and slow pacing.
-nothing really
-the graphics aren't too bad but suffer due to some annoying effects and wooden animations
-dull story, amateurish narrative, terrible dialogues
-drawn out cutscenes
-clumsy jump scares
-minigames feel out of place
-uninspired puzzles
-terrible English translation
Morphine feels, simply put, like an uninteresting and dull chore as you play through it. The gameplay consists of simply walking around, picking up diary pages and going through cutscenes with a few minigames or puzzles thrown around (lockpicking, making a campfire, opening certain dorrs or, sigh, fishing). Said puzzles and minigames are uninspired at best and can sometimes become annoying due to being set in dimply lit places or requiring you to find small objects in a certain room.
But the story and pacing are the main culprits here, seldom have I played something so tedious. Dialogues are cliched, slow (no voice acting and there's several seconds between lines) and basically all revolve around the fact that people at school are bad. Even cutscenes suffer from the same problem as they're filled with moments where nothing happens or your attention is drawn for several unnecessary seconds over certain things in the area. Heck even after you finish the game there's a small credits screen and then you're forced to go through several more minutes of cutscenes basically recapping what just happened, why? why would you do that?  The stumbling English just makes things even worse and can sometimes also get in the way of a puzzle (like calling a safety pin "a buckle" or small branches being referred to as "bushes". Even if you discount the aforementioned problems the story is uninteresting at best, leaves no lasting impression and can at times just feel a bit pretentious.
Unless you desperately need to get rid of that insomnia that's been bothering you I can't recommend this one: horror games are a dime a dozen nowadays and Morphine is subpar both in story and gameplay.

A quest of the two eponymous characters to find a magical cure for their ill father, where you get to control both of them at the same time in a sort of puzzle-lite third persons' view co-operating-with-yourself adventure game.
It's essentially a very visceral, very interactive fairy tale. The control scheme, the environmental puzzles with quite obvious solutions to push the story forward.. It is all about creating practically a physical bond between you and the brothers, via the controller, to feel their struggle quite personally.
The tale takes you to strange places along the way. That also includes variety of emotional places, there are times to be happy, and to be sad, and perhaps to be scared, too. And it can get very intense at all of them. Yes, this is definitely about the journey not the destination. Even the achievements accentuate exploration and doing side activities not on the main storyline - this is exactly what you get rewarded for. You get exactly zero achievements for the main "quest" (which probably also serves to well, avoid spoilers).
All this means you are doing everybody a great disservice if you're just watching some let's play or something. I think any single player game with a story is meant to be a GAME, therefore something for you to experience personally not via watching others do it (unless you've done it already and want to relive via someone elses eyes), but this is especially true in this title.
It's best experienced in one go, to keep you in the emotional flow, it's at most 4 hours long if you like to smell flowers along the way (you can even literally do just that at places.. well not YOU-you but you know what I mean, the characters you play as) and you probably wouldn't want to leave a movie in the middle and come back later, would you?
Also, it's obviously designed with a twin stick controller in mind, controlling each brother with one of the sticks and triggers. For example things like cranking a winch are just felt more personally if you're actually "cranking" your sticks. But - it
have keyboard bindings, WSAD for one brother and arrow keys for the other, so it actually
playable without a controller despite the warning on the Steam page, you're just somewhat missing out and I imagine keyboard control can be rather frustrating, I mean even the twin sticks almost cross that line often but luckily the game isn't hard so that's never an issue.
Seriously if you're a PC gamer and do not have a controller yet, then you were asking Santa Klaus or your regional equivalent for wrong things. Because you are missing out in titles that were designed primarily with controllers in mind, and this game is perhaps the best example yet of just how much you're missing (otherwise the design with controller in mind usually just comes from a mild form of consolitis). But mind you, you don't need anything posh and expensive, you're probably somewhat worse by not having things like force feedback but otherwise there are pretty cheap controllers that do the job just as well, you may just need something like x360cemu if it's not an xinput controller.
All in all, I highly recommend playing this game. I mean I'm personally not entirely sure why TotalBiscuit hails it as perhaps the best game of all time as far as he is concerned, it must have had much higher impact on him, but nonetheless it is truly a great gem, exemplifying of just how well controls can be integrated into a game, and how a game  can present you various emotional states not just cashing on one.

This game is like an interactive movie. Playing the game is not difficult at any point, the player needs to do very little to get the reguired outcome (usually just move next to an interactable object and press a button) and most of the "action" parts are very pre-scripted. There are puzzles along the way but they are very simple and easy. There is very little exploration involved and you can't really change anything about the story or events.
The reason why I would recommend this game is that the things it does (above I tried to say what it doesn't do) it does very well. It shows this remarkable world in a very beatiful and deep way. Even though most (if not every) of the wonderful little things about the world are very common in many fantasy settings (like trolls, magical trees, etc.) this game presents them in a magical way that I (a grown-up) felt like a little boy who is introduced to possibilities of imagination for the first time. I played this game through in two sittings but would have played it through in one if I hadn't had to stop playing during the first time I launched the game. It truly was like watching a good movie, I didn't want to stop wathcing until it ended on its own.
I personally liked the concept of playing in coop with myself. It was on the other hand kind of sad that the possibilities it can open weren't fully explored. I'm sure that there are people who find these "difficult" controls to be a turn-off but anyone willing to keep an open mind should find out that it works well. I personally was very surprised how well the camera was able to follow the protagonists. I very rarely needed to adjust the camera manually.
Another thing that this game does very well are the achiements. Usually achiements in games are gained by just playing the game. Nothing extra is needed. Just by finishing the game you get something like 80 - 90 % of all the achiements. In this game you will get 0 %. They are all kind of like "side-quests" that you end up completing just because you were so drawn into the world that you wanted to interact with it and its people/creatures as much as you could.

A simple but touching puzzler played out in a stunningly beautiful fantasy setting (good use of the Unreal Engine). Controls are quite unique, steering both characters in real time, but may cause occasional brain meltdowns (at least to those who do not master the art of mental multi-tasking) - playing with an XBox 360 (or similar) controller is highly recommended, but even then it can be a bit fickle. Amosphere is great, as it all starts out quite colorful, but the game gets progressively dark and ominous as the story plays out. Sound effects and music are simple but effective, and speech is of the 'The Sims'-gibberish category. Not that understanding the 'dialogs' would be needed to understand the story.
All in all highly recommended if you're looking for a nice change of pace between hectic fragging, hacking, looting or racing sessions.

I've got a large map of the UK on my computer room wall and I often search YouTube videos to get additional information on the railways there, particularly the historical stuff.  And, oh yes, the North American routes are great too.
Super piece of software.  Thanks RailWorks.

I've been playing this game on and off for 9 years, before I even had a Steam account. My favorite thing in the world is showing my friends how to play and then sending them off to make their own ridiculous creature. There's so much to customize, and the things people are able to make just with the parts included in the base game is insane. I'm constantly in awe of the cool dragons and Godzillas and Predators that talented players share on Sporepedia. This is still my go-to game for worldbuilding inspiration.
Whenever things get a little dull, like in certain areas of the Civ and Tribal stages, I remind myself that I have the power to change the way things work. At any given time, I can just throw all my peacemaking plans out the window and burn down the nearest settlement. It's that sense of control and freedom that keeps me coming back to play Spore. Your choices MATTER. You're the one telling the story of your species; the game isn't plopping you on some predetermined plot-on-rails that you always have to follow. You don't have to kill ANYTHING the whole game if you really want to (apart from some Space stage missions), or you can decide to murder everything in your path. It's all up to you.
I'm immensely nostalgic for this game. I've put in probably hundreds of hours combined across all platforms messing around. And I still have yet to "complete" it, despite the years that have gone by. I don't think I ever need to though. The process of going from a small, flat-colored cell just trying not to get eaten to a world-class Space Captain exploring the universe within HOURS is always amazing to experience.
I highly recommend this game. The graphics are not the selling point; it's the storytelling.
Remember to save often, and make it a game YOU want to play.

At its worst, HuniePop is a weebo, after school before mom comes home, pathetic anime dating sim.
At its best, HuniePop is a strategic, memory based puzzle game likened to Bejeweled/Candy Crush.
Having played for 15 hours, I will say it wasn't until hour 8-9 that I fully understood all the elements of the game. It is more than just "match 3 colors and see boobies". To make the most out of the game you must talk to and learn information from all the girls (8 initially). The Bejewled/Candy Crush element makes for addicitive fun, plus the dating items alter how you think of the puzzle board.
My main complaint would be risk/reward factor. There is almost zero repercussions for not learning about a girl or screwing up on a date. Till the last minute I played I would regularly get questions wrong when girls are quizzing me on stuff we talked about. "Oh you forgot when my birthday was...oh well lets bang!"
With addictive puzzles, decent humor, and anime milk bubbles, I would recommend this game for anyone looking for candy crush with bazongas.

One of the best slice of life type VNs I've had the pleasure to read. Couldn't put it down and ended up wishing for more once I finished. Lot's of decisions, mostly related to the different dating aspects of the game (which girl you end up with). I've only played through once thus far (Yuuna), but there seems to be replayability to go the other routes/partners based on what I've seen and read. For those looking for anything more than a well written VN, you might be disappointed, as there are no mini-games or combat involved, despite the mechs. The art was vrty nice and the voice acting was really well done. The only things I can think of as less than great were the music (which was just alright) and the fact that the end seemed kind of rushed (maybe funding was getting tight?). Nothing major, but enough that it didn't really fit the pace of the rest of the story and left a bit of a flat feel to the conclusion. In any case, overall a great VN that leaves you looking forward to more from PixelFade.

is a sublime poignant experience, characterized by its ability to convey affecting emotion without any intelligible dialog. It carries you through a fantastical world never uncertain of what it wants you to see and feel, and does so in such a effective manner that it never needs to say anything to make you connect with your two characters, and leave a lasting impression.
story is not one that can be spelled out on paper, and really does require you to experience it for yourself in order to understand why it is so powerful. The way in which each piece is woven and rewoven together creates a world that feels connected and draw out despite the immense ground covered and the drastic changes undergone by the environment, as well as the short length which leaves little time for exposition. I honestly do not feel capable of doing it any sort of justice with this review, but know that this is the type of narrative journey that comes along rarely for a reason, that being it is very hard to do successfully especially to such a level as is shown here.
I once read the way
plays described as "single player co-op" which is the perfect definition for it. You control both brothers concurrently with the two analog sticks and triggers. It's a disorienting rewiring of the motions we've become so accustomed to and requires you use both sides of your brain at once, but once you get accustomed it allows for an array of increasingly ingenious occurrences. The ways in which it forces you to work together (with yourself) are brilliant and within the first opening moments completely sold me on the unusual control scheme and only continued to impress me with the cleverness that the developers managed to play with mechanic.
As compelling as I found the gameplay, I was simply struck by the unequivocal beauty of the visuals. The texture work and lighting effects bring the prodigious creativity and imagination to life in a vibrant and ever changing display of wondrous locals and characters. The breathtaking and dramatic soundtrack is perfectly timed to every action that occurs, with a dynamic range of sounds that sweeps you through the world as an irreplaceable part of it.
There are few games which I feel deserve the title, but the level at which
accomplishes everything it attempts and the skill in which it executes the different components, warrants the term masterpiece. It is an impressive achievement in both interactive storytelling and original game design that left me in a state of wonder with each passing moment. Disregard the fact that you can and likely will complete it in one sitting,
is something that needs to be played and a game I will surely be singing the praises of far into the future.

There are a lot of mixed reviews about this game, and this probably stems from similar issues of taste and perception to a great or lesser degree, that those which occurred with 'Dear Esther' or 'Gone Home'. IF you liked those, I suspect you'll love this.
This game is beautiful, atmospheric, and utterly immersive. It has a wonderfully simple way of developing story and character by viewing the characters interactions with the world, and responses to the environment, and it allows you to do this by trying things, and testing things for yourself, there is no HUD or tutorial beyond one instruction at the start. The levels are simply visually stunning and varied, and absolutely beautifully designed and structured. They are complemented perfectly by the soundtrack, which highlights the levels and story. I'd go so far as to say this is a great example of the maturity of the gaming industry. I have seen some criticism of the story, but I think this perhaps a little literal, the game feels more about the emotion of the story, and how the story is told, but I guess everyone must judge this for themselves.
The controlls and situation are innovative, but intuative, but from a gaming perspective were underused. I played through the entire game with only dying once, and that was easily avoidable, I was just seeing if something was possible. The following may be considered gameplay *SPOILERS* as much of the game is about working things out for yourself, but you cannot fall off most the edges, you don't actually have to balance on narrow beams, some of the action sequences you literally only have to press the run button and it does the rest. It is not a gamers game, if that makes any sense, you can't fail, it may just take you a little longer.
However, I'd say thats completely not the point of a game like this, which is about story, situation, emotion, beauty, and provoking thought. It is very engaging and I got 2 play throughs for my few quid, one to play the game, and a second to pick up the few missing achievements, and just experience the world again. I can't reccomend it highly enough.

This game is a lot of fun. The simple name made me leave it to linger on my wishlist for quite a while, thinking it was probably just another simplistic indie game that wouldn't offer much. But that was a snap judgement that this game did not deserve.
Space Run has plenty of depth, a pretty great upgrade tree for your barge to incorporate into itself as you go, and ultimately the most important thing of all; fun gameplay. More than just fun, it's also quite challenging and the game manages to land that perfect balance of easy to learn but difficult to master. That isn't easy to pull off, but Space Run does so with aplomb.
This one is worth a look at full price. If you are lucky enough to land a copy during a sale like I did, then it's really a steal. Well worth your time. To the developers I say "great job". I will keep my eyes open for more work from you guys. This is a fun imaginative use of a reasonably tired genre that I keep thinking has crested. But folks keep coming up with ways to make Tower Defence interesting again and again, and this one is worth the time and money to play.

While the price might be a little steep for a game that doesn't revolutionise the formula, since it's appreciably higher than most other games in the genre, one can't deny that it is a well-designed and good-looking entry into the genre that adds it's unique spin on things.  Definitely one to pick up on a sale, at least, however.

Mobius Final Fantasy is probably one of the better mobile games out there that Square Enix has put out, it looks beautiful and the production values are pretty high for a game that was previously played in the palm of your hand.
Mobius Final Fantasy is an alternate Universe Final Fantasy I which was released on the NES and Famicom, if you're familiar with the game you'll immediately recognize familiar names and terms like Warrior of Light, Garland, Cornelia and Princess Sarah and the "core" jobs being in parrelel to Final Fantasy I. The game does resort to recycling models from XI, XII, LR and XIV but the game still feels like its own world and I applaud it for that. (The Red Dragon feels like it belongs more to this world than it does Lightning Returns :P)
The thing that really sells me on this game is Echo and the events.
The events are humourous and often poke a bit of fun at the enemy you'll be facing once you scale the tower and Echo well she's a welcome companion to have traveling around with me, the Warrior of Light and the fairy are an excellent duo always playing off each other and I look forward to every event where they might have an exchange with a boss character.
This isn't really a review more of what I enjoyed about this game.

I've only just started playing visual novels and dating sims, but so far, ACE Academy is my favorite of those genres. There's a lot to like.
You make choice after choice after glorious choice as you guide your main character through his new life in Japan as a transfer student in piloting at ACE Academy (which reviewers call a high school but seems to me to definitely be a university). You join a team and pilot your GEAR (robot/mecha) through various battle matches, which are quick and simple to play and are bookended by strategy sessions and postmatch analysis. You go to classes and sit through or skip lessons and assignments. You adjust to a new family life at home with your charming little sister Nikki and your fun uncle Kaito. You have natural, rich, meaningful relationships with your friends and teammates. You crack jokes, play pranks, and encounter numerous weird pop culture references. And through all this, you learn about your GEAR and what connection it may have to the loss of your parents. All of this makes ACE Academy a fun yet moving game that took me about ten hours on the first playthrough. (Steam says I have 3 hours, but it stopped counting after the first day for some reason.)
What this game handles best of all is the relationships between the characters. With so many choices, you have a lot of control over the main character (although not complete control: occasionally he does something I wouldn't do or chose not to do). The game is long enough for the characters to reveal their depth, to one another as well as to you. And the relationships develop naturally.
On my first time through, I decided not to pursue any of the four possible girls but instead stay open to whatever might happen. I spent time with the girl I liked the most, but then she signaled that she was uneasy about our feelings and didn't want to pursue them, so I backed off and we became great friends. Meanwhile, I was unsure about another girl, and I took things as slowly as I could... which gave us the chance to really get to know each other, until one day she said something that made me realize that what was happening between us was real, so I chose to kiss her, and we ended up in such a close relationship that by story's end, I felt sure that our characters would end up marrying each other after graduation.
Some reviewers are disappointed with the story's ending, feeling that it's a big buildup with no payoff, but I found it satisfying. In my playthrough, the major plot points were resolved in a striking way
, yet leaving the satisfying feeling that these characters still have their lives ahead of them. Even though our story ends, theirs will go on.
There are a few quibbles with this game. For example, some of the backgrounds get reused, the pop culture references can be a bit over the top sometimes, and I wish there were an option to make the main character's relationship with his sister sweeter and more supportive without the teasing. And the story is so deep that it might keep me from replaying the game any time soon. The game seems to let you skip scenes that you've played before, but I would want the whole experience again... and if I take another route it might be bittersweet to meet my girlfriend again knowing that we're not getting together this time.
All in all, ACE Academy is an immersive, intriguing, fun game with mostly likeable characters, and a story that you get to participate in with active choices rather than just passively observe. You'll have to decide for yourself if you like it, but I really do. Highly recommended.

The Mount & Blade series. An amazing game I thought about for years before I actually knew it existed. 'How cool would it be if you could be a Lord with a castle, host an army of varying troops while you conquer your enemies?'.
I first started playing the original Mount & Blade, which was already a really fun and immersive game to play. At that time I was quite broke as a teenage boy so I downloaded the game (shame!).
Mount & Blade: Warband is the sequel to the first game with a tonne of improvements in graphics, gameplay, roleplaying, units, etc. This game is worth every penny if not more. The community offers a wide array of mods for each and every taste. Ranging from music mods (this way you hear the awesome music of Rome: Total War while you vanquish your enemies) all the way to brand new worlds with new factions, gear and units.
Multiplayer is fun as well, however it is not campaign based. You fight different battles or sieges and you earn money by killing opponents. This way you can upgrade your character with new weapons, armor and horses.
Personally, this game is all about the singleplayer. From a developer that doesn't care about useless DLC with content that should'ev been in the basegame to start with. The Napoleonic Wars DLC is a different style altogether in a different era. Focussing solely on multiplayer with a fun player base.
As of this moment (Summer Sale '16) this game has a pricetag of €5.-. If you have ever doubted about this game and did not want to pay €20.- then now is your chance. Give this baby a go and you, sir or madam, shall not be disappointed. If you're a medieval era fan or just like to charge through your enemies with a heavy lance dealing infinite damage to their groins then this game should have a shiny spot in your library.

It's a puzzle platformer where dying leaves a body behind, which is actually a resource necessary to complete the level. For example, if there are floor spikes you can't get past, you can jump onto them and die, leaving behind a body that your next character can safely land on. Over the course of the game, the use of bodies gets increasingly creative, with buttons, conveyor belts, gravity beams, etc.
The game is well-made, and never gets overly difficult, instead opting to periodically introduce new mechanics. In addition, there are 3 bonus objectives on each level: finding a monster named Jeff, completing the level within a time limit, and dying a minimum number of times.

For anyone who might be a model railroader, train watcher, or someone who generally enjoys trains - you will love this game.  For anyone who doesn't like trains much, this probably isn't for you.
There are many different routes and locomotives to choose from (tons more if you include the DLCs).  You have three options of how to play, carrier, scenario, and free run.  Carrier and scenario both give you a set goal with a set train.  This could be a passenger train with scheduled stops, a freight train with cars to pick up and drop off, or a freight yard locomotive switching cars around. Skill system is a spiritual successor to Diablo 2's skill system.  Works by giving special bonuses to skills every 5 skill points invested.  Also, no prerequisite skills lets you truly pick what skills you want instead of having to throw away skill points for the sake of picking up "syngergies" and required skills for other skills.  Aside from the skill system, it's still basic Torchlight gameplay but with a more Diablo-esque feel with a larger world to explore instead of just taking stairs down to the next level.  Each class also has special resources which grant them bonuses such as giving extra damage to specific skills or even triggering an enrage effect on the character. (For example, the berserker, upon reaching maximum of his/her resource, is guaranteed 100% critical strike for the duration of his/her "enrage," where the Engineer's resource builds up charges he/she can use to increase the effectiveness of specific abilities.)  Worth 40, easily, so 20's a steal!

After spending over 50+ hours in this game, here's my thoughts.
PROS:
+ Addicting
+ Very nice graphics for a mobile game
+ Plays smoothly at least on my computer
+ Cards system is fun but can be tedious
+ Job system is great to customize your character
+ Midgar is in the game
+ Cloud Strife is in the game
+ Great Soundtrack
+ Bonus rewards lets you play without spending real money.
CONS:
- Very repetitive
- Main story is incomplete
- Bonus rewards run out after awhile
- Stamina runs out after awhile, which you'll need an elixer or wait a day to refill
- Getting rare cards is extremely tedious which requires a lot of luck or patience, or spend a fortune with real money.
- ingame currency is useless, in otherwords in order to play this game without spending real money requires a lot of patience and time.
So here's my final thoughts. I think it's worth trying out, especially since it's free to try. The game gets you addicted by rewarding you greatly at the beginning, but unless you spend those rewards wisely, you could be wasting a lot of time on this game. That being said, I don't think it's worth investing too much on this mobile game, it's a time consumer that's all it is, and the game is not all that rewarding especially since the main story is not fully complete yet. So my score is 7/10, it's good but incomplete.

Moon Hunter is probably one of the best purchases I've made for my Steam library. It is story-rich, family-friendly, intuitive and has good replayability value thanks to randomly generated maps and players' RPG-styled choices. Moon Hunters is the RPG equivilent/alternative to board games, only that instead of reading manuals and dishing out cards or game-pieces, anyone can jump in regardless of prior gaming experience.

I wanted to enjoy Moon Hunters. It is (in theory) a narritive heavy game that focuses on personal choices and has consequences for your actions - which is a genre I normally enjoy. The problem is that the game is bogged down by tediously repetitive combat, uninspired  level design, and barely any recognition of your choices. I played through a whole campaign twice with a friend only to, at the end, be given practically the same results both times despite attempting to play differently and picking different characters.
For what I paid, Moon Hunters was enjoyable enough. But I won't be getting any replay value out of it, and my friend will be giving me♥♥♥♥♥♥for the rest of time for convincing him to buy this game.

I first discovered this game years ago through its Napoleonic Wars expansion (henceforth to be called "NW"), back during a period when I had an itch for musket warfare. As far as the genre and era convergence, that expansion is the best game available. Because I bought the game during a sale and picked up the full collection, I also got the "With Fire & Sword" expansion.
As I continued to enjoy NW I began to explore the rest of the game, including WF&S and Native ("vanilla") and that was one of the best game-related choices I've ever made. As I got engrossed in the single player and started to exploring mods, this game took me from Napoleonic warfare to the low-fantasy (no magic, monsters, or elven bs) land of high medieval Calradia where 6 factions traded blows and sought your blade for hire. From there the mods took me from Native's version Calradia to the Roman Imperial era, to a recreation of Europe in 1257, to several completely different fictional lands such as recreations of Westeros, Middle Earth, and the Warhammer world, as well as completely original lands such as Pendor and Perisno, and then brought me back to tweaked versions of Calradia- maybe it's calradia in 1400 or 1500, or maybe the mod only covers a small part of Calradia such as Swadia, or maybe the tweaks are as small as new troops and equipment.
The game features a unique sort of double genre-system. Your character and companions are persistent and your stats are managed in traditional RPG style, but in combat you not only fight yourself (with a very original directional system - move your mouse the way you want to swing or block) but you also command your troops using the F(number) keys to give orders. (tip- hold down f1 and point at a location to give your troops the order to stand there; this took me a couple hundred hours of playtime to figure out thanks to the lack of directions on hotkeys and command). When not in battle you travel on the overland map, which is where combat is avoided or initiated and from where you reach villages to recruit from, castles to meet lords in, and towns to make purchases in.
The game definitely has a learning curve as the combat doesn't immediately feel natural (with time it will likely become your favorite combat system ever, though) and there are a lot of things in the game and world that the tutorial doesn't tell you. Once your buy it your FIRST order of business should be to find a starter guide video, and your second order should be to search online for all the keyboard shortcuts, especially the use of the ctrl key to speed things up.
This is my most played game and it's earned that place for a reason. You will come to love the game's unique charm, well-designed world, and unique combat, and I can almost guarantee that the kind of gamer who's had sleepness nights playing Total War or Skyrim because they didn't notice the time go by will be able to look past the dated graphics, quirky AI and UI, and let this game infest their heart like it has done to me.
Once you've got the feel for vanilla, though, you absolutely must move on to the many many marvellous mods available, including the paid DLC Viking Conquest which has overcome teething troubles to become a valuable member of the Mount & Blade IP, featuring increased difficulty and set in Britannia during the period of Viking raiding.
The Module system makes switching between mods dreamily easy, as each mod keeps its own savegames separate from those of other mods, so you can easily have several games in progress in several mods and switch between them fluidly without fiddling with 3rd party managers to put all the little tweaks correctly in their places as with Bethesda games.
If you manage to read this before the steam sale ends, if you have even a slight idea that you might want it, buy it anyway and the money will likely not go to waste. Between native multiplayer, Napoleonic Wars (which is only MP, unfortunately- however, there is a single-player mod called L'Aigle that takes place during Napoleon's reign), and the countless overhaul mods available, there is something here for everybody, and many things for people who like to get engrossed in a game to lose themselves in. This is a must-have title.
P.S. - It's prequel, M&B 2: Bannerlord, will be releasing early next year. As it stands, that game is looking like it may become the best game of all time, and Taleworlds is self-publishing so you can rest assured they'll deliver a product that they feel is great and they will release it when they know it is finished, no sooner. The game seemingly features an almost identical combat and overland system to Warband, so if Bannerlord interests you then Warband is practically a prerequisite if you want to start in Bannerlord's multiplayer without being slaughtered by veterans, and if you want to jump right into its singleplayer (although TW has promised more help for ne players in Bannerlord), then I reccomend you get Warband now so you can teethe yourself on M&B's uniqueness sooner rather than later.

I really do wish I could give this a positive review, because there is so much about this game that is fun. The graphics are good for the war style game that it is, and every game you play will throw different challenges and scenarios at you. However, as great as that may sound... 2 matches of that could easily turn out to be about 3 hours of grind, lagg, crashes, and so much more. I feel that it's abit hit and miss as to wether you get a good game or not.
Firstly, the squad update. In the words of Argus Filch - "Oh dear, we are in trouble." That being the devs, and also many players, as they experience the peformance issues that the new update has presented. They claimed that after testing they had improved the perfomance by x% ...  If anything, it's worse! On top of that, the game now likes to crash on you, at certain points. Just within 4 hours of gameplay today, it has crashed about 5 times. However, some postivies about this are the fact you don't have to entirely re launch the entire game from your desktop- you can simply press the red "launch" button from the already running Heroes and Generals menu. Furthermore, Reto have given out a code for 24 hours of Veteran as a way of apology i presume, for the bad update. I redeemed... So i'm not going to complain about that. :)
Now, onto the actual squad system. Bloody useless! Okay, maybe that is abit harsh. Although it doesn't seem to be any use at the moment, what they were trying to create was overall more positive and looking to better the gameplay experience. They wanted people to work more like a team. How does the squad system do this? Ah yes, it highlights your squad green. A way to encourage users to use it, is the xp that you can get from doing certain things. Despite the above sounding more postive about the Squad update, after 18 hours of gameplay using Squads, I can confirm it is a waste of time. At some point when joining a match, you are just plonked into someones squad, or someone joins yours. I am rank 7. I am placed into a rank 3 squad. They are now telling me that I need to capture point O2, despite the fact it's surrounded by about 5 tanks and swarming with their infanty units. I am now getting ordered around by someone who has no idea what they are doing.
Another complaint of mine is the queue times. I was queueing for war for about 6 mins earlier, where i just gave up and ended up in some 30 min assault match. Cool. Now, for, quite possibly, my biggest problem. THE GRIND. All those matches, all those valient battles where you bravely fought to the last second to defend point B. Congratulations you now have a new pistol. For me the game actually becomes a chore. There are an annoyingly large amount of obvious hackers in the game, which clearly ruin the game experience. Overall just what should be a fun experience, is far from it. Yes, I do recommend this game - but you need to know what you're getting into.
"Arma 2" is a serious simulation, not a "shooter." It's complex, and brutally unforgiving. Make a mistake, even a small one, and you will take the one or two bullets necessary to die. You will be fired at - very effectively - by enemies you can't see. You are probably not going to be casually taking down armored vehicles and helicopters while dismounted. The TUTORIAL can curbstomp you with vicious efficiency.
Let me put it like this. "S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow Of Chernobyl" is a cakewalk compared to this title.
But the game (if you can call it that) is beautiful. That is, it's beautifully crafted, with oceans of effort apparently invested in it being authentic. That authenticity - or what appears to be authenticity to a layman like me - is what makes the experience so lethal.
And engaging.
I barely scratched the surface of the game's content, even after putting in over 20 hours. I ended up quitting because I couldn't manage the difficulty curve, but my total experience was one of being very impressed. There's a lot to do, and a lot of freedom.
I do dispute a review that says the game rewards patience. Sometimes it does, and sometimes it punishes your patience with devastating force. Then it punishes your impatience. Then it punishes your patience again. That's not a flaw. That's the nature of simulating war.
The flaws that I did find were mostly related to AI and event triggers. Sometimes, what I thought would happen after issuing a certain order or carrying out a certain task is not what ended up happening. I also found the "command" interface to be rather strange. I made it work a fair bit, but I never really got the hang of it.
Even so, I feel that this piece of software is a masterwork, and worth experiencing if you want to try something different...and something so difficult that "Nintendo Hard" doesn't even begin to describe the ride.

Not entirely certain what to think here :/ I thought this was going to basically be a horror game played from the viewpoint of a school bully's victim and exploring the pschological suffering and terror that go along with it. Blah blah - fancy words, fancy expectations.
What I got was a bizarre mixture of overly loud scream effects, guiding faerie lights, and the Donnie Darko rabbit with a serious case of steroid abuse. I honestly feel that this could have actually been an awesome game with a bit of polishing. But sadly, the only thing this game is, is a hodgepodge attempt at artsyness wrapped in chaotic failure. Cheesey, badly executed and predictable horror effects have been sprinkled to and fro and inbetween the cookie cutter characters: your default ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bully, your default girl of your dreams, your default creepy creature, your default terrors, your default troubled nerd glasses kid... the list goes on. Oh, and just because: needless lockpick and door opening minigames. IMHO a game can be "wierd and artsy" but if it relies solely on that, the results end up being stale and somewhat cheap, as the story felt extremely flimsy and predictable here.
And I feel bad saying all of this, because the idea and the concept of the game are quite neat. One other thing that really really bothered me was the atrocious english translation. One or two little mistakes can easily be ignored, but the game is saturared with bad expressions, faulty grammar, and flimsy translations. English is a difficult language to master - even more so when you're not a native speaker. But there are so, so, SO many people right here on Steam who would have been delighted to proof read it as well as help out with the grammar, spelling and what have you.
Blaaaaaaaargh. Not my cup of tea, for sure. I tried to like it and give it a chance. But I wish the dev good luck in the future!

Space Run is a clever little game, a nice twist on the tower defence gameplay. Lots of different weapons and modules with which to outfit your ship make for some interesting combinations. Some micromanaging is required during some of the more intense fights, as you are constantly trying to maximise damage output while minimising risk to your own vessel.
the only downside I can find so far is the fact that some, if not all runs, can not be completed with full points on the first try. Unless you're lucky off course. Enemy waves pass your vessel from all sides, but during levels not every side of your ship is attacked with equal ferocity. This means that building a symmetrical ship is usually a bad idea, either because it costs too much, or because you have dps pointing in a direction that is seeing no action. This problem is most felt before the mission begins, when you place your key delivery structures. These take up space you might need. If placed on the wrong side of your ship, you may not be able to defend against the enemy waves effectively. This means several plays of the same trip will probably be required to find the right set up for each mission.
A good game, nice mechanics and gameplay, allthough a little frustrating from time to time when you get blindsided by that last enemy wave coming up on the side of your ship you can't effectively defend.

After spending over 50+ hours in this game, here's my thoughts.
PROS:
+ Addicting
+ Very nice graphics for a mobile game
+ Plays smoothly at least on my computer
+ Cards system is fun but can be tedious
+ Job system is great to customize your character
+ Midgar is in the game
+ Cloud Strife is in the game
+ Great Soundtrack
+ Bonus rewards lets you play without spending real money.
CONS:
- Very repetitive
- Main story is incomplete
- Bonus rewards run out after awhile
- Stamina runs out after awhile, which you'll need an elixer or wait a day to refill
- Getting rare cards is extremely tedious which requires a lot of luck or patience, or spend a fortune with real money.
- ingame currency is useless, in otherwords in order to play this game without spending real money requires a lot of patience and time.
So here's my final thoughts. I think it's worth trying out, especially since it's free to try. The game gets you addicted by rewarding you greatly at the beginning, but unless you spend those rewards wisely, you could be wasting a lot of time on this game. That being said, I don't think it's worth investing too much on this mobile game, it's a time consumer that's all it is, and the game is not all that rewarding especially since the main story is not fully complete yet. So my score is 7/10, it's good but incomplete.

I have no idea if you are going to like this game. It's a weird, hard to control, bizarre game. People compare it to QWOP and to the extent that it relies on playing twister with your fingers that's true, but it's much more than that. Each surgery is like a puzzle, trying to figure out which tools work and don't, finding the most efficient route through it. Achievements incentivize creative play. I mean, the most amazing thing about the game is that it exists at all, it's so absurd. But I think if you get past the initial curve you'll find a compelling score/time attack game.
I'll also add that if you have people over to your house, non-gamers LOVE watching this. A casual hammer to the skull here, a drill dropped in a chest cavity there, accidentally throwing the replacement heart away. It's all good.
You're looking at 8-10 hours for completion of every surgery with good scores, maybe 12-15 if you want to go to A++ on everything. The developers have also repeatedly updated the game with new free content, so I think it's fair to say that if you're the type that buys games to support a developer, this is a good choice.

ike any game it has its quirks, but, overall, Defiance, is a PVE co-op player's game.
Sure there's PVP, but for we who do not PVP this game has something to do almost all the time.
You're ego can go from where you start at 1, to 5900, it gets rough around 4400ish and some of the ways to increase and max, basically your level, are things I won't do, like PVP.  So I'll never max my character, but I find reaching for 5000, and likely 5400 will be satisfactory.
Whatever you do find a place called Headlands transit.  Vehicles can be bought there for the game currency, make sure you get at least a duni.  And, when you can affor it, get a Dodge Caravan.  The Duni maneuvers well, you'll be surprised, but the Caravan hits hard, and a most morbid thrill for me is running around killing mutants with my vehicle haha
If you're into zombies, seek out the afflicted, and make sure you get a BMG weapon.  You'll be laughing over and over every time you use it against afflicted, not the most powerful weapon, but that's relative anyway.
Defiance uses a scaling system, those who play Rift will be familiar with this. and the scaling system can make life a pain, but that usually means better rewards.
And, as far as metacritic is concerned, I look at it this way.  64 is 14 over 50, and with most game reviewers being PVP elitists, they will never give Defiance a great review, always slightly above average because their PVP bias weighs so heavy in their scoring compared to the game itself.
You can't find a better game to play that's free, that has a lot to do, has great clans and great atmosphere, is sci-fi, has aliens and zombies, had a pretty good sized map, has just a lot going for it as a real game, with a storyline that generally follows (a season behind) a syfy television show, with good cut scenes and voice acting.
Oh and, no requirement of ground travel to towns, once you find it you double-click and are there.
Additionally, and I don't care who thinks this is "unrealistic" no damage from falling, or landing off a cliff, or jumping too high.  The game wants to be played, not cursed, and isn't trying to stop you from enjoying what you want to enjoy.  Not many games anymore do that, most game Devs seem to think their job is destroying anything the players enjoy, while complaining sales are down... Apparently most do not understand the simple principle of cause and effect haha.  Trion has its issues, has had trouble with ups and downs, but they do know how to make a fun game, a challenging game, that once and a while is too much for me, but not so much I curse the game, and the company for being arrogant and not caring about their market and community, because, as I said, overall Trion does deliver what it promises to the player in Defiance.
Download and enjoy Defiance, I had my issues with it at one time but they fixed that, and some of them were just me being wrongfully picky hahaha
I may soon download the DLC for Defiance, and that says a lot coming from someone who doesn't like to pay to play anything since NCSoft's player abuse by closing Tabula Rasa 2 days before its 2nd Black Friday.

Old Review begins here:
Defiance has its own client and a really great salvage system so you don't lose money you spent previously on upgrades/mods.
Easy to play.  Challenging missions and encounters.  Ability to play with all levels together.  Weapons have a great range.  You get a vehicle at the beginning and can upgrade to newer vehicles through faction.  Just all and all well thought out, well planned and appears to be catering to a very broad market, with a game for everyone.
A great feature that is missing in many games is being able to set preferences so you don't have to be a PVP player, there's also a shadow conflict area (PVP) that just shows up over cities and areas of the map.  Thus you can participate if you want but are never forced to be a PVP player.  I bring this up as a strictly PVE player who is amazed how large the map is, how they have encounters yet gave us a way around them.  The game seems so designed around the player and the player experience compared to many games I've played, such as Firefall, Face of Mankind, and others which are less well known and/or older.
I was really into Tabula Rasa, which was closed due to a lack of advertising that appears to have been coordinated for corporate politics at NCSoft, Defiance is as close as I can come to Tabula Rasa.  There have been others that came close until they made radical changes to their game and chose paths away from as broad a market as they could have (and therefore able to afford the game being open).  Some games, however, are choosing narrow markets which is of course their choice.  Defiance appears to be, since it's based from a SyFy television show, appealing to as broad a market as possible and is designed to do that without these markets segments of gamers with their own designs as to how they'll play the game trespassing on each other.  So I'll say something that my friends will find rare:  Definance is a great game design which, when you play Defiance shows in the graphics, shows in the options that open up as you advance, just a clear demonstration that Trion took the time to really think out the game, while coordinating missions to episodes too.  Definance has a lot of side missions, a lot of content outside of what you can just do to level, and the side missions have their own rewards that you'll want as much as leveling.  I am finding Definance a great game with enough depth to play for a very long time.  I just hope they don't make some radical change in the future away from what will get them the greatest chance to be a great decades played game success.
Defiance has their own client too, Glyph, and apparently are no longer going to be played through steam.  You'll note I have no time played showed and this is why -- Been playing for 8 days straight now, it's a lot of fun, a lot to explore still, only partially in San Francisco.
Download Defiance, it's free to play, though I believe PVPr's will want to pay some since it appears a bit P2win for that level of game play, but for PVEr's it's just a lot of fun with a great story, in a world where you have no home, no bank, and write your story as you play.

I just now got this game on Steam, having some 100 hours on my hard copy, but nonetheless it is an amazing game. It's also good to occasionally gaze up into the Martian sky...seeing the beautifully rendered Heavens above, with a comet streaking past every so often.
Let me talk for a minute about the destruction engine: off the top of my head, there are 2 things that cannot be destroyed in this game: the terrain and those big♥♥♥♥♥towers in the games last stage. Every other building, however, you can destroy essentially brick by brick, with any non-energy weapon (even your fist). The engine also understands that if you take out critical points of a structure, it will fall much easier than just randomly blowing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it.
The EDF in this game are also very realistic (on the highest difficulty at least, I haven't played medium or easy in such a long time), as in they behave like police. However, I'd like to talk for a moment about the hilarity of their pilots and drivers. The EDF will often flip their cars and crash into each other or even drive off a damn cliff when they're pursuing you, and they will often just fly their gunships into tall buildings, mountains, or even each other. It's really ♥♥♥♥ing hilarious and I'd say buy this game just to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the EDF.

It was a great visual novel and much more that the sum of its parts but I'll go into those parts anyways below. The short answer about this game is that if you like VN's, several choices of women in dating sims, a cute and funny slice of life story placed in the future you will like this game. For those who have come to this game to experience the "story" rather than the dating sim turn away now. Many parts of the story including the "ending" are driven by your choices in the datiing sim.
All in all I will reccomend this game, my full review is below.
The dating sim worked well, and unlike many other VN's of this type there was no question as to who you want to date. The game figuired that out based on a couple of your early game decisions. The way that they did it made everything feel very natrual. The dating sim portion gets a 10/10
The fighting sequences were easy, and the engine that they were using to program it doesn't usually support combat sequences so the way that they went about it was fairly smart, however there are other games that used the same engine that did it better such as the SUNRIDER series. Unlike the sunrider series though, if you fail by scrolling up you can try again. The Fighting sequence get a 5/10 for lack of action.
The story was amazing. It took me about 5 hours to complete one path and then only a couple of hours to complete the others. i skipped quite a bit on those other playthrough because I wanted to look at the ending. The plot was amazing however the ending left a little to be desired. There was no denouement or in layman's terms resolution to the story. The main conflict that drove a huge portion of the story is never resolved. For that I have to give the story a inc/10 for being incomplete.
I give this game a 8.5/10 with 1 point being able to be earned back by either making a sequel or by adding onto the story, and .5 being redeemable if they ever fix their combat sequences.

ACE Academy is one of the best western visual novels I've played to date, even if quite limited in scope. It doens't offer incredible production qualities, as it was made by an indie team and the story is not as expansive as in some top-tier games in this genre. The replay value is also a bit limited, as your choices in most cases don't radically change the storyline or provide very distinct endings like in School Days or Fruit of Grisaia.
Still, while not as "big" as those Japanese games I mentioned above, it presents an engaging, well-written story with tasteful approach to both the main intrigue and the romance arcs. All characters are distinct enough and have intriguing qualities that makes you want to learn their stories and see different interactions protagonist might have with them. They do not deviate much from the typical tropes of the genre (a shy girl, a tsundere etc.), but they're done well enough to be entartaining and not completely predictable. The two romance arcs I've followed (Yunna and Kaori) were both really well done and compelling and the family storyline of the protagonist, especially his interactions with younger sister, were surprisingly good. The art and music complements the story properly and while the game would probably benefit from more sprites and more dedicated drawings for various scenes, it never felt "cheap" enough to make it problematic.
Also, as I suggested earlier, I very much liked the approach to romance it took, even though some my find it overly tame. I find this aspect of many visual novels rather exploitative than compelling and the slow pace of the relationships here felt very much natural and appropriate for the characters. Also, the "dating sim" component never dominated the story and rather complemented it, with benefits for both aspects of the game.
One negative I will have to mention is that with the limited replayability and around 7-8 hours for full playthrough, for many it probably won't be worth the full asking price of 20$. I've bought it on -75% sale and was very satisfied with the content provided, but I think paying more than 10$ would be a bit too much.

Now, I have only played three hours but the hours that I did play were disappointing and kind of boring. I wish I liked the game more but it's difficult to force myself to play any more than I already have. Moon Hunters is clearly a game made with lots of talent and passion but it lacks in so many aspects.
- Disgustingly simple combat: you're limited to three abilities and you can never change them. Only upgrade them to make them stronger.
- Combat lacks responsiveness, it's never clear when you've taken damage and things just sort of happen. The spacebar ability for most of the characters feel weird. You don't feel like you're dashing somewhere smoothly, you kind of bug forward from my experience.
- The goal and how to solve it is unclear. I understand that the game is designed around multiple runs but it's still incredibly vague at the start and you end up running around with a giant question mark above your head in confusion.
- Lots of bugs. Like, a lot. I played with a friend and despite us unlocking Songweaver, I couldn't play her. Our seperate characters's actions got mixed up somehow? What I did play of singleplayer was cut short as no enemies spawned and I got locked into a combat arena thing with nothing to fight.
- Procedural generation is kind of bland and stale in this game. Level outlays are predictable and repeated too often, lots of emtpy space with nothing in them to pad out game and only elongates the amount of time you spend with your set of abilities.
- Traits changing happens too easily if you ask me, you'll go from a compassionate person to a vengeful one with just one action. You never feel like your personality is being tested or that your traits last - it's all very temporary and it never feels like you're making unique individuals.
Otherwise the artwork is really good, music is great with the exception of the ones you constantly hear when traversing the padded out areas. The character designs are really good and I'm deeply enamored with it. I wish I liked this game but it's hard to when it's so boring to get through.

I feel like this game has a lot of heart, a LOT of heart, so I feel bad discounting it.  However there's a lot to be desired from the basic mechanics of the game.  While it has a couple different classes, each only gets a couple different moves none of which have much depth to them.  Between that and a fairly cut and dry enemy roster, you're left spamming the same buttons in roughly the same way for an hour until you get to the end of the run.  In addition, the risk/reward balance of the game is fairly non-existent.  Currency from killing monsters gets spent on mechanical upgrades to kill monsters more effectively...but most upgrades add very little to your stopping power and most enemies go down easy anyway.  In fact, most enemies can just be outrun without much consequence.  Even dying isn't much of a threat, it just brings you forward to the next area.
Despite these gripes the feeling of lore, deeper story, and creating the myth as you go all feel great.  I ran through the game a couple times just to experience the style of the game alone.  That said, once I figured out how irrelevant combat was I spent most of my time just ignoring it entirely and skipping large sections of what was definitely meant to be an intergral part of the game.  It's sad because this feels like a balance issue which could be solved by moving a few numbers around and changing how the difficulty works, but without that fix the game is essentially just a fairly nice visual novel with a lot of running from point A to point B in the middle.

The basic premise here is to run a train from A to B, maybe doing some things on the way. That's it, there's no other meta-game here other than that. No economic layer, no strategy, no career mode other than to collect points and level up for no reason other than to level up. You run a train down a track. I'm not a train nut, but I like trains enough and the setting is simulated well enough for me to enjoy this. Anyone not interested in trains or picking this up for a lark will probably be better off staying away.
There is enough here of the same things I tend to enjoy about ETS2. A chance to maybe explore the track-side of a country or place (or time) I may or may not ever get to visit. For me, there is that same sense of chill about cruising down the track that you get from cruising down the road, just not with the same sense of freedom ETS2 tends to have. Keeping things at speed and on time has a certain challenge to it that has proven engaging and frustrating at times.
(One thing that never fails to get me to chuckle is going past a platform in the pouring rain or snow and seeing people waiting or walking around the station without coats or umbrellas. "Why is that lady wearing a sleeveless dress in this weather?" Then I go: "Oh yeah, its a GAME".)
It's a train simulator, and as such it suffers from the usual types of complaints these simulator games tend to get. Not realistic enough, too hard, too easy, wrong color paint on the ABC-123 exhaust cover, et al. I tend to think these complaints are more about the expectations of the user than the game itself. Things do get updated from time to time, and yes, the community management strategy of the developer can be questionable, DLC is expensive when not on sale. If you are getting in late to the game, my advice is to stick with the more recent and future DLC, which seems to be to a higher standard (admittedly expectable) than stuff from earlier iterations. Stick with a route and equipment on that route that you tend to be interested in.
Here is what I have to say: This game is a train simulator, and it delivers on that promise. It simulates the operation of a train on a track with the expected degree of versimilitude. The models look pretty good to my eyes, the trains run like I would expect them to, and its enjoyable to me.
Well i was surprised how good this simulation really is,Would recommend this to all you budding train drivers.

It's a puzzle game where you have to impale, burn, catapult, and generally sacrifice your previous characters (knights who have absurd titles and a growing array of hats and weapons) to get through the levels.
Comedy is apparent throughout the entire game, from the weaponry/apparel your knights equip to the victory screen where the massive VICTORY that appears is enclosed by a much smaller font, condemning how that victory was achieved.
The levels are innovative and novel, ranging from more basic can-find-it-in-every-puzzle-game layouts (which are mostly just near the beginning of the game while mechanics are still being introduced) to challenges that are wholly unique. Each level has a fuzzy monster (Jeff), and one of the challenges (the other two being time and killing as few knights as possible) is to feed one of your knights to Jeff. Sometimes, getting to Jeff can be harder than finishing the level (which is marked by getting to the cup found on each level).
After finishing a level, you're able to see what the cup you achieved does (and it's all very inconsequential stuff, such as headache relief or something that harms rather than hurts, like a cup of strafe) The cups do nothing but to motivate the premise, which is the king of the knights is sending them to find the cup of life so that he may never die. They have to go through countless other cups first to find the cup of life. The
can easily be ignored while playing as it's really just there for context and atmosphere rather than having any impact on gameplay.
The graphics are surprisingly good, and each set of levels has a unique look to them (the first set is in some mines, and all the levels have a certain feel to them while another set takes place in the mountains.) Each set, to assist in setting the atmosphere, has a unique soundtrack to go with it. While the overall soundtrack has many common themes, it distinguishes itself in each set to give a refreshing sense of
to each set. Levels themselves are also distinguished from one another with each one posing a new challenge (especially the bonus levels, which are designed to be even more of a mind boggler than the usual ones.)
The game, overall, is lighthearted, hilarious, visually & audibly beautiful, and sometimes rather challenging.
10/10, it's completely worth $13, and not buying it during the current sale is a veritable crime.
