I am the biggest sucker for exploration games. By that I mean I will play anything that gives me a wide open world to explore, and doesn't make it too onerous to explore. Platformers usually do exploration the metroidvania route, but there are a few quality indie games that just let you run freely around their world. Lunnye Devitsy happens to be one of those, a relaxed platformer in the vein of Knytt but without the sort of sprawl that really defines those games.
The only story you're going to get is that you're a tiny alien who fell off his tiny planet and onto a great big mountain. You want to get home, and as it turns out there are six wholly different and pretty entertaining ways to do that. But you'll have to find them and piece together a few puzzles to make them work. Some are as simple as jumping on a springboard, some are as complex as building a rocket, and some defy any sort of logic whatsoever.
You can run and you can jump, and that's all you need to start unraveling Lunnye Devitsy's secrets. The running takes a little getting used to, since you have to build up momentum before you really get going, but there's plenty of space to practice your sprinting. You also can't die here, which takes any possible edge off the game. Anything that looks lethal most assuredly is not, and falling off the screen just wraps you around to the other side.
It's not hard to sink a few hours into this one trying to divine its secrets, but without any sort of character progression, collectibles, or story, it's also not hard to get bored quickly. I certainly appreciate it for its stark, otherworldly atmosphere and simple exploration, but not enough to suss out all the endings. Still, I got a bunch of them and thoroughly enjoyed my time working them out across the charming alien landscape. If you're looking for something light to while away a few hours in, you could do far worse.

I bought this game as part of a bundle along with Wake, for $5. Yeah, this is one of those games (along with Wake) that you kinda are willing to spend money on just because you can. "Ah, I got like 5 bucks left... Can't really buy anything. I guess I'll just take this..."
At first I was intrigued and relaxed. But upon only finding half of the ways to get to the moon, the game because so boring, I had to quit in order to save some sanity. So, I got a better computer and played this on it as one of the first games to test its intensity of RAM (since it lagged like crazy on my laptop). So yes, I gave it a second go. Appearently, it was not my laptop...
The game was just so SLOW paced that you can't get anywhere in a decent time. The level design along with the slow paced gameplay makes finding all the endings take probably more than several days. That's just not how to design a game. I explored every area and got two powerups, then there was nothing to do, so I stopped. For good. I will never come back to this game because I'm one of those people who want to experience everything for themselves. If you tell me what powerup you get in a game, that will suddenly render the game unplayable for me, because I want everything to be exciting, new, and not spoiled.
I don't like writing down rates for games that are pretty good, but really, this belongs on a flash website. It's one of those flash games that you really shouldn't spend money on. Not because it's short or anything, but just the amount of enjoyment you'll get out of it. Again, it's soooo boooring. I understand it's supposed to be atmospheric, and it was. But after about halfway through the game, you just simply cannot find any ways back to the moon, no more upgrades, and literally nothing to do.
Call me biased because I didn't technically complete the game, but a human being cannot go through so much loss of sanity by playing a game like this. Again, it's "okay" but the pace is way too slow, goal way too indirect, and progression even worse so.
I don't know what else to say for this other than to save your money. I don't know about anyone else, but I'm one of those people that would rather spend on a game I end up disliking due to genre or whatever rather than a game I just end up not enjoying because of its experience. Buy it if you want, but I don't want anyone else losing any sanity or time either.
My suggestions to developer (even though I know the game won't get updated ever):
- Smaller level design or less filler areas just to slow you down
- More quick movement speed and not so much "moon" gravity
- Add a decent title screen with some possible, oh I don't know, options, then tell the player what to do in some way fitting to the game's atmosphere (basically, not a tutorial, but still telling them what to do)

Have you ever played the tabletop game 'Galaxy Trucker'? If yes, imagine a single-player version of it, mixed with Real-Time Tower Defense.
If you haven't, well, a few more words.
Personally, I'm not a fan of regular tower defense games, but generally the more irregular ones (e.g. Dungeon Defenders) do strike a chord for me. So, along comes Space Run. I bought it more on a whim, because it reminded me of the above mentioned tabletop game, which I immensely enjoy.
So, what is it with this game?
Essentially, you're a guy tasked to ship stuff from A to B, as fast as possible, and hopefully without losing any of the stuff you're supposed to ship. To fulfill this task you get an empty ship made from hex-tiles which you can then populate with weapons, defenses, and of course the cargo you're supposed to transport.
However, you only place the cargo (and generally a single cheap engine) at the beginning of the round. The rest you have to build, rebuild and manage when and as the situation demands with funds you gain during the rounds from destroying random asteroids, enemies and such. The placement of your constructions is a key feature, e.g. engines can only be built on tiles that face space behind the ship, while turrets can be placed in any direction at the edge of your ship, but then can only fire in the directions they can reach. So you'll soon find that one of the most important creeds of your game is going to be 'Location, Location, Location'.
While the first levels (imo) were starting out pretty easy, the latter ones do have a tendency to become rather hectic and challenging, especially when you have to start to compromise (or rather, optimize) wether you need more space for engines to meet a higher quality deadline or rather place another turret to prevent your other engines from getting wrecked by enemy fire.
Inbetween rounds you have then the Engineering section where you can upgrade the constructions you already have or unlock new ones from the money that you received during your missions. You can repeat your missions as often as you like, so running your favorite runs multiple times to gather up some money is not a bad idea, especially since getting the best ratings in the later levels really requires the good stuff, in addition to your knowledge how to best use what in which situation. All constructions have 3 upgrade, 2 of which are active abilities, that all differ immensely (at least in the weapon section), and one passive.
The "story" of the game is pretty weak and is basically nothing much more than an explanation of 'You're a guy shipping stuff from A to B, so here, ship some stuff from A to B.', but honestly, that doesn't really matter, because, hey, shipping stuff from A to B is a lot of fun here. The game is split into several 'chapters', each with their own type of freight to be transported. Those freights will give you different handicaps that make your life only harder.
As for replayability: Well, I'm not sure what happens when you have all the high-scores on all the tracks with all items unlocked, but I guess nothing. So even if I wouldn't say it has insta-replayablity value once finished (which might take some time; I haven't unlocked all the missions yet, and don't have the top-scores on several of those I've done already), but I definetly can see myself coming back to it from time to time just for a few fun rounds.
So far I've been enjoying the game very much and would recommend it. I've heard that some people complained about lags and crashes, but it seems that I had the luck of not being affected by any of those, so the game ran fine for me.

I genuinely enjoyed this game. I played few Visual Novel games before, but this game shot up to one of my favorites. Normally, I go through VN games questions as I, probably, would do in real life and usually ignore the other paths/endings. However, in this case, I binged through the game and experienced all the endings. For the most part, I liked all the characters that were introduced to us. I orginally ended with Kaori's ending then continued to move through the rest of the characters. And one character's CG scenes (not going to say who) actually made me feel unsettled and made my heart skip a beat, which was intended.
As I played through the game, I was always saying how certain scenes were "cute" or "that's adorable". What can I say, I'm a sucker for things that are cute.
One of my favorite things about the game were the hilarious choices you could make and the many referances that the game makes like celebrities, TV shows, movies, devices, a semi-direct referance to a game their currently working on, and even throws a light punch at VN game cliches. The game is packed with many choices compared to othere VN games, which I always enjoy in any game. The game is fully voice-acted and is pretty well done in my opinion. And something that I haven't seen in a VN game that kind of thrown me off at first were the quick-time-choices. I didn't expect that some of my choices were going to be timed, but you quickly get use to it since the game gives you plenty of time to choose.
They're four romance options in the game with personalities that are, somewhat, cliched but still enjoyable as you progress through the story. Speaking of story, admittedly, I didn't quite enjoyed it as much as I would have thought I would have. But is it bad? No. I just simply enjoy games with a really deep story line. Without trying to explain to much of the story, I would say it's average. And as for the battle scenes, it was I would expect it to be; not great, but not horrible either.
And as for what's bad with the game, I don't think there's a lot to talk about other than personal preferances or nit-picky things. On a rarity, lines from characters aren't voice and sometimes doesn't match with what the text box says. I feel like they could have done something a bit more to the battle scenes. I know it's only a VN game and is limited to do so much, and I understand that. Just could have wished for more intriguing battles that were more memoribly. But, my major complaint has to do with the ending. It left to many questions and so little answers, which was probably what they were going for. Still, I'm fine with open endings, but this one left kind of left a combination of a sweet and sour taste that makes me can't tell I liked it or didn't.
Overal, the game is pretty good and would highly recommend it to other VN Gamers out there that would just like to relax with a game like this. Good and fun way to spend some time on it.
A definite score of a 8.5/10.
And, as far as I know, this was PixelFade's first game that was punblished and am excited to play their new games that they are currently working on. I'm definitely going to keep track of their new games to come. And I know it was a joke thing they did at the end of the game, but I really do hope they make a sequel to Ace Academy in the future.

This game is so disappointing. Reading the description I was hoping for a game involving building and running a railroad or even a decent simulation/puzzle instead this game involves around not hitting cars buses at road crossings and not running into other trains. Not a signal in sight though. Would have been better described by the title Train Crash.
The only skill you need are fast reactions and good mouse control.
This is a puzzle game designed for children and young ones at that.

You've got 45% planning and 45% timing to work with, but that last 10% is left to pure luck and sometimes you'll need every bit of it.  But I guess that's how trains work, right?  Or maybe I'm just not that good at this oddly named puzzle game, but either way it's a pretty entertaining game that has a lot of content – most of which will have you questioning just how good you are at multitasking.
If there is one thing that this game exposes you to quickly and without warning, it's that any contact between a train and another object results in a near-nuclear explosion.  That was a common theme for much of my experience in Conduct Deluxe.  That’s the first and probably the most difficult task to complete and one that does not let up as the levels progress.  The secondary task is to move your passengers from one station to another.  The types of passengers vary by color and each level can sometimes include several varieties and their respective drop-off stations, or fewer if the map has other complexities.  What often ends up being the biggest conflict are when tracks overlap with other tracks and roadways.  The only things you’re able to directly influence are whether your passenger trains are stopped or moving and status of the switches on the track that change the paths for the trains.  This presents what appears to be a hands off experience but in reality involves very meticulous operating of these two options.   In order to avoid freight trains, cars, and colliding with your own trains, you have to ramp up your multitasking abilities and keep your eyes on what several trains are doing simultaneously – all while at least attempting to get your passengers where they’re trying to go.
Conduct Deluxe presents itself as a very simple game.  With its roots on mobile, it can’t have overly complex controls and it certainly doesn’t add any additional for the PC version.  It does seem to add (or perhaps maintain) a very large collection of levels, each of which can present a very complex set of tracks and train movement.  This can easily be overwhelming and put off someone wanting a game that appears so casual to actually *be* casual, but for those willing to take up the challenge, you’ll certainly have fun.  That being said, Conduct really feels like a game that’s at home in small doses, which is probably what lead to its popularity on mobile.  On PC where sessions generally last longer and involve much more of a commitment, it can seem like too much to get involved with it for more than thirty-minute blocks.  It’s nothing that would keep me from recommending the game, but it’s certainly something to consider if you’re looking for a game that is either more hands on or is less inherently frustrating due to difficulty.  Either way, Conduct Deluxe does have all the necessary parts to appeal to an audience that has patience and has fun keeping those gears turning.  However, the base price is probably a little excessive considering the scope of the game.  Make sure there's at least a moderate discount before you jump on the decision to pick this up.  While it may feature a healthy assortment of levels, you're not going to find a lot of depth and I've always felt like the $10 level of indie games is where games are supposed to graduate from one-trick ponies to something a little more rich.

Yaiba: Ninja Gaiden Z is nothing more than your every day hack and slash gorefest and that's the strength it plays to. Fight hordes of zombies and other enemies in glorious, flashy fast paced slashing action.
Graphically it isn't the best and there aren't many variations when it comes to gameplay. You go from point A to point B and brutally murder everything in your path while purchasing some upgrades for Yaiba a long the way. What really makes the game shine is the humour. Think Borderlands meets Ninja Gaiden. Yaiba is a reckless, ruthless and funny rage filled character that will keep you entertained.
I got this on the sale and it's more than worth that price for a couple of hours of switching your brain off to engage in some gory action.
The game runs incredibly smooth, I've not encountered any FPS drops, any crashes, any freezes or any graphical issues. I've also not encountered any gameplay bugs so far either. For a fast paced combat focused game running smooth and being as bug free as possible is a must and this game seems to nail it.
I will say though if you're a hardcore Ninja Gaiden fan (1, black, 2, 3) then this game likely isn't for you. It has nowhere near that level of difficulty and combat depth and certainly isn't as "serious" as the main franchise games try to be in tone.
If you're looking for any deep sort of gameplay then I'd move on but if you're just looking to murder hordes of the undead, give it a go. It's worth it.

OK, I now have over 1600  hours playing this game and my mood towards it has cooled somewhat.
The routes that made the game fun originally are still fun, but a large number of the DLC that I have bought since acquiring the game has been sub par at best.
In fact my last purchase "North London Network" almost finished me with the game, broken scenarios, missing consists and appalling physics of the locos featured.
Verifying files, re-installing the game from scratch, neither made the slightest difference to issues experienced in the game or other routes.
My computer is capable of playing any route at maximum settings, yet the broken bits still remain, and that's the bottom line, the game has atrocious quality control, routes and locos etc are rushed out without seemingly the slightest care as to whether they are fit for purpose, and when one does complain, no solution or fix is forthcoming, it's all very much a case from DTG of, oh dear, how sad, never mind.
Some notable examples of shoddy build are as follows.
Northeast Corridor, bought in good faith, never worked and is full of missing speed signs, broken consists and scenarios that can't be finished due to AI issues.
Then there are the Chinese routes, they are to sum it up, dross and unplayable.
Again with many of the German routes, missing locos, speed signs, broken scenarios and random derailments.
At present there is no real competition to the DTG game and this has allowed DTG to release the most egregious dreck and ignore the moaning customers.
The game still has its virtues and if one is careful when buying routes and reads the reviews, you can be assured of some real fun; sadly the misery and disappointment of the purchase of a poorly made route can really knock the joy out of it.
In conclusion an 8/10 for play value and 3/10 for build quality.
I'm dubious about buying further routes just in case they're cack like the ones mentioned above, or as truly abysmal as Return To Maerdy or the Chinese high speed route.
Caveat emptor as they say.

This is a very interesting game that's a challenging take on the tower defense genre. There's more emphasis on speed than there is in most tower defense games, but that just makes it more interesting.
The game lets you put your ship together as you want, which is a very interesting touch.
Overall, I would recommend Space Run if you like tower defense games and space games.

Space Run has humor, charm, wit, and a very decent challenge that is well designed.
The basic concept of Space Run is tower defense, but it takes things in a surprisingly exciting and original direction. Given a ship, a cargo, and an engine, the player constructs weapons, shields and many other devices as needed, all constrained by the limitation of space that the hexagons of the ship represent.
The feeling of flight, of speed is palpable, as the ship soars past planets and asteroid fields, threatened from all sides by every manner of trouble. Pirate ships, tumbling rocks, and even other space truckers all present either a danger, or an opportunity to make cash on the side.
The goal is to protect the cargo and deliver it as quickly as possible - the faster, the better the payoff. But there are strategies that pay well in doddling too, and there are times when it is sensible to hunker down, and times when putting everything into engines is better. It is the diversity of choices, and the continual unlocking of new weapons, shields and engines that make the game entrancing.
Cultural and media references abound - there are nods to everything from Red Dwarf and Blake's Seven to Babylon 5, and more.
Above all, the game is just plain fun. I highly recommend it as a light, enjoyable diversion. Each run takes about ten to fifteen minutes, making it ideal for a quick break or that waiting time before dinner.
This is a casual, but not unchallenging game, that holds a lot of fun in a small package.
It is worth the price.

Surprisingly wonderful story. It’s rare to find a Visual novel with a focus on story.

Cons:

A Visual Novel from a western developer who for the most part actually understands how to make a VN. (Theres no eroge so they are sort of missing out there but thats not a 100% requirement, it would be nice though.)
Pros:
A slice of life story that isn't boring. (This is hard to do for the most part, especially without eroge.)
Romance that develops overtime and doesn't seem to happen too fast or in a stupid way. (Which can happen, expecially when a developer is lazy.)
Some really funny references to other media (mostly japanese or online stuff) that really shows the developers know there stuff.
Some really great art for the most part. (some of the backgrounds and male characters look a bit off but nothing distracting.)
Really solid from a technical standpoint, at least in my case. No bugs or CtD's or anything like that, which can happen, even with Visual Novels made specifically for PC. They really put in the effort here.
A really good if not large soundtrack!
Cons:
They could have spent more time in QA. There are several voice lines that are spoken incorrectly or the voice actors let there accents slip near the end of sentences. This isn't an insult to the voice actors, from there work in game to what I have heard on there patreon they are some of the very few western voice actors that seem to have passion for there work. Also some of the lines in game have some errors but the amount is small. (Less than half a dozen.)
Now this might put some people off but I really urge you to reconsider, this is a con but one that could and most likely will be rectified by the developers in future. The game ends but the story doesn't really. The game is actually 4 chapters of ACE Academy. They finished these 4 chapters and left them open to return to later while they develop another game.
[Minor Spoiler] One thing I don't particularly like but doesn't come up very often is the fact that they are in Japan and the voice actors are speaking English. Yet as it turns out they are meant to be speaking Japanese basically the whole time. I would have thought they could just get Seiyuus for this instead of getting English voice actors (like another company has done before.) It is to me at least, cringe worthy. But like I said it doesn't come up very often and from what I know of the developers they didn't have any shady intentions behind doing so (like some marketing trash to "reach out to a wider audience". Yeah I'm talking about you Moe Novel you pieces of human filth :D)
So in closing, if you like romance stories, a good slice of life (good because its not boring :P) and some mecha thrown in, this is a great little VN for you!
I would highly recommend you check out there patreon and there next game! You can support them and get the first chapter of that starting in Q1 2017. As well as voting on what could be in that game (romance choices and origin stories etc, which on a side note was done for this game. Only two people were romanceable in this at first but the devs put in more after feedback on there patreon.)

Playing through the relatively short story was a joy, the puzzles embraced the mechanics and the world was one of the most detailed I've seen. The story was kept simple and through the gibberish dialogue there was a tale to be told between the Brothers.
It's emotional at times and many can relate to the sibling relationship of older and younger. You empathize with the characters because you know through the game how they interact with each other. It's a beautiful way of storytelling and I look forward to more from Starbreeze.

Definately a game worth getting, especially since it's on sale right now.   You need to use a controller; the left side controls the big brother and the right side controls the younger brother.   It makes for a cool puzzle game.

This game is short but beautiful, a gem truly worth experiencing. During the entire game not a word of any language is spoken. But the message is perfectly conveyed by the emotions the characters exhibit.  Games like this aren't just games, they are stories that we in a way live and experience.
TLDR; Go buy a controller then buy this.

I've been a gamer for a over 25 years (since I was 13). This is one of the most unique and beautiful games I ever played.

If you haven't played Brothers yet, play it now!
Don't watch a video and ruin it for yourself, play it!
This is quite possibly my favorite game this year, I was absolutely surprised by this and honeslty didn't expect more than just a few puzzles and straightforward story about two brothers trying to retrieve a cure for their father, but it goes a lot further than that. The gameplay sort of reminds me of Ico and Limbo for some reason, but that's a good thing, both those games are amazing. I have to give the developers hefty amounts of praise, the only other game that really made me say "Wow!" this year has been Bioshock Infinite, and honestly I think Brothers might have topped that. I can't say much without spoiling the game, so please just go try it for yourself, I can't recommend this game enough. The only complaint I really have is that I beat it in 2 hours. might be able to make it a 4 hour game, max. Either way, money well spent, this is a quality game and story! Truly an adventure unlike what I've experienced in this last generation of gaming.

Known in Japan as "Brothers: Two Sons: A Pair of Male Siblings who Share a Common Mother and Father", Brothers takes a page from Ico and crafts its powerful story through the gameplay mechanics themselves rather than through dialogue in a way that had my jaw dropping by the end.

The closest thing there is to an interactive fairy tale. An extravagant art style, a unique (and sometimes frustrating) control scheme, and a touching story told without any real dialogue. A short game, to be sure, but a meaningful one, and one of the best of the year.

As the trailer suggests, this game is a humorous cross between puzzle platformer and lemmings, where you take advantage of the deaths of your predecessors to progress through the different levels.
With an unlimited number of knights at your disposal, you control one until it dies, then another, and so on, and on each try to die in a way that your corpse will be of some benefit to your next knight. But doing well at a level means using fewer knights (wouldn't want them to die in vain, right? ;)
Progressing in the game uses more of your puzzle skills than your platforming skills, and for considering you will only be using 3-4 buttons, the game gets surprisingly complex.
Completing the various levels and achievements feels reasonably satisfying, and it can be amusing to overcome any obstacle by throwing numerous knights at it in various ways.
The game contains several references to other games, most of which I found quite amusing, but more than anything else I found myself laughing out loud at many of the messages describing how varyingly successful I had been at the end of each level.

My review for the other Lunar Pack game, Wake, was scathing.  So I am please to say, this game isn't that bad.  It isn't that good, either.
The game is the definition of minimalism, for better or worse.  There are no tutorials, no menu screens, no help at all.  In a way, that harkens back to the old Atari days, I suppose.  If you guess correctly at the start, you will see signs that tell you what buttons to push.  Of course, these buttons do not work.
There may or may not be a goal to this game.  Damned if I can tell.  You wander around a complex of caves and water.  Seems nothing, not even lava can hurt you, but it is horribly easy to get lost or stuck.  While you explore, you find items such as moons, which so far, don't seem to do anything.  The game is very slow-paced, and aside from exploring, there isn't anything to do.  No matter how into games you may be, you will be bored by this game.
Like Wake, the game is poorly optimized, and for all of its minimalism, feels very sluggish.  Not only does the game play at a snail's pace, it runs at a snail's pace as well.  It is not unplayable like Wake was for many people, but it is noticable.  I have also had it crash every time I have run the game, sometimes on exit, sometimes on the start.  It also caused an odd behavior while the game was running.  My shift key acted like D, as did X on my gamepad, and Y acted like the w key.  Somehow this game managed to make it almost impossible to type while it was running, even when alt-tabbed.  Perhaps this is why the buttons didn't seem to do anything?
Despite being basically a bad game, there is some value to the Lunar Pack.  If you buy this game on a sale, the card drops will more than pay for it, so you might just turn a profit.  But is that kind of suffering worth it?

Okay, so i´ve played quite a bit of this game now and i´m going to tell you(The consumer) what I think.
Conductor deluxe is a full time strategy game that heavily relies on timing and strategic planning. It was published and made by Northplay, consisting of a development team of 4-5 people.
Originally this game was released for iphones and android phones. Recently however, the game was ported to pc and released on steam. The reason i wanted to check it out, was because one of my good friends recommended it to me(as he had played it on his phone). And well here we are.
In this game, you(the player) posses the power to take control of trains and rails(and for some unknown reason, you have the title of "conductor", despite you clearly being a god)
First of all, this game is incredibly fun and addictive and yet extremely challenging at times. The game also provides a ton of content, at this point in time of me writting this review, i have over 4 hours played, and i´ve only made it through the 3 first overworlds (24 overworlds total). Not to mention that i have barely touched the custom level creation. Yes you heard that right, this game has custom level creation.
However, you have to earn certain structures such as "longer rails"(don´t worry you still have unlimited basic structures fo you to use) you unlock these structures by opening chests which you occasionally are rewarded from playing the main game. I do feel like this is quite unnecessary, also let it be known, at this point in time of me writting this review, there is no way of buying these chests. Maybe in the future the devs will change this system in which you earn chests or just remove chests altogether (the second option is prefered naturally).
The custom level creation also offers deep customization and details for you to add, to your custom levels(finally my detail fetishes can be satisfied, it´s like cities skylines all over again).
There are also quite a few alternate trains/skins, which you are also rewarded with occaisionally. you can change what train type you want to use at almost any given time. It´s a bit underwhelming, maybe you could add to it with some paint jobs or "custom grafitti" maybe, but hey it´s still something.
All in all, i would strongly recommend this game, great challenge, plenty of fun and with a ton of content for you to utilize. And all of this for only 10 bucks!

Space Run is an interesting little take on the tower defense formula. It is good that for the most part what you are defending is immobile(as far as gameplay is concerned), and it lets you concentrate on enemies coming to you, which is how I personally define a good basic Tower Defense game. The game is not difficult to understand, and the upgrade paths are reasonably forgiving, at least at the beginning when you're starting to get comfortable with how -you- plan to play. Gameplay can get a little frantic, and could probably use a pause button to let you catch your bearings when things start getting overwhelming(and to let you focus on easy-to-forget things like repairs), and the way it judges performance is entirely fair for the context of the game.
Most importantly, the game pushes you into situations that make you think creatively. You have to decide whether you'll use space on your ship for your cargo that could be used for valuable engine and weapon emplacements. You have to decide -which- weapons to use, and what will be most useful for the trials ahead. The game does reward replaying missions, both with currency for upgrades, as well as the reputation needed to unlock new equipment. The fact that you can easily replay missions, even coming back later with better equipment to earn better ratings, and get a sizable reward for doing so very much evens out the game's inherant difficulty level. Because the choices are so diverse and useful in their own ways, this has the effect of making it not feel like grinding is required.
I would recommend that anyone seeking to play this game be comfortable with the idea of learning hotkeys(they're simple and laid out around the WASD keys) because every second you can squeeze out of your interactions will save you time later when you need it. Said hotkeys would be a lot less necessary if they later patch in a pause button.
Good luck, and may the winds be at your backs!

Not perfect by any mean, but still one of the best VNs I've ever read.
Pros:
-Phenomenally written. I could barely stop smilling as I read.
-Lots and lots of meaningful and seemingly meaningful choices. Troll choices are always welcome.
-Well voice acted *in English*. (I just can't understand why some certain VNs written in English went for Japanese Voice Acting. I really don't. If I want to listen to Japanese, I can read any of the many Japanese VNs)
-Music is very nice to listen to, though rarely I do feel that the music playing doesn't match what was happening on screen.
-Art quality is usually very nice, though I feel there's some inconsistencies in some scenes
Cons
-The Dialogue choices aren't always representative of the Protagonist's choice of words. Most of the time, it's just mildly different and the choices I see could be seen as shorter versions of what he would say but in some cases the results give completely different feel than what I thought I choose to convey.
-The ending, or lack thereof.
As this is, in essence a 'Novel', the most importance factor in judging it should be the quality of the writing and the story.
The writing passes with a flying colour, and I can't really recall any VN I have more fun reading in recent memory.
What we have of the story easily passes as well, though if this was a play, I would say that it lacks the entirety of its third act, and I was shoved off the theatre in confusion right after act 2 ended. Not the best feeling ever, especially since it's so good.
It was short and sweet, more of playing a make your own movie than a traditional game but i loved the characters and wish for more.

I really wanted to like this game.
This game has been on my radar (and later my wishlist) for a while.  Then, I saw Total Biscuit's Top 10 of 2013 and I badly wanted this game - waiting each day hoping the game would go on sale during this winter extravaganza.  Then, it did...and I finally played it.
*Forgive me for this bit of backstory* I loved a game called The Adventures of Cookie & Cream for the PS2.  The idea of using both analog sticks to control 2 different characters really was fun back then, and I hoped for a new take on the potentials of using the controller in a new way.  Additionally, to provide an introduction to my review (and of course since I do not do this for a living or in any professional capacity) I also just finished a totally different game – Bioshock Infinite – and watched Total Biscuit’s review.  He has a long opening providing his rationale for providing a contrary opinion to the overall critic base praising that game.  I feel like I am now in his shoes…
Brothers does have moments of beauty.  The visuals can be picturesque and the use of nonsense Sim-like language actually benefits the narrative the game designers create for the player.  The story and the world give the player reasons to connect to the overall plan of the designers.  There were a few moments where the combination of the music, story, and visuals really pulled me in (but this is of course very subjective – see Total Biscuit who loved it).
But, in the end, this game does not deserve the high scores or the praise.  This does not mean I hated the game.  I just did not like it.
I wanted a puzzle game, instead I got a game that had nothing but unbelievably easy obstacles (not puzzles) for the player to move through – not work through.  I wanted a challenge – instead I got a simple and easy set of moments with absolutely no choice, danger, difficulty or need for pause.  I wanted a story that was moving and engaging – but what I got was mediocre and similar to many books I’ve read and games I’ve played (the developers left the limited language, music, and landscapes for the player to project onto – which isn’t bad, but did not work for me).  I wanted a world I could revisit, or at least enjoy the time I spent in it - but the world was not unique *spoilers in black*
.  I wanted a little bit of length – I feel like the game lasted maybe 2-3 hours (this is not always bad, but it feels like I never got to live in the world).  If nothing else, I wanted the overall picture to matter more than the individual parts, but I felt myself constantly wishing the game was better in all the areas listed above (maybe I’m a victim of the hype train – also a fair critique of my own review).
In the end, I guess I wanted more than I got.  The game is worth a few dollars if for nothing else that I hope more developers play with controls and story, but I have to disagree with the chorus of praise.  Tread carefully and limit your expectations.
If I could give it a vote of Meh instead of up or down, I would.

This game is both a joy to look at and to play. Despite knowing it'll be free on the PS+ network next month, I bought it during the sale and even 75 minutes in, I don't regret it. I expected to be frustrated by the "single player co-op" as the game calls it, but the controls are intuitive and the puzzles that involve both brothers make sense. Even if you don't know precisely *how* to do something, you can tell exactly *what* you're supposed to do at a glance.
As a puzzle platformer, it's probably very easy. But it's not about that. It's about the bond that's built as you play both of these brothers, interacting with each other and their environment. Like I said, less than 2 hours in I already feel a deep sense of attachment to them. I find myself moving the older brother first, to protect the younger one. But the younger one is always the first to interact with new people, because it feels like it's in his nature to do so.
With no dialogue (that you can understand--though context is easy to read here), this game relies on action to tell its story and reveal the personality of the characters, and so far it's done a phenomenal job. Highly recommended.

Taking the rules of death in gaming to a completely different place, this game is devilishly fun.  The graphics and physics of this puzzle game are very well done for this independent company based in Edmonton, AB.  Well worth the time and money.

Death. It has always been something that is best avoided in video games. Also real life would be the other main place. But as Life Goes On, an indie puzzle game by Infinite Monkeys shows, sometimes it can be used to solve environmental physics based puzzles.
The hook of this game is a little tricky to wrap your head around, but simple to understand once you see it in action. Basically you control an infinite number of little knights and want to get them to the golden chalice at the end of each level. To do so, you can respawn a knight whenever a death occurs and make use of the previous body to further your cause. For example, you might be faced with a spike pit which is too wide to jump over. In this case, simply jump a knight into the middle of it, respawn and use the lifeless body as a stepping stone to get to the other side (The game gives each character a name, but you'll never bother to read it).
It is a base mechanics that works extremely well. If you played the demo (and you should) you would quickly have got into the swing of using your minions to get a little bit further each life. It is clever and the initial levels make great use of the different possibilities the mechanic presents. Unfortunately, like a lot of clever ideas it runs out of steam far too quickly.
Life Goes on just doesn't have enough good variety to maintain your attention. By the end of the first set of levels you will have had your fill of the different types of puzzles and so it is a let down that the next set is more or less repeating things all over again. The levels get longer and the challenges more difficult, but really the game is just chaining the same challenges you have already faced over and over again into growing chunks. Worse, whenever a new mechanic is introduced, it tends to lean more towards frustration rather than fun, especially when compared to the very solid base (trying to avoid activating respawn points is never a fun time).
To be fair, although the 3rd "world" on drags a lot, there are still a couple of memorable stages here and there. One in particular pays homage to a popular steam themed game and the "final level" in each group represents somewhat of a boss battle, that is much more fun to play through. If only these levels had been the norm, rather than the exception this review would be a lot more glowing. As it stands the game only shows glimpses of potential and innovation, perhaps a lesson for the developers next game (quality of puzzles over quantity please!).
Mixing it up is the set challenge of beating the clock and set number of deaths for each level. You will also have a "fuzzy" creature to find in each level which will eat one of your knights. While this promises diversity, the reality is it just means you are beating the level three times with a slightly different focus. Sadly there doesn't appear to be much scope for earning all three in one run consistently and there is seemingly no payoff for doing so anyway.
The rest of the package is well put together. The graphics are functional and the sound and music is nicely done. The menus work, but are a little uninspired (think ios style) and there is basically no story to drive you on. The environments are nice though and have a lot of good touches such as moving power cables. There isn't a lot of variety in the caverns, but later levels do at least provide a slightly different colour palette.
In terms of gameplay, the knights themselves are perhaps a little inconsistent as platforms (you'll often try to jump on one and "miss") but this isn't something you can't adjust and plan for and there is a very low penalty for failure. The controls in general are tight and it is nice that the game automatically "grabs" you onto other knights so this is nowhere near as fiddly as it might have been.
Is there enough content for the asking price? I'd still suggest that there is, at a push, but it is walking a very fine line (looking at 4-5 hours I would think). The base game here is so solid that I highly recommend everybody tries it, but the lack of ideas means even the demo might just be sufficient (or waiting for a deeper sale might be the best option).
So ultimately a bit of a disappointment despite still being a solid game. But then, life always goes on.

Well to start off, I picked this game up off of a Humble sale for pretty cheap. I sometimes like to buy and play ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games just for the hell of it. While some are enjoyable in how awful they are, like Legendary, some are just truly bad. This game is one of the latter. It's just bad.
TL;DR - It's bad. If you like awful,♥♥♥♥♥♥games pick it up on sale. If not, just keep away.
Pros:
-The cell shaded art style of the game is solid. Nothing special, but it doesn't look poor.
-The game runs well with high frame rates on high settings
Cons:
-THERE IS NO CAMERA CONTROL
-The writing is just god awful (the intended audience has to be preteens when it's probably rated Mature)
-The game is weirdly difficult, but not in an intuitive way (feels more unfair than hard)
-Generally uninspired
While the game looks good and runs well, that doesn't save it from being an utter shitpile. The game is weirdly difficult, which is nothing new to the Ninja Gaiden series, but it's not intuitively difficult. The other NG games made you want to "git gud" and beat the difficult areas/bosses while this game is just frustrating. Enemies are plentiful and you can only take a few hits worth of damage. Then there are tons of gimmick enemies that are super powered and while fine on their own, become annoying and difficult as they send multiple at you at a time. The weapons you have to deal with them are uninspired and feel sub par, taking like 2 light combos for one generic enemy. The more interesting and special weapons are gated behind killing special enemies and you lose them after a period of time. Leaving you with just the normal boring weapons again.
What makes the game the most difficult is the lack of camera control. Not being able to move the camera at all is the worst decision you can make in a game like this. Enemies get in the way of the camera and it's way to easy to lose your character after getting knocked around. No camera movement plus enemies that obscure the screen make it nearly impossible to see what's going on in certain situations. I feel like most of the difficulty stems from this awful camera which just makes the game more difficult in general.
Poor controls + uninspired weapons + terrible writing means I cannot recommend this game. I tried to as hard as I could to play it thinking 6 hours (howlongtobeat) was doable, but I just can't do it to myself anymore. Just save yourself the bad feelings and skip this one.

What a boring game. No plot, no purpose, no puzzles, nothing interesting at all.
It's like Exile but without the puzzles or inventory.
It's like Limbo but without the atmosphere, sound effects or puzzles.
It's like a 2D version of Kairo but without the puzzles.
You wander round and round and round this huge map with no clue as to where you're going or what you're supposed to be doing, occasionally picking up collectables. But you're not told what they're for or how many you have to collect, or even if you have to. Some give you new abilities, but you're not told what they are, so every time you pick something up, you have to stand and press every key on your keyboard to see if anything different happens.
And it's S...L....O....W.... your character walks like he's wading through treacle, even after you pick up the "run" powerup (which I wasn't aware I'd even done until I read on a forum about it) and you can just hold an arrow key down for minutes at a time as your character crosses the barren map.
Also, the developer couldn't be bothered to put in an options screen. You can't change the resolution, or adjust the controls, or alter the volume without manually editing the config file. Many people only found out by accident that pressing 'F' makes the game go fullscreen.
I left the character underwater for ten minutes hoping he would drown, but not even that relieved the tedium as absolutely nothing happened.
The game has achievements? That's a joke, right? Surely the only one it needs is "Put up with this drivel for ten minutes."
Please don't tell me that I didn't "get" the game, or that I obviously only like FPSs. If you'd check my profile you'd see that I'm a great fan of both indie puzzle/platform games and 'arty' games - I have Kairo, Braid, The Path, Dear Esther, The Graveyard, They Breathe, LIMBO, Thomas Was Alone, Botanicula and Gone Home. It was tough not to recommend this game, because I did enjoy it for a while.
At first I really appreciated how organic the game was: there were no clear directions, controls were written in the ground, no options, and you had to hold down esc to make your screen slowly fade into an exit. The game had nice spare looking style and sound.
The goal in the game is to return to the moon in a few different ways. The first few puzzles were extremely simple (for one of them you just wait in a post office and the mailman delivers you to the moon), but then a majority of them ended up being exercises in tedium.
Lunnye Devitsy is lacking. It has open world that is not interesting and stops being mysterious fairly early on. Sometimes messing up means having to trek back and forth between the boring areas. The controls and character are also a bit finicky and take more maneuvering than I think should be required. There are also puzzles that are all about guess work rather than puzzle solving (a completely blind maze, and then cannons take brute trial and error). And the "organic" aspects just got on my nerves:  you can edit a text file to turn post processing on and off, you can enter full screen with "F" and you can't pause or change any other options.
This isn't a terrible game, it's just a game with terrible pacing and some poor choices. Its not even that this game is challenging on a puzzle or platforming level, because it's really not. It is quite simple, and, aside from the mentioned nuisances, the platforming is easy. The problem is that the game seems to deliberately want to inconvenience the player.  Instead of being open, this game would have done better to be contained with levels and/or check points.
The price may be tempting, but I think you should consider other games.

I generally don't leave reviews, but I kickstarted this game and feel like I should, based on the low number of reviews currently.
Pros:
* Multiple characters that play differently
* Gorgeous
* Great soundtrack.
* Differnent choices throughout the story that shape your character. Not in a Deus-Ex way per se, but more of the constellation locking bit.
* New experiences and story interactions each time you play
* Overarching unlocking system, which means that regardless of how poorly you did, you might still get something out of it (Sorta like how with Rogue Legacy, over time you unlock better and better gear. Same concept in that you unlock and learn things over time/runs, but not same in terms of gear)
* Multiplayer! (which is currently a con as well)
* Cool boss fights!
Cons:
* Somewhat repetitive fights. Usually, getting into melee isn't a great idea, so if you spam one of your ranged abilities, its almost always a better idea. While there are different types of enemies, I still haven't found a scenario in which I should risk going into melee over using ranged abilities.
* Co-op/Multiplayer is YMMV. To be fair, haven't played in a while, so maybe its been patched up. But last time I played (Aug 2016) with a friend, he got frustrated after a disconnection lost us our progress roughly 1/2 hour to an hour in.
Bugs aside, I'd highly recommend this game. It is clear that a lot of tender loving care went into this game. It's highly polished and it shows the devs put blood, sweat, and tears into this game. It can both excite you in combat, then relax you when camping at night and interacting with NPCs. It's fun and engaging, which should be what people are looking for in a video game. The two cons are not enough to detract from this beautiful game. Again, high recommendations, and buy some copies for your friends.
P.S. Again, I stress that the stability of the online play is essential. The devs are aware of the situation and quite active, so hopefully it gets resolved. While I recommened it, its a conditional recommendation (at least if you're looking for the multiplayer aspect) until thats more of an anomoly than it currently is.

If you happen to survive the HOG without a cornea transplant then you immediately get treated to a puzzle in the form of a jigsaw, a puzzle slide, a rotating disc slider, or a find the 20 differences puzzle. Once you complete that you recieve a postcard and you get to do the whole thing again and again 25 times until you collect 25 postcards from 25 different landscapes from Anozira.
This brings us to the story. Anozira contains 5 main characters all demonstrating b grade voice acting skills coupled with acute brain damage, probably due to incest as they have been cut off from the main world for far too long and want to drum up tourism. Our main protaginist of the game has a light bulb decision to create 25 postcards and send them out. What this has to do with finding 12 items in each landscape and solving a puzzle I will never know. Neither will I nut it out how postcards will bring the masses to this fictitious town filled with grand dad jokes worthy of the skip button being mashed with your forehead.
Each character apparently has a different dialogue and so if your game and want to go blind you could play this 125 times just to find out all the secrets of the town. The only secret I want to know is why the main characters at the beginning have mouths that move like their some sort of ventrilloquist puppet where the puppeteer really has his hand jammed up in there and is desperately trying to get it out. Seriously their head and mouth have an eplipetic fit like a hummimng bird being electrocuted and then out of sink voices start coming through. It would not have started to surprise me if their heads suddenly did a 360 turn and green stuff came out of their mouths.
In all seriousness the game was really easy since you have 5 hint possibilities and 5 time extensions which you can constantly build up and even over the 25 landscapes youll eventually gather 5 skips which will allow you to skip a puzzle completely. Surprisingly I found the timed version of the game very relaxing, but apparently there is a no timer option also available, which is very, very, very, very, very, very relaxing. This is for red necks so dumb that their dogs teach them new tricks.

This is a decent HOG with a western theme. If you played Al Emmo the Lost Dutch Mine, you will be familiar with things here. if not, that's okay. The game works as a stand alone experience too. You start out by selecting one of five playable characters. I thought this was a nice touch, as each character has different things to say and their own audio speech for every postcard collected. Game play involves finding a list of random objects in each scene before the timer expires. Along the way you can find different types of tokens to assist your game. Points tokens, time increase tokens, and skip puzzle tokens. There are 29 levels to solve and 29 postcards to collect from completing scenes at various locations.
PROS:
*Nice colorful scenes
*A large variety of hidden objects
*5 playable characters, individually voiced. Good replay value
*With 29 levels, it's quite a large game
*There's a relaxed game mode without a timer
CONS:
*At times certain objects were hard to see
*On a few rare occassions there were some doubled objects in a scene (like 2 coffee cups) but only one of them would register as the correct object.
*Resolution could be higher, but I suppose this is a limit of the AGS engine.
*Some non-HOG puzzles may grow a little tedious (Find the Differences puzzles)

---My Train Simulator 2015 Review---
First and foremost, this is an honest review.
Train Simulator 2015 is an OK simulator/game.
I'm going to simply list some of the pros and cons that I have:
PROS:
*Decent graphics.
*High quality audio.
*Nicely modeled locomotives.
*Somewhat decent scenarios.
*Good physics.
CONS:
*All the DLCs are really expensive and completely useless.
*You don't even get a "full game". In order to get the "full game" you need to buy over $2000 in DLC locomotives and routes.
*Poor support. One time I emailed them and never got a single response back.
*Not fully compatible with Raildriver.
*The "free updates" are basically just DTG correcting grammatical and text mistakes.
*It's a shame that all the DLCs combined are worth over $2000.
*Not enough scenarios, even with people from the Workshop making them.
*DTG seems to forget about some of the decent routes, like Cajon Pass, and Castle Rock Railroad. I have no more scenarios to play for these routes and all of the ones from the Workshop need other DLCs just to function.
*About a month or two after they release a DLC, they forget about it and don't even attempt to push out updates and fix bugs.
*You really think anybody at DTG cares about their customers? Nope, they don't. It's all about money.
***PLEASE, DON'T WASTE YOUR MONEY ON THIS!***
I do NOT recommend this game!

Have some time to relax? Check out Lunnye Devitsy, a casual exploration game where I think the goal is to find different ways to hit the moon. And yeah--I think that's about it.

Lunnye Devitsy wants to tell us the story of an alien that inexplicably falls from the moon onto a huge mountainside on the planet below each time you make him fall, only to then spend the next few minutes finding a way back up. The problem is: there is no story, the only known thing about the alien is the fact that he needs to return to the moon, and yet each time he does he will fall again only to do the same thing all over again. The entire point of the game is to explore the map and find six different ways to make it back to the moon in one piece, only to unlock the seventh way, but since even then nothing new will happen, achievements are probably your best motivation to make it that far. Apart from that, you know absolutely nothing about the alien's life, the planet, the random creatures you will find on the planet or even the purpose of the entire game; aside from two or three easter eggs that will award you with an achievement each once you get to them, the entire map is a empty maze in which your only purpose is to get to the other end in order to collect a part for something that should take you to the moon. As much as the game focuses on exploration, as it leaves menus, instructions or quests behind, there really isn't much out there to explore and without looking it up online you will have a hard time figuring out what you're supposed to do with those random pieces you find scattered around the map. Even with seven different ways to make it back to the moon, the entire experience feels repetitive and mediocre, as almost all the routes will require you to collect a number of items from around the map, not knowing in what direction they might be, bringing them back to an NPC which will then present you with another way to make it back. This is one of those games that it's painful to watch or play as nothing interesting ever happens and even when the challenge is supposed to make it better, there will be issues that will stop it from being enjoyable.
Lunnye Devitsy fails to follow the first rule of any platformer: being fun to play; instead of that you get a boring, frustrating and luck-based experience that you won't miss once you press the escape button. For the first bit, Lunnye Devitsy wants to give you freedom of exploration, giving you the choice to take on the six different endings at your own phase and theoretically figuring out each one of them on your own. However, the game has absolutely no instructions whatsoever and even though you will bump into an engine part or a moon piece frequently, it will take a while to piece them all together and figure out where you're supposed to go once you have collected them all, time in which you will simply move from one edge of the world to the opposite one trying to find that object that you're supposed to interact with, as there is no hint to the whereabouts of that object or NPC, or the action you're supposed to perform in order to interact with that object / NPC. Once you do eventually get back to the moon six times, a seventh ending will be unlocked which is supposed to be longer and more challenging, but ended up being nothing like that. In order to get back to the moon the seventh time you must collect all the coins scattered around the map, some of them in almost unreachable areas, so this is where your abilities were supposed to interfere, making use of the double jump techniques and the cannons, which were useless before, however the cannon shooting mechanic is completely broke, sending you way off track from where you're supposed to be and in different directions each time, no matter if the cannon is positioned at the same angle it was a try before, making reaching those hard areas a game of luck rather than skill; combine that with the double jump mechanic which randomly stops working at times after you come out of the cannon, even though you obviously need it to reach the ledge near you, and you've got yourself an almost impossible to finish game. Believe it or not, that was only the core of the problem, as there are many more issues such as your character randomly being transported on the other side of a wall or getting stuck for a few moments in the floor.
The resolution is for some reason fixed, which works fine if you play the entire game in window mode using only a portion of your screen, but if you do decide to go fullscreen, then that becomes a problem since the resolution is nowhere near HD. The map is relatively small and even though it's somehow divided into different areas, they all look alike; the black is always dominant and there are little things to differentiate one area from another, and because of that until you get familiar with the layout, it will be easy to get lost. The visual effects will always be around in some way, whether it's rain, fog or a combination of both, but they only make it harder to see, something that can become extremely annoying later in the game when you you have to jump from one platform to another and the fog or rain effects will cause you to miss your target.
This game sounds just as mediocre as it looks, there are few sound effects and the ones that are there feel like they've been extracted from a 90's basic effects pack. While that song playing the background as you jump around isn't necessarily bad, you will eventually grow tired of hearing it, and after the four or five hours you'll spend with the game if you're into getting all the achievements for returning to the moon seven times you will be glad it's over. Even though the game has a lot of issues aside from audio related ones, it would've been nice to have a background story narrated while playing, at least offering some details on why the alien that you control keeps jumping from the surface of the moon, or at least make some jokes about it.
Completing the game takes around 3-4 hours depending on how long you take to find everything and if you're using a guide or not, something that you will probably do at some point since there are no indications to what your objective is or where you should start looking for something, but even so most of the players will probably give up on this game in less than an hour, leaving you with a question if you really do want to complete it or not; I did, and I already regret wasting 4 hours of my life with this.
Lunnye Devitsy is a bad idea with a worse execution, and that's the kind way to say it; the story or the purpose of the game makes no sense, the bugs and technical issues will sometimes make the game impossible to play and on top of that most of the players won't even know what to do without a guide since there are no indications whatsoever. You can, however, grab the game for only a few bucks, so if you're still interested you can try it without spending too much and give it your verdict.

I picked this up on a whim when the Lunar Pack was on sale, and I've been very pleasantly surprised and pleased with the game. It's a nice little platform-puzzler, especially for the Lunar pack price.
Enjoyable if:
-You like games with very little guidance--there's no tutorial and there are no hints or clues.
-You like games with an atmospheric story rather than a written or spoken dialogue (there are only a few symbols, no text, as far as I've played)
-You like games where you can find your own way
-You like pixel art.
If, on the other hand, you prefer games with lots of hints, levels, and a clear game trajectory, this is probably not a game you'll enjoy.
Small drawbacks: There's no way (that I've discovered) to restart the game if you get stuck in certain areas of the game, other than quitting and restarting the game.  This is only a real problem at the beginning, though, before discovering moves like the double jump.  As progress in the game is saved, this is only a minor annoyance. Also, occasionally the various filters are a bit much.
Overall: 8/10

Oh, boy. Let me tell you about this God-forsaken game, Lunnye Devitsy.
You play as a cute little alien that falls from the moon and you need to find your way back. There are several ways to get back, 7 in fact. That's the premise of the game. There are no enemies, nothing can kill you... it's pure puzzle platforming. The design is ALL atmosphere and what an atmosphere it is! Further, there is zero guidance, no on-screen instruction, not even a main menu of any kind. This minimalistic approach isn't for everyone, but I appreciate its purity.
The game comes includes with a map file. Use it! The game is virtually impossible without it! I advise against using online guides of walkthroughs, that way you can get a decent amount of time into the game... probably over 20 hours. Your time is spent finding all of the different ways back to the moon by looking for visual clues, as there are no words. It will test your attention to detail, patience and platforming abilities.
About 98% of the game is the perfect little puzzle platformer, but there is one glaring design flaw that nearly drove me to the brink in my playthrough. Eventually, towards the end of the game, you need to collect coins around the entire map to unlock the final method of getting back to the moon. Of the few dozen coins to collect, there is ONE that is infuriatingly frustrating to collect. Getting this one coin took longer than unlocking any other method for lunar return. To get the coin, you need to launch yourself from a cannon onto a certain platform. This cannon needs to be aimed PERFECTLY. By perfectly I mean PER-FREAKIN'-FECTLY. There is maybe a 2 pixel window that makes up the sweet spot. Whether you're using a joypad or keyboard, the aim is WAY too sensitive. On top of that,  everytime you miss and get back in the cannon, it resets. Even when you do get it right, you then have to traverse what is probably one of the hardest platforming obstacle courses in the history of the genre. And if you mess up and fall? Back in the cannon! So you spend the majority of your time firing the cannon, missing, firing again, missing, firing again, missing... over and over and over and over. This is not fun, this is not challenging, this is bad design and frustrating more than anything else.
However, I can't decry the entire game because of this one puzzle. In fact, if and when you do finally pull it off, it's quite the sense of accomplishment! That's something many AAA titles can't claim. At the end of the day, it's a visually appealing, unique and tough puzzler that makes you think and challenges you. You've been warned.

Forget your Clannads and Grisaias, this is the top dog of VNs.

Surgeon Simulator 2013 brings the humorous web game to a more feature rich version that brings as much fun as the original prototype. The goal of each operation is to remove a failed organ and replace it with another, often with realism taking a step back for the gameplay. The controls can be likened to QWOP with its confusing and awkward controls, although getting a feel of them doesn't take too long to do each of the operations. Each operation can be summed up as break this bone or cut exactly here on the organ and remove it, and is loads of fun trying to flail around your hand. Graphically and musically it plays as parody of TV medical dramas like the first game with good music and funny yet semirealistic medical objects and organs. There's a small amount of operations with some variations, but the appeal is in the controls, physics, and humor. As an update to the popular web game, the full version of Surgeon Simulator 2013 brings humor and silliness to surgery to a very enhanced and appealing experience.

Spore is a great unique game, a hybrid of open-world sandbox, strategy, and creative design. If you are looking for something graphically stunning, this is not it, but I personally think it aged well. Spore has five unque stages: molecular, creature, tribal, civilization, and space. Here's my thoughts on the different stages.
The molecular stage is pretty fun (think pacman open world) and it does not take too long, probably less than a half hour depending how long you take designing your creature as it evolves. The design system is fairly intuitive and very enjoyable, they use the same system for all the creature/building/vehicle design throughout the game. The only thing I would really like is an "airbrush" feature to add or layer color/texture.
The creature stage is like (in a way) a third-person adventure game. In order to survive you must forage/explore, fight, and interact. How much fighting, socializing, or exploring one does depends on the person. I personally spent a long time gathering more dna (the 'currency" needed to add features to a creature) and making allies with lots of different creatures. The design system is the same as the molecular stage but now adds in flying, walking, jumping etc. Eventually, I had maxed out the creature so it wouldn't let me add any more parts :/ The controls for the camera can be a bit klunky but overall not that bad.
The Tribal stage was the stage I disliked the most, although it was still pretty good. You are basically commanding your tribe around to destroy or ally different tribes (all the same type of creature). At the same time, your tribe must evolve what types of weapons/tools it uses. But it is almost like an RTS which involves managing resources, defense, diplomacy, and offense. It loses its savor fairly quickly and for me was a bit of a grind. I enjoyed the resource gathering/tooling of the tribe, but the main goals of socializing and/or fighting were not as fun in comparison to the creature stage. I also didn't like the limitation on tribal buildings, there are (I think) 8 slots to put building but 10 buildings. Really though considering all the many stages and things spore has to offer these are small negatives.
The civilization stage was more of an RTS/city building game. I found it very enjoyable as the building creation process, the goals, and ultimate conquest were simple and fairly intuitive. At first, trying to take over a city with loudspeakers, if your civilization is "religious" seems non-intuitive, but after a while it is fun and makes sense (in some odd way). I especially enjoyed the building/vehicle design as you get to be an "architect" and a auto designer - very awesome!
The space stage is arguably my favorite stage. Terroforming, creating alliances, exploring space and trading are a lot of fun. For me, I thought the "main quest" of dealing with the Grox is kind of annoying. I almost wish there was a way to "turn off" the main quest for a while, as semi-consistent Grox raids are distracting when one is trying to explore and terraform. Before starting this stage I think the player should figure out how they will make money (or spice) in space. There are clearly more valuable commodities of spice and the player should have a plan.
In sum, I think Spore is a great and unique game. As of the writing of this review, this is my third time playing through the game and i have only enjoyed it more every time I have playe it. If you are a creative person and enjoy the open-world sandbox type game this is a must play.
