Moon Hunters is a simple, easy-to-play game about decision making with light roleplaying and combat elements.  A full game can be played solo in 10 minutes to an hour.  Each play through adds to a chronology of characters which are stored for review.
PROS:
The game is rather casual and easy to pick up and put down
Controls are not very demanding
The difficulty is very mild which puts more emphasis on the decision making process that is core to the game
In game references to past characters adds weight and scope to the gameworld in spite of it's short length
CONS:
Multiplayer has some de-sync issues that interrupt gameplay and ruin some of the experience from time to time
Difficulty does not appear to scale much and can become easy to the point of tedium
Character classes are not balanced, some are quite powerful relative to others
The combat portion of the game is quite repetitive
Overall I enjoy the game, but don't expect to get 10+ hours of playtime from it right away unless you really enjoy the completionist nature of the constellation system.  I feel that the game is missing more opportunities for boss style conflicts to add a sense of climax to each 'day' of a playthrough.  The quirky gameplay mechanics, however, are very charming and I hope to see more from this developer

Both the writing and the voice acting (in English, for a change!) are excellent, and well worth your purchase.
The characters are very likable (both those with romance routes and the side characters).
There's a lot of great banter between your character and Nikki, your sister, which helps sell her as "real".  (She doesn't have a route, lest the siscons get too excited.)
There's lots of dialogue choices throughout the game too -- most of them don't really matter in terms of choosing a route but they add more flavour and overall make the game more enjoyable and give it more replay value.
The combat system is a little meh (mostly QTEs) but it doesn't happen often enough to be annoying, and fits in reasonably well with the story.  How well you do in combats does alter the story slightly as well, which can be interesting for repeat playthroughs, but there doesn't seem to be anything major hinging on it.  (Which is a good thing, in my view.)
Romance is handled tastefully; there's no "adult patch" or anything like that.  It doesn't need one, the stories are still amazing.

My Tower, My Home is a third person tower defense game developed by Shoor Games, that mixes a distinctive paper cut-out art style with quick shoot-em-up tower defense gameplay.
The game’s premise is pretty simple: survive waves upon waves of enemies trying to overtake your tower (which is also your home, hence the title) wash, rinse repeat.  Now, under normal circumstances this would be a recipe for a fairly simple game that’s little more than a time waster, but somehow My Tower, My Home ends up as a rather crude execution of the tower defense genre.
The game is varied, yes -- it has all sorts of ways your little silhouetted man can protect your tower from the waves upon waves of enemies that it faces, ranging from turrets, to mines, to shotguns, walls, and other things like that. But while it has a very large quantity of things to do and ways to do them, it just falls flat.
Now, if you’re going by variety of ways to play, with that being all you need in a game in order for you to like it, then you’ll probably find no issue with My Tower, My Home, and will go about your time building interesting little ways to defend the tower. But, the issue lies with the fact that in-game, there’s really not much of an impact with the things that you do, there’s no real sense of progression to it.

The thing that I was most interested about in My Tower, My Home was the combination of an action shooter with a tower defense game. Being a big fan of tower defense games I am always interested in games that try to do something new with the genre. Even though I haven't played the game a ton at this point, I have had fun with the game. The controls work well and if you think the concept sounds interesting, I think you will enjoy the game.
My biggest problem with My Tower, My Home is the difficulty and the fact that you will be replaying the same waves over and over again. While there are quite a few different strategies in the game, some seem to be better than others. Until you find one of these strategies you will die a lot. Being difficult is not necessarily a bad thing but it does force you to keep replaying the same content over and over again as you try to perfect your strategy. If you don't like the idea of playing the same level over and over again, the game may frustrate you.
Overall I had fun with My Tower, My Home. I liked the combination of the 2D action shooter and tower defense genres. If the premise sounds really interesting to you I think you could like My Tower, My Home quite a bit. If you are only curious about the concept though I would probably wait for a sale.
Note: I received a review copy from the developer but received no other compensation for this review.

Red Faction Guerrilla is a free-roaming third person action game set on Mars. This game departs from the FPS genre and while that might offput some (it did for me at first, but I got over it), it does well to distance itself from the failure of Red Faction 2.
Red Faction Guerrilla is one of the few games that I've actually played to completion. I loved the original Red Faction FPS game, can't say the same for RF2 and I was hoping this game would restore the franchise.
In the spirit of the original Red Faction, Red Faction Guerrilla totes a physicals engine that allows for physics based destruction of buildings. Unlike the original Red Faction, this game actually does produce gameplay around this aspect. The building destruction physics is fairly well executed and destroying buildings can be extemely satisfying.
8/10

Brothers is a very pretty game. It is definately charming with its lack of a discernable dialogue and gorgeous graphics that look hand painted at times. The story is 'touching' I suppose, but it's nothing you can't see coming from a mile away.
The control scheme has you controlling one brother with a left analogue stick, and the other with the right. Each trigger controls a contextual action each brother can take, making the controls very simple, but you can get yourself tied in knots trying to control each brother, which is kind of amusing. You'll feel good when pulling off certain tasks in tandem though.
On the downside is the fact that the game is around three and a half hours long, and there is little reason to play again unless you really want those achievements. I think the $15 price tag is ridiculous for such a short experience, good as it is. Pick it up for $5 if you can, $10 if you really enjoy these 'games as art' joints.
Overall I recommend Brothers to everyone, even to family members that you want to try to get into gaming. Barring that though, get it on sale to take the sting off the price.

Oh my... where to start with this game. First off Id like to say that I have read plenty of VN's both from steam and off the platform. I have seen the good, the bad, and the excuse to make a porno versions of VN's. That being said, through all of the stories ive read through, writing that I have critisized and had to re-read , and Listening to my fair share of "interesting" voice acting I have come to one conclusion. This VN is HANDS DOWN the BEST Visual novel I have EVER read/played. The Story itself gripped the MC with intelligent writing, great pop culture refrences (hello ceonardo dilaprio), plenty of moments of teenage hilarity that caught me with my pants down and gave me a good laugh, and in tandem with brillant voice acting it pulled at my heartstrings in both the sad and the warm fuzzy moments. you would look at this game showcasing different girls routes like its a dating sim and it kinda is, however it revolves around the main characters story and the relationships that the player can CHOOSE to develop or not makes it SOOO much better. Now that ive ranted I want to break down what makes this game so good.
First: writing and plotline
Im very impressed with the quality of storytelling in ACE and through my reads the writing was always clear and there were no mispellings or incorrect uses of the english language during any of the parts 1-4. The story made me laugh, feel like a badass during the mech fights, feel warm and fuzzy during the moments you spend with the S.O you have chosen and with the family members that surround the MC throughout the game.
writing gets a 10/10 for adding the choice "swiggity swoogity, im comin for that booty" <-- seems perverted? nope, it makes you laugh and allows the MC to display a more animated personality than whats usually thrown at you.
2nd Visuals and music:
first off the character sprites are all well detailed and each with their own clear persona defined in how they look and act. I found each supporting character to be in sync with how the devs made them look and even when that transferred to how each characters gear was visually designed made it that much more in sync. The music was a nice add on to the game that never got in the way of the gameplay or voice acting. It pumped you up during action scenes, made emotions come out more in both sad and happy moments and overall was just great to listen too.
visuals and music, 10/10
3rd isnt something thats directly part of the game but rather focuses on the people behind it. While this game was in early access the devs of this game set out to put it together in parts of 1-4. I joined in the game when they had just added part 3 a day after I had bought it. going through the news and seeing the release of part 4 I was very happy that these devs were constantly communicating with players through feedback and were very timely with content releases. Oh and another thing about each release, these guys didnt charge any more  money for each new release of content! you buy it at the beginning for the reduced price and you get the full package the second it comes out. This kind of loyalty reward is something that most devs overlook or try to exploit in players who want their games so Im just giving a shoutout to the guys at pixelfade for doing it right!
If you have doubts about this game or wether or not Its truely worth your money Im here to say that you need to stop doubting and just jump in already, your going to love the ride!

This game has so much potential, the art is beautiful, the music is touching, and the dialogue ranges from silly to memorable. But that's where it stops for Moon Hunters and it makes me sad...
The combat is lack luster, it's the same every time, and their new expansion turns it from easy combat that's simple, to annoying combat that's still easy. I've played the expansion already and while a free DLC update is 100% amazing, the DLC doesn't fix the game or anything, if anything it adds more things that break it.
The story is lack luster. While yes the game relies on you as the player to want to live, die, repeat, it takes away from that with a lack of enemies, only a few good endings, "constellations" that act has kind of titles/achievements that aren't meaningful in the slightest, and really even the first 2 days of the 5 DAY STORY. Are ALWAYS the same.
The bugs are crippling. There's so many it's absolutely silly, I've found NPCs with no names, my friends spawn on different maps than me but are still in my games, but all they see is me glitching through rocks and I see them doing the same. Whenever you leave the game or press continue after beating it, the game closes completely. There's a LOT more on the discussions and more I've reported but it gets... so exhausting to report 2 bugs every play through.
The co-op is broken. In more ways than one does the word "Broken" apply to the co-op. For one, having more than 1 person playing this game makes it easy as hell, you breeze through enemies the "bosses" are push overs, it's all too easy. Then there's the glitches that come with it, you get stuck IN eachother, the maps like I said, load in differently so my friend is in the boss room but I'm talking to a trader while another friend is walking up a pathway to a shrine. Whenever you finish areas you all have different quotes, as in for me it may say "The druid was peaceful and helped all who he met" while for my friend it says "Quietly the druid sat under a tree" or something along the lines. Even at the end of the game there's bugs! When you finish the game ALL of your friends have different from what they say, I was "Kid the Fox" but for my friend I was "Kid the Monkey" and my other friend "Kid the silver-tongued" the game has no smooth co-op aspects AT ALL.
So sadly, I can't recommend this game, it's lack luster, it falls flat on what SHOULD be its strengths but makes them burdens. Like I said it has a lot of potential, the music, the art and the characters really help this game stand out, but once you dive in deeper the game ends up being a lot more shallow. It is a very sad feeling and I wish I WISH I didn't feel it, remember just cause this is a negative review doesn't mean I want this game to fail, but I have to warn people of how this game is, it is NOT finished to the standards of a game without the "Early Access" tag on it's store page. It has a lot of work to do, but has the potential to be a great game from a small team. For now, I can't recommend it, but in the future, I may change my mind.

Note: Games for Windows Live (GFWL) is GONE; it has been completely patched out of the game.
Red Faction: Guerrilla is a satisfying mix of an open-world Mars, GTA driving elements, relatively basic shooting mechanics, some unique weapons, and a rather standard rebel-against-the-oppressive-government / corporation story. Recommended for its tough enemies and unique building-destruction mechanics.
Mars is really large, even if it might not look that way on the map. There are no bodies of water, despite the terraforming; it is a dusty, rocky, generally red landscape (as you might expect), but generally well-detailed (if occasionally low-res). Vehicles have some decent variety, and the driving is generally entertaining - which is good, since you'll be doing a lot of it. When not driving, you'll be shooting. The shooting mechanics work well enough (though iron sights are strangely bound to F, while melee is right-click – the reverse of most other games I've played). The weapons themselves, while not as insanely fun to use as those in Red Faction: Armageddon, are still great: the Nano rifle instantly vaporizes ANYTHING (including steel beams), but ammo is limited, so pick your shots. The Grinder shoots throwing stars. The Arc Welder can handle mobs with ease, hitting around 8 or 10 enemies at once with a chained electrical field.
The enemy AI and weapon damage provides plenty of challenge for even the most mundane task. Unless you find and seize an actual tank (which is possible!), you won't be able to “tank” anything. Playing Rambo style will get you killed fast. If you like to camp and shoot enemies, you'll die just as fast; enemy AI flanks quickly, and does a lot of damage, even if you acquired armor upgrades. The best part is the destructible buildings. If there's a sniper on a roof I could (of course) try shooting him from a distance. Or I could just shoot the beams under him, collapsing the building and killing him instantly.
Not everything is completely satisfying. Vehicles are floaty and hard to control. They're manageable during most missions, but challenge changes to annoyance in several of the timed “drive-this-vehicle-back-to-the-safehouse” missions. This would be a minor nit-pick if driving weren't such a large part of the game. Save points don't save your location in the world; they save you to the nearest safe-house. The constant red landscape is cool and all, but it can get visually boring after a while.
Red Faction: Guerrilla is a great game that gives you some trucks, some guns, and tells you to go free the planet from the evil forces controlling it. One of the few games to combine challenging enemies with an open world.
Worth noting is that when THQ went bankrupt, the Red Faction franchise and IP was purchased by Nordic Games. Nordic has undertaken extensive patching in recent months, removing Games For Windows Live (replacing it with Steamworks), adding DirectX 11 support (DX9 mode still exists for those who need it), stability patches, a field-of-view setting, new multiplayer maps, the Reconstructor from Red Faction: Armageddon, and many more. At this time, Nordic is very interested in maintaining this franchise, and with developer Volition saying they'd love to do another Red Faction game, we might not have seen the last game of this franchise.

Americas Army 8/10
Been playing AA off and on from the start and have always loved it. Things that make AA a title I always enjoy.
1. It's free, totally free, always been free, and always will be. It is a recruting tool for the Army of USA, and as such it's paid for by good ol' tax dollars. If you never felt as though your taxes went toward anything fun for you, pick up this game to feel better about it all.
2. Server performance has always been top notch. Not always perfect, but better than most for- profit games.
3. A shooter with class. Team play, good conduct and friendly compitition are always promoted because they wish to instill those values in those they recruit. It shows in the game and I really like it.
4. The survival of the game and the quality of it are not dependant on how well the game is doing at any time. Like all games, populations wax and wane, but in AAs case, if it goes through a lean patch it won't bankrupt the army. The game chugss on.
5. Really good graphics and player control. Climb ladders, slide down them, run and slide, kneel, prone, lean and support position. Fatige effects, good flash bang reaction graphics and a hit position indicator that almost makes up for what you cant "feel".  Even melee and choke outs. Good run pacing, realistic jump and climb. Decent at realistic control of a human laden with heavy gear. I wish you could drag a buddy out of fire, but who knows they may get to it.
6. Many good maps, and a user map editor. C'mon. That's awsome!
7. Not a respawn game. I enjoy it, cause it really makes it important to fight like you mean it. Getting knocked out of a round in the first 20 seconds because you tried to pull a Rambo wiill teach you quick. Buddies can pick you up once unless you have been secured by an enemy player. This makes team play very important, and while not realistic, serves to promote the habit of taking care of each other. Seeing a complete reversal of defeat into a victory is a regular thing and is a great reward for the team that has each others back.
8. A nice community. All the years I have been playing this, one thing stands out. The players are for the most part very quality gamers. I have seldom if ever heard anyone get mad becuase a noob is on thier team and they are loosing because of it. They tell you to hang in there and they have all been there. I really like everyone I have met in the game.
9. Quality control. AA dosnt tollerate ashatery, cheaters or trolls. Seeing how the community isnt paying them, they feel no need to make griefers happy and will ban a cheater no problem. I sort of like the idea of playing a game where messing with the servers is attacking US govenment Army property, and they have the resources to deal with it. There is even a disclaimer warning you when you sign up. I'm the sort of gamer that never cheats, and I like to play with those sorts of people.
10. Everyone is an American soldier, you just percive the other team differently. No need for team stacking or balance issues.
11. It's Americas Army. We're OP bro. Get freedom or get r3kt. It has a solid past and will have a solid future.
12. A really nice authentic military feel all the way around. I never served in the military, so this is a nice little way to vacation there and keep my hair.
Thanks Americas Army for your service and this game. Not only do you fight for my freedom, but you made a fun video game to play free too. That's freedom on top of freedom making love to freedom to birth more freedom.

TL;DR: At only 2 1/2 hours long with frustrating controls, and effectively zero replay value I'd struggle to recommend this game even at the Holiday Sale price.
You play as two brothers (simultaneously) on a quest to find the cure for their dying father by solving a bunch of puzzles and finding the "Water of Life".
The game runs about 2 1/2 hours through a strictly linear story. The puzzles are all incredibly simple, and the only real challenge comes from the controls (and not in a good way). While the concept of controlling both characters at the same time was interesting at first, more often than not I simply found it frustrating. This is compounded by an often less than helpful camera, and unncessarily "picky" trigger areas especially in a number of the jumping sections.
The game seems to be going for more of the artistic and is probably better compared to a movie than other games (puzzle or otherwise). In that regard I will give it points for its visual style which is relatively interesting, and for the most part consistent throughout. Story wise however I feel the game again falls short. I will agree with others that the game does a great job conveying emotion and telling the story, but the trouble is, there's just not much of a story there to be told.
As I said above, you play as two brothers who have set out to find a cure for their dying. There's not much more to be said about it without completely spoiling the ending. The entire "story" happens in the first and last 15 minutes of the game. The other 2 hours consist of (1) meet random person, (2) help person solve puzzle, (3) person points you in direction of Giant Tree containing Water of Life, (4) wash rinse repete, sprinkled with a few reminders that you're playing as brothers who care about eachover.
The ending, which everyone seems to be praising, felt drawn out and contrived. It doesn't really fit with the rest of the game's narative, and just sort of comes out of nowhere. The game slaps you in the face, says "we're ending this way now", and then you spend the last 15 minutes going through the motions to one predicitble outcome after another.

Players must match tokens of the same type in lines of three or more in order to build up the goal meter. You only have twenty moves to do so, and the game gets harder as you complete puzzles, making for a great challenge.
There are eight different types of tokens, four of which are 'normal', four are 'special'. The four 'normal' tokens fill up the meter when matched. Each color (red, orange, green, and blue) has a different strength, which changes per puzzle. Matching stronger tokens fills the meter faster, while matching weaker tokens fills it slower. Sometimes, tokens included in four-token lines will become 'power tokens', and will fill the meter a lot more than normal tokens. The four 'special' tokens all modify certain stats when matched. Pink tokens increase a score multiplier, yellow tokens give you one extra move, cyan tokens give you three 'credits', which will be explained later, and the purple tokens remove a large amount of points from the meter, matching these is detrimental.
On top of all of this, there are special items that you can recieve that, when used, change things about the puzzle, either immediately or gradually. You can have up to six items in a puzzle at a time. Some items consume all tokens of a certain kind, some change tokens into other tokens, some cause more of a certain token to fall, some give special bonusus for matching sertain tokens, some do completely different things. One even nullifies certain side effects of other items. Each item costs a certain amount of 'credits', the amount varying on how effective and useful the item is.

All of this added together makes for rich strategic gameplay, requiring you to plan out your moves, accounting for the random token drops. You must strategize about how you will use your items, what move will benefit the board the most, how you will move a token to shift another into setting up a huge five-token line, how many 'credits' you need to collect to use your items, how to chain matches together, etc, there is so much to think about in this amazingly designed puzzle game. My one complaint about HuniePop is that if a token falls into a four or five-token line match, only three of the tokens will be consumed. This is most likely a result of how tokens engave with each other in the passive state as opposed to the active state of being moved manually. I can forgive this, since the game wasn't designed to be a masterpiece. It was made as a fun casual game that ended up allowing really deep strategy.
HuniePop is an incredible puzzle game experience, and iI implore anyone who is a fan of the puzzle genre, casual or competitive, to check out this gem of a game.
Also, there's explicit female nudity, but that has nothing to do with the core game itself.

I rate the game ARCADE GAME SERIES: Ms. PAC-MAN 3/5. Okay.
If, on your computer, you want to play Ms. Pac-Man EXACTLY as it appeared in the arcade with very few frills or fringe benefits (other than a few steam awards and some fun alternate settings which, incidentally, will prevent you from earning any steam awards if you modify them away from their default paramaters) then this game is for you.
However, even given what it attempts to achieve, this game is far from perfect. The system requirements for this game are stupidly high given what this game allows you to do and it says nothing about whether the game is designed to run on a smart phone (which would be cool if it does). Why does Ms. Pac-Man need 2000 megabytes of RAM? Why does it need at least a 2.3 Ghz processor? These system specs are completely insane for a game of such utter simplicity.
Sure, this game runs fine on my computer but that's entirely missing the point. Ms. Pac-Man should have been designed to run fine on ANY remotely modern electronic device which has any kind of screen and some sort of controls. The fact that the game designers didn't purposefully attempt to reach a far wider audience (all phone users which exist) is baffling and absurd. This version's designers simply weren't ambitious enough and somehow caused this game to have system requirements which were completely undreamt of when this game first came out (the year 1982) and that seems to me to be either a little crazy or very lazy.
I wish this game's requirements simply said "Any electronic device which has any kind of operating system which has been made since the year 1990." That would have been a cool programming achievement to attempt but Nooo! The makers of this version didn't even try to get close to that fairly obvious concept. What's next in the future, a classic version of Ms. Pac-Man that requires two GTX Titans? Or worse still, a quantum computer?

As of this review the game is currently on Ep.3 and let me say its a cliff hanger. Now this is my first time actually engaed in a visual novel, most of my gaming came from playing First.Person.Shooter as a kid, like Halo, or Medal of Honor. The game, story wise is incredable, with its cast of lovable charcters that grow onto you as you progress as a male transfer student to the ACE Academy in Japan.
There is combat during the mech matches (ie. you fight in giant robots "plot of the game"), but in reality its mostly quick time events, and choices that requires you to press an option in about 3 seconds or else it will pick randomly or fail you on it.
Romance is prevelent as theres a total of 4 girls to choose, each with unique personalites and the small decesions you make with them if you want to be friends or more.
Voice acting is great although you may here when the voice acter speaks a little too far or close to the mic giving them an echo effect sometimes, but really its nothing that ruins the game. As for the art its very sleek and clean and has lots of details in it. Although background charcters like workers, gaurds, generic college students and professers are just black cut outs, yet they have voice acters, so they're not just black silhouettes  with nothing to say but text.
As for the story its really engaining with the occasional pop culture refrences to anime tropes, popular animes, memes and movies like the God Father hidden in the dialouge. Each charcter has a hidden past you must pry into as everyone even your self is getting to know each other and part of the game is to interact with everyone but becarful of what you say and risk hurting relationships with others.
Price value is a bit high for a game I just played for 5 hour (till Ep. 3, game is still incompelet at the time of writing this), but its worth it as theres animations, insted of still art charcters, some 3d modeling, and great moments that will make you just laugh.

Before this game, I tended to avoid early access games. However, the premise and visuals swayed my decision and I gave it a shot.
What followed was the most entertaining visual novel I've played.
The story is very sound, with a appealing theme (you attend a school that lets you pilot giant robots. What's not to like?) and plenty of interesting characters to interact with. On those characters; they're very fleshed out and each have their own funny quirks, even if they do tend to follow certain stereotypes (tsundere, shy rich girl, mary sue girl, seductive girl and goofball best friend). But rather than drag the experience down, these characters help make it that much more entertaining. Shou is by a big margin one of the funniest characters I've seen in a VN, and yet despite that even he has a level of depth that helps you fall for these characters.
As far as voice acting is concerned, there were only one or two that could potentially be annoying, yet I found these negligible. Also noticed however that some of the silhouetted characters shared voice actors. I can understand why but it was noticable. The music was good too, and fit the scene, though could get repeditive at times. The art design was pretty cool and, for the mechs at least, improved greatly after episode three. As far as mech battles are concerned, they were nothing more than quicktime WASD segments before becoming timed choice options. While a part of me wishes the battle system could be a little bit more advanced than mere quicktime events (maybe something like from the Sunrider series), it's only a minor complaint, given the mecha combat isn't the main focus of the story.
And as for the story, while it does have choices, the game will eventually steer you back onto the main story path. That said, the options you're given are interesting to discover, leading to a greater replayability than most other VNs I've played. Plus, with four possible love interests (the fourth added after community pleading), it opens story options up even further. While the story did end with much less oomph than what I was expecting, it was still a satisfying ending well worth the wait.
TL;DR
This is a great VN, very entertaining and you'll be replaying it again and again to experience all it has to offer. A few nitpicks here and there, but overall one I'd highly recommend.

A game heavily inspired by System Shock 2, Spirits of Xanadu is an excellent game with lots of small touches that help to make it what it is. The game tells virtually the entire story through audio logs and piece of paper but its able to use those limited sources to create an interesting story that slowly makes sense as you go through the entire space ship. Speaking of the space ship, the Xanadu is a bit small but for a game thats only $10 it does the job, emulating the exploritory nature of the first few decks in SS2. The whole game can be beaten pretty quickly once you know what you're doing instead of just blindly wandering around but the game has enough small easter eggs and minigames that to do everything the game has to do will take probably around 2 hours. While the game's combat is not incredibly deep (only 3 weapons and 4 types of enemies) it is just enough to make the first areas of the game feel tense and recapture the feeling of SS2 and other early survival horror games. The game is interesting and able to capture some of the magic of SS2 while also telling its own unique story though a very organic form.

Okay. I decided I needed to give Red Faction 3 (this game) another chance. I'm loving it. It's like GTA, but it's on Mars and it's fun. You don't really wander aimlessly (as my previous review states) doing odd jobs. You just do mission for the Red Faction. It's fun, challenging, and... just FUN. I can't strees enough that this is like GTA, except it's fun.
I guess my problem with the GTA series has always been the lack of direction. It's TOO sandboxy. I loves me a good sandbox, but GTA just felt like there was no driving plot. No real reason to do one thing over another. RFG has a very central plot. There are some side missions, but it's not a game full of side missions with a plot thrown in that you can follow if you want.
It feels like they took the GTA engine and decided to make an actual game with it. For me, this is even better than Saints Row (another, more blatant GTA clone). That series has some drive, but still no real "story" to be followed.
RFG hits you with action and plot right off the bat, and gets you involved in what's going on in the game setting pretty quickly (if clumsily). The lack of cinematics is almost a blessing. The few in the beginning are just painful to watch.
Like many games on Steam, this one does not work with a gamepad. Let me re-state that. This game doesn't get my usual gamepad complaint, but it's equally non-compliant with how I want to use my gamepad (which is not odd in any way).
I had everything working perfectly (so I thought), until I got into a vehicle for the first time. Suddenly, my look up/down axis inverted and there's no option to fix that. Rather, I already fixed it. I wanted my look up/down axis to be inverted (for some reason, "inverted" means "when I push the control stalk up, my head points up"), so I set it that way immediately. I can switch it back and forth each time I get in/out of a truck, but there's no option to make it be the same in both places.
So I'm stuck with mouse-and-keyboard for this action game. The upside is I can turn very fast; the down side is I can't move slowly.
Some other good things about the control scheme. Both "zoom/aim" and "crouch" can be set to toggle as opposed to hold. Personally, I feel that this is the best way of doing things. There's nothing more complicated than holding down ctrl (to crouch), alt (to walk slow), Z (to aim), S (to walk backward) and A (to walk left). Okay, fine. But it takes a bit of brain power to release the correct key to stop doing just one of those things while continuing to do all the others while tracking targets and avoiding enemy fire. Much better for crouch and aim to be set to toggle instead of hold. Also, reloading automatically stops aiming and sprinting automatically stops crouching. Awesome brain savers.
I do wish "aim" was bound to right-click by default (as in Borderlands) instead of to F, but I understand why they did it that way. And if it really becomes irksome, I can switch my keybinds. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ a console-to-PC port that lets you swap the mother♥♥♥♥ing keybinds. I get that this game is over two years old, but I just wanted to point out how far things have back-slid. Thes console-to-PC port not only has keybind options IN-GAME, but it has mouse-keyboard controls that work properly and don't limit your functionality (Space Marine is absolutely unplayable without a gamepad because of how the mouse-keyboard camera control "works").
So I retroactively give RFG a B-. The fact that I can't use my gamepad is a big deal, but I'm still really enjoying the game.

Red Faction Guerrilla is an amazing game by Volition, and they decided to make a sandbox game as opposed to a linear first person shooter.
What Guerrilla brings to the table is it's primary selling point, it's destruction system. Which is so well implemented I'm extremely surprised it was never really focused on in games since then. The game allows you to destroy literally every building in the game with it's revolutionary destruction mechanic. All the buildings are built with foundations, levels and fall apart due to the strain of gravity. So it takes a great deal of strategy inorder to destroy a building using as minimal resources as possible.
Indeed much of the mission structure and sidequests in the game revolve entirely around the destruction mechanic. Add to that it has an engaging world to explore. Full of little niche references to the original while maintaining a totally different stylistic design. There are of course elements from other games like cars and firefights but it pales in comparison to the well incorporated destruction mechanic. Believe me, once you destroy your first building you will go on an odyssey to return Mars back to a desolate wasteland.
Thankfully RFG has had Games For Windows Live patched out. So now you can play it and it's multiplayer properly. I can't recommend this game enough.

Easily one of the funnest games I have ever played and in my top 3 games of 2009, Red Faction Guerrilla is a masterpiece of destructive fun. Volition just knows how to make a great 3rd person, open world game that is simply enjoyable to play (Saints Row being their other fantastic series). Very few, no seriously, very few games can match the destruction and physics that RF:G has available to the player. You'll need a decent PC even by today's standards to keep the framerate up during some epic facility colapses. Sadly, Games for Windows Live has infested this game and until it is patched out, you cannot save your game. It is a shame that such a great game must be sheltered due to such a failure of a 'feature', but once GFWL is cleansed off this planet, you owe it to yourself and the pleasure centers of your brain to play this game.

First, the obvious out of the way. This is MW remastered and not remade. The campaign is 7 hours, so for people who lament the good old days, they weren't that great either.  The game has all the annoyed bits of a game from the 2000s, with a fresh coat of paint. You will absolutely loath the sound of flinch. Enemies keep spawning and on higher difficulties, they are everywhere seemingly blasting your face with constant full auto even from a distance. Needless to say, you will die...alot. The good parts are great. The famous ghill suit level is still epic. And some fire fights are fun, when enemy squads (NOT whole armies) arrive, deploy and take cover, requiring you to flank.  Its pretty satisfying.  The worst are the timed sequences, that throw seemingly dozens of enemies at the player, while you have to fight your way through. And your squad is beyond useless, because of course, their guns don't insta kill on full auto. So its you against the game. Some may find that fun. It was very intense 10 years ago, now needless to say its a little dated.
I haven't tried multiplayer, but I'm sure its largely dependant on the community, which is probably dead a year after release. Will see.
Overall, its tough to recommend at full price. Best deal is part of the Infinite Warefare full package. But for people looking forward to it, that was a bit of a dik move on part of Activision in 2016.  While not a deal by any stretch of imagination, its a better price. Although, IW is a little older now. It got the whole thing on sale for around $85 cdn, so its not too bad (incl season pass).
If you've never played, and you don't have an old legacy computer to play the old one on, this game is worth a shot on sale. Just don't expect to be blown away, pun intended.

Think of a game like System Shock 2, or Dead Space.   You arrive (or wake up) on a space station, and everything's gone to hell in a handbasket.  Implausibly, you're the only person who can fix it (and/or die trying).    In this instance, you're someone being bussed in from afar to fix a space ship that's broken down and not responding.
To resolve the situation, you will need to run the usual obstacle course:  There'll be security systems, locked doors, roaming androids, broken things to fix, dark sections needing a torch, toilets,  a general plot to uncover,  audio logs, humorous notes, a few little mini-games, and a multi-choice ending.
OK, so you're thinking "about 20 to 30 hours of gameplay".  Yup, that's about average for an older game.  Newer ones tend to be "short and sweet" at about 8 hours, or "money's worth" at about 40.
Well, Spirits of Xanadu takes another path.  It says to you "You know all that running around and doing things?  Well, all those /other/ games make you do it over and over and over again, the same task.  Not me!  You get to do everything once, or only a small number of times (max 3).  That means you get all the core gameplay elements of a AAA space FPS RPG, but in about 2 hours, maybe less.
Indeed, once you know the codes, you can speed run the game in under 7 minutes.  But to get to that level, requires a few playthroughs!
SoX is unusual because it's ultra low-poly.  This game has almost no texture mapping in it, it's just plan low poly models, That makes it feel really old school, but a few shadered glass panels which seem so incongruous.  However it's shockingly badly optimised, so you'll still need a relatively fair graphics card to play it (my laptop can't handle it, but my PC can).     The low-poly reminds me of some older 16-bit 3d games like Cybercon III or Corporation, and the way the game plays is very oldschool too.
I've played this through about half a dozen times to get all the achievements.   There is a LOT of replay value packed into this simple little game.   You can run through and complete the "success" ending, however there are two other endings (one of which you are hinted about while playing, and the other requires a LOT of experimentation, searching and derring-do!)..
There are a lot of nice achievements for doing fun things, and the great thing is that the achievements sometimes act as hints for how to better play the game.
SoX was a great little purchase.  Thanks to Nightdive for bringing it back from the dead.  It's not for everone, but if you like the sort of SS1, SS2, DS1, DS2, type games, but want sometime a lot simpler, and a lot faster, then grab this and have a play.

Nightdive let me down with this one, They tried to make something akin to their rehash of systemshock and failed horribly. They left us with a game that looks like it was put together in one afternoon with some basic/hacky entry level unity code.
Interesting concept for a plot, but even Marathon did it better back in the 90s.

The obvious inspiration for Spirits of Xanadu is System Shock 2 - you have a variety of weapons in an FPS style, you're stuck on a lonely space station, crazed robots are after you, you find audio logs, piece together a story, it's spooky but not too spooky, and get the place up and running in order to complete your mission.  It's on the short side but there isn't much filler at all, and the weird moments remain weird and interesting (there are multiple endings, too).
The layout of the ship is a little goofy at times, and some enemies tend to be a little annoying, but it's a solid few hours of entertainment if you like the style.  Voice acting was surprisingly solid for an indie game, and there are a lot of little details that make exploring worthwhile.
This one's a hidden gem.

Unless you're getting this game very, very cheaply ($2 and below), don't buy it.
Exploring the vessel is interesting and that's about it. There's only two actual puzzles, if they can be called that, concerning turning generators on by adding certain amounts of voltage without going too high or too low, and putting a tank of liquid nitrogen into a cryosleep tube. That's it. Everything else hinges around searching the ship to find pages and audio logs.
Combat is very unsatisfying. You get a charge pistol, and if you can find either, a submachine gun and shotgun. No resource management or reloading, just keep clicking until stuff explodes. Enemies are basic and uninteresting. It's kind of like Receiver except without any of the things that make Receiver fun and interesting.
The game gives you no direction at all, which is a good thing, and though the ship is laid out well and you'll naturally drift from one part to the other as you bring the ship's systems up one by one, it's ultimately pretty small. There's absolutely zero replayability value. The endings are unsatisfying and uninteresting, offering you no answers or explanations to the events preceding your arrival.
The story is paper thin and pretty much EXACTLY as it's laid out in the trailer. There's nothing more to it than that.
This is a game that gives you an hour or two of playable content, with no replay value and no staying power. It does some things well, namely just giving you a situation and letting you explore it at will, but the only appeal to the game is its mystery. Going in blind is the only way to enjoy it.
If you really, really want a brief sci-fi experience that has you unravelling an (admittedly shallow) mystery and exploring a derelict space ship, then buy this game. Ideally, buy it for $2, maybe $3. If you want anything more than that, and any kind of staying power out of this game, then don't buy it.

Defiance feels like the ultimate tourist MMO.
It starts out with seeing the show on TV with the built in commercials.  "Hey, that place looks shiny and neat!  Looks fun, we should visit!"
Then you buy your tickets, take the flight and arrive.  You wander gawking at everything with wide innocent eyes, having zero clue what the hell is going on, but man it looks cool!
After a while, you get tired of sightseeing, so you suck it up and decide to dip your toe into the pool, test the waters.  You grab what looks like a quest, studying the map for a minute, make a vague guess as to where you're supposed to go.  You hope on your rented ATV and head out across the country side.
As you're riding, you run into what you think are locals.  They're mean and grumpy; they call you names and are zero help.
You put up with the angry locals for a day or two as you try and find your way around.  Eventually, you *think* you have a general idea of how the quest system works; you how know how to get to one or two key locations in town.  You know how to avoid the dangerous locals; you stick to the mildly annoying ones.  How you're having some fun getting into minor fire fights, picking up bits and pieces of armor and weapons as souvenirs.  You're amused, you're satisfied.
Next thing you know, a week has passed.  You're bored with going back and forth to town and the sections you're familiar with.  Branching out to new areas feels like too much work.  It's been a week; you've had your fun.  Vacations over, time to go home.
You uninstall, move on to the next game and tell your friends, "eh, that games was all right for $5", and now you feel more connected to Julie Benz every week when you watch the show because "You've been there".
And that's all right!

If the pieces match the interest of your partner, it gives more affection needed to complete the date.
Along the way the girls send you pictures (three picture messages per a girl). Two quite normal pictures and then they usually send a naughty/teasing picture. The final picture comes after the 4th date (or any date after) if it's completed during the night. Completing that date will lead into a so called "bedroom stage" which basically equals having sex.
In this mode you have unlimited moves and there are no Broken Heart tokens (during a normal date, matching these would lessen your Affection points). After completing the stage, the picture is basically just an after picture of the act. Usually it's just them topless (if playing as a male character they're covered in your liquids as well).
These things you mostly pick up during the game, but overall the game is like a f**ked up dating simulator.
You ask girls the things you should never ask in real life, for example their:
Age, weight and cup size
The game itself is fairly well known, because most of the people play it with only their left hand (the right hand is busy doing something else...)
However, while it does have its own entertaining side in it's pornography, it still is an extremely entertaining game.
I totally recommend it... for both of these reasons...

My advice, if you want this game, buy it when it's on sale for at least 50% off.

Fantastic, atmospheric, short indie game with a slight nod towards System Shock and Deus Ex. Take a slow pace, explore, learn to figure things out for yourself and you'll have a good time. Rushing around doesn't work well and there is minimal (if any) handholding.
You could easily finish this in one sitting, but collecting everything and getting all endings will take some time. Pay attention to what you read, the audio logs you listen to and the visual feedback the game gives you. The voice recordings and music are superb. The graphics are basic but work well for the 80's inspired sci-fi environment, plus you can alter things like bloom and film grain.

Don't be deceived by the basic graphics, as the game is eerie and gets quite creepy.
Recommended.

BLUFF:  For me to consider a game worth it, I need to get at least 1 hour per $1 spent on it.  This is a buy it on sale game.
Not a huge hurdle, but one that this game only achieved because I bought it on sale.  All achievements unlocked in 5.4 hours of gameplay, and that included cooking dinner with it paused.  Four playthroughs, one of which was well under 10 minutes for the speedrun.
I'd rate this as a scavanger hunt game with mild, mild combat.  More than that, there is little replayability once you have achieved everything because, well, the ship is static, nothing varies over time except for maybe randomly generated robots.  The ship's layout and item locations is always the same, and I've seen bigger ships in various construction games.  There are some hidden objects, which I will admit I got lucky finding as easily as I did.  Another scavanger hunt on a ship game I've played recently does it much better.  The ship is far larger, the enemy smarter, and the ship and item locations are random each playthrough.
If you can pick it up for a buck or so, it's worth it as a sort of interactive mystery.   But I wouldn't pay full price for it, sorry.
Recommended, but only on sale.

I can't really complain for the price, but I still think this is very far from what I might consider to be a "complete game." There is nothing wrong with a short game, but this one lacks a lot of substance, the story doesn't really feel real to me and I don't have a chance to identify with any of the characters, despite the audio logs sprinkled around the map.
I also draw issue with the gameplay itself, as it seems to be caught somewhere between attempting to have gameplay, and wanting to tell a story. There is no downside to dying, and the combat is minimal at best, so I don't really see the need for it. On the other hand, the game wouldn't be worse if a more elaborate combat mechanic was added.
I think the world is somewhat charming (though I could do without the setting being in the 1980s for virtually no reason other than it seems to be the trend lately) and the bones of something a bit more engaging are here, but for the time being I cannot really recommend this game.

text:
A two word review of this game might read, "surprsingly strong."
At the end of the day anime-style dating sims (and I say this as a fan of the genre) are generally bite-sized snacks of games that favor pretty picturs over deep and fascinating gameplay or any sort of complex storytelling. Huniepop strikes a stunning blow against the tired cannard that games with anime♥♥♥♥♥♥can't also be engaging on other levels of game design as well.
The chief challenge in Huniepop is the date puzzles that you need to complete. These take place on a 9X9 (?) grid filled with different types of tokens. You have 20 moves with which to fill up the affection meter, which is fueled by succesful token matches. Other types of token matches give you a resource you can use to deploy items for a boost, and another makes token matches give you more points.
Huniepop may call itself a token matching game but the resource management aspects, the items, and the move limit give it much more of a hook than just "match the colors." And as the game grows progressively more challenging you'll have to optimize your item loadout and plan your moves in advance to really succeed.
One thing that may frustrate is that there is an element of luck to which tokens you get on the grid. Sometimes you'll make a match and the game will thrown down the ideal tokens to make your affection score explode. And on other dates you'll struggle futilely against a grid that has grown cold and distant and fat, and threatens to take away the kids.
That being said I only very rarely felt like luck wasn't on my side. For 99% of dates if you just take your time and really look around you'll begin to see good options.
Gameplay aside, for me this game's most compelling attribute was also the one I expected to be the weakest. Namely the characters. Don't get me wrong the story in Huniepop is mere window dressing, the dramatic stakes never get higher than simply "you need to get laid."
But in spite of that each girl has a unique and believeable personality (the latter attribute having 4 obvious exceptions) that make them entertaining to talk to and observe. And the way this information is conveyed is really quite elegant. To illustrate my point I'll give a slight spoiler.
****
One girl you pursue is Tiffany, a vivacious and hardworking college student. She's a regular all-American, a sweetheart cheerleader in a schoolgirl outfit who's ready to study her cute little butt off. And while she's no prude Tiffany gives every indication that she is loyal and commited to the player once they enter a relationship.
So far so good but what really made me regard her more deeply is her off-screen relationship with another girl you date, her mother Jessie.
Jessie is a porn star who gave birth to Tiffany at a young age. And even though she seems to have done a good job getting her daughter into college and instilling in her a solid work ethic, Tiffany wants nothing to do with her. It is deeply ironic that the porn star would value family far more than the supposedly goody two-shoes schoolgirl and yet here we are.
And what's especially neat about this little wrinkle of characterization is that it isn't thrown in the player's face. You have to suss it out through the snatches of dialogue you get from talking to the girls. Granted you don't have to be Sherlock Holmes to make the connection but it is nice to be given a bit of legwork to do. Especially in a genre that seems to always revert to clicking through text boxes that bare all.
***
It's my hope that in whatever project the devs decide to tackle next they will build on the foundation of Huniepop's storytelling style while upping the dramatic ante. It may not be innappropriate for them to consider adding some visual novel aspects to what is currently a dating simulator♥♥♥♥♥puzzle game.

This game surely is quite an interestingly executed old concept used in Snake and idea-sakes, with the only difference it's actually you playing as an apple, only either to escape or to be eaten by a snake (or, like, two snakes, differs from level to level).

Guys have also added the "snake mode", which is a regular Snake game, with the addition of those pesky running apples and teleports they use to evade you.
The only thing that kind of disturbed me a little is roughness of the interface, but that's rather my point of view (I would have executed it a little bit different) and this won't really take your attention away from good-quality gameplay and the sounds of the Apple, which, as someone has already pointed out, begins to feel a little prick really quick.

I want to begin with noting the length of the game.  This game could easily be completed in fifteen minutes up to an hour if you want to find everything on a blind run.  That being said let's being.
In Spirits of Xanadu you control a nameless female space detective on a mission to investigate what happened to the crew of four on the space vessel 'Xanadu'. While on the ship, everything is done in the 1st person perspective almost in the exact way as System Shock. You get two weapons, you figure puzzles to turn on computers, get passcodes to doors, etc.  All the while you shoot at, hack, or escape robots which try to kill you.  Without revealing too much more I'll leave it at that and say it's an eerie and welcome experience for so cheap.
Get it if it's under $10.  It'll get your System Shock urges down until the real deal releases from this very same company later in the year.

If there's a subgenre of games called "stuck alone on a space ship", then Spirits of Xanadu would be in it. You began the game docking with the Xanadu, a ship that's gone silent, contracted by a company that wants its valuable investment back. As soon as you touch down, all the lights go out. Good job you brought a flashlight, because you're going to need it - for a while at least. The first thing you'll find upon exiting your ship is a hand gun. It's probably no surprise, then, that you can expect some resistance. This isn't a particularly difficult game, and death is... well, it's not the end.
If Spirits of Xanadu reminds you a little of System Shock 2, let's just say it's probably not unintentional. There are nods all over the place to that game, from the design of some of the enemies, the consequences of dying, the audio logs scattered around, and even a functional basketball court. It even sports a similar low-poly, angular look, but this is no sprawling FPS / RPG hybrid. It's a much smaller game with very modest ambitions. Your goals, as you'll quickly discover, are to get the ship functional again, and secondarily to find out what happened to the crew. This latter component actually turns out to be more compelling, and while the tale that's told isn't particulary original, it's told well and effectively through scraps of evidence, notes scrawled on white boards, emails and audio logs. The way you complete the game (there is more than one ending) will depend on it.
It's not a long game, although you can add an hour or two of replay time for alternative endings. If it wasn't for my backlog I'd be almost tempted. The game also has an optional "peaceful mode" which deactivates all enemies, allowing you to simply explore, fix the ship and figure out what's going on. This takes away a certain degree of tension, especially considering the respawning enemies, but I can see the appeal. The respawning mechanic is fairly mild, but it does keep you on your toes. Overall I enjoyed Spirits of Xanadu. It doesn't quite have the oppressive atmosphere of some other "stuck on a space ship" entries, but it's a solid little game.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
SnakEscape is cute and colourful casual turn-based puzzle game in which you control an apple that has to collect stars before making its way to the glowing golden exit on each level, usually avoiding hungry snakes along the way. I think I got that right.
Graphics - Graphics are colourful, blocky, and cute. Your green apple (a Granny Smith?) is well animated and portrays expressions well: either general happiness or fear, depending on how close he is to being eaten by snakes. The snakes are less animated, and just move around the level with blank expressions on their snakey faces, but they're still well animated and cute.
Each level is shown as a series of floating connected squares, usually with a few platforms populated with blocky scenery. It's a tried-and-true formula and it's done well here, with the platforms slowly bobbing up and down and small animations adding a bit of life to the cartoon-like scenery.
Menus are easy to navigate, if a tiny bit slow, and include large colourful buttons. They're easy to navigate and look good.
There are no graphics options to speak of -- just the normal Unity detail level and resolution settings -- but the game looks nice and runs without issues on my old gaming laptop, so anyone with reasonable hardware bought in the last five years should have no problem with it.
Sound - The music is a mix of ambient and electronic beats and is quite pleasant. The credits don't disclose it as being taken from anywhere so I suspect it's original, in which case I'm impressed.
Sound effects are minimal, but sufficient. Your apple makes some cute, worried sounds when the snakes get too close, and there's a Pacman-like 'wubwubwubwub' when you fail a level, which seems fitting.
Gameplay - SnakEscape is played through a series of isolated levels in which you must manoeuvre your apple towards the glowing golden exit square, avoiding snakes, dodging around obstacles, and (hopefully) collecting three stars along your way.
You control your apple either with the WASD or arrow keys, or by using the mouse to rotate the screen until a little transparent apple marker appears on the square next to you in the direction you want to move, and then left clicking. Rotating the screen with the mouse is a bit slow and to me seems to rotate backwards with the default settings, but you can change it from the options and after that it's fine. You can also zoom in and out with the mouse wheel, or toggle an overhead view with the X key, to help you navigate around obstacles.
In typical puzzle game fashion there are plenty of levels (four 'worlds' of 15 each, I think), and you unlock each level in each world by completing the previous levels or earning a sufficient number of stars. It's a completely unoriginal progression system, but that's fine; it's easy to understand and it allows you to move on to new levels even when you're having trouble getting a perfect three-star score, although new levels require enough stars to unlock that it's easy to become stuck on a handful of levels quite early on.
Oh, and I've given an extra plus because each level has a name, which I like. They're not as amusing or crazy as Jeff Minter's classic Mutant Camel level names, but it's still a good tradition to uphold.
Pros:
+ Pleasant music
+ Colourful, cute graphics, with well-presented levels and nice animation touches
+ Each level has a name
+ Steam achievements and trading cards
Cons:
- There are some minor errors in some of the level names and other game text
- Gets very repetitive
- Hard! Difficulty ramps up quickly and you need a lot of stars to unlock later levels.
- Snakes don't eat apples!
SnakEscape is a nice simple casual puzzle game. It's cute and colourful and looks professional for the most part. It's no contender for game of the year, but it's not trying to be either. Pick it up for a bit of puzzling every now and then.

However it's too bad that Spore is actually another piece of crap that generates frustration!
It crashes. At first it wasn't such a big problem. The game would crash once every 2 or 3 hours. I found that to be bearable, but I attempted to start it today and it crashed 5 times in a matter of minutes. I hate it when companies publish games with crippling bugs like this. I am considering asking for a refund then downloading a pirated version. That would be fair since I paid for a product that I can't USE and the EA support page is of no help, as expected.

UPDATE: Came back to edit this review since the amount of frustration this game generated me is insane!
I did manage to work around the crashes. I noticed that once you get to the final stage, the game is pretty stable, but of course, something else had to be wrong, because games that you can enjoy from start to finish are simply put insanely rare.
Whoever designed the final mission is a complete retard! It's the classic difficulty spike that ruins a what would otherwise be a great game (if you don't count in the bugs). Basically you have to play the crap out of it and get lucky in order to make it to the end. To me, this type of thing ruins the entire game. I never could understand this BS in gaming. "It's the last boss fight, therefore we must make it as difficult as possible." The result? You are playing because you are invested in the game, you want to see the ending, without using cheats, but you are not enjoying it. It all turns into an unpleasant task because of the stupid decisions that the idiots working on this game took when designing it. I had tons of fun, but it all balances out in frustration at the end of the game.
I'm playing on easy and it's still next to impossible to finish the last stage. It's not just me either. People complain about the same thing on the forums.
So to sum it up, Spore can offer a great experience, if you don't mind the constant crashes and the fact that you are not going to be able to finish it without serious dedication and frustration.

The Xanadu has gone silent, and it's your job to wake her up, and bring her back home to earth.

You may ask why the graphics seem dated...
This game takes place in an alternate 1980s where man is already visiting other planets, so I think the developer was trying to get the graphics to reflect that.
I personally feel this was not necessary. Did they dumb down the movie Watchmen? No.
I also felt that the puzzles were either direct and to the point, or very vague in what was needed to figure them out.
The battles with the robots got old quick, as they became obvious in their patterns.
The gameplay and controls are very simple, and solid, that anyone can play with no issues.

This is literally the most underated gem on steam! It's like a mix of System Shock 2 and Alien with a mix of easter eggs. It isn't particularly scary, but it had a very eerie atmosphere, and a great narrative story with no hand holding. It's the sort of game where you have to work out what's going on yourself, not press 'tab' to see what your goal is, you have to do it yourself.

I don't really think I would class this game as horror, although it does have very slight psychological horror elements in the story telling.
But that aside the game is mechanically competent, the graphics are decent and the price is good. Also worth mentioning is the voice acting delivered via audio logs, which is excellent throughout. The gunplay is functional, but its not really the core of the game so I don't hold that against it. Also the puzzle elements are pretty light, and nothing too taxing.
Biggest gripe is how short the game can be - once you know what to do, and where to go you can speed run it in less than ten minutes. However if yuor willing to explore, read the documents and listen too the audio you can make the first play through last a couple of hours.
However with three endings to get, plenty of secrets and easter eggs to find I feel this game is worth the asking price overall.
It's a great game in the spirit(pun) of the System Shock kind of game. If you don't mind the simple graphic then you will have a great time. Okey now i have to get back to play the game :)

I didn't know what to expect out of this game, (especially when I found out recently it had a KickStarter project under the name of Kendo Crush) but I decided to give it a try because it was part of an anime-centric sale. I like to say it was a good investment for Ace Academy held my attention by the end of the demo.
Rarely do you get a fully english Visual Novel, and it feels a bit more interesting to me than a regular japanese subbed one. It probably helps that all the characters are well voiced and that you can hear how well they suit their characters. Like Shou Shinjirou, the male best friend. If I didn't know better, I'd say he sounded like Yuri Lowenthall (particularly Yosuke from Persona 4). And it feels fun to hang out with him despite the obvious dating sim with other girls, if only because he seems to have his own romance subplot that you can either help out in or watch from the distance as he remains oblivious.
In fact, the whole slice-of-life story is quite enjoyable with all the characters. You have the cute but at times annoying younger sister, the laid back uncle, and the kind and popular ace Ace pilot. And then you have a bunch of girls that you can date; there's the mean captain with a soft side, a smart and shy support with an obvious crush on Shou, the shameless flirt of an engineer, a kind stickler to the rules manager, and possibly a friendly rival to the captain but with bad history. As vague as those descriptions are, that's the gist of the cast.
It's actually hard for me to pick which one girl to follow at first, because they're all likeable in their own way. They have layers to them that only through extended hang-out sessions can you see and also realize in how to nurture your friendship with them. Of course, I might have cheated because there's a "rollback" system, or at least being able to load to an earlier save or autosave file before picking a different option.
And the music is top notch. The instrumental version of the trailer song as you load it up is very catchy and seems to capture the general feel of the game. Upbeat and awesome.
Of course, I wish the game would make some changes for the full release. While the slice-of-life aspects are fun, I have little to no understanding of the world lore, despite the little sprinkled in class scenes talking about Gears. Gears are a big deal in the world; there are even movies and TV shows that are like ours but have the world Gear in them; That 70's Gear, The Gear of Thrones, The Lord of the Gears...
We hear so much about Gears on a technical scale from their tools to their weapons, including the safe "recreational" ones. And yet at the same time don't know a thing. They're a common thing in this world, have their own toy line, and yet there doesn't seem to be any sort of big scale robot war with them. Why do college students have to fight each other? Why are there sponsors for so many pilot teams? What's the benefit of being a Gear Pilot? What do Gear Pilots do when they graduate? It's not like we have Gears of our own in our world so it would help to get some context. It can't be exactly as the same as running tanks or planes because we don't use those to beat the snot out of each other.
And what's more, I like to agree with the general consensus that the fast reaction time keys of WASD is kind of bland for what I'd expect in a visual novel with actual gameplay. For the first few matches I wasn't even sure if I was doing something right because there were two points where the gameplay elements screwed with you; first was when you had no weapons and could only dodge and block as your HP dwindled down and your enemy was completely fine (not to mention you couldn't even choose the action; it was automatic after pressing the button indicated). Then there was a match where you DID have weapons, but you got your scrap♥♥♥♥♥kicked anyway because the weapons weren't calibrated. I thought it was another mistake based on the weapons I could choose (and you only get to choose once in this Early Access, between three sets of guns and three sets of swords).
They were all story-based defeats that meant to drive the plot a bit more, but I thought I was actually doing something wrong. There was little to no explanation in how to fight other that "use the weapons at the right time". But you don't get to chose to go all sword akimbo because the 4 button commands change it every time. You have no control of your protagonist's Gear so it feels less like a cool robot fight and more like a game of slap the coin before your opponent does.
My suggestion is that if there is going to be fighting that incorporates the swords, guns, thrusters and shields, let the player make their own choices. Make into rock-paper-scissors, kind of like Fate/EXTRA. There are four buttons, so each one can make a command. Gun beats Sword, Sword beats Thrusters, and Thrusters beats Gun, with the Shield command as an all purpose guard. You still take damage, but not as much as if you got hit with the wrong counter.
Still, I was hooked until the end of the 3rd Episode; where it literally ended on a rather tense cliffhanger. Up until then, there wasn't any sense of drama or tension aside from school related problems, and most of those were easily resolved in time. But I think after all the build-up and introduction that there might be a change in the story, as well as an answer to most of the question I listed here.
Ace Academy is a very fun game. I would have kept playing until the end and/or got bored if possible. I'm not sure if I can recommend this to anyone, but I certainly enjoyed running at least 5 and a half hours in it. It sounds short, but with a lot of choices to build your camaraderie and possible love interest, as well as some hidden choices depending if you picked a strong, smart, or charasmatic build when you start the game, it has the potential to go on even longer by the time it goes full access. I personally can't wait to play more of this game/

You might look at this game and think it's some kind of odd piece of pornography, but actually in essence it's a very polished combination of a bejeweled like puzzle game and a dating sim (the latter being something similar to the kind of dating mechanics you'd find in something like Harvest Moon, where you have to respond to certain prompts in the correct way to earn more "hearts" and ultimately get a woman in bed). The "porn" aspect is just the aesthetic style of what is quite a well constructed game overall.
What you notice about it after a while is that a huge amount of effort has gone into making the mechanics balanced. In fact I found it a little off putting once I noticed that - the game is almost rigged in a certain way to make it so that it's always beatable but never easy. Each move in the "bejeweled" part of the game will shape the next tiles that become available, the food you have to buy girls to talk to them exists so that you can't just grind your way to huge numbers of level-up points by asking one girl the same questions all the time, and so on. It's quite clever when you start to appreciate how it works - the mark of some fairly mature game design (rather than the sort of amateurish effort you might be expecting if you think this is just going to be cheap tittilation).
Overall I bought this out of sleazy curiousity, but came out of it admiring the game design more than anything else.

There will be spoiler in this review.
The game has lovely art and a good concept. That's where the good ended for me unfortunately. I took me longer to complete it than most because I completed it 100% but I was also complaining to my friends while I did it. The characters and the story lack depth. There are holes. The choices don't matter. At the beginning the writing almost sounds like the MC looks down on the people who live in that rural area with her, making her sound pretentious. (In big part due to the particular wording that's rampant across this game.)
The MC is made out to be intelligent, yet I found myself incessantly baffled by her choices. You've been taking the train for
long, and you're seriously questioning that you just never noticed this stop that it never stopped at? Yeah sure, let's walk into a spider demon's house for tea.
And this was right after I was so proud that she finally have a reasonable response upon finding out a strange man kidnapped her by running away.
The game makes her go through trials to get back home, but the trials all feel worthless. The MC doesn't actually learn anything new or change and grow as a person. She is pretty much the same as she started. What was even the point other than busy work and making friends with all these yokai? Yokai, which by the way, are known to be tricksters and demons/monsters/spirits but are ever only makes strides to be her friend. It felt like yokai were used as a flavor different from human than actually taking to heart that these are non-human creatures.
I never understood why the train was going to stop running, either. Is
in that rural area ever interested in going to the city? They're just cutting contact entirely? Do they all just drive when they get old enough? I have no idea.
It's a shame the art is fantastic and the idea for it is so promising. Rather than explore and develop this game, instead if feels like they just wanted it over and done with and released the most basic game they found acceptable and called it done. It also frustrated me that sometimes the dialogue box just up and covers the entire screen even though the text never warrants it. Why? The backgrounds are beautiful and you're covering it with this thin layer instead of letting it shine.
It's a shame because I really enjoyed Forgotten, Not Lost. I don't know what changed between the two games, but hopefully their upcoming game A More Beautiful World doesn't retain the same problem.
TL;DR I pretty much went through the entire game mystified with the permanent question of
Characters and story lack depth and the things the writing claims doesn't match the behavior of the MC.
