The legacy of System Shock lives on in Spirits of Xanadu.
It would be very difficult to deny the influence of the landmark PC classic (as well as the film Alien) as you timidly explore the tense, creepy corrodors of the Xanadu, attempting to repair the ship and discover what happened to the missing crew via emails and audio logs.
The minimalist texture pallett on offer might make this look like an asset-flip on first glance but it is often a beautiful, haunting experience, capable of some stunning visuals.
While the combat is a bit on the easy side and you'll soon run out of enemies to block your path, the feeling of isolation and terror lurking around every corner and watching from the shadows never leaves you; it's a fantastically atmospheric game. It's even more amazing when you consider it was made by just two people and knows more about horror than the entire towns' worth of staff wrking on the last Resident Evil!
Spirits of Zanadu is short but you certainly get your money's worth. It comes off as a passion project and you can tell that the developers put their all into it. Night Dive Studios (fast becomming my favourite developer/publisher) as well as Allen Trivette & Lee Williams have done a fantastic job.

I was quite looking forward to this game, as I love a good Sci-fi game setting. The concept sounded good, some good reviews also helped sway my decision to purchase the game, however I think my mistake was probably playing Alien Isolation before playing this game.
Both these games have a very similar storyline, both set in space and on an abandoned space station where strange things have happened (we'll say no more to avoid spoiling it for anyone}, and of course we go in by ourselves to find out whats been going on. On paper the story is sound but in practise the Spirits of Xanadu left me feeling like I was back in the 1990s. The visual style can be forgiven somewhat, as I was fairly prepared for that after seeing the video on the store page. What I didn't expect to find is a virtually non-existant learning curve when it comes dealing with the kamikaze style robots onboard who immediately start shooting at you almost as soon as you set foot on the station. You have a weapon of course too which comes in pretty damn handy straight away, not like in Alien Isolation where you picked up weapons over time, but at least in that game you didn't have quite a much to deal with from the start, and you were very capable of sneaking past the enemy and avoiding any combat.
In Spirits of Xanadu however it was almost a regular occurrance, and one that is immediately so frustrating that for me anyway I decided it was too much too soon, and gave up. It seemed like gaming had taken a gigantic step backwards in terms of playability.
I can appreciate that combat in games like these is a necessary requirement, but when there is very little (or not at all in this case) learning curve to ease you into a particularly simple and dare I say it 'old style' of shooting game, reminiscent of playing Doom many years ago, just with plainer graphics and simpler but just as deadlier A.I.
Yes I am over 40 and have played many games of this kind before, but frankly this game needs a lot more work to become a more enjoyable gaming experience.

This isn't a terrible game, though it did irritate me a couple of times across the 3+ hours I spent with it - once again I wish there was a "whatever" or "neutral" choice, rather than just thumbs up or down.  Deadwood is simple and direct, without the customary frills of Hidden Object Games right now - no map, no penalty for loose clicking, no achievements; just a very basic game and a hint button that seems intended to be pressed freely, and often.  Also no collectibles, so I'm not sure in what way this is a Collector's Edition.  /shrugs
What others say is true: some of the objects are exceptionally hard to click on - there's one pair of scissors that led me in particular on a merry chase, more than once too, and an errant hourglass and a few other objects were also quite hard to get.  And there's a lot of go-try-it-again play, going back to search in locations already visited.  As the cursor doesn't spontaneously indicate active areas, this involves a lot of random clicking.  Overall it's a quick and tidy experience, in which I rarely felt I had enough information to avoid leaning on hints for the next step forward.  I put this on top of there why?  Just because?  Well, whatever.  Sound was a bit muddled, but that may have been my aging box.
There's some good variety in the approach to hidden object scenes: sometimes outlines, sometimes descriptions, and other times just a dozen or so objects of a type.  The assets themselves are used more than once, without regard to context, so there are ballet slippers in the crypt and also in the library (just an example, I don't recall if the slippers are in those actual locations).  That always bugs me some.  Deadwood may work best as a beginner's game for a precocious kid to play; as a HOG fan, I found it a little bland and arbitrary.

Grand Theft Auto: Mars is one of those games you hear a lot of good things about, then when you finally play it for yourself it leaves an odd taste in your mouth.  It has some good points and bad, and the result feels rather mediocre to me.
The thing that this game does best is the destruction.  After all, that's what Red Faction is known for so it better be good.  It's a much more dynamic system than a game like Battlefield 3, allowing you to take out building supports and even collapse upper floors of multistory buildings to collapse the lower floors.  It's also a hell of a lot more fun than the chaos system in Just Cause 2 since you do more than shoot fuel tanks and throw grenades at satellite dishes.  Nearly everything is destructible and it's great fun running around destroying things.  Strangely though, hitting just about anything with a sledgehammer, even foot-thick metal barricades, causes them to splinter into pieces.  There are various explosives you can use as well, but their limited ammunition, even with upgrades, makes them of limited use.  Sometimes the best choice is to hijack a heavy APC, since those drive through buildings like there's nothing there.
Driving works pretty well as well, though cars can be difficult to control in the low Mars gravity.  The vehicles themselves are rather unique, taking cues from various rover designs used by Nasa with some Volition style added.  You can find some really cool ones, though they pretty much all function the same.  Many vehicles have mounted weapons which auto-aim at enemies to help your destruction sprees.
As for bad things, I found the alert system to be astonishingly annoying throughout the game.  The main way to advance through the game is to destroy EDF structures and do other missions that♥♥♥♥♥♥the EDF off.  When your alert level has raised up, they will constantly spawn near you with 10+ enemies shooting at you at all times, and they kill you very fast, even on normal difficulty.  This results on you being teleported a long distance to a safehouse and having to drive back to resume your task.  Dying during a mission seems to be completely random whether there's a checkpoint to retry from or whether you will have to restart the entire mission.  You will be doing that a lot.
With this in mind, I found many of the side missions were designed to be quite annoying or very tedious.  There are vehicle recovery missions where you have to return a vehicle to a safe house.  The game always chooses one 2 sectors away so it takes you 4 or 5 minutes to drive there.  Other missions will put you at a ridiculous disadvantage such as requiring you to destroy 30 enemy vehicles on foot without dying.  I found these side missions so annoying that I just skipped as many as possible.
The story is decent, though not terribly well presented.  It is advanced through short story mission briefings and a couple cutscenes with reasonable voice acting.  It's broken up into very rigid sections, where you progress through each sector of the map in sequence.  I never really got a feel for the characters which is unfortunate because they could have been done a lot better.
Overall, while running around destroying things is fun, I feel like the rest of the game falls a bit flat.  It's fun, but the frustrating parts really get in the way.

I have found this program/software to be, in one word, brilliant. I am using an Xbox One controller, with a Microsoft ‘Chatpad’, connected via an Xbox USB wireless adapter to a Windows 10 computer.
I’m pretty sure that the Chatpad is detected by ‘plug and play’ on start up as a normal keyboard would be. I personally find it easier to type quickly and it allows me to login using the controller. Controller Companion’s onscreen swirl keyboard is not affected and is still fully functional.
When the controller is turned on it will automatically connect to the software, as long as the software is running (mine is set to run on start-up and has had no issues what so ever). When you turn off you system it will turn off the controller for you which is awesome because I nearly always forget (flat batteries are no fun).
Something that sets this apart from the freeware I was using before is that controller companion will turn off the key bindings when it detects a full screen program. This means if you jump in to a game like Assassin’s Creed 4: Black Flag, which has its own controller support, the two different inputs won’t confuse the game. This can be overridden with a shortcut on the controller if, for example, you full screen a movie and don’t want to lose control.
I could go on but the videos on the product page do a pretty good job of explaining all the features. In my opinion, ‘Controller Companion’ is the best solution to controlling a Windows 10 PC I have had the chance to use. It makes console-like, living room computers much easier and it just works which is what I need.
Controller companion is really easy to use and set up. This program is a big help for me since I have a bit of carpel tunnel and my hands need a break from using the keyboard and mouse.

Spirits of Xanadu it's not what I expected. It caught me completely off guard. It's weird, but in a good way. A way that I like. At first glance it looks like a low polygon sci-fi generci shooter, but believe me it's more than that. It's hard to talk about the game and not spoil anything. I'll try my best to avoid spoilers.
There descent amount of video options here – resolution, fullscreen, V-sync, shadows, film grain, FXAA, SSAO, depth of field, bloom and motion blur. For some odd reason when everything is on high, my framerate drops to 30 and I exceed the system requirements. So I had turn off V-sync and SSAO. But maybe the problem is in my PC, I don't know. No matter if you put everything on high it won't make the game pretty. It have this simplistic art style and I love it. This is a design choice. Also the keys are rebindable and you can find a ton of different options in the options menu like Field of View, Difficulty, sound volume and so on. Overall you can find a lot of settings.
The year is 1983 and you are send to the research ship Xanadu. She calmly stay around the orbit of a mysterious planet. From a few months her crew hasn't send a single messege. Now alone you have find what happened on the ship. Piece by piece you will put together the story by finding audio logs and pieces paper. Usually I don't searching for both in other games. However in this case I don't know why, but I don't have a problem with that. Keep in mind that this is the only way to understand what happen. The great writting help a lot too. The story begs for more than one playthrough. It have three distinct endings with different requirments to see them and there are a lot of things to find, events to be interpreted. I saw some weird things and make me curious and I wanted to know more, what the dev try to tell with all this symbolism. I like when a game or movie crawls under my skin like that. For me this is smart storytelling.
The gameplay is simple. When you arive on Xanandu, you immediately find a lazer gun. So it's part shooter. But the other part is more interesting for me – scavenging hunt. The game is not all about shooting. It's more about adventuring and finding what happen. There three weapons in total – pistol, shotgun and SMG. The shooting is just fine. I complete the game only with the lazer gun, because I didn't find the other two and it's not necessary. They certainly would make my life easier. Like I said it's about the story. There is even a optional “Peacfull” mode. If you don't like shooting robots, you can enable it and just explore the ship, solve puzzles and find what happen. This is such a cool idea.
Puzzles are not hard and most of them have common sense. Get something, put it there or remove this. Simple puzzles. Some are kinda obscure and I complete them by accident. Others are obvious, like find a code for a lock door, but where is it, it's the difficult part. There a lot of hidden stuff.
The enemies here are all different type of robots. Some are flying and shoot electricity, other shoot lazers, third suicide by exploding near you and finaly a turret with shield. I think it's enough variety, considering the length of the game.
Except sound of your gun, the robots you encounter and a little ambient sound, most the time there isn't something else to hear. They are great. This is not a horror game, but it  defenently have a creepy atmosphere. Still, you are on a space ship with missing crew, aggressive robots and weird things happening around you. There is almost no music, which is a great idea.
The only voice acting you will hear is from the recordings and it's really good. The actors do a great job to let you know how they feel – sad, desperate, drunk and so on.
The level design is good. The ship is not a huge and you will familiarize quickly with Xanadu. All room are distinct. There are crew quarters, laboratory, bridge, offices and so on. You have to walk around the ship to piece together the story. The ship is interactive. You can open cabinets, lockers and so on to search for clues. You can even eat, drink and smoke. It's not necessery, unless you want the achievment for that. It's a neet little thing. Also there are mini-games. I found only one, a simple kill all zombies. One of the coolest things here is no hand holding. Not even where to save your game. You arrive on the ship and you are free to go wherever you want. The only way to know where you are are is a map on the walls. It shows your current location. As a whole the ships feel like it came out from 80's sci-fi movies and it's awesome
Rarely i've been invested in a game or a movie like this. As i mentioned in the beginning at first glance it's doesn't seems to be anything special. The game don't have high production value, but it doesn't have to. I feel the graphics are a design choice. Don't write off the game. The shooting is solid, but it's not the center of the game. It's the story. When you find out what happen, you can see it's not entirly original, but the way unfolds, what you see, the symbolism is what caught my attention. It's well crafted story. The only thing people might not like is the lenght. I beat it in 2 hours, because i wonder around the ship exploring. Some reach the end in just an hour. But the game begs to be played again and that's why i think the lenght is perfect. I even found something, a secret, that can ease my second playthrough. One final thing. People are saying if System Shock and Deus Ex are making a baby and Kubrick shooting it, this will be the result – Spirits Wideshut 1983 Space Odessy. Actually this is my interpretation of the words. The say it have a System Shock and Deus Ex vibe with a pinch of Kubrick. Go now and buy the game. I highly recommend it.

Having bought this game with no prior knowledge of what it was all about, I had no expectations when I started to play it.
And without exaggeration, I'd have to say that it blew my mind.
In essense, Spirits of Xanadu is a mystery thriller adventure with first person perspective and occasional first person fight, that can become a hindrance if you play the game on a very difficult mode. The gameplay revolves around your investigation of a mysterious spaceship called Xanadu, communication with which was lost months prior.
Your job is to locate the survivors, but more importantly, to locate its cargo. What happened to the crew and what can happen to you is for you to discover and is actually entirely optional.
And I guess that's what makes this game really brilliant - it's a free roaming game, set in a single large level where you can pretty much do whatever you desire, including going into the ship recreation area and just playing the "game within the game" zombie shooter that is just sitting there.
And although graphically, this game is not particularly exciting, I found it to be very beautiful, for the setting it's going for and to be honest, the grahics are not paricularly important for this genre of games. Music and sound, including the sound track, are brilliant, and there are tons of voiced dialogues.
But the most important part is of course the gameplay and this is where Spirits of Xanadu takes the cake - it is just really really good. The attention to detail, the little secrets and achievements and of course multiple endings, all make this game a must play in my book. Don't be deceived into thinking that this is a run of the mill horror game though. As not only is this game very unique, but I'd also have to say that's it not horror. I'd called it a space opera thriller with mystery elements.
However I should mention at least one negative aspect because no game is perfect and in this case it's the length. I was able to finish my first run in about 3.5 hours and really, wanted more. As a matter of fact, I did the second run to find another ending in the same sitting. But having seen the game for sale at 5$ very recently, I'd have to say this would be an incredible purchase if you decided to go with it.
If you're still not sure, check out my playthrough here:

There's been a problem on a space ship far away. It was on an important mission, but communications have gone silent. You're sent to see what happened, make repairs, and have orders to bring the ship back if possible. Of course a mystery awaits when you arrive. I won't go much farther than that as it's a game best experienced without too much description.
I consider Spirits of Xanadu to be an excellent game, with a good mix of first person action, exploration, stealth, mystery, and light puzzles. The story and method of exposition is excellent. There's just enough to clue you into what's happening and keep you moving forward, and the writing and performance (via audiologs) is effective in allowing you to see clearly. (I'm sometimes frustrated by games where the writing tries to trick and confuse the player w/ the unreliable narrator thing, and Xanadu does not do that - it lays out the story for you to discover without the intentional misdirection that some games use.) I got stuck at one point and had to seek out a hint, but it's probably something I should've figured out myself if I'd been more careful w/ my exploration.
Another thing I like: the environments have a good degree of interactivity which helps make the world feel real and lived in. I enjoy games that reward exploring, and there are quite a few little "extras" that are not central to the game, but exist to help make the place feel real.
So yes, I recommend this game. Quite an achievement for a small team - and I understand there was one developer doing the coding.

Greenlit the game, bought it, played and now I'll recommend it.
Despite being short, the game feels very complete, there are many things to interact with and tasks to perform around the spaceship. One very good point is that the game doesn't babysit you, if you want the solution to something that's going on you have to search, look for a tip, think and figure it out by yourself.
The FPS part is very simple, not much depth, just a few guns, the basic for you to survive, shoot to kill and don't let them get you (though a "stealth" approach is possible to deal with some enemies). There are also different difficulty levels to satisfy your playstyle.
But what this game really excells at is it's atmosphere, the mystery, the experiences you'll have, whether you understand them or not. The plot isn't given to you, you have to find out about it, imagine what happened, how it happened and why. All in all,  Spirits of Xanadu is a short but very solid experience. well worth playing.
PS: Did I mention there's a zombie shooting mini-game?

Ghost Encounters is a pretty standard hidden object game set in a dead Western town. It may not win awards with its writing, but its many good hidden object scenes certainly should put it on the map of any HOG fan.
After playing through Ghost Encounters: Deadwood, I’m somewhat baffled by the abysmal Steam ratings. Sure, this hidden object game isn’t a masterpiece, but it is far from being bad.
The story has a fairly average premise: a paranormal investigator decides to get to the bottom of the curse of a desolate Western town hunted by a vengeful spirit of an outlaw. What she sees there though is anything but a predictable HOG story. Nothing ground-breaking, and the voice-acting is rather mediocre, but it has its own moments and even a few well-written surprises.
Gameplay is simple and the puzzles quickly get repetitive, probably this is why we get tons of hidden object scenes instead. As a feature presentation, they work great: the scenes are crowded, but only to the point to be fair in their challenge. In my book, this aspect alone should earn Ghost Encounters a spot in most HOG fans’ libraries.

The highlight was one HO scene with a belt arranged in a loop, which was not only half hidden behind the interface, but the game wouldn't accept that I found it until I clicked the empty space in the middle of the loop.
Might be forgiveable if the rest of the game was good, but the story is bland and the puzzles are incredibly lazy. A lot of them involve finding the pieces of a lock, and then suddenly the lock turns into a really bad jigsaw puzzle and you have to put the pieces together, because anything more complicated would be too difficult to program, or something.
I played the whole thing (about 2 hours long) because I apparently have no better outlet for my newfound masochistic tendencies. Don't be like me.

Ghost Encounters: Deadwood puts you in the shoes of a paranormal investigator sent to a ghost town, named Deadwood, haunted by a criminal spirit. Will she lift the curse? Will she save those who are apparently alive?
The story is good and sad. Many ghosts are staying because they're not at peace concerning their loved ones or because they're tied to earth by stuff. Also, many twists will let you scream "NO!!!!!". Yeah, true, the ending is happy in the sense where Deadwood is uncursed. But is it really an ending like you would have preferred?
Anyway, the problem with the game isn't hidden objects scenes or puzzles. They're just what you need. However, by moments, you don't know what you have to do and it's frustrating. Another big problem is the "get back to a previous scene". In almost all games, you have an arrow just above the inventory that lets you go back. Here, nope, you have to click an arrow next to the inventory. When you're used to the standard way, it's hard to remember that.
Anyway, the graphics are pretty good as the soundtrack. While you're in a town set in the far west, you visit a lot of places: mine, saloon, even the funeral home!
Would I recommend it? Yes. But wait for a discount.

Fantastic game. It may not have the most high end engine, but the developers still managed to created some breathtaking scenes and various aesthetically pleasing environments throughout the game.
Where this game truly shines though is the gameplay, with it's fairly origin control and vast variety of puzzles. The game itself is only 3-4 hours long, but every minute of it feels fresh. It's short and sweet. The controls are dead simple, yet challenging to master. The puzzles are not too easy to get you bored, nor too hard to have you screaming in anger at the screen.
The slightly weaker part of the game is the story. Don't get me wrong, it still is a neat little story which complements the gameplay nicely, but it's nothing revolutionary. The soundtrack isn't very memorable, but the sound effects are quite high quality and usually make up for it. In general, although the story felt like it was trying to be emotional, I wasn't really able to feel any strong connection, even at the darkest scenes. Personally, I think it was the music, but who knows, maybe I just wasn't in the mood.
Overall, definitely a game worth playing. It's a unique perfectly crafted and not too long experience.

Wow. This game... just wow.
Brothers was an absolute joy to play. The largest reason being that Brothers is extremely immersive, connecting the player to the game better than almost any other game I have played. This can be attributed to the unique "single-player co-op" mechanic whereby the player uses a single controller to control two in game players. Just as the controller cannot be ripped in part at will, nor can these Brothers. As a player you are connected to the brothers immediately and that connection only becomes stronger over the next two an a half hours as you travel the stunningly beautiful lands, solving puzzles, meeting other creatures, and exploring the world, all in search for the elixir to save your ill father.
While the game is short, and the gameplay is very easy, Brothers as an overall experience is beautiful, immersive, heart-wrenching, and pleasurable. I highly recommend this game, it is fantastic.
Pros:
• Well written and rich story.
• Simple, elegant presentation.
• Stunning visuals.
• Extremely immersive controls.
Cons:
• Graphical fidelity suffers at points, mainly close ups.

I'm going to try and keep this simple and to the point. I am not much for words but I'll try to condense what I think about this game.
Pros:
1. Huge potential. Large seamless maps. You can drive, fly or run across km after km. Towns, roads etc.. Basically entire detailed islands.
2. Great military sim taking advantage of the above. Realistic damage from small arms as well as vehicle weapons.
3. Lots of realistic military vehicles and aircraft. Even boats.
4. Multiplayer is fun, especially coop.
5. Speaking of multiplayer, Dayz mod is something special. Very fun and you can waste hours and hours in it.
6. The single player story is alright, I guess. Nothing to tell mom about.
Cons:
1. Bugs, glitches, more bugs. Absolutely unbearable, game breaking, punch your monitor and throw your computer out the window kind of bugs. Because you can only save 2 times per mission and the mission mught be very well broken before your first save and you won't know it until the end, which can take 1 hour or more if you take your time like me. All sorts of bugs. AI pathfinding drives your teammates vehicles off of cliffs. Mission scripts break and you can't complete the mission. You may fall through the floor and injure yourself badly or die (especially annoying in Dayz). I could write pages detailing the bugs, you get the idea.
2. Second most annoying thing is the interface and the interaction system. You have to scroll through a list of actions to change your weapon, get in a vehicle or perform some other mundane function which shouldn't be that complicated. There's a key for everything and then some. It's very clunky, slow and prone to you pressing the wrong button or doing something unintended. Controling your squad mates and telling them where to go, what to attack is tedious at best.
3. Clunky player movement? Even cars drive like crap and those are the easiest to control.
4. Inaccurate helicopter controls. Don't even get me started, whatever you read on the net, trust me. The heli controls are bad and make no sense. I have no idea what they were thinking when they decided that the helicopter would start acting like and airplane above 50 mph. I can fly no problem in flight sims and the Battlefield series. I even fly RC in real life. This is innacurate, plain and simple.
5. Devs had plenty of time to address these bugs/issues and this is a problem. What a bunch of underachievers. Their strategy is like this: For every new iteration/expansion, focus on adding more crap and complexity built on the same shoddy engine/interface and ignore all the bugs. Then collect money and develop the next uncooked iteration.
Arma2:OA isn't that much better, either. The missions bugs are fewer, but everything else is the same.
The bottom line: This is the kind of game you play because you know what to expect and you still want to play it because there isn't anything like it. You have to be a cult follower, or else you will hate it. The main reason you might get this is to play Dayz mod, which is great, but expect to be killed falling through floors, off ladders, killed by zombies walking through walls, etc... Definitely not for the casual gamer.

What we have here is either a really, really short shooter on a spaceship or a very, very deep atmospheric adventure in space. You're pretty much free to play the game either way. As the sort fo person who hates Adventure games and crawling over every inch of a level just to find an item I really appreciate the open design.
If you play this like a shooter you will probably get the bad ending and, if you can't get into the atmosphere, you won't have much fun. The game has the steady pace and mystery of Alien, and once you've killed all the robot enemies the ship will become very quiet.
There are two things I didn't like: the length and overuse of the shellshock effect. The game felt so short it was like getting a teaspoon of a new flavor of icecream and then being told to go home because the shop is closing forever. It actually upset me a little bit. Sure, you can extend the length by hunting down all the pages and masks and nonsense but that's boring and annoying when your only companion is the shellshock effect.
What do I mean by shellshock effect? I mean that flash followed by an approximation of the character's ears ringing. The screen flashes and your ears ring far, far too often for the effect to remain anything but aggravating. Plus I played shooters through the CoD era so I've experienced the shellshock effect so much it's become a painful cliche. I thought it would stop after a while but I never seemed to reach a point when I was safe from it. Part of the reason I'm accepting the bad ending and leaving the others for YouTube is simply so I don't have to put up with anymore shellshock.

System Shock with simplified combat, minus RPG elements, boiled down into a 3-4 hour experience.
The game has some very obvious System Shock (2) influences -- the layout of the ship, the sound of your footsteps on metal, the select-fire laser pistol, and even the audio log icons pretty much all scream "System Shock 2". And despite the game's length, it's also home to a surprising number of other sci-fi game and movie references.
As mentioned, there is no real RPG-like progression, and even though you have a weapon, it's almost more of a tool for solving problems (in the form of enemies).
The writing is surprisingly competent, as are the puzzles. Even more surprising is the quality of the audio log voiceovers. They're at least on par with SS2, if perhaps even a bit better than some of SS2's voice actors.
Graphics aren't exactly impressive, as you can see from the screenshots, but they get the job done and at the very least don't hurt your eyes. I think there could've been improvement on making more obvious what items can be interacted with though, which would've helped with some puzzles.
As a warning, this game does contain some moderate atmospheric tension. At times you'll experience some environmental surprises that keep you on edge, but there are no cheap jump-scares, unless perhaps you run around a corner too fast and run into an enemy.

If you like mystery, exploration, and psychological horror, this is a wonderful way to spend 3 hours. (More, if you want to take the time to earn some of the achievements.)
The story has themes and tone reminiscent of Solaris (especially Tarkovsky's film adaptation), and also The Quatermass Experiment. Both are excellent reference points.
There are some good puzzles in the game, that are not impossible to solve if you are patient. The ship is small enough that you won't feel frustrated with going back to look for clues you might have missed.
I'd also like to thank the developer for supporting Linux!

Subtlety is a concept that too frequently seems to get glossed over by developers of horror games. I guess they're scared if they don't throw a jump scare at you every fifteen minutes the player would be dissatisfied with the lack of♥♥♥♥♥♥in their pants and quit the game. Spirits of Xanadu isn't afraid to trust that players have an attention span greater than that of a goldfish, and as a result, is one of the greatest horror games I've ever had the pleasure of playing.
The year is 1983, and you're an engineer hired to make some repairs and check on the crewmembers of the titular ship, Xanadu. Within minutes of stepping aboard the craft, it's evident that something is amiss. Robots patrol the hallways eager to aerate you with laser blasts, as you trudge from room to room, discovering pages from books, audiologs, and even the occasional weapon. Xanadu is a shooter after all, and you'll be able to find three different weapons scattered around the ship, some harder to reach than others. You'll want to find a replacement for you starter laser pistol as soon as possible because frankly, it's pretty ♥♥♥♥e. The shooting itself isn't great either, and aiming down the sights makes the controls disgustingly floaty, so I'd advise sticking with hip fire as much as possible.
There's four enemies you'll encounter as you navigate the xanadu, some easier tod eal with than others. There's your basic sentry bot that patrols the ship's corridors and rooms that can be dispatched with your guns or by shutting it down with the panel located on its back. These guys are fairly basic, but in numbers can be somewhat challenging. Then you have small flying robots that zap you with burst of electricity, and stationary turrets whose shields have to be deactivated before you are able to blow them up. Finally there's these self-destructing robots that will run up to you and wreck your♥♥♥♥♥♥These guys can feel a bit cheap at times, as the time it takes to kill one of these guys seems to be greater than how long it takes for them to blow you up. Luckily, dying in this game doesn't really have any negative effects, as you're just transported to the brig of the ship, where you'll have to trudge back to whatever area you werein where you died. Once you kill an enemy, they're gone for good, so by the end of the game the ship is empty as can be, which emphasizes the lonely atmosphere of the game.
Speaking of atmosphere, Spirits of Xanadu oozes it out of every orifice, and it's only bolstered by the audio logs left by the crew of the ship, which are the main medium for the story to be delivered. These are both written and acted out incredibly well, and some are downright chilling. I found myself stopping in shock as these logs detailed what the crew experienced, which are reflected in your own experiences. You'll also find pages of a book scattered throughout the ship that hold parallels to what has happened on the ship, and are a nice touch. I really don't want to go too deep into the story, as it really is the strongest aspect of the game. Seriously, if you're a sucker for atmoshperic space horror, this game is outstanding.
Visually, the game is simple, but it gets the job done. There's some nice lighting found throughout the ship which adds to the look of the game, but it's still not really anything to write home about. The sound design however is, pardon the space pun, stellar (save for the weapon sounds). The creaks of the Xanadu and the hum of the robots in nearby rooms had me constantly checking behind me, and cautiously approaching each new room.
This game is chock full of secrets and mentions, from secret rooms and hidden weapons, to Kubrick and other classic films and pop culture referenced. These for the most part are insanely well hidden, and really require you to take your time, poring over every nook and cranny of the ship if you want to find everything. This game overs no tips or hints, and aside fromt eh general objectives you're given at the start of the game, it's up to you to figure out what to do and how to do it. Your basic objectives are to restore power to the ship and plot a course back to Earth, but you may just find other alternatives based on what you uncover. I love that they are really hands off with the player in this game, and it means every piece of information you discover through the aforementioned audio logs and pages, as well as the occasional email you'll read all hold another piece of the story and clues as to what to do and how to find secret areas. There's no big arrow at the top of the screen pointing you to the next objective, so whenever you finally accomplish your goals, it feels like just that, an accomplishment.
The game offers three different endings, all of which are great in their own right, and none are really objectively better than the others. The game is short, too just over an hour or so long depending on how thorough you are with your explorations, so I was eager to hop right back in and find out what else there was to discover after I had beaten the game the first time.
The game is obviously not without faults, like I said, the shooting is underwhelming and the enemies can feel a bit cheap at times. And while I like the lack of directions given to the player, you can find yourself scratching your head wondering where to go next. Luckily, Xanadu is not a particularly large ship, and with the aid of maps spread throughout the game, you'll learn your way around the ship pretty quickly, which is good, because there's a lot of backtracking to be done here.
If the combat really doesn't do anything for you, you can play the game on peaceful mode, where the robots won't attack you, but that really gets rid of a lot of the tension that comes along with fighting the rustbuckets.
The game offers a concentrated dose of excellent storytelling and atmosphere, all based in a very interesting setting. For fans of creepy games or even just fans of great narratives, this game is a great way to spend a dark night alone.

Spirits of Xanadu is pretty much proof that a game doesn't need to look 'next-gen' to be worth playing. It's a neat little first-person adventure/shooter, with a psychological premise, more than a blood and guts free-for-all.
This little gem popped up in my discovery queue after I had been playing Cradle for a while. It was on sale so I thought, why not? It seemed to have a similar type of theme and story so I gave it a go. I'm not good with things like jumpscare or torture so I was relieved to find this game did psychological horror perfectly without the need for such gimmicks. From beginning to end you feel incredibly uneasy, jumpy even. Every corner, every hallway makes you look behind you and every so often, you'll find yourself asking if what just flickered in your sight, too brief to catch, was ineed real.
One of the most intriguing concepts of the entire game are the little 'events' that trigger from time to time. Without giving anything away, it catches your attention every time and keeps you alert and if nothing else, nervous.
The story is extremely well written in it's simplicity and gives you just enough about each character to visualize their personalities while still letting your own mind shape the bigger picture. There isn't a lot of story 'visible', it's all hidden in the bits and pieces of the logs left behind by each of the crew. The story unfolds itself only if you seek it out actively, rather than force it upon you. This to me is much more rewarding.
The controls are rather straightforward, if a bit awkward at first with a controller. However once you get started it's smooth and responsive.
It's a short game, 4-6 hours if you take your time, but it's a GOOD 4-6 hours and worth an extra playthrough if you're looking for the multiple endings. Not all games have to be long to be memorable.
This look of the game really does fall in with the 80's sci-fi vibe they were going for and the simplistic visuals actually drew me in more than pushed me away. No graphic glitches to be seen and let's just say trying to line up that basketball shot is nearly as difficult in game as it is in real life. The space, despite it's simplicity feels in scale and there's a ton of small things to investigate. From the old boomboxes that play actual music, to a toaster you can interact and even donuts and soda you can snack on in passing, it's clear the Devs were looking at the little things that bring you into a scene.
One of the most memorable things to me was seeing the signage on the ship written in both chinese characters and in English, and how that detail emphasizes more about the crew aboard the ship. A lot of care went into crafting the small universe.
It's worth picking up for sure if you have the chance and like a sci-fi story that doesn't hand you all the details on a plate.

This might just be one of my favorite games.
Now don't be fooled, this isn't a shooter, at least not really. It has shooting in it, yes, but that's not the focus and there are a limited number of enemies which will never respawn. The map is also fairly small but very easy to navigate once you've been through once or twice (and get the lights on) I'd say this is far more of a puzzle game with an incredible atmosphere. The majority of the gameplay revolves around puzzle solving while occasionally shooting robots. The puzles for the most part aren't all that difficult, with the exception of one which leads you to one of the three endings. The minimalist style might be a bit offputting depending on your sensibilites but I personaly thought it looked pretty nice. (again, after I got the lights on, Before then it COULD be a bit difficult to figure out what you're doing or where you're going)
Now, onto the thing the game get's REALLY right: atmosphere. This game scares the absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me, but not because of cheap and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jumpscares. From the very second you step out of your little pod you are instilled with a deep sense of dread and a feeling of "something ain't right here..." There are a handful of scares but you could go through the game and completely miss all of them because there isn't some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ musical sting to startle you and in most cases when they happened I spent a second asking myself "Did I actually see that?" and that is what I love so much about this game, it's smart with its scares and baths the entire experience in a rich atmosphere that stuck with me even after I turned the game off.
The voice acting in this game is incredible as well, at least for the most part. I personally thought the voice actor they had for Solomon Agnew stole the show and the other two voice actors they had weren't quite on par with his performance. Not to imply they were bad, quite the contrary, they just weren't quite as good and it was pretty noticeable to me.
The game however is pretty short (maybe 1.5-2 hours if you're quick about things, 3 if you take your time a bit) and despite being very replayable I don't know if that's really worth the $10 it's being sold for. Additionally the game doesn't seem to be optimized very well. I'm not playing on a very poweful machine but I can generally get away with playing most modern indies on mid to lower settings, but Spirits of Xanadu had very frequent framerate drops and even on the absolute lowest settings I was barely pushing 20 fps most of the time so if you're running on a budget machine keep that in mind. The default controls are pretty wacky as well so before you start the game I'd highly recommend going through and changing everything to your liking, as well as lowering the mouse sensitivity. Speaking of the mouselook, perhaps it's just me but the mouselook didn't feel very great in this game. I can't quite nail down what it is but now matter how much I fiddled with the sensitivity and whatnot it just never felt quite right.
All that said though, if you're looking for an atmospheric horror game with a super solid story then Spirits of Xanadu is gonna be exactly what you're looking for. Seriously, please please please play this game and give these guys your money, they really deserve it.
UPDATE: So sometime before I wrote this review an update was rolled out that was at least partially focused on optimization and the game runs like a dream on my computer now. There are also a few things I wanted to mention but left out of my inital review because at the time of writing I hadn't actually played the game in some time and was just going off about a dozen or so YouTube videos. 1. You can choose between a female and male character. It literally doesn't do anything other than change the grunts you make when you're injured but it's a neat little addition nonetheless.
2. There are 4 different difficulties, one of which being a peaceful mode that makes it so the enemies won't attack you unless you shoot first. I particularly like that one for repeat playthroughs because for me the second (and subsequent) run through the game was a "Lets find the things I missed the first time!" kind of run and it's nice to not have to worry about the bots going after you.
3. The endings. I mentioned that there was more than one ending but I didn't go any deeper than that and I thought I should. There's your standard good and bad ending (Although they won't be exactly what you think, at least not right off the bat) and there is also a really neat ambiguous and kinda trippy ending that I really like but is a massive pain to actually achieve (there are walkthroughs for those of us who simply don't have the time/brain power to figure it all out) Those endings are part of what provide the game wiht so much replayability.
4. The characters. What kind of reviewer am I to mention voice actors without mentioning characters? Well it's simple, I'm not a professional. Anyway, There are three main characters in the game; Solomon Agnew, Lucy Zhao, and Cornell Johns. You never meet any of them throughout the game but in listening to the various audiologs in the game you really get a sense as to who each of these people were. I felt like I really knew these chracters as people which makes it all the more hearbreaking as you piece everything together and learn of their fates and that really is a testament to the strength of the writing and voice acting.
Another thing I absolutely need to mention is that the mouselook is fine. The issues I was experiencing I think were directly related to the low framerates I was getting and had absolutely nothing to do with the game itself. After the optimization update it feels great.

Gotta rewrite my review.
I bought this game on early access since episode 2 came out. there are quite a lot changes.
And i'm also more matured as a VN reader.
First just want to let you know that, i've been reading VN quite a lot. But not really as much as those in fuwanovel forum. At least i've read some of the best and popular ones like, KnS 1 &2, Fate, Hollow ataraxia, Katawa Shoujo, G senjo, Majikois, and some others. So i can assure you that this review is not coming from someone who just got into VNs. And also, i didn't really into mechs so i never read something like muv luv or watch gundam. But ACE Academy for me i think is an exception to that.
Now, lets talk about this VN.
- The most important part is story, for me its considerably a bit lighthearted. You know your typical romance/school/sci fi/mech, etc. Those kind of genre that is pretty familiar with some of the recent anime that just came out.. But to be fair it's not bad. actually not bad at all. Cuz it's more like real life experience. That is what i like about VNs. Most of the stuff is relatable to us because we can choose how the story is going to progress. And even more in this VN, because you're dealling with your daily college stuffs, friendship, business(maybe?), family stuffs, and romance ofc. Unlike other hardcore VN that will just throw us into some unknown situations to us and let us decide on things that we didnt even know what to do about it.
But in ACE Academy, it's not that hard to understand what's the story will progressing if you choose a certain choice in the game.
- The humour is so good, i fell of my chair once.

This is my first review so I can't really go in to full detail, (especially since I've so far only followed one storyline up to the cut off at the end of episode/chapter 2...) But I would like to talk about my Pros and Cons for this game.
Pros:
1. Diverse cast of characters; Cute little sister, Shy girl, flirty foreigner, Tsundere and of course, the idiot male friend.
2. Diverse focus. Even if you're focusing on one character to get to know them or get romantically involved, at some points you HAVE to talk to someone else and it shows character development for all the characters.
3. Not just a date sim, just because it has a date sim doesn't mean that's the focus of the story, in fact some of my FAVORITE dialouge is silly banter between Shou, the male friend, and your character.
4. Character artwork is JUST as good as the character personalities.
5. Full cast voice acting. We have voice acting  and not just for the main characters like your family and friends, even the faceless background characters like classmates and teachers have voices.
Cons:
1. Again with Artwork, some of the full cut scenes are not necessarily poorly drawn, but they need to be redrawn if nothing else for the sake of functional anatomy.
2. Voices, some of the voices for the main characters sound... off, not necessarily bad, some just don't fit the characers, and others just sound like they were recorded on a terrible mic. Other than that voices are great.
3. The "Gears" I am 100% fine with the name, but the mech suits, in my opinion, look very bland and need a little bit of visual flair. There is one acception being somthing that happens to the main character's Gear after a certain point in the game BUT that new look is temporary and I don't want to spoil anything more.
4. Combat, Quick time events are used throughout the game including quick reaction dialogue and such, but  the combat mechanics are severely lacking. it's just a mater of you have about three to four seconds to press either w,a,s or d as it appears on the screen, you fail to press it in time or press the wrong one, you take damage. As a counter to my arguement, this game is 1) still in early access, and 2) not a fighting sim. I know this, but I feel once the game has a bit more story done to it they should go back and refine the combat system just a little bit that way it's more fun to fight in your big robot.
Again all of my complaints are either only a problem because the game is early access, or can be fixed in an upcoming update due to the fact it's in early access. Over all for an uncompleted game with a few quirks that may bug me but Certainly don't take much away from the game if at all, I give this game a 9/10. Depending on how they finish it it may jump up to 10/10

Before I go into my review, I must first make it clear that the game is not really a Free to Play. I say this because after you hit level 30, you hit subscription-based paywall. With that said, though, the features players pay for are totally worth it in that you get hours upon hours upon hours of fun (I have over 1000 hours in the game...).
Pros About the Game:
- Unique MMORPG (superheroes man, how much better can it get?)
- Insane customization
- Decent character creation
- Game community and Daybreak (game company) communicate well and creators listen to players.
- Monthly DLC is gone and now replaced with larger DLC packs being released every few months.
Cons About the Game:
- "Free to Play" is almost false considering the pay-to-win structure of the game (ie: Utility Belt)
- Missions are fun, but get pretty boring
- Not really much replay value with regards to low level operations
All in all, I really enjoy this game; I wouldn't have played over a thousand hours of it if I didn't. That said, the game is really meant to be for those who are ready to pay for DLC or subscribe to a membership. If you can't afford to do so, for whatever reason, you may want to re-consider hopping into this game. If you can afford it however, then I highly recommend you give the game a try; I mean it’s free until level 30 anyways so there’s nothing to loose and everything to gain!

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, was such a crazy, emotional rollercoaster, that it would be hard to find the right words to describe it.
In essence, it's about two brothers that go on a quest to save their ailing father. Along the way, they conquer several trials and tribulations using a combination of their unique attributes. What would've been impossible with one becomes managable with two. This game however, is not co-op based. The player controls both brothers at the same time which adds a unique twist to the platforming puzzler. This feature might be a little annoying at first, but in the end, you will find yourself sorely missing it (you'll understand later...) The puzzles themselves aren't frustratingly impossible, but are still challenging and the gameplay is quite satisfying.
The graphics are simply gorgeous. Treasure your first playthrough, take your time going through places and interact with the insignificant little details in the environment. The saying "a picture is worth a thousand words" was made with this game in mind. Without a single line of dialogue, the game manages to weave an epic tale jam packed with emotion that can and will leave you in wonder, shock and sorrow.
This game should be enjoyed like a good movie. So set aside a good 3-4 hours, sit down by yourself and just play. Lose yourself in the game and let the story wash over you. It's quite the treat and you won't be dissapointed. 10/10

5/5 stars! This app does it all! It took me a few minutes to figure out how to change button mappings (settings > profiles > add new profile > recent processes), but once I figured it out, I was in HEAVEN!
• Allows you to map any key/button/action to your controller. This means you can use your gamepad to play games that do not support controller function (example: Binding of Isaac 1), including non-Steam games (example: Hearthstone)
• Allows you to change mappings for games that support gamepad but do NOT allow for customization (such as changing "right trigger" to the "A" button) NOTE: I am still trying to figure this one out. It might be necessary to disable gamepad support IN-GAME, then map your keyboard keys to the controller via Controller Companion. If there is an easier way, I couldn't find it after looking for a few minutes.
• Each game/application has a unique profile, so once you have customized your controls for that game, it will remember them every time you play.
I am by no means a controller fanatic; in fact, I generally prefer mouse/keyboard. But occasionally, a game is just better suited (or at least more comfortable) with a controller. One of my biggest complaints about controller mappings is that developers seem to think that the right trigger should be the primary action button... when it is one of the most uncomfortable and awkward buttons to press while holding a controller normally, and it only gets worse during long-term gaming sessions.
This app changes all that. No more being forced to use sub-optimal controller settings, chosen by short-sighted developers. No more being forced to use a keyboard and mouse to play a platformer or directional game. THE WORLD IS YOURS! Highly recommended!

I have never been impressed by any controller software since Xpadder came out. I love native controller support for PC gamers nowadays, but I have been mapping my mouse and keyboard controls to every controller from a Gravis Gamepad to my Xbox Elite Controller for years.
That said, I gave CONTROLLER COMPANION a shot because I was interested to see the Steam Workshop and all the available custom profiles for everything from emulators to DOS games, all actively maintained and contributed to. The auto switch from mapped game or native game to the default Desktop profile, which enables controller mouse control and a virtual keyboad to boot - friggin ingenious. It works great in either fullscreen games and apps or windowed games and apps. Once your game loses focus, the desktop profile activates on your controller, so you can do anything from your couch or comfy chair.
It's seamless to map the xbox guide button to the windows task switcher or start menu or steam big picture. Feel's console-like when you jump from game to access FAQ infos, change a podcast, or view a funny cat video and then jump back to game, all without touching your mouse or keyboard.
Best thing about this software? THE VIRTUAL KEYBOARD RULES!!!
I dunno why the neverending reel of characters allow me to type so efficiently in comparison to the square boxes for pointing and clicking letters. I mean I do know why. It's science and relates to how in some games or dashboards that consoles use you can't scroll past the end of the letters to go to the other side but instead have to go back or up and down to switch letters. It's magic how your virtual keyboard works. The neverending spiral is so intuitive as to make me think you should patent it. It's wondrously better than anything except a real keyboard. Next level. Like there is typing with your mind (lol), keyboards, CONTROLLER COMPANION's neverending spiral keyboard, then all else ever. Amazing really.
An idea I have is if ya'll make the overlay have some sweet keyboard button textures on the spiral and a little "blob" or 'booba" bubbly noise or something to confirm the rotation and clicks. It's just a little rugged looking for such a smooth interface. That's purely an asthetic qualm in my taste of interfaces and in no way changes the fact that this working as intended, and it's great.
The only con and it's not really a con as to say a possible future update. Macros. One thing I like in xpadder, is the ability to map a virtual script of keyboard presses, mouse clicks and include custom intervaling, press/unpress detection, variable rapid fire, toggle, etc. Seems like CC is begging for this because of the strong workshop support. Imagine users supplying a mappable Mortal Kombat profile that auto fatalities on a single button press by simulating the presses and timing nesseccary. That's the killer app right thur.
You can do this in xpadder already and I would look more into it but I don't play MK. I have made one button special moves like fireballs and dragon uppercuts using this kind of button simulation macroing in xpadder and I make less complex shortcut buttons for games like combo mouse/keystrokes allowing me to click and drag (I play Baldur's Gate with a controller like a boss), but that's all lacking at the moment from CONTROLLER COMPANION.
Imagine adding this kind of flexibilty coupled with the seemingly motivated user base of PC gamers looking to add controller functionality to tieing their shoes and this will be my end all, be all, go to controller addon.
It still is tho, since CC wonderfully allows Xpadder to take controller presidence over itself if you map a button to xpadder. That means you can run both and get the complete convenience of CC in all ways and if I need to use more advanced button assignments, I can open xpadder and map there.

Multiplayer review?
On launch day; only 134 players in the past 11 minutes, in the last 24 hours there was 451 players, all time was 6,075 players (stats from SteamCharts).
You WILL be spending most of your time in lobbies. At this point, someone should create a Discord server so that people that want to play the game can get into lobbies quick and easy with players that also want to play this game. Mostly everyone is playing either TDM or HC TDM, all I want to play is HC SnD.
I personally only bought it because the original COD 4 on PC never had a workable lobby like on Xbox 360/PS3, only a server browser. So Infinity Ward never gave and/or stopped supporting Official servers like what MWR has. I searched for a lobby in HC SnD, we had 5 players and we needed 1 more player to play. A guy in our lobby stated "this might be the first time I might actually play HC SnD." Believe it or not, we didn't play, we found no one. He told us to switch to normal SnD to see if we can find a match there, nope, same results.
What Activision should do is give a chunky discount to users who have COD 4 in their Steam library.
Pros;
- The game itself, oh my... The memories.
- Graphics
- Game lobbies
- Some of the guns got improved sounds, some should have just been left alone.
- Better animations
Cons;
-- The price, I paid $49.59 (from its standard $80, during the MWR standalone launch sale) for the deluxe edition to have both IW and MWR. The MWR price, then with the expectations to buy the DLC (I didn't) also to play on all the maps, the standard price point of MWR is stupidly high for a remastered game that has a dead community.
- MWR is filled with Activision’s greed. Microtransactions up the bum hole.
- New weapons, are they really needed? Including melee weapons, really? Can you just leave that for other crap CoD titles?
- No dedicated servers, all peer to peer host connections like normal CoD.
- Game modes show a % size, instead of an actual number. This means you don't know actually how many players are in a game mode.
- Small community = only x amount of game modes can actually be played. Everything else is a ghost town. Most, if not all game modes have "< 5%" of people playing/searching for that game mode. In reality, it's probably like 0.5%. Get into a lobby and it says 'No Match Found.'
- The snipers. You were able to quick scope easily in the COD 4. In this? It's slow and horrible.
- It has 0 Steam integration whats so ever in-game. When I click on a player names, it should have the option to go to that users Steam profile (like how Xbox and PlayStation has one to go to a users 'gamercard/profile).'
Bugs/Glitches:
- At times when people are talking during the process of the match being over and goes back to the main lobby. The game freezes for a few seconds and the players voices just repeat.
- Even with extra video memory available the game can easily lag and hiccup when loading into a match. It will then lag and hiccup again once you get into a match, but after awhile it doesn't do it anymore.
Tips:
- Upon starting the game, be sure to pre-cache the shadows. If you don't you will receive server timeout messages when entering a match due to all the shadows that you need to load.
At this point in time, they should just do cross-platform with Xbox/PlayStation so that we can play with them.
MWR multiplayer is not worth it right now. But, if you have the extra cash lying around get it. It's not that bad if you just close your eyes when you see the paid DLC and microtransactions.

THIS GAME IS RAD.
It’s got a really simple visual design, but it is still very atmospheric to explore.
The game is KIND of a shooter… there is definitely shooter gameplay in it, and the shooting feels just fine, but what you are really looking at with this game is an ADVENTURE GAME that also just happens to let you shoot robots with laser guns.
The premise is sort of like the first Dead Space. There is a vessel that has gone silent for some reason. You are sent to the vessel to assess the situation and then fix anything that needs to be fixed to assure that the vessel will return to earth properly. The difference is that in Dead Space, this is just some explanation for getting you on board the ship full of aliens so that you can start shooting aliens. Sometimes a guy on a radio tells you to fix something and you press A to fix it. But in Xanadu, you actually have to like… figure out how to disable the rogue turret outside the engine room, then disable it, then break into the engine room and look at the engine to figure out why it’s not working, which is partly obvious (replace fuses, unjam the cogs, etc), but it also means performing some quasi-Myst-like gameplay where you fiddle around with knobs and switches and buttons until something interesting starts to happen.
There are also audio logs and text notes you can find, as well as computers you can log onto to read emails and such, which fulfills the part of the mission where you’re trying to investigate what happened. But the weird thing is… and this is coming from a guy who nearly always HATES audio logs and note pages… I actually am really enjoying finding them and reading/listening to them?
They are actually really well written (and the VO is not bad at all), and there is an interesting element of the story that adds an interesting quirk to a lot of the messages. But I also like that the logs and stuff you find aren’t just exposition dumps. You also find the sorts of notes and things that people would actually write down. You might find the recipe for an omelet, or a scrap of paper on which someone has simply scribbled down the Konami code (ha ha). One of the audio logs was made by one of the crew, who got really drunk and basically just drunk dialed his voice recorder. I literally laughed when he starts talking about his girlfriend’s hair for some reason and about how it looks “very Roman… like the hair a Roman would have”. The sort of weird, incomprehensible babbling your drunk friend would actually say.
The most obvious sign this is an adventure game though? I've never played a shooter where I had to get out a pen and paper to SOLVE ONE OF ITS PUZZLES. But you will have to do that at least once here. Don't be scared, though. The puzzle quality is very good. Just remember to be very thorough.

Brothers plays like a fairy tale yet is so much more than that. The scenery is absolutely beautiful, music and sounds are quite enjoyable, and the story excellent. Without spoiling the ending, this is a game I would enjoy playing again, though I would need some time after the final chapter.
I did beat this game in a matter of 3 hours (5 hours to complete all achievements), taking my time to enjoy the scenery while scaling walls and "conversing" with some of the NPCs. For example, the engineer/scientist and the younger brother have a fun interaction and I have to admit I watched them for a good 3 minutes! The entire game was a bit shorter than I expected, but enjoyable nontheless.
I would like to note that at first I thought I was set on another language. However, after checking it was on "English", I determined that it was nonsensical speech, similar to what you may have heard playing The Sims. And this is what really makes the game shine: it is the facial expressions, the body motions, the interactions, that convey the story though you don't understand a word. It drives you deeper into the story, an immersive quality I haven't experienced with many other games (the closest being BioShock Infinite and the relationship you develop with Elizabeth, and that doesn't come close).
For games that require a controller, I use an Xbox 360 controller that I bought specifically for PC gaming. With that being said, this game was a pleasure to play, though I found myself confusing the two brothers on screen occasionally. (Hint: it is easier to play if you have the older brother on the left and the younger brother on the right.) However, I did notice that there are keyboard controls in the menu (WASD and arrow keys for both brothers), so it doesn't "require a controller to play" but it sure is nice.
Had it been a few hours longer I would say it was worth the full price, but if you see it on sale, pick this gem up. This is a game I am proud to have in my collection.

I had picked up this game mainly because I kept hearing it brought up constantly during the Giant Bomb GOTY deliberation podcasts. It was something that was completely off my radar.
I cannot describe how spectacular this game looks. Each "Level" had its own atmosphere and the transitions between areas does not feel forced. It provides for a fluid flow through the game. It is something that will need to be experienced firsthand in order to appreciate it. Even the game realizes this by providing small moments where you can just take in the scope and detail of the scenery. All of this is exemplified by a truly outstanding score to go along with this game, I had played through with a decent set of headphones and throughout the entire game the music just added into the experience in a very impactful way.
Game play is a little odd to get used to. A controller is a must, while there were keyboard mappings in the options you control each brother with the separate analog sticks. It takes some getting used to, and even towards the end I was still confusing the two onscreen on screen with the controls getting their positions reversed. But it ultimately gets the job done, I had never found myself blaming the controls.
This was something I finished in a single sitting. I think that is the best way to experience this due to the nature of the gameplay. The motivations for the character seem a little weak, where you are attempting to cure your sick father (Which you get very little screen time with at the start of the game) and you set off on an adventure. The charm of the environment and the pacing through the game bring everything together even with the loose story creating an ultimately enjoyable runthrough.
Put on some headphones, grab a controller and set aside a few hours and just enjoy the experience.

There is so much room for improvement in this game and I feel that the developers should continue polishing this game as in my opinion, the game doesn't feel done at this point. There are many user interface issues that I feel can be improved on. The levels feel vast, open and dull and the encounters are not challenging enough. Some areas are way too open and the pacing between encounters are too long and causes boredom. Allowing the players to disable the map doesn't really have any functionality at all other than provide a better screenshot if one feels the need to take it. Exploration feels punishing because after going down one path and reaching the end only to discover a well, the player has to travel a pretty long distance back to where the path branches off. This is a frustrating process and gets old very quickly, giving me more reasons to quit the game. Please do not stop polishing this game. It has a lot of potential.
One thing that I feel is done superbly, is the music. The music is SO beautiful. However, the cutscene dialogue seems to conflict with the singer's voice and competes with each other for the player's attention. Some cutscenes (like the intro), cut off so abruptly it makes me wonder if I was missing something. A simple fade out of the music would help a lot.
Given how short a single run through of the game is, the simple mechanics and the low interest curve, it definitely doesn't justify the price this game is going for. I do like the art style.

Moon Hunters is, well, kind of just an average game. I wish it were more than what it was. I was really excited for this game initially, but the end result is pretty bland and repetitive.
It sells itself almost as a roguelike or "roguelite" kinda deal, hinging on the idea that you play through it multiple times, and each playthrough is different. Each "run" is procedurally generated, you encounter different stuff each playthrough, that kinda thing. But ultimately the game ends up being way too samey, to the point where you end up seeing everything the game has to offer in 2-3 runs. There's all these different unlocks and stuff, but they don't really ADD anything to the gameplay. Not really.
I felt no desire to play after my 3rd playthrough. There just wasn't enough there to really hook me in. I think the core gameplay loop is flawed, to be honest. You start out picking a character, picking their starting location, and going from there. You have several "days" until the run ends automatically by forcing the final boss on you. Each time you visit an area, whether it be a level or a town, that consumes a day. Either way, each playthrough is stupendously short.
The story's supposed to be a bit of a hook as well, but I found myself not really caring about it. For a game that's toting the story as one of its strong points, I feel like they failed on this end. Part of the idea behind the story is that you're "building a legacy" for your character, to be remembered for what they did. But it's completely irrelelvant in the long run, it has no implication on anything other than "well here's how your run ended up". But even then, I felt like it kinda just decided things on its own. I was playing a character and making choices to be a big ol' jerky jerk, but in the end it painted me as being kind and gentle. Wait, what?
The combat's not great. It consists of super basic AI just kinda throwing themselves at you, and you spamming abilities. It gets really repetitive and monotonous as you just button mash your way through everything. There's upgrades for certain abilities or your autoattacks, but a lot of the time you mostly just want to focus on one particular thing. For example, the Spellblade has a knockback ability, but it sucks, so you just want to upgrade his autoattacks.
You can make yourself pretty OP, but often it doesn't matter, because the game is way too easy. There's almost no difficulty, and you have to try REALLY hard to actually die. Some characters are a lot better than others, while some are much worse than others, so the balance is kinda all over the place.
When I played the game initially, it was ridden with bugs. Online co-op was UNPLAYABLE, there were several game-breaking bugs that prevented progression. Even in single player, like straight up skipping the opening and ending cutscenes without a way to rewatch them. It boggles my mind how the game actually came out in that state. I don't know if they've fixed the bugs since, but it left a really sour taste in my mouth regardless.
They've been patching the game as well, adding new encounters and events and such. But it all doesn't really matter too much, because it doesn't really add anything to the game and it doesn't solve the issue of the game's core gameplay loop being unfun.
There were a lot of cool ideas at play, but the end result is that nothing really comes together to form a cohesive gameplay experience. The game really feels half-baked, it felt like it was kinda rushed in the end, and ultimately it's just not that fun.

Due to the word limit, I cannot post my entire review here.  What follows is a summary of my thoughts on this game.  To read the full review, complete with a video and pictures, visit
.
I have been puzzling over how to approach this review for a few days now. On one hand, I think about how much I enjoyed the game early on, with its unique and colorful hand drawn art work and fascinating mythology. On the other hand, I think about how much I despise several of the classes and how horribly unbalanced and repetitive everything gets after about two hours of play, and I am torn. This is a divisive game, as divisive as I have ever seen or played.
Visually the game is actually a treat.  I love the hand drawn style for the cutscenes and character portraits, and the sprite work and generally style of the game is great.  The regions can feel samey at times, with all forests/deserts/mountains/swamps basically identical, and in some cases even repeating the procedurally generated terrain (Seriously, in one forest I ran across the same ruins twice), but overall its possibly one of the best features of this game.
The other great part of this game is the Soundtrack, and I am VERY happy the devs gave us a key that included said soundtrack, because the music is awesome.  Sadly, it seems that each type of region has a specific song, and it can become repeatative quickly.  For example, when in a forest....you will hear the same song no matter WHICH forest you are in.  At least each town has its own track.  The boss battles all share the same track as well.
Where the game fails is its gameplay.  Its a roguelike, so its designed to be repeatedly played.  However, it quickly loses steam after a few hours.  You start to see the same events over and over again, and get the same endings over and over again unless you are really lucky.  I know there is a 3rd ending, but the events needed to trigger it are events I have not seen over 7 playthroughs of the game.  I have only gotten the bad ending and neutral ending.
The other issue is one of balance.  You see, you have 6 total characters, 2 of which are unlockable.  However, the only ones worth a damn if you play solo are the Swordmage and Occultist.  The other two, the Witch and the Druid, are barely playable.  I was able to finish the game with the 2 secret characters, and the Witch, Occultist, and Swordmage.  The druid however is so poorly balanced I could not get through the first zone without dying.  Whats really funny is that the character most people consider one of the weakest, one of the two hidden ones, was far easier to play then any others simply because her attacks do not root her in place.
Truthfully, the Occultist is so overpowered in design that if you stack INT you can stand in one spot during the final boss fight and murder him before he ever gets a shot off, its really bad.
The mythology of the world is actually really interesting, but the lack of depth and replayability absolutely kills this game and I cannot in good conscience recommend it at full price.  If you can get it for say $5 then sure, its worth a few hours at least, but beyond that, don't bother.
I am, however, interested to see if KitFox games can take what they learned here and maybe try again, and do it better!
