There are a lot of games that have an infinite world as a major selling point. This game's world is infinite-er than all those others. The geometry is strange and takes some getting used to, but it has some really interesting effects that really shape how the game plays. The world is divided up into regions with different biomes, every region is infinite -- only possible because of the weird geometry -- and every biome feels distinct from the others, with new twists on the rules and new ways of employing the strange geometry.
I recommend using a mouse to play -- keyboard is possible, but not at all necessary, and the grid is made of 6- and 7-sided cells, so the 8 directional movement on a keyboard doesn't map really well. The controls are very simple, and everything is done through movement, so you don't need all of the key-bindings that most roguelikes have.
I first fell in love with version 4.4, since then the content has been massively expanded with new biomes and new challenges.
A simple and entertaining roguelike with an atypical movement and exploration system. Very straightforward, but surprisingly addictive, and gets challenging quite fast as you rack up the treasure.
+A billion thumbs up for Dune references!
This is an extreeeemely cut down roguelike with some uncharacteristic dimensional atributes, you can see upcoming danger an almost infinate distance away for example.

This game is definitely worth $1.
The only action you can take is to move to an adjacent space, possibly killing the monster there. There is no equipment and no stats. This is about as minimalistic as a rogue-like can be, and yet the developer manages to do so much with so little. Each of the ~10 zones feel different and completing the game is a nice challenge.
Because you can't accidentally kill yourself due to the turn order (the game stops you from moving in to such a space) you're free to speed through the easier parts of the game. That doesn't mean you can't die though as getting stuck between two enemies (much like checkmating a king in chess) is still fatal and happens way more often than you'd expect. It's a great little mechanic that makes the game both faster and more thoughtful.
I do have to say that the hyperbolic geometry is mostly just a gimmick, but it does make it very easy to get lost, which serves the mood of the game fairly well.
I would definitely recommend this game.
Edit: Version 5.3 added a Euclidean mode which proves that the game does benefit from the hyperbolic geometry more than I thought. (The Euclidean mode isn't as well tuned, but it does highlight a few interesting differences.)

I kind of put off reviewing this game until it had a year to sort of work out the bugs and content, as most MMOs do. To be honest, I feel a mixture of pleasant surprise and disappointment.
We'll start off with that the game is definitely worth the $10 asking price, especially for the in-game bonuses you get if you also play RIFT. You are an ark hunter, out to make your fortune in the terraformed San Francisco Bay area after an alien immigration. The story is fairly interesting, though I personally do not have a special attachment to mission based storytelling.
The gameplay is great. The gunplay is fun and functional, with weapon modding and several familiar systems with a little bit of Defiance uniqueness to it, but not so unique as to be esoteric to a newcomer. Imagine Borderlands 2 as an MMO, sort of. However, the missions and side missions consist of go here, kill this, activate that and come back. Then never deviates from this formula.
Though to break it up there are regular arkfall events, which are large scale multiplayer events in which people get together to take down randomly spawning minibosses to unlock a massive world boss, which if defeated will reward the participants with big rewards depending on their contribution score. Simply tagging the objective and walking away will not give you full rewards as it does with RIFT.
There are also smaller emergency events which happen throughout the map on a constant basis, in which you'll have to clear out a nest of enemies or help friendly NPCs in some way.
The game does not require a subscription, but runs on microtransactions and while people tend to shy away from this word, a huge majority of the items on the MTX market are purely cosmetic with free versions obtainable in-game with in-game currency or through achievements. There are a bunch of boosts available, but it is hardly pay to win. All in all, the MTX market is purely an "I want it now!" option for people throwing money at their screen.
My biggest complaints about the game right now are the repetativeness in the missions structure and the graphics. The graphic presentation of the game is not representative of what we should expect from a game released in 2013. I would even go so far as to say that the hardware limitations of the PlayStation 3 and XBOX 360 (especially the XBOX 360) do not excuse the graphic quality of this game. Even on the highest graphic settings, I would say that the visual quality is about on par with a game released in 2005 or maybe earlier.
Overall, I would give this game a 6/10. The content is definitely worth the price tag, but if you are looking for an MMO that will have the draw and lifespan of the giants like World of Warcraft, this isn't it.

Krator was a pretty decent game although there were drawbacks that made me from playing it all the way through at times laying it down and playing it again maybe a year later from an old save. What made me do that? Well I'm going to tell you.
I won't go into the good parts of the game like its graphics. Voices for characters the looks of your guys. Other things that made it good. But instead only its main cons that made me very upset with how the developers made the game.
1. Barely no customization. None what so ever in changing how your characters look. Except for the weapons they carry. The only way is to buy a new character that looks different but the same class and scrap the other one basically. Or keep  the old one and keep them as backup.
2. Only a 3 man squad at all times even though your party can be huge. Say 9 people are partners going about the wasteland and helping eachother except in battles or dungeons only 3 of them are fighting and doing missions for the ENTIRE group. Where is the backup? The other backpackers? The sniper helping out? NOPE! None. Only 3 guys of your choosing at all times. Theres not even mods that change this which could of been excellent for the game but no, those never came up. This made it really hard to complete the game which I still haven't because the bosses and enemies can get so hard its not even worth playing anymore without a friend coming to help. If only you could use your whole party and not only 3 of them that you could actually get things done faster and better. Whats the point in spending all your hard earned cash on new followers if you can't really have them out with your whole team. They need backup. This basically made the game dead for me. And extremely hard and not worth playing for a long time. It made it very grindy because while your old characters are out and doing the missions the others are not getting any experience and fall down the usage wheel and basically become dead weight cause they can't fight any of the higher level enemies.
So with those two out of the way thats the only two main cons that made a lot of people upset. Its those two choices they made that really set the game level to drop for playability. And made it frustrating.
The stories are fine, going through the map is fine, enemies are fine IF you could actually use your whole team and not just 3. Perma-death is awesome and makes you think over your choices except doesn't really have much of a point if your team isn't really helping all that much. All in all I can't recommend this game all that much cause of the future people who play this game that will get frustrated with its bad developer choices that made this game dead for me. But others may like it and I did like the story and I do want to finish the story.
If they make the parties bigger it would be a huge major help for us singleplayer users that don't have a friend that wants to play this game to boost your party to 6 characters that go on the map. How is that fair for us as singleplayer users I might add? It makes the game easier but way more harder and frustrating for single player.
If anyone that made this game sees this review, please, please, please make us be able to have a bigger party out for the single player users. Thank you.

I'm reluctant to give this a bad review, because the artistic quality of the writing, visuals, music, etc. is quite high. Still, the experience as a whole leaves a tremendous amount to be desired. Here are the things that really come up short for me:
1. The Combat
It doesn't feel like there was a comprehensive vision for this. The game simply vomits enemies and makes them run towards you. There is no real enemy AI from what I can tell. This means that combat isn't particularly interesting to begin with, quickly becomes very repetitive, and despite how the game is marketed, combat is definitely its core loop.
2. The Polish
Scenes often smash cut from one to another super abruptly, with no fades or other transitions of any kind. The multiplayer is, as others have said, simply busted. There are just a lot of these kinds of little(?) details that make the game feel unfinished and rushed out the door. They say you gotta do the first 90% of a project and then the second 90% - Moon Hunters often feels like that second 90% fell by the wayside.
3. Narrative Structure
While the quality of the writing is quite good, the way that the story and characters are presented is a pretty hot mess. I understand what the game is trying to do in terms of allowing you to work out the story through multiple playthroughs (FWIW, I've been through the game five times) but in practice it doesn't function well. Character prologues would help, a little more linearity on initial playthroughs might help, there are a lot of things that could be done... Moon Hunters simply throws you into deep water without any real sense of how to swim.
There is a really great game somewhere in here, and a lot of the pieces are already in place, but so much of it just comes off as half-baked and barely-there. If this was in early access and coming to consoles a year from now, I'd say god bless - but it seems like Kitfox believes this is a fully-finished, ready-for-market game.
I can't see how you can play this, eyes open, and believe that.

I know that there are people who rag on Spore, they say it didn't live up to what it could've been. By far that is the most common complaint that I've seen out of the game. However, while it is entirely true, Spore could have been MUCH more, what we do have is still fantastic. First thing about this game you should know is just how acessible this is. I clearly remember being around 8 or 9, playing it at a friends house for the first time. The first two stages show a gradual curve in complexity, if you are young, you can easily grasp the idea of how to play the game. The cell stage, if a little simple, is still a fun and challenging experience. If you find the game too difficult, crank the difficulty up to hard mode, even the cell stage can be a challenging endeaver. Next up is the creature stage, this stage's premise is simple, however, it uses this lack of complexity to add a lot of depth. The creature creator the game is known for shines most in this stage. There are a handful of both social and combat abilities that you can use in order to progress through the stage. If you are smart, you can completely deck out your creature, though if you do not plan well, expect to get crushed even on lower difficulties. Tribal stage is the point where a lot of people I've heard from, say the game starts to get stale. While an RTS is much less immediately satisfying to play than a real time RPG, this stage is still fun. When I was younger, I had no  idea how to play this stage, so I just played creature stage more. Once I finally learned how to play though, it became my favorite stage. Managing attacks from other tribes, gathering food and adding more tribe members, it is a very exhilerating experience. The game has just enough difficulty, and enough mechanics to make this stage interesting and a ton of fun. Next off, civilization. This stage is very good, and by that I mean, really good. It's not by favorite by a long shot, though I will admit that the entire stage is always a great time. This stage teaches you a lot of the fundamentals that you need in the space stage, very subtly without tons and tons of tutorials like the space stage had. Learning to establish trade routes, protecting your cities and grabbing up as much spice as possible. All of this is done in real time, so you have to manage that, potentially at the same time somebody is attacking you. Then, the jewel of this game, everyone's favorite, space stage. Now, I could spend hours talking about why space stage is absolutely fantastic. The progression system, tools, complexity of the mechanics. However, what I want to say is, the game is slowly teaching you the entire way how to play space stage. It's really clever how a lot of concepts are introduced to you early on, that if you pay attention to, you will do well in the space stage. Overall, this game is fantastic. I can proudly state that this is my second favorite game of all time (Only behind Fallout New Vegas). I would reccomend it to literally anyone, because for all the flak it gets for not living up to its potential, what we did get is still a phenomenal game on its own.

America's Army: Proving Grounds
The game does have some pros, but these are far outweighed by the cons.
+ Free download, no cost whatsoever.
+ Graphical improvements compared to America's Army 3. The game looks a fair bit better but it's still not anything amazing.
+ Really interesting United States army recruitment videos, showing you how they train and the opportunities that exist while serving.
+ More options for weapon selection. The developers have listened to player feedback from America's Army 3. You now carry a secondary firearm (pistol), along with one primary weapon, either a sniper rifle, M249 SAW, standard issue rifle or a shotgun.
+ There's a nice mix of maps available, keeping the game fresh.
+ Hardcore mode. Thank goodness they implemented this into the game. The problem is, nobody uses it, probably because they would all suck if they did (lol). There's not many servers for hardcore mode. It erases the stupid features which make the game less strategy oriented, like enemies being marked on your map and unlimited medical revives for teammates. You can actually bleed out from wounds, similar to America's Army 3. However, hardcore mode doesn't solve the inherent flaws in gameplay, such as the bad shooting and lack of teamwork. Ideally, it should have been the
mode for the game. As you'll see from my negatives below, the main game mode which has been coined 'user friendly', is atrocious and should never have been released.
- The main game mode for America's Army: Proving Grounds is less skill based and more generic than America's Army 3. It follows in the footsteps of mainstream First Person Shooter titles, which are not focused on teamwork.
- The main game mode is much more unrealistic than America's Army 3. If you're shot in the legs or arms, it doesn't affect your ability to run or aim steadily. You can be on 1% health in America's Army: Proving Grounds and still sprint around, jump onto objects and shoot the enemy as if nothing ever happened. It's simply ridiculous.
- You can now medic yourself using bandages an
of times. Have you been shot? No problem, just heal yourself. Have you been shot again? No worries, just heal yourself. Were you shot a third time? No problem, just heal again. I don't know what clown came up with this idea. The only way to die in the main game mode is to be secured by an enemy team member (which involves them pressing a key while standing above you). If you're shot in the head you can still be revived if you haven't been secured, lol.
- It's extremely difficult to locate enemy soldiers who are firing on you, this is because of the poor visual game design and colours used. It's a frustrating chore.
- The maps in America's Army: Proving Grounds are complex, which you would think is a benefit to the game. Alas, this negatively impacts upon player interaction and teamwork. America's Army 3 was successful due to the small map sizes, which were easy to adapt to and understand. This fostered teamwork, where players stuck together and fought to control important areas. Because the maps were straightforward, most players were able to provide detailed intelligence on enemy locations. America's Army: Proving Grounds suffers from large maps, where a great number of individuals have no idea how to tell their team where the enemy is. There is very limited exchange of conversation on microphone, which is a shame.
- The shooting is bad, it really is. The guns are inaccurate and annoying. Weapons from America's Army 3 were not precise either, but they were reliable and could hit targets.
- The game is boring, what can I say? It's not fun at all, unlike America's Army 3. Many of the best players I know from America's Army 3 consistently die in this game now, myself included. Sure, they're still better than other players, but the game doesn't reward them for playing tactically.
Overall Score: 3.5/10
I've played America's Army 3 in excess of 1,000 hours and I'm experienced with the gameplay. It was the only First Person Shooter I've truly enjoyed. America's Army: Proving Grounds destroys the series and is a pure embarrassment, one that has sadly resulted in the end of my America's Army career.

I appreciate it when devs go to the trouble of weaving story elements into the searches instead of just throwing in meaningless objects. There is a unique mechanic of using mirrors to change from the living world to the spirit world and transporting objects from one to the other which I really liked. The artwork is great; I would love an HD upgrade if it were ever available. I especially enjoyed the effects used to enhance the ambience in the rooms where you can see that it's a dark, windy, rainy day outside. I found myself staring longingly out those windows, wishing I could go out there and enjoy the storm. The game is surprisingly long. There are many locations, so many that you start to wonder if the mansion could actually contain all of them in the physical layout implied, but this is one of the rare inconsistencies. I like the "area is cleared" notification, saves a lot of time knowing you're done with a room! This HOG contains very minimal backtracking, and I thank the devs for that! If you enjoy curling up on a rainy day with a pleasant mystery HOG, this is well worth your money, even if you don't catch it on sale. One of the better HOGs on Steam, highly recommended.

I currently have 13h on the beta version of the game.
First of all : Even if it looks like an action packed Mana game serie, be aware that this game is about the journey, the seek and the poetry more than fighting (but there are fights if you like them, and in co-op, it will feel like a Gauntlet)
You are seeking for a goddess that you might or might not find and different things happens each time you play, even when you make mostly the same choice. "Each time you play" means "each time one of your character become a legend in 5 days and nights", which happens kinda fast to be honest.
So here it comes : the Main features :
- Rogue like concepts.
- Fast, easy-to-learn-but-hard-to-master fighting system. You might die a lot, especially with the bard, but don't worry, it's part of the story to run away sometimes.
- NG+ mechanics A LOT. In most rogue like, you spend a lot of time in game but you rarely beat the final boss. Here it can happen really often, but even if you die against it, you'll unlock new features anyway.
- Poetry ! Songs and winds whispers are delightful !
- You didn't read dialogues in game since the old RPG era ? This game might make you actually read the dialogues again, and wanting to read it, which for me is incredible.
Conclusion : Blend Gauntlet with rogue like elements, put an extra 110% poetry and "play again if you want to see what I have to offer" and you have a solid, original and enchanting game.

Brothers uses an interesting gameplay mechanic in that you control both brothers simultaneously, one with the left joystick and the other with the right joystick.  To interact with things you use the left or right trigger depending on which brother you want to use.  Now, there are some "puzzles" that test your brain's ability to control two characters at once, and this is where the game feels really fresh and cool.
The game has a wonderful, somewhat sad, but heartfelt story.  The art style and music are very well done, and they invoke the correct emotions at the correct times.
This game is very short; I believe it took me under 4 hours to complete.  The short journey you take place in is well worth the small admission price, and the only gripe is that it was over so fast.
Definitely recommend this game.  Don't forget you need a controller!

I'm going to give more of a neutral rating for this game, as opposed to the many overwhelmingly good reviews that this game has.
I will start off by saying yes, this is a good game at what it does- the world is beautiful and the story is told well; BUT, it is not for everyone. Do not go into this game expecting more than a good story and some simple puzzle solving. People who want amazing gameplay should probably pass on this game.
I foolishly allowed myself to get really hyped for this game after many people calling it "one of the best games of the year if not of all time." While it was enjoyable, the story personally did not carry an enormous amount of weight for me. Don't get me wrong- I love story driven games. I really wanted to get moved by this game, but this game just did not click for me as it has for many people. After the 2-3 hour playthrough, I just felt like I was missing something. Yes, it was a good story; yes, it told it well, but it just wasn't the second coming on Jesus.
All in all, I am not bashing the game- I still recommend it to people who like a good story. I just wanted to offer a different opinion than what most people are saying. Do not allow yourself to go into the game expecting one of the greatest stories ever told, as it will surely diminish the effect the game has, as it did for me.

The most apparent thing as soon as you start up, the graphics ain't exactly all that and a bag of potato chips. The game is fairly ugly, even by 2010 standards. The size of the world and the battles make up for this in spades. With battles to be fought, wars to be won, cities and castles to conquer, and fair maidens to court and marry, this game has nearly everything I want in a medieval game.
The combat is somewhat clunky, but much more enjoyable than a majority of first-person combat systems. You can attack and parry in four directions (up, down, left, and right), shields block as long as you are looking at your attacker, but break after enough damage. Overall, the combat is fun, exhilarating, and, assuming you don't turn down the difficulty options, challenging. Dueling more than one target can range from difficult to nigh-impossible.
The real meat of the game comes to building armies and sieging other kingdoms. Your army starts out fairly small, maybe twenty-five unless you pile all  your points into charisma and leadership, and grows to upward of two to three-hundred soldiers the longer you go. You can become a vassal to one of the kings in the game, assisting him and other lords with things from conquests to simple bounties. If you don't like the idea of serving under an existing king, you can choose the more difficult option of raising an army and starting your own kingdom, or assisting claimants with the right to rule certain kingdoms with overthrowing the current king of said kingdom.
Overall, anyone into medieval combat and the time period in general will have a blast. Fans of action-RPGs will enjoy this too. There's a multiplayer that many people absolutely love, but I have little-to-no experience in it, so I can't supply much more than that.

Krater is a game which can neither be wholly dismissed nor whole-heartedly embraced. The tactical team-based RTS/ARPG hybrid battle-system is exciting, innovative, and well-implemented, while various tweaks to the typical ARPG formula show the thoughtfulness of passionate game design.  The graphic design is consistent and thematically appropriate throughout. Sadly, Krater plays like a concept demo - a few hours of fun as you acclimate to the control scheme and unique design elements, followed by a steep drop-off in variety. The crafting system is essentially a grinding-incentiviser, and character progression is bizarrely limited in ways which are obviously designed to conjure up more grindplay. While the four classes do allow for some interesting combinations and teamwork, each class has only two skills. Although these skills can be tweaked in a variety of ways thanks to the unique augmentation system, the actual gameplay is largely unaffected by these tweaks and runs together in a wash of habitual button-mashing.
In many ways Krater succeeds - the writing is quirky, the world interesting, and the graphics stimulating. Unfortunately at the core of it all is an exceedingly repetitious experience. If your love for grinding or your desire to explore outweigh your distaste for repetitive gameplay, there is a unique and rewarding experience to discover here. Otherwise, avoid investing yourself in Krater: its innovation is only skin deep.

This has been a ton of fun for casual play. In past MMOs I've played, the two biggest pet peeves I've had is lack of character customization and mobility at lower levels of play. As a casual player, I don't usually find myself playing at the higher levels where the cooler-looking gear and mobility options are found in other MMOs, DC Universe Online takes a different approach.
Character creation, from the onset, gives you a wealth of starting looks, powers, and tweaks to choose from to make a variety of unique-feeling characters. Medieval barbarian with fire magic? Go for it. Futuristic flying robot with machine pistols? You can do that to. You even have some choices with different idle and movement animations, which helps even more with making your character feel distinct.
Character movement is also a blat from the game's start. There are no mounts in this game. Instead, you choose from one of a few movement capabilities  such as Flight, Super Speed, and Acrobatics. All of these make transit between quests as much fun as any other part of the game. I personally love using Acrobatics to scale tall buildings, leap from them, glide across the skies of Gotham, and land with a ground-shattering smash at my quest destination. I've never played an MMO where going from point A to point B was so much fun it itself.
Another aspect I enjoyed was the integration of DC comic characters in most of the quests you undertake. I have a passing familiarity with the DC roster from days watching the Justice League/Justice League Unlimted cartoons, so seeing various heroes pop up at the end of a quest for my villain character to immolate and punch in the face provides a lot of entertainment value for me. There's a lot of voice-acting done here, including the iconic performances of Mark Hamil as the Joker and Kevin Conroy as Batman.
The game is definitely not perfect. Much of the content is behind paywalls, and Daybreak will not hesitate to remind you of this every step of the way; however, I've been able to experience much of the game without paying a penny. The combat is so-so. There are some cool combos and tricks, but a lot of it revolves around chaining together "stun lock" loops. They're satisfying to pull off at times, but the game comes to a standstill when a swarm of NPCs are doing the same to you all in unison.
Overall, I'd recommend this for folks who want a fun casual MMO experience where they can create all sorts of goofy characters and have them run around the world of DC comics.

There is so much to like about this game, such as the historical accuracy (with creative license for the sake of story, of course) and the change in Town attitudes, supplies, and contraband depending on the course of the Civil War.
It's a fresh release, so there are some bugs still being ironed out.
It follows the tropes of a family member passes away and leaves you the business and there's a rival trying to take it from you.
The problems difficulties I face most are:
Only being able to take a mix of about three or four cars, depending on the strength of the engine.  My current config is one Passenger car, one Cargo car (cargo usually needed for passenger luggage, as well as goods to sell/trade), and a Caboose for my defenders.  At my stage in the game, I can only haul 18 units of cargo (depending on weight) and 4 passengers.
My biggest challenge is Reputation.
I've not been able to participate in all but two auctions just because my standing with a certain town/faction wasn't high enough to let me in.
With all the timed missions, there's just not enough time to grind for Rep on the side.  All my time is consumed by timed missions and raising money for repairs, upgrades, and supplies.  In some towns, I can't even do their Rep missions, because they hate me so much, so they just continue to hate me.  So many Rep ups are at the cost of a different Rep down.  Yes, that's realistic, but the numbers are so close to 1:1, that it's Catch-22 all the dang time.  One time, I went back and forth between two towns, just so I can pay the Bandits' fee and get +5 Rep until they vanished.
I've "lost" at least two auctions for my company shares *just* because the town literally wouldn't let me into the auction.
Based on the Bandits, Rep costs around $100 for one point.  In my opinion, you should just be able to buy Rep outright for $1000 a point in Town.
Cars and Engines lose quality.  While this is a nice taste of realism, why the hell aren't my repairs restoring them?  We know some of these engines lasted decades, and these barely last a year.  It's a massive money drain and time consuming when you have to travel and find "the right" car to buy and upgrade...and the cannon(s) to put in it.
One of my own damn siblings sold his company shares to Mr. Evil after I found and helped him!  He said he "needed to money so badly"...but never messaged me asking for money or saying there was trouble.  Just, "oh, by the way, I sold the shares I promised you, MY RELATIVE, to the guy trying to steal/kill our family's dream, just because I needed a stiff drink.
That alone almost made me uninstall the game.  F*** you, that's messed up.
Some missions don't tell you how to accomplish them, and some of their notes don't get updated.
Example 1:  Get a necklace.  You have to meet a few people, in a few different towns.  The note only says the original quest, so you have to remember who to find in which town.  Fortunately, this isn't timed.
Example 2:  You have to "let someone vanish in an accident."  It doesn't tell you how to arrange it.  Just where to get the guy, and return to the client with news of his disappearance.  Even talking with Bandits in 50+ Rep, there's no "hey, make this guy vanish" option.  I hauled him around over a month trying to figure out where to get rid of him without visiting the town he had to arrive safely in.  Eventually, I gave up and delivered him, harming my company's shares.
I'd love to see the ability to give engine/car sets to your siblings so they can earn money and rep off-screen for you, instead of the option to join your crew.  Same for your hired staff...how about hiring them to run their own line with their own lines?  You run a Company, not just your Engine and 1-5 cars.
But, this game is still fun and I enjoy it.  It's just so frustrating right now.

After my first few playthroughs, I didn't really "get" Moon Hunters.  But as a kickstarter and beta tester, I felt compelled to give the game a chance to show its full hand.  I ended up playing for a little over 20 hours, and received several different endings including the good, the bad, and the non-combat ending.  And as I kept playing, I hoped I'd "get" the game eventually.  Well, I think I finally did get it, and I'm ambivalent about what I got.
The game is pretty and atmospheric.  The combat is decent though not challenging, and the classes are different enough that you have to change tactics to use each one effectively.  The game's real weakness is the story.  Whether or not you get to experience any of it is a total crapshoot.  Most playthroughs, it's like the game gives you two pieces each from three different jigsaw puzzles.  There's a slim chance you're going to assemble anything recognizable from them.  Every now and then, the randomness will align to allow you to complete the right encounters to build the right attributes, and talk to the right NPCs in the right order on the right day, and make a little progress.  But things don't usually align that way.  This would be somewhat tolerable if you could cumulatively build your character up over multiple playthroughs (like Rogue Legacy) but you can't. And Moon Hunters' moment-to-moment gameplay isn't compelling enough to warrant playing just for play's sake.  Sure, there are some unlockables, but I feel like I only unlocked them because I forced myself to play long enough, rather than having the unlockables motivate me to keep playing.
So I think they did a great job with the graphics and sound.  The mythology seems to have potential, and the combat is pretty smooth. I hope Kitfox will take these pieces and make a coherent game with them someday.

I feel compelled to leave a review because I'm seeing a lot of misinformation about how this game "takes an hour to complete". That's completely untrue. You can get to the boss and defeat him in an hour, but you won't "complete" the game in a single run. There are multiple zone types that are only unlocked by beating the game multiple times. There are multiple encounters that can only be attempted if you have certain Traits, and you won't have every trait on every character.
Roguelike players will have been trained to expect multiple failures before "beating" the game, but Moon Hunters isn't about that. It's a game about stories, and you can't see the whole story without playing through the game multiple times.

There are a lot of things to like about Moon Hunters. The game is fun to play. If you like 2D action/adventure games, like Zelda or Diablo, I think you will have a lot of fun with the game. The controls are pretty simple but are responsive. The game works better as a co-op game but you can still have fun with the game in single player. Moon Hunters probably works best in group settings where some of the players aren't experienced gamers since the game is pretty easy overall.
The story is interesting and I like that every decision you make has an effect on gameplay as well as the ending. Each decision you make gives you stat boosts that help you in the game. When you finish the game you also get a little story about your journey telling the legend of your hero. This legend gives you details about what happened to your hero after your journey. Combine this with great music and good graphics and Moon Hunters creates an engaging environment.
The biggest problem with the game is that each game is quite short (30 minutes to one and a half hours). This means you will quickly start running into repeated material. While the worlds appear to be randomly generated, the events that you encounter start to repeat themselves quite a bit. A good example is that the final boss of the game seems to always be the same (unless I have yet to find events that change the final boss battle). While this doesn't ruin the game, it keeps it from being as good as it could have been.
If you like 2D action/adventure games you should enjoy Moon Hunters. If you want to fully explore the game's world you can get quite a bit out of the game. If you don't like to repeat a lot of material though you may not get as much out of the game as you were expecting.
Note: I received a review copy from the developers but received no other compensation for this review.

Moon Hunters might be described as a co-op personality test, but its beautifully painted environments, evocative soundtrack, and wonderfully malleable narrative make it so much more than that. As a kickstarter backer, I'm thrilled by the sheer amount of mythology and personality that's been packed into this game, not to mention the subtle humour and surprising twists in the narrative that kept me constantly engaged. The reputation system, which adorns you with particular traits based on your in game decisions, is a key driving force behind Moon Hunters' replay value because it makes one playthrough vastly different from another. What makes the experience slightly repetitive at times is the combat, due to its simplicity and the fact that enemies attack in groups and follow you relentlessly, and occasionally the geographical appearance of certain areas is the same. Furthermore there are some random bugs and the game crashed very rarely, but that didn't detract from the overall experience. Moon Hunters has some serious staying power and I adore its sensitive exploration of abandoned religions and traditions-especially one that focused on something that humanity has been fascinated with for centuries, the moon.
What a magnificent story.

have spoiled me.
is a reasonably good HOG with familiar story elements, adequate length, maybe a bit on the short side, and graphics and sound up to the genre standard.
What it lacks are all the extras that a modern HO game tends to have.  There's no map.  There's no secret collectibles.  No achievements.  No trading cards.  Essentially no puzzles or minigames worthy of the name.  There's just the story, the HO scenes, and running objects back and forth from place to place in order to progress.  This is hidden-object gaming pared back to its core form, but those core elements are quite decently done.
The hidden-object experience is here, and quite satisfactory, once you look past the absence of all the bells and whistles that other HO games have trained us to expect.  That's good enough for me to recommend it.

Brothers uses an interesting gameplay mechanic in that you control both brothers simultaneously, one with the left joystick and the other with the right joystick. Now, there are some "puzzles" that test your brain's ability to control two characters at once, and this is where the game feels really fresh and cool.
The game has a wonderful, somewhat sad, but heartfelt story.  The art style and music are very well done, and they invoke the correct emotions at the correct times.
This game is very short; I believe it took me under 4 hours to complete.  The short journey you take place in is well worth the small admission price, and the only gripe is that it was over so fast.
Definitely recommend this game.  Don't forget you need a controller!

Defiance: a mix of bullets, rockets, grenades, ATVs, cars, buggies and Hellbugs.
I've heard alot of people say it sucks, and, admittedly, it has some shortcomings. However, I find Defiance is not for everybody, as many are too used to fantasy MMOs, or the more realism-focused Call of Duty series.
Overall, I like Defiance. The weapons are customizable, the vehicles are plenty, and road rage is ALWAYS a valid option in the field. I would say one of the things it needs is a menu showing the built-up bonuses one accrues from using weapons and vehicles consistently (like the Reload, Recoil, and Fire Rate bonuses on weapons).

A cult favorite of mine, and the first MMO to ever coincide with a live-action TV show, Defiance is a unique MMO to say the least. Trion Worlds is most famous for there other MMO, Rift, however Defiance features a unique blend of open-world combat, free-roaming and large scale boss fights. In terms of weapons, think of Borderlands. Defiance has hundreds if not thousands of different weapons, shields, and more.
The game also sports a vast collection of vehicles to chose from including a limited edition 2013 Dodge Charger specifically designed for the vast and rugged terrains of Defiance. There is also a huge amount of character creation, including tons of in game armour's along with some purchasable items such as hats, armour's, shields and more. The grind is real, but it's not a big issue in Defiance because the ranking system is fairly balanced and easy to rank up.
I'll admit that the quests are a bit repetitive feeling, but the overall game is very enjoyable and it remains in my top 5 MMO's I have played thus far.

Krater is a game I really want to like, although it has some shortcomings.
First, the postitives:
+ post-apocalyptic, yet "fresh" setting (a krater in future Sweden)
+ nice art style
+ doesn't take itself too serious (also some nice pop-cultural references)
+ very cool system to modify skills and chars (via boosts/implants)
+ crafting system
+ "meaty" crits and nice fx
+ teleport to world map from everywhere
+ good loot is scarce (a plus in my book)
+ great name generator
Now the not-so-positives:
- booooring dungeons (only a few tile sets and it gets repetitive fast), almost no interactive objects or surprises and only a few rare special bosses
- much back-tracking if you want to explore the whole map
- opponents are just static groups in regular intervals in the dungeons
- not much tactic involved, more like button-smashing
- chars aren't really unique (with the exception of the DLC chars), they are randomly assembled and you can hire them in many towns
- chars have limited levels, which you can expand with money to a max of lvl 15 (which you can reach in maybe 2h per char), after that there is no char evolution other than gear/implants
That being said, this game would have had huge potential. Better maps and more interesting battles would have helped much. It just feels too generic as is.
Imo, the best thing would have been, if the game had had turn-based or rtwp-combat with a deeper skill system. I'm sure it would have been a  (indie) success with that.

Let's have an actual review for this game:
Despite my minimal hours on this game I have completed the Campaign and have played my fair share of multiplayer.
Rather than showing my bias and one sided opinion on this game I will elaborate on the pros and cons.
I bought this game with Infinite Warefare and do not regret it. The campaign is undoubtedly the best part; it is 100% true to the original, which I played for hundreds of hours on my xbox 360. With the exitement of the Death From Above mission to the iconic All Ghillied Up mission.
The multiplayer in this game is probably the biggest let down. Although there were no performance issues; there is just nobody playing this game.
Due to the unpopularity of Call of Duty on PC, and by releasing it with the very unpopular Infinite Warfare, there are very clear reasons as to why there is nobody playing this game on PC. Perhaps if they had initially released it as a standalone game there could have been a chance for this game. But we can't dwell on something that didn't happen. However, if you are playing with friends or against bots the multiplayer is ultimatley brilliant and extremely fun. Yet repetitive, but I suppose that is just an added feature of Call of Duty multiplayer, no matter what game it is. If you do end up finding a game you will find that you earn COD points.
If you are surprised by this, I am shocked. A Call of Duty game in 2017 without micro transactions? I do not think so. However, unlike its predecessor Black Ops 3, the added weapons are actually achievable without spending any money. It may take a while, especially with the inability to find a game, it WILL take a while.
I had no issue of running this game, I run at around 150fps and it is smooth and not junky at all. The graphics are all that was promised if not more. Running at ultra settings as well as the lowest settings, this game is absolutley and undeniably beautiful. Again, despite all of the negative comments of the poor porting; I had absolutley no issue running this game. And perhaps with some settings adjustments or anything, you should be able to run it smoothly.
In all honesty I think all the negative comments are complaining because it is easy to trash Call of Duty nowadays.
I genuinely enjoy this game, and hopefully if you decide to buy it, you will too.

First, let me state this is a pretty fun game.  I bought it when it was 50% off ($12.49) and I have enjoyed every minute of it.  What I like most is it provides you with a different type of game playing style.  A little RPG mixed in with a little bit of management style gamind and garnished with a tad of train simulator.  The graphics are pretty good for the game type and minus a few bugs I list below the playability is pretty nice. The combat is pretty unique and I like that you can perform combat while the train is moving or not.  It adds for a new dynamic. The storyline is pretty good as well, however I think it could have been drawn out a little longer to give you more gameplay time in the campaign.  Now for some of the not so likeable features.
There area few bugs the developers are apparently aware of such as enemies getting stuck in certain comabt maps which really draws from the excitement in the game, especially the combat.
I'd like to go over a few of the key aspects of the game and what I liked and didn't like about them.
- I really loved this aspect of the game. It allowed me to really hone the characters to my gaming style.  There are quite a few abilities you or your companions can have such as gunslinger or marksman which give you bonuses with revolvers or rifles. Then there are abilities that help you run or repair your locomotive, fight fires, heal, and so on.  You can pick up different crew members along the way, paying for most of them of course, that can have a variety of these skills.
- There is a pretty wide range of equipment you can choose from however I think this is an area for improvement.  There are quite a few varieties of revolvers and rifles, however there is very little differences between most of them. One of the biggest missed opportunities here is the range of your weapons and their effectiveness at different ranges.  They are pretty much all th same.  You have the same range for a pistol at the same accuracy as a rifle. Really there is no difference except the damage they do and the amount of ammo. It would have been better to have a range scale for each weapon so that as your range increased your % chance to hit and damage were adjusted accordingly by firearm and type.  I think this would have made comabt mush more enjoyable and realistic.
They also included the gatlin gun and another automatic fire weapon and I think the implementation of those was handled quite well.
- I've noted some of my issues with combat previously, however another 'missed opportunity' is cover.  There really doesn't appear to be any, except for the bad guys who can hide behind a tree stump and crates.  It seems the bullets just rip tight through the train no matter how high you have the armor level which I think is more for the train not taking damage than you! I may be missing something here but this defintely needs to be improved.
Why are the native americans the only ones attacking me on horseback?  Not all train robbers blocked the track with rocks, which by the way, I shoudl be able to destroy with the dynamite!  I would have made the rock barriers have occurred much less often and increased the escape distance to allow more horseback chase fights.
Another improvement could be made by allowing your crew to exit the train to fight and make use of the same cover used by the outlaws or to perform flanking maneuvers to get a better sight on your target. This would also add another element to the game which would be to get your characters back on board the train if you try to out run them.
- I think overall the developers did a nice job here.  The trading is pretty straight forward and implemented nicely.
- The locomotives are implemented very well and you have the ability to upgrade them to get more power or durability, etc.  I would have like to have seen more diversity with them.
There are a few different types of carriages.  Some carry cargo some carry people and some have specific purposes such as the hospital car.  There are also cabooses which carry your crew and you can mount the gatlin guns where ever there are gun mounts.
There are a couple of areas that really need attention here as well. First, you can only have one caboose. Now I know that sounds stupid "A train only has one caboose" duh, but this is the ONLY way you can carry crew.  Now you can place you crew anywhere in the train, but the largest caboose only carries 4 crew members. A typical gunfight has 20 enemies sometimes with the same or better firepower than you and with much better cover. So your crew has to be REALLY powerful or your need numbers which you just can't have with only a single 4 crew caboose. Once again, maybe I missed something here it's very possible as I only played it through one time ( about 20 hours playtime)
It would have been nice to see gun cars or the ability to add two small cabooses (2 crew each) and place them at different points in the train for better coverage.
- The story is very well put together and I think they have really set themselves up for a Bounty Train 2.  The entire story and map takes place east of the Mississippi River and your goal is to take back the company your father started. There is the greedy train baron that is your nemesis throughout the game and you have to work hard to race for controlling shares in your father's company and you have to reunite your family during this process.
Reuniting your family happens in the first hour or two of the game.  I think this should have been drawn out across the campaign better. After that it is basically a mad rush to get money so yo can get better stuff.  There are what seems to be auction events at regular intervals or specific dates in the game where you can get back shares of your company.  When these do pop up its a mad rush to gain influence in that city and come up with the funds for the auction.  This gets repetative pretty quickly. There doesn't seem to be any real logic to the auctions and after one or two your pretty much know how much the shares will go for and even though there are other 'moguls' involved in the bidding they never win and it is always between you and your nemesis.
There are a few non-shares auctions which allow you to buy up property in the various cities.  I really liked this aspect as it allows you to expand your little empire and have an alternate source of funds, however those are few and far in between.  Another missed opportunity here I think.  This could have also brought another dynamic to the game by allowing you to 'help' your business out by moving passnegers or cargo to/from cities where your businesses are located.
I know it looks liek there are a like of bad aspects to the game, however I still had a blast playing it and if you can pick it up for $12 then I highly recommend you doing it. If they ever develop BT 2 and/or make some improvements  to the existing one then I think it would be worth the full price.

Bounty Train is actually a really lovely game. You follow the story of Walter trying to get back his father's railroad company from some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who wants to destroy natives.
Pros
+Very realistic to how trains worked back in those days
+Missions are very nice to do and not just simple and linear there's actually many choices you can pick
+Trading varies from city to city depending on what's in 'shortage' therefore will sell for more etc. (It's not just that's the base price in this city, it fluctuates which is pretty awesome).
+In game events actually matter (ie. more authorities patrolling the borders when♥♥♥♥♥♥happens therefore harder to smuggle)
+A really good map of all different cities
+Passengers, traded goods, jobs that cities can provide for you all give you good money
+Requires you to actually think and plan out your journey and maximise each trip
Cons
- The biggest problem I had is that it's repetitive sometimes. Autosave doesn't always work and if you f*ck up along the way you have to start from your last save. In my case I've had to redo sometimes 6 months worth of in game time because I keep forgetting the autosave feature doesn't always work. This was the main frustrating point of the game.
- Coal is sketchy to buy as they don't consider decimal points. (If you have 3.8/5 tons you MUST buy 2 tons to fill it to 5 wasting 0.8 tons and your money. This means the coal's auto buy feature is useless and you must manually buy coal everytime at the market. (Hopefully this will be fixed)
- Train malfunctions to my knowledge apply randomly regardless of whether you fully upgrade your train or not. This was pretty annoying to deal with.
- Repair and hospital time is AGES. It can take 1-4 days to fix your people or repair your train.
All in all a good game. A few things that can be looked over or perhaps redone.

You have to constatnly end the game via Task Manager and reload. Also the penalties and chance of getting caught are NOT at all balanced. I had the medium cargo car with full bars on the concealed compartment skill. ! had two crates of guns in with tobacco, 69% chance of being caught. Same city with a full load of guns was 69%, as well. When you are caught, your rep drops immensely your first offfense, no one will do business with you in that city and it takes FOREVER to reclaim good rep.

I've read alot of reviews claiming that dcuo's free to play model is false advertising but this couldn't be further from the truth.
The amount of time it would take you to complete all the free content could range anywhere from 40 hours to hundereds depending on whether or not you go for all the feats or just rush through the content. When dcuo was released it was a $60 release that sold very well, held a strong playerbase for many years and went free to play to offer players a way to experience the game without having to invest to see if they would like it first.
but as all free to play games will, dcuo has its ways of genereting a profit to pay it's dev team, this is broken down into episodes you can purchase that act as dlc's. none of these effect the base game. all orignial content as well as the first two dlcs are completely free. may even be more but i have paid to have a membership since the switch to f2p so i can't say exactly how many dlc's are part of the free package.
The only valid argument about how bad the f2p model is comes from the fact that they do limit the mount of ingame cash you can carry on your character as a free member. this is annoying but not hindering to progression, since anything you would buy with in game cash is purely cosmetic aside from gear mods which you don't need until you get into the dlc's anyways.
Now.......to the review.
i've played thousands upon thousands of games in my life time, none of which can hold a candle to dcuo. when i tried to get my fiance to play it she thought it was boring the first few hours. fast forward three years and she's clocked over a thousand hours and wont play anything else.
the exact same thing happend to my buddy when i showed it to him, he wasn't sure about it the first couple days, now dcuo is his all time favorite game. also putting in over a thousand hours.
For an mmo the combat is fast and fun. the movement is in the vien of games like protoype and infamous where you can fly, freerun, or zip around at lighting speeds like the flash. each power is unique and requires a different mind set while using them, content pacing is good and story development is colorful and fully voice acted from the tutorial to the latest dlc. only reading you have to do is when your choosing your skills/powers.
PVP shines in dcuo, though buggy at times it plays more like a arcade fighter then your typical mmo. Where blocking at the right times and following up with a hard hitting combo will reign supreme over following a predetemed skill rotation.
character customization is better here then any game i've played. your "styles" are choosen and edited seperately from your gear. so you never have to choose between looking the way you want and being geared with the right equipment. in this case you can have your cake and eat it too. this leads to a ton of inspired characters, leading to many nights that had me and my friends flying around for hours just checking out everyones characters.
as far as end game content goes, its never a dull moment. the content will bring you defeat if your not paying attention, but it never means more then respawning and trying the fight over again. with each tier of gear you get drastically stronger and it gives the vibes of something quite similar to reaching that next level of super sayian if you where goku.

Moon Hunters is an aesthetically driven rogue-like where the story is also randomly generated and iteratively unlocked as you re-play more and more rounds.

If you die early in your round often, it's hard to unlock future elements of the game. Also, your character attracts monsters like crazy and it's difficult to stealth or avoid them if your health is low.
I am still recommending this game because I do think it was ambitious in its design and I can see how all the characters strengths integrate really well in the multiplayer version. I think this game works best as it was originally designed but the single-player combat experience is not fun for me.

Moon Hunters is a procedural mythology game about weaving stories, defining characters, fighting monsters, uncovering secrets, and telling tales. It's a lot of fun, looks beautiful, and has a gorgeous sound track.
As a little extra: Moon Hunters understands a lot about how to make procedural generation more meaningful. In most procedural RPGs, you come across little events or random encounters, and that's it. That feels underwhelming - it's a bit like being dealt a hand of cards. You might not have seen those cards in that combination before, but it doesn't make it special. Moon Hunters is a bit more like a tarot reading. The encounters you have become compiled into who your character is and what they're doing, and they become part of a little story about you. So you didn't just come across a chest with a thing in - because you were Patient, you meditated under a tree and understood more about your quest for vengeance. Or you didn't. Or you found a cat instead and that was way cuter.

Haunted Past: Realm of Ghosts is one of these games in my backlog that I decided to play after stumbling upon it on Big Fish games, when I was adding to Neoseeker the series Haunted Manor. Haunted Past was the game just under. When I realized that I had it in my library, I told myself why not?
So far, I liked the plot. I also liked the twist in the game. Sure, it's not the plot of the year. But at least, you're not discovering the truth early on.
The gameplay is the standard one: find items, use them, clear hidden objects scenes and solve puzzles. However, here, you have a special feature: the ghost realm. Indeed, through mirrors, you can access the same room but in another realm and in its previous state. Items found there can't be brought back with you to the real world, so you have to hid them in the ghost room and to find them in the real world. While it's true that these areas are cleared fairly quick, it's still a nice way to influence the world (example: a cushion was put in the real room but in the ghost realm, it's not there. So you use your brain to make one with the items hidden in it... and tadaaa, the cushion in the real world will have them!). Also, to help you, each time a room is totally cleared, a message is shown. And last but not least, some doors are closed because of evil magic/spirit. They can be opened by doing the right glyph you'll find around...
Everything is easy, apart for same areas that you can't really see. It might have been influenced by the weather here, as it was a little sunny and that I had to move my screen to find a correct angle (as I'm playing hidden objects games on my laptop mainly).
The graphics are quite good, very darker in the real world, as the estate is abandoned but when you go to the ghost realm, it's very bright. The soundtrack is also good.
In other words, for 5 bucks, you have a good little casual adventure game, with a good plot, good graphics and interesting features. It would be sad for you to miss it. Go for it, whether it's full price or discounted.

I hesitate to refer to Brothers as a game. You control two characters simultaneously, and that is a bit of a challenge at first. But the focus is more on the story and the world than anything I would recognize as gameplay. The puzzles are simple and quick, which is fantastic, because anything more complex would have slowed down the revealing of the majestic and amazing world. It is short, two to three hours for most I'd imagine. This is not meant to be played across multiple sittings. The way the story unfolds, I couldn't imagine going cold and coming back to it a week later. To me it is more of an interactive art piece, played via characters drawn with simple but effective strokes, instilling genuine emotion and empathy in the viewer. Brothers is fantastic in many ways, but for me two elements are the crown jewels. The beautifully crafted fantasy world, slowly revealed in its awesome grandeur, is one. The other is the wonderful relationship between the two brothers. You understand why they must do what the plot has them doing. Their trust and love for one another is the only thing that sees them through, and the connection that they share is made real to the player by the end. This isn't just a game to be played, it is a experience to be enjoyed and shared. I cannot compare this to many other games, but to me, it was like reading a good book. I was left with thoughtful emotional introspection and an internal analytical discussion about the nature of storytelling. I whole-heartedly recommend Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons.

As far as hidden object games go, it's a decent one for the collection.
The HOG genre are all very similar in terms of plot lines and gameplay, so it's hard to review these kind of games in detail without all of these reviews sounding the same.
The plots are always treasure hunters, old time detectives or historians looking for a special artifact, a murderer or just plain ol' answers. They're always set in spooky houses, old ruins or other planes of existence. History is revealed, secrets are unraveled and generally just all that kind of stuff really.
Despite hidden object games being all very similar to each other, they are a guilty pleasure of mine as i do just enjoy the hidden object scenes and puzzles you find in these games.
This one is set in haunted house. You need to find what happened, whose behind it and destroy the evil entity. The story was interesting, it was nothing amazing but it kept me playing which is always good.
In terms of puzzles, there wasn't really any in this one. It was more so just clear each room and move on. I quite liked the pace of the game as i was only looking for a short few hour game to complete so it worked for me!
This game also has an interesting feature of being able to switch between two planes of existence. You can find items you need in the other realm and hide them somewhere for you to find in the real world. This kind of switches the gameplay up a little bit and it's always nice to play the slightly more unique HOGs.
In terms of the object finding, the scenes weren't too cluttered to the point your eyes hurt, and the items were well blended into the scenes. So all around good on that part in my opinion.
All in all it's a decent one, if you enjoy the HOG genre then this is definitely one you can whiz through and add to pile.
TL;DR : It's decent for a hidden object game, pretty standard but it's enjoyable.

I have played on and off for a few years, it has come a long way since it came out, it offers a good amount of gameplay. It is likely what you would expect from a free to play game, a well made one. There are many things you can unlock and earn, albeit through some grinding, you will notice that a few weapons are different in their behavoir but some "endgame" or final unlock weapons in a catagory are not at all some massive upgrade (some), I personally feel this is good as this requires a crazy amount of grinding to get them, I can say that the basic equipment you get can let you go on a rampage or any other gun if you use it right (even the tiny baby pistol I unlocked let me rack up some kills in one life, mostly from sneaking behind a few squads though). The game is very skill based, you will have some matches where you mop the floor with the opposing side, and other matches where you find yourself spending half the time respawning. An important bit is to upgrade your guns as this is the main way to make a gun in a catagory op. A good bit is that you can also pick up any dropped weapon from a dead comrade of enemy soldier, which lets you have a good bit of fun playing around with their gun. Aside from the infantry aspect there are motorized, tanks, and planes that will come and affect your game. motorized are fairly important for of course getting around quickly, some are armoured and others have AA guns, you can go find out yourself, it will take time to unlock these. Tanks come in a few teirs from light to heavy and tank destroyers, these are kind of WWII common sense in, done expect your american training tank with only machine guns to takeout a german king tiger tank. the tank combat is good and easy to learn and get into, but always beware of the guy who is using his tank as a giant sniper rifle, he will get his aim, and he will see you, and he will kill you and spawn trap your team, be warned. the air combat I have found is a bit...special in its controls... I say this as a War Thunder player, this game is not the smoothest in its air combat but you can easily just kill a bunch of ground targets with little resistance 4/5 times, air to air combat is greatly satisfying but again, do not attack a fighter with your light scout plane and be surprised when you end up falling out the sky in flames, but be happy when you take them down. All vehicals can also be stolen when they are not manned, for example you sneak up on a tank and the drive pokes his head you to get a good view of the area, you happen to fill said head with a bullet, you can "unlock" his tank and drive it around freely, same with a plane, rare but it happens if there are a few airmen in a game, one will land and try to repair their plane, that is a prime moment to show them you want to prove your ability to fly too, and possible shoot them down once they have spawned it. The game is objective base where you capture and hold and capture several points till you either take the map or it can become a battle of attrition where both sides are too good in defending two opposing points, this results in your team killing the other team till all the resources or tokens of one team is gone. war is fun but really doesn't matter unless you are commanding the war or using the bonus for playing a faction you don't usually play. The game is overall a skill based game where you can mop the floor with your first gun while seeing the whole of the enemy faction your fighting have top quality weapons. of course each gun is ment to be used differently, don't snipe with a pistol at a guy with a fully buffed sniper rifle from 1000m away and complain when somehow he shoots you dead. when it comes to vehicles, land and air, they do matter but infantry gameplay is very flexable and you can get what you want and use it forever if you like it. I would recommend this game you may indeed love it or find it boring as it is not always super intense combat, sometimes you have to run for a few minutes to get into the action, you may find it pay to win and that is yes but not really true (excluding vehicles cause dat boi is pretty based on how expensive the vehicle is) you win if you know how to use your guns strengths and how to hit your target, no amount of money you spend will make your own aim and practical understanding of what a sniper/smg/pistol/rocket launcher/battle rifle/assault rifle (StG44) is ment to be used , although yeah a scope will help but only in certain situations. It is about as fun as you can make it, and can take a bit to get a good understanding of the game. It is a good game, not the best for me personally but it does draw me back to play a few matches every month or when I see an update, a good variety and I personally have fun when I jump in a match for an hour or two. only thing are unlocks and the veteran membership teasing you about how much you can earn more then without it, unlocks do go on 25-50% discount, I've picked up enough guns to know which one I wanted and I unlocked it, so the crazy grinds are much to me as I know what I want and focus on just those, so I am personally satisfied with the game, but damnit stop telling me how good veteran membership is. 8/10 don't tease me about veteran anymore unless I want to know it'll cut grinding in half, please stop.

game doesn't overly appeal to me, as it just tends to be a grindfest, which is what SOE MMORPGs are known for. SWG, EQ, EQ2 all were focused on grinding, and DCUO is no different.
This game seems fairly large, however is only two main adventure zones. You can play in Gotham, or Metropolis, or travel between them. Missions will take you to both cities, although I do use the term "Missions" lightly since there isn't really a storyline. Sure, there might be some vague story buried under the grind, but nothing that's going to reach out and grab you.
You do have the option of being a good guy, or a villain, which is unique, but even as a bad guy, you still feel like a good guy, since the missions tend to revolve around stopping an alien invasion and beating up other criminals for one reason or another. You don't really do anything bad! except plant bombs on cops...i guess there's that.
Still, if you are a huge fan of comics(Particularly DC comics) and love MMORPGs, then give the game a shot. It's not as interesting as Champions Online, but it does look better and has a setting that maybe more familiar to more players than the champions setting.

Haunted Past tells a simple, yet exciting ghost story with an excellent atmosphere in the form of a hidden object game with a few nice mechanics.
A female protagonist in a haunted house unravelling a ghost story is basically hidden object game making 101. What makes Haunted Past: Realm of Ghosts different is how the developers made sure that the player is interested and invested in their tale.
Their greatest tool was the pacing, which involves just enough backtracking to shake the feeling of being stuck in a corridor, but not too much to make anyone run around in circles (thanks to the room clearance indicators).
The game has no traditional puzzles, only item gathering point ‘n’ click style, and lots and lots of hidden object scenes. These two elements are often combined into single-room challenges, called ghost rooms, where you must find and hide items to use them later in the normal world.
Sadly, not even this abundance of hidden object scenes could save the play time that barely reaches two hours, which may be too short even for such an engaging game.

That describes what I am feeling about the game. First, it isn't a bad HOG. But it's very short (my 8 hours of playtime were caused by me, getting some rest and dozing off). Second the story is interesting. But the riddles and puzzles are quite easy to solve, some of them are literally self solving. The graphics look great, but some of the full screen animations do lag and the sound is at times, best described as... "crunchy" - though the voiceacting was very pretty.
If I follow my own Rules and Regulations this game lies in the 50% area, because there are good and bad things in the game, overall it would be a "Not Recommended" for this game. Which actually I will give. To clarify my stance with this game I will give the Pros and Cons and then describe why I don't recommend the game.
Given the age of the game, this game isn't all bad - but it lacks a lot which games of the genre and this age already had, there are a lot of similar games which did truly build up a suspense. The game also isn't quite perfect on case of technology, the lagging was encountered on all of my machines. The crunchy sound might have to do with some of the effect filters used, to make the voices sound ghostly. The too easy puzzles/riddles were only a small anoyance compared to the really short playtime (actually about two hours).
All in all this game is nestled in the 45 to 50 % Value, because all of the encountered problems and annoyances. If you want at all to try this one out, try to get it bundled, or at a sale. But, please don't make the mistake to gift this game to a newby of the genre, he might lose his interest in HOGs forever...

Haunted Past is another game from the developer of Princess Isabella, Gogii Games, and is pretty clearly a more recent creation. The graphics are cleaner, the art is better, and the scenes are more detailed in terms of animation and sound. It also feels like a more mature game in tone and design. The haunted house motif is done without jumpscares or loud stingers, and the puzzles are quite a bit more challenging than the ones in Isabella. It's a very polished game, though still a bit dated. One strange omission I should mention is that there's no map, and thus no fast-travel between rooms, but the game flow is quite linear and they had the good sense to include a few shortcuts where backtracking is needed.
Gameplay is a lot of point-and-click puzzling through rooms, with the hidden object scenes almost a secondary feature. Worth noting that with the better graphics, the hidden object scenes are actually easier since everything is more distinct. The big gimmick of the game is the "spirit world", which is alternate ghostly versions of rooms where you can find additional items. Not only do you have to find the items, you have to "hide" them in a place you can retrieve them in the real world, because ghosts will steal them or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ I don't remember but it was dumb. These aren't particularly challenging puzzles but they add a little much-appreciated variety. Unfortunately, the main draw of the game, the puzzles, suffer from some really obnoxious design. Two examples:
- You have to match up the birth and death years on some funerary urns. These dates are on gravestones in the cemetery, but finding them isn't enough. You HAVE to find three pieces of paper and three pieces of charcoal to make rubbings of the gravestones, and THEN you can match up the dates. It's a completely unnecessary step that got me stuck for awhile because I had no idea why the urns wouldn't let me move♥♥♥♥♥♥around.
- You can't use items on other items directly, which lead to a couple aggravating situations where you have to use a piece of paper on a SPECIFIC background spot to lay it down, and then use a pencil or whatever on it to get the thing you're trying to do done.
If you can deal with some outdated puzzle design, this is a solid 2-hour game that actually falls more on the point-and-click end of the spectrum than hidden object, but should suffice for either.

I only reccomend getting this game in a bundle or on sale, do not pay full price for it!
Let's get the worst part out of the way first, why you should not pay full price for it. You can see by my hours played that this is not a very long game. It's by no means a bad one but it is short so if you want short entertainment, a few dollars dropped on this in a bundle with other games is worth it. Otherwise, do not pay full asking price because it is not worth it.
That being said, it is a very fun hidden object game. In terms of hidden object scenes (HOGs) there are a handful of them but not so many that they become annoying. This game is very inventory item heavy in that a lot of game play is finding an item to use later on. One good feature is that areas will have an Area Cleared banner on the top of the screen after everything is done in the area so you don't have to worry about not knowing if you missed something or not. There arn't a ton of puzzles compared to other HOG games but there are some fun little puzzles occasionally.
A main mechanic in this game is traveling back in time through reflective surfaces to obtain items in the past, hide them and get them in the future. Sometimes this doesn't make sense logically (you hide some in a baby's crib so sometime between the past and the future no one thought to check it?) but since when were HOG games a place for logic? This is a neat little feature but I feel they could have done some more with the time traveling part other than just hiding items like maybe areas only reachable in the past due to things breaking.
Storywise it's a bit typical, dead mother, haunted house... You get more story from reading the diary and papers you find laying around otherwise the story can pretty much be ignored. The voice acting isn't too bad and I found it slightly better quality than most other HOG games.
Graphically this game isn't HD quality but it's not Minecraft pixelated level graphics either. I'd say 7/10 around since it's not so bad that it hurt the hidden object scences but not high enough quality to make that a selling point.
I noticed maybe two annoying things, one, the hidden objects often have a small clickable area so you need to be precise in your clicks. The other is if you spam using an item (I KNOW THIS ITEM WORKS HERE STOP TELLING ME OTHERWISE GAME) it will keep playing the "this isn't going to work" message lines as many times as you clicked. Which can be annoying when you finally give in to the games logic and want to click the area to see what hint it gives you.
One really nice feature is that custom difficulty options it gives you. You have about three options for the most part on how long the hint button recharges as well as how long until you can skip a puzzle and if active areas glow. It's nice if you want certain things to be easier and others to be harder like if you like not using hints but hate puzzles and want those to be skippable faster. That is a nice feature.
Overall its a good fun game that will entertain you for one night and then you'll hide it in your Steam library and forget all about it.
