On launch day there were bugs that were deal breakers for some players.  For me in particular I had a game breaking issue when I tried to remap the keyboard and mouse keybindings.  The developers at Kitfox Games have since fixed a large number bugs and performance issues and even provided a full additional iteration on online multiplayer functionality.
Bugs at launch asside, MoonHunters is excellent in many ways.  It has very pretty visual artwork and music.  It has a play time that is shorter than a full FTL run, but like FTL you really don't experience the entirety of the game without replaying it quite a bit.  There are multiple endings and many locations impossible to experience in even a few playthroughs.  Each time you play your choices become a legacy for you that then gets written in the stars of the game, and your choices affect what happens to you in the game.  It's cool how in future playthroughs you see statues honoring your previous heros.
This game breaks the mold in many ways.  Mechanically there is no traditional level up system.  Instead your characters gradually gain stats and purchase abilities over the course of a playthrough.  Neither is there death in the traditional sense.  Rather, if your character dies you simply crawl away skipping the rest of that location and unable to gain any additional benefits from it.  In addition, all your choices in the game contribute to your character's personality. This then is factored into how you are able to interact with characters and events creating a noticably reactive world.
As you can likely see in the art this game is not set in a world of high fantasy or sci-fi, but rather one that is built around mythologies of ancient Mesopotamia and especially the Epic of Gilgamesh. This setting is a welcome breath of fresh air.
Visually the game looks amazing, somehow managing to use both pixel art sprites and detailed (what I think is considered) watercolor portraits and backgrounds.  Give the soundtrack a listen as well and you will find that it is nothing to sneeze at.
Multiplayer mode is very fun.  In single player mode I often go in and out of battles while maintaining max health.  Not to say that it's easy, you need to be focused and patient to do so, but on multiplayer I often find myself and teammates with less than half health and enjoying the game all the more for the tension it creates.
I consider this game well rounded.  I'm not sure how else to say it.  There's a lot of meat to it, like a lot of different aspects of the game are strong.  Many games fall short in one area or another, but this game has good art, music, story, choices, combat, and replayability.  It does all this without feeling like any of its strong points are borrowed from other games.
The mystery of the misssing Moon Goddess keeps me coming back right now, but even after I know the mystery I'm sure I will want to come back to enjoy smashing pots, flirting with npcs, and fighting all manner of strange beasts with my friends.

is a tactical action RPG set in post-apocalyptic Sweden.  Sounds awesome, right?  Well, with a little more patching I think it could be, but right now the game is far too buggy to recommend.
The first thing you'll notice is that despite looking and playing like a
mod, this game runs like♥♥♥♥♥  The framerate is lower than one would expect given the graphical complexity and apparent number of objects on screen.  This isn't game breaking, but it's still unpleasant to look at.
The cursor is insane.  Its actual position does not match up with the arrow point, and its location is inconsistent: sometimes it will be a few pixels above the point, sometimes it's on the arrow's shaft.  This can be really jarring before you realise what's going on, and almost convinced me to quit before I figured it out.  There's also noticeable input lag, which is not something you want in a real time tactics game.  This input lag really shines when a character dies, as the camera does not automatically center on the next character, so you have to waste precious milliseconds double clicking a portrait so that you can continue commanding or start running away.  These issues make it needlessly difficult to micromanage the troops and greatly diminish the game's tactical aspect.
Aside from that,
has potential.  The level-up method is quirky and allows for a good amount of character customization.  The setting is interesting and the game world is pretty big.  Maybe the developer will eventually patch out the problems, but until then I don't recommend this game.

I've bought Krater as Early Access. And I can tell you that this game was one of the reasons why I am now completely cured of this Early Access. It looked promising, so promising in fact that I bought the unfinished product, even if this kind of game is not my cup of tea. Oh boy, was I disappointed.
I will not speak about game mechanics, since there are already enough well written reviews covering that up. I will only tell why you should not buy this game, not matter how cheap it is sold in the next sale.

The devs fixed some smaller things, forcing me to start over and over again, because everytime the update broke my save games. It still crashes, it still has problems with the webcode. But to me and other players one of the biggest problems of the game is the tiny font. As in "You need the Hubble telescope to read things" tiny. You can barely read item descriptions and crafting becomes a nice game of "squint & guess". People were complaining about this since the beta, but the devs just give a crap.
This game was already abandoned shortly after its release. The tiny font thing was never adressed, most of the bugs were never adressed. They released a single player character for 6 €, cashed in an went off to never look back.
Sadly, with a bit more work Krater could have earned a recommendation easily. It has charm, a great soundtrack, tons of fun loot, a nice crafting system and a great soundtrack. It even looks nice. Unfortunately the devs decided to leave this game alone and, considering Kraters still unfinished state, you should too.

I feel bad for Krater
You don't have to be good at RPG's or even played Krater as a whole game to notice that it has some great missed potentials.
It just makes me sad to see it there on my desktop catching dust never having been played again after four tries. But I am not gonna let you stay in the dark about why it's that way;
point 1 - the freedom you get from it
In Krater, you have the freedom to pick from 4 different classes, build a team out of them however it pleases you, change the loadout of your characters and get to explore an everchanging postapocalyptic version of what seems to be Sweden.
Now in seriousness: Some classes are just obviously overpowered compared to others (slayer to regulator) You have eight and I am not joking here, EIGHT different skills to chose from in the entire game. Each class has two available and the teams you build can have three characters maximum.
Now to the loadout. Every character has two slots in the inventory. One for a weapons and one for a gadget. Each weapon can only be used by one class and they normaly differ from one another like some flowerpots.
And finally the map: Instant traveling to a point on the map is not only a thing required to get from one end of the game to another, it's also slow as hell because you get to see a little blinky ping representing your team going wherever you told it to on the map in a speed that makes you wonder if a one-legged pensioner taking his dead pet slug for a walk would be this slow. Also the stages are either so small one could call them 'tight' or are equaly tight tunnel systems which seamingly end up in postapocalyptic Russia.

Point 2 - Atmosphere
It is obvious that a lot of love went into the graphical developement of Krater but there are still some things that just get annoying over time; NPC's mainly looking alike, a nonexistant plot and the ...ugh... music.
Whith 'a nonexistant plot' I just want to underline that the game starts with all your characters being kicked out of a town which they seem to have drunkenly terrorised and joining some kind of mercenary force which operates all over Krater. BAM raiders, freediggers, wildlife, reference to a country which cannot totaly be a reference to Germany in of itself
why is everyone having bears and mooses in ther cellars? Why am I fighting people who dig holes into their own estates? Oh wait... I am not fighting them? And why do i still not know any main villain? AND WHY HAS EVERYONE BECOME PYRO?! (ok the last one was unnecessary)
Last point was also listing the music... Well, this is what disappointed me the most about the game; there are 18 tracks in this game which are used mainly as themes for the different places, but why do 16 of them sound almost the same?! I literaly tried to memorize them as different songs with all their individualities but still: 16 of them sound like one giant synthetic smooth jazz remix, one is a rock song and one is medieval fair music, but you have practicaly no chance whatsoever to tell the first bunch ones apart! I wish they had put some more diverse tracks into this game. The atmosphere is just depressing if every place sounds the same! And I mean the bad kind of depressing. Also the music is nothing special. Not only is the sound of it never changing, it's not even good.
Although it's a failure in my eyes as well as a waste of money I just can't stop myself from feeling pitty for it.
Thanks for reading.

A fun casual game with a low level of challenge. If you're looking for something you don't have to think too hard about while playing this is a good pickup. I might wait until it's 50% on sale. This game is definitely designed for an expansion. Hopefully that'll address some of the concerns that I have.
PROS
+Creative, variety of ways to earn money
+Story is mildly interesting, and feels "natural"
+Slowly expanding explorable territory keeps you from being overwhelmed
+Interface is clean and responsive
+Good reputation system
CONS
-Bugs, none of them game breaking, but there are a LOT of them.
--Characters stop shooting at enemies
--Several NPCs in the game have bugged quests. One will eat 20k of your money for no reward.
--Enemies stay at their spawn zone and never leave. This causes huge problems because you cannot go out to fight them so you get stuck in encounters until the rocks timer counts down.
--I ended up with a fist in my inventory
-The way you win is by getting 51% of the shares. After a certain point the only way to get shares is at random auctions. I spent a great deal of time just spinning the clock waiting for these auctions to come up. I would literally sit in station and let months pass by.
-Late game is essentially broken. They need more higher level content.
-Strange design decisions. More of the game's encounter system should have been built around operating your train (driving it) while fending off attacks. In MOST attacks you have to deal with a stationary train. Sometimes you get a rock in front of your train with a timer on it. You can't do anything but wait for the timer to tick down. No explanation as to how the rocks are being moved, or why there's a timer, or why the timer has different values in different encounters.
-Characters are stuck on the train even when the train is motionless.
-Considering the pitfalls of getting caught smuggling, it's never worth doing.

This feels a lot like Sid Meier's classic Pirates! but with an 1800s rail setting - no bad thing.
I recommend it, but with some qualifications. The below review is with a full playthru on Normal mode. There are no story spoilers (but the story isn't Oscar-winning), just some gameplay spoilers.
To start with the negatives:
* Combat and urgent real-time runs are largely stats-based and thus unneccesary. Would love to see these upgraded a bit because they're great in theory but pretty boring in practise. Rare is the fight that is close: either you're beaten to a pulp early in the game or by late game you have a train loaded with gatling guns and even a mortar car that can blow even the strongest Rebel or Yankee force to bits. Indians don't even bear mention. You'll spend longer waiting for them to respawn than mowing them down.
* The depot/carriage options should be available in the newspaper just as are the freight options. Having to remember them is irritating.
* The 'random' events trackside are pointless. Wasting 36 hours for $180 isn't economical at any stage in the game, even the very first run. These feel tacked on.
* The only way to reliably make a ton of money is city contracts. Passenger carriage isn't worth it at all, and freight trading is only worth it if you can't get a suitable contract.
* The faction system - cities, Union, Confederates, Indians, bandits - is a little underdone.
And plenty of positives:
* The main story mode gives structure to the game and is pretty well done so far, although I'm not too far into it.There are plenty of side quests, many of which are worth doing and some of which are entertaining.
* Beautiful setting. Very evocative of its era, especially at stations. Nice little NPC touches here and there add character. It does feel like you're running across the New World on the railroad.
* The music is tremendous. I'd love it if they added a few more tracks but even without this it's a joy to listen to.
* Overall it has an addictive quality and the little micro-deadlines are compelling.
* Satisfaction when you can finally upgrade to a new engine and trick it out (although the final and best engine is so far ahead of the others isn't unreal, and as such it's a rush to get the 20k-and-upgrade fees, then the rest of the game is plain sailing.)
* Lots of companions add variety, even if their skillsets are a bit random, although it'd be nice to give them side quests.
Overall, I doubt I'll play this again until there's an expansion out, but I'm glad I got it. If you like rail games, trading games, Americana games, or any mix thereof, give it a chance. If not, you will find better things.

Quite a good game, I really enjoyed 10 hours playing it until the game actually lost its lure for me after the second evolutionary stage (out of five) as the focus of the game abruptly changes and it becomes something like a city management type strategy game. In summary, the first two stages are nice and fun to play; from third stage on, the game gets tedious. If you love strategy/action games, I still recommend this game as the first two evolutionary stages are indeed fun to play. My overall score: 6.5/10. If you are interested in finding out more about the game, you can read the rest of my review below.
There are five evolutionary stages in the game where you play through Spore's five evolutionary stages: Cell, Creature, Tribe, Civilization, and Space. The first and second stages are related to biological evolution: you first try to survive as a single celled organism in aqueous environment and evolve as you gain DNA points by eating food (the type of food depends on your Spore choice: herbivore or carnivore). You can spend your DNA points, for example, by adding flagella to your spore to move faster or by adding spikes as a defense mechanism, which adds the strategy component to the game. You eventually set foot on land where the second stage starts. During the second stage, you fight or ally with surrounding nests (you send them to oblivion or make them your allies through various social skills: singing, dancing, posing or being somewhat charming). You find various evolutionary parts which you can equip to your Spore to increase your chances of survival along your travel along this stage.
The third phase is where you lead a tribe. As in the second stage, you can also be friendly with the other tribes or destroy them. However, the biological evolution compenent is completely stripped off from the game which, for me, is the main reason why I lost interest. The fourth and fifth stages are in essence similar to the third stage where you compete with other cities or civilizations. For me the game actually ended after the third phase that’s why my review also ends here.

I've been trying out several controller mapping softwares trying to find the perfect application for my HTPC setup.  Controller keyboard support for the desktop is attrocious, there isn't a single on screen keyboard that supports use with controllers or even arrow keys.  Along comes Controller Companion, with a built in controller supported on screen keyboard, one that looks really easy to use too.  I thought I'd found the answer.  I had not. Controller Companion doesn't meet my needs at all, for several reasons.
First off, the mapping capability of the software is no where near powerful enough. It lacks advanced custom key combinations (holding one key down, tapping a few others, letting up on the held key, and tapping a few more, or tapping a key, waiting a few seconds, then tapping it, or another key again, etc) as well as lacking advanced controls (such as doing one thing for tapping a button, another for holding it down, or different button combinations depending on how far you tilt one of the joysticks and in what direction, etc).
Second, it's limited to only one profile and two layouts in that profile per game, as well as hardcoding the layout switch to the back button, and only while held down. Xpadder also limits you to one profile per game, but allows for up to 8 layouts in that profile. Pinnacle Game Profiler/Padstarr are limited to 5 layouts per profile, but can hotswap any number of profiles in a game. Both can assign layout shifting to any key, as a one way, toggle, or held down control.
Third, CC ONLY works with XBox style xinput controllers. No playstation controllers, no old directinput controllers, no joysticks/joypads, no steering wheels, nothing. Just xbox style controllers.
Fourth, last, and really most important: There is no null profile. Controller Companion will turn itself off when you're in Steam Big Picture Mode, and while playing any games launched from Steam big picture mode, but other than that, it is ALWAYS on, unless you manually shut it off (yes, easy with the start+back button combo, but not automatic). I don't use Steam as my main game launcher (I use Launchbox's Big Box for this), and I do a lot more than just games anyway. Kodi has built in controller support, a lot of games I have from outside of Steam have full controller support built in, and I have games and applications where I want other controller mapping software to take the controller. A blank profile in CC leaves the controller unable to do anything, and setting every application where I don't want CC to do anything, but hasn't been launched in big picture, to just emulate xbox buttons is not only extremely tedious, but you never know exactly what is actually going to come out when you've got two controller mapper programs both trying to modify a controller's inputs at the same time. So, while most of the programs that I want the keyboard function in would do just fine with the very simple control capabilities given by CC, CC otherwise gets in the way of everything else I want to do with the controller outside of Steam Big Picture.
So while Controller Companion has that sweet, sweet on screen keyboard, it's otherwise no where near as powerful in the controller mapping as its peers, and gets in the way of using those more powerful programs (that otherwise work automatically), as well as getting in the way of using any games with native controller support outside of Steam's Big Picture mode.
Until Controller Companion either becomes just as powerful at the controller mapping aspect as Pinnacle Game Profiler/Padstarr, or adds the capability to switch controller intervetion on or off based on what application currently is active and in focus, thus allowing me to set which controller mapping software I want (or don't want) on an application by application basis, I just cannot reccomend Controller Companion to anyone that owns games outside of Steam.

(Full disclosure- I'm a friend of one of the developers!  But let me give you my honest opinion.)
Moon Hunters plays a bit like Diablo in the monster bashing sense, and a bit like Zelda in the world exploring sense.
The coolest innovation in Moon Hunters is the myth-building aspect.  As you play, you'll make choices that determine your character's traits.  These traits will unlock side quests, pets, encounters, and interactions with NPCs.  At the end of your run, your character's Myth is told to you, based on these traits.
The next coolest innovation becomes clear on multiple playthroughs!  Each playthrough you do will unlock new content for future playthroughs, expanding the world and the options every time you play, and revealing more and more of what is actually going on.
I haven't yet been able to get online multiplayer working yet, and the combat can be a bit easy at times- though I personally was sufficiently challenged a few times each playthrough.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who likes the idea of playing a solid couch-co-op game with their friends, exploring the world and learning more about it, and making entertaining character based decisions to find out what changes happen as a consequence.

This dynamic way of playing is new and fresh in my opinion. It allows the player to be flexible in terms of their time investment, whether that be a large investment or small.
I want to compliment the art direction of this game. I have seen a lot of harsh comments in other places that the game is ugly looking. However my opinion is that the game is the complete opposite of ugly. It is in fact quite beautiful, especially when you factor in all the different settings, towns, enemies etc. are all quite unique as well as make use of a wonderful range of pastel colours throughout the world. Scenes look like pixelated watercolour paintings.
Gameplay wise it actually is like a diablo/zelda style. Its not nearly as deep as diablo though so don't expect that. Its a very light rpg. Unfortunately the game is really easy. This in my opinion is the game biggest flaw and they really need to improve the AI of enemies because once you understand the mix of your abilities and start gaining modifiers and skill ups, you become super OP. The reason to keep coming back to to discover the world and all the unlockables (places to see, things to do, new classes, new pathways) however if the game was more challenging that those things wouldn't be such a cake walk to find.
Definitely buy this, once you indulge deeper into the games systems they grab a hold of you and make you want more. The world of Moon Hunters is compelling and definitely draws interest, but the level of challenge is fairly low. Nothing a few AI and balancing tweaks wouldnt fix.

Moon Hunters definitely feels like something a bit special. A gorgeous melding of co-op ARPG and emergent storytelling. With choices that genuinely shape your character and the world (or rather the heavens) around you.
Pitched as a "co-operative action personality test RPG" it does have all those traditional RPG elements you might expect to find - Assorted class specific heroes with their own unique abilities. Character leveling and ability upgrades. And enemies (and cacti) that explode into loot if you hit them hard enough. But where the game really shines is in how it feels different each time you play.
You play as one of 6 heroes (4 starter classes with two more unlockable characters that can be found in game) whose quest is to find out why the Moon Goddess has vanished from the land. What's more you only have 3 days to do so.
As you travel across the procedurally generated world you come across random characters & objects and the way you react and interact with them not only changes your personality traits but also unlocks new characters, skins, villages and even familiars that can play alongside you. Though more importantly it helps write the legend of your greatest feats and failures in the stars above.
Each playthrough is about an hour long is definitely designed to be played with friends but more importantly to be played multiple times in order to unlock everything.
Admittedly the game is not perfect. I have come across a couple of minor bugs here and there (character names not appearing properly or hero skins changing mid conversation). The enemy AI can easily get caught on objects. And whilst there is a ton of content to explore the game is not infinitely replayable as you will soon get used to the various environments and start skipping encounters you've already made.
That said I wholeheartedly recommend giving Moon Hunters a go. A fun adventure on your own but even better with friends.

Get ready for an absurd amount of trial-and-error puzzles and a truckload of dark humour in this horror-themed episode, which is possibly also the high point of this season.
Humour that comes out of absolutely nowhere and seemingly leads nowhere: this is the main principle most Sam & Max stories were based on, especially during their early comic book years. This kind of humour we get plentifully in the Night of the Raving Dead, where things happen not because they have any reason or logic, but because they can be funny.
I mean, just look at the basic premise we see before the title credits: New York’s streets are flooded with dancing zombies, so our heroes set out to investigate the problem at its roots, which is naturally Stuttgart.
From here, the story evolves into a series of parodies, subtly or obviously mocking things like the stereotype about Germans lacking any sense of humour, or classic stories like Frankenstein. This is where Sam & Max are in their natural element, and it shows here.
If something negative can be said about the episode, then it’s that most of the writing went into dialogues and little to the puzzles; there are too many trial-and-error ones littered all over the place, often halting progression. They payoff is always great—if a bit dark sometimes—but the road to the next hilarious joke can be a little more bumpy than needed.

However, and this is important, this game is made by comic book nerds for comic book nerds. They have entire chapters dedicated to the weirdest parts of marvel- their wild west and mideval England comics, the Inhumans, all that stuff, then just randomly around the map is an unlockable assortment of marvel's weirdest. They have Throgg, they have Ursa Major, they have Ms. Marvel, they have Gwenpool... It's glorious.
The story focuses on weird characters too. You'll have your standard popular movie character- usually Spider Man, Thor, or one of the guardians of the galaxy, then they'll throw you something weird like Spider Man Noir or Sting Ray. It's something only someone who'se wasted a significant portion of their lives can truly appreciate it... But I love it!
And the hub world! My gosh- They came up with a way to pretty much ignore reality in favor of smashing a ton of crazy settings together. Tired of snowed in and dreary Manhattan Noir, it's okay! A couple steps north and you're in ancient Egypt! Easy as that! West of there is the Wild West, and if you keep going, you'll get to a destroyed Asgard.
So... Here's the deal- if you're looking for challenging and engaging gameplay, you won't find it here, but if you're looking for the most glorious fanfic ever invented, then buy away my friend. The great and mighty Throgg awaits!

I love this game. I can't find another game like it. Out of the Mount and Blade games, this one is by far my favourite. I usually play this on my laptop screen and have Youtube or Netflix playing something on my TV as you can Alt+ENTER in and out of windowed mode (usually) without any problems.
Its an RPG/RTS that allows you to recruit a warband consisting of both generic soldiers that follow an upgrade tree and NPC heros that offer different buffs depending on there skills which you upgrade in same fashion as your own character. You can traid goods, join one of the waring factions, raid villages, fight in tournaments, buy businesses or even take a castle or city as your own if you're feeling brave. Missions are not just given to you (appart from the very first one), you have to travel from place to place asking people if they need your help. The motervation to make money comes from the fact that you need to pay and feed your warband.
There are two sides to this game, the world map and the 3rd/1st person view used on the battle map. The world map looks similar to a Total War game map with icons of characters moving around. You switch to 3rd/1st  person view when you enter a town, city or other location or when you engage an enemy. In battle, you can issue comands to your soldiers using the numbers and the F-keys. For instance - 1 (infantry), F1 (Hold possition). Strategy is key to winning a battle when you're out numbered.
There are tones of mods for this game as well, from minor enhancements to total conversionsas. So when you get fed up with the vanella setting, you can change it to something else like Lord of the Rings or Game of Thrones or Warhammer or an original concept setting. This game has kept me busy for a while still.

I'm just going to get the couple of bad points out of the way as quickly as possible.
The Combat is quite clunky and a bit buggy.  Line of sights are difficult to predict and sometimes your crew ends up doing nothing because the character sprites run into each other.
Also the "free" mode (without the campaign) feels soulless and unfulfilling.  It is in the campaign mode where this game really shines through.
The best things about the game are the multitude of depth this game has. There are plenty of upgrades to your train and crew. Managing your efficiency and income is the number one priority for this game.
Trains aren't just limited to purchasing the next greatest thing.  There are a few different types of locomotives, such as one being slower but pulls more carriages or another that does both well enough.
Your trains also lose durability over time which makes them break down more and thus forcing you to purchase a new (same) carriage to avoid such losses of money and time.
Take on different jobs in every city you pull into the station in.  Go to the market and check the latest market prices and buy low and sell high.  Post office may need to send urgent mail and need somebody with a fast engine.  What about they guy who wants you to send a love letter in the direction you're going anyways?
Your crew levels up and you can shape them up to be whatever role you need them to be.  Need a sharpshooter? You can hire one.  Need somebody that can heal your crew up in a real gunfight?  Grab the healing trait. Don't have a healer? There are medicine and herbs that can fix you up in a quick pinch.
Combat isn't just about killing the other side, you can outrun your enemy if you are outgunned if you have a good fast train and someone with an engineer trait.
Over 25 hours later, I'm still hooked and I can't wait to get back into playing and beating the game.  This game is really that good.

This is a long review, so feel free to scroll to the end for a list of pros and cons.
Bounty Train is an enjoyable game that unfortunately falls short in many ways.  The premise is that the US government is trying to build a transcontinental railroad in the mid-1800s, and in order to get the winning bid, your company must accomulate a majority of the stock shares (51%).  In order to do this, you run cargo, passengers, and mail from one city to another, complete missions, recruit people to help run and defend your train, negotiate with different factions, and build up your assets and capabilities as you acquire more and more wealth.
Thematically, Bounty Train is wonderful.  Events from history drive the game forward, such as Civil War battles changing the market demand for weapons or medicine, as well as different historical characters that you can interact with, like Samuel Colt or even Abraham Lincoln.  The map (expectedly) constrains you to territory east of the Mississippi River, but there are plenty of towns to visit and things to do in that region, so it never feels cramped.
For a good part of the game, it's plenty of fun to play.  Sure, there are some minor issues, like people that appear to be there to talk to but never have anything to say, inconsistencies in game text ("town hall" versus "city hall" in the same city), the camera set up in a such a way that gun emplacements in the market are either covered up or off-screen, the apparent lack of a bank in Washington despite the icon, or the fact that there's a greater variety of music in the menu that you spend all of 5 seconds in than in the game itself, which plays the same track over and over.  However, from the start of play through roughly the end of the Civil War, there's plenty to do, and plenty of ways to advance and improve your train and characters.
Unfortunately, it's at that point that the game simply runs out of content.  You've explored every city, talked to every person, purchased every upgrade, and almost no quests appear beyond an auction for stock shares every few months.  There's nothing to do but run cargo back and forth until you get another chance at those company shares.
And the thing is, it's not like I was slow-playing things.  You're constantly competing with one of your company's rivals to reach 51% stock shares first, and I'm positive I pursued (and successfully completed) every chance to acquire stock for my own company and deprive my opponent of stock for his.  And by the time I was at about 40% of the shares (and he had about half that), I had run out of things to do.  I had already purchased the best equipment by about halfway into my playtime, and there was no longer any real goal for me.
And that's just the most obvious flaw to me.  There are plenty of others, like the seeming impossibility of improving your reputation among the different factions once the missions run out (I had 75% or higher reputation in each of the Confederate cities, yet my faction reputation hung around 1-3%), or the utter incompetence of your party members in combat situations.  Then there are the specialized train cars, like the mortar, the hospital car, or the armored cargo cars, but it's far simpler to just pay off attackers, since even the best engine in the game can't pull all of that with any degree of usefulness.
Still, I had fun.  I enjoyed it.  I loved the concept, and I truly had a good time while playing it; I just wish the game was more polished.  Even though it's an official release, Bounty Train feels like it's still in Early Access (albeit near the end).  It's not quite a finished product, but I would definitely still recommend it.  At any rate, there are worse ways to spend 20 hours.
Pros:
+great atmosphere and theme
+many facets of gameplay
+variety of missions to complete
+RPG elements with character leveling
+easy to keep track of market prices and availability
+easy to keep track of ongoing missions
+historically accurate background and foreground events that affect gameplay
Cons:
-dull late game
-unclear how to change faction reputation
-no way to cancel a trip (say, if your train breaks down midway and needs repairs)
-limited background music
-NPCs need hand-holding in battles
-limited use for some train cars
-market items can appear off-screen or covered
-difficult to keep track of where you can buy certain train equipment
-some mission summaries aren't clear where the target is ("Talk to Joe" with no mention of a city)

Bounty Train's strengths lies in its mixed bag of gameplay mechanics: trading goods based on economic needs, transporting passengers, wild west gun fights while defending your train from boarding bandits, RPG character leveling up/skills/loot, and random events occurring along your travels. The mechanics are simplified to make these tasks less daunting. I specifically found the economy-trading mechanics to be addicting and lucrative, which made it easier to purchase new carriages, locomotives, crew, and upgrades.
For those who quickly play through the campaign, you have sandbox mode. This is where you strive for the best Train equipment and crew money can buy, and of course, try your hand at being the best Bounty Train Bandit in all the land, or you know, you can always stick to being a boring, law-abiding citizen.
Bounty Train has a lot to offer with miles of track to cover, and although I particularly didn't like the frequent game-flow-interrupting loading screens and I lost a bit of steam when the game started feeling repetitive, I think Bounty Train is still worthy of a ride.

A nice short trading game where you are incharge of a single train and drive it from city to city (Note: You can only have one active train at a time, so you cant setup a 'trading empire' in this game). A lot of background events simulating what happened in real life history for the first year of the game add a good amount of flavour to the game (Sometimes too many in the first year as they happen one after the other and you lose track). However these are few and far between by the second year which is a pity as the game feels a little stale.
Game still has some bugs (One which made be have to restart- I was only a couple of hours in so it was fine). Devs do read the comments posted on steam though which is a plus.
To make money, goods are really the only way to go (Whether its you doing manual trading or accepting goals/missions). Unfortunately, I found that passengers were not feasible as a money maker as passenger carriages carry far too few people (2-4 passengers each) and the short timeframe you get for passengers before you fail their 'mission' means you have to go directly to their destination, so its hard to pick up multiple passengers from multiple cities and take them to multiple destinations. If capacities were doubled or tripled and the timelimits doubled, it might be possible to setup 'whistlestop tours'.
Although purchasing industries is possible, they are very rare and by the time you can start purchasing them, you will be hard pressed to earn back your initial investment. It would have been good if these were more common, available earlier and you could also build them rather than having to wait until auctions.
Overall though, I still enjoyed the experience. Replay value is not its strong point so I view I have 'finished' the game for now, but might pick it up again some time in the future for a freeplay game

At first, Masters of the World looks like a deep, engaging and thrilling simulator of worldwide politics. If you made the same mistake that I did by purchasing the $70 bundle with the game, updated content, and the modding tool, you'd better hurry and refund that. If you really want to see what this game has to offer then you should just buy the base game.
Unfortunately, the problems with MotW appear immediately. Right off the bat, the tutorial was unable to figure out that I had successfully changed some spending priorities as it had instructed me to, preventing me from progressing further. Armed only with the knowledge of how to navigate the map and modify the budget, I tried to start a new game. It was extremely difficult selecting a leader that wasn't of the same party as the current leader, turning the start-up process into a mess as I accidentally changed unrelated settings attempting to figure out how to change the leader. I eventually figured it out - though I can't even remember how I did - and entered the game.
Immediately, the game became campy and even amusing. To communicate to the player even basic messages, an ugly and poorly-rendered person takes over your screen to talk to you about how well you're doing. The voice acting was so robotic and unnatural, the first 7 hours I played I was certain it was just a text-to-speech software. These messages quickly become repetitive: whenever there is a terrorist cell in a foreign country, someone will come on the screen and deliver a useless, rambling explanation of the "Brown model" without giving you any real information (they'll mention percentages and numbers that sound important, but turn out to be repetitive filler that doesn't change situation to situation). Afterwords the game will give you a static text box telling you the real information: where the cell is, what it does and how to contact them. You can skip these messages (and thankfully by doing so you're not actually missing anything), but the fact that Eversim put so much effort into something so unnecessary - and in fact something that hinders the gameplay experience - shows where their priorities are.
The rest of the game's graphics do not fare well, either. The game has extreme and severe lag somehow, even when countries are basically trees, lakes, and geometrically simple cities that consist of about a dozen buildings. As mentioned earlier, the character models look horrendous, but the developers seem to enjoy showing off. The interface is a problem (which is not uncommon for an Eversim game), with the developers trying to make fancy-looking infographics hidden behind dozens of menus and tabs.
If these problems weren't major enough, the game is buggy, crashes very often, and Eversim has completely given up on it. Eversim has a history of spending about 6 months on a political game, updating it rarely for a 6-month period, and then disappearing to work on a sequel. Their sequel to this game is coming out soon (the release date has already passed with no announcement) and judging by the trailers, it preserves the terrible graphics and confusing interface. If Eversim settled on a game, kept updating it, used a reasonable price, and actually made a working tutorial, they wouldn't have a 42% positive score on Steam.

Time for a good, bad, and ugly review. (NON PVP player) Final verdict at the end.
****************  The Good things *********************
Character generation – IMHO more MMO's should adopt this style of both character creation, and customization.  Your stats and abilities are almost totally independent of your characters appearance, and there are a LOT of appearance options to customize your hero.  I personally Cosplay my DC character as Starlord from the Guardians of the Galaxy movie, and it looks and feels awesome to play!
Action/fighting/button mashing combat – If you are like me, you are sick of the action/hotbar style mmo mechanic.  This game has a more traditional action game approach to controls, and works BEST with a controller, but also well with a mouse and keyboard. If you like Games that give you button combos, active dodging and countering, you will like this.
Story – It is clearly a “theme park” mmo in every sense of the word.  IMHO it does this well, each story arc is mostly fun, and only a handful felt boring or like something I couldn't wait to finish.  Nothing too deep, nothing too shallow. Nice bite sized plots that you can finish in a few hours at a time. Great for casual gaming.
Gotham – The city of Gotham is legit, and makes you feel like you are in the Batman animated series in many ways.
Sound and graphics – for an MMO, these look great with everything maxed out.  The colors, the characters, and the environments (especially gotham) are full of eye candy.
Gameplay overall – The game play is very addictive as I mentioned before, even just flying/running/climbing around the cities is fun. The fighting action is great. But another great thing are the movement modes, I find acrobatics/grapplinghook to be the most fun to play, and flight to be the most useful.
Free to play – This is kind of both a good and bad – the free to play model being used here is what I prefer to call – the Extended preview model.  The free elements are enough to level you to 30 and beyond, but you will be limited in a lot of ways, and won't get to experiment with all the possible power and weapon combos.  As free to play games go, if you enjoy the game you will be getting a LOT out of the game even if you never buy anything.
********************* The bad things ************************
Grind - The level range is only 1-30, and when it finishes, the game devolves into repeating content for marks which you use to buy gear that raises your level (similar to destiny's light level).  This is fun for a little while, but once you see how long it takes to grind for marks, and how much content you have to repeat to do it... you will likely quit, most people I know get their full Tier 1, then either quit, or make a new toon experience another storyline up to thirty, then quit.
Lots of empty space – I can't tell you how often I'm traveling around, especially in Metropolis, and feel like the city is empty and unfinished.  Huge sections of the map have almost no reason for going there, except exploring for collectible elements.  No random enemies to fight, no quests... I'd say only about 1/3 of the map for each city has actual content in it, the rest is just travel and exploration fodder.
The hideout system – This is boring to me, it's got a lot going for it I suppose if you like these things, but I just can't get into the layouts or designs.  However, unlike most other MMO's where a home is just a fun vanity collectible box, you NEED a hideout or else you won't get certain upgrades, buff and perks... My hideout is basically an empty warehouse looking place with a few key elements so I can get my buffs...
Low level instances – The balance on the low level 4 player instances can be frustrating.  They can be very difficult to beat at the level they claim to be designed for, and often a high level player will be in it, which seems to make it harder for everyone else.
It's not really free to play – This depends on your perspective, for me, I don't expect games to be totally free... either I need to buy it, or buy things in microtransactions, or pay for monthly. Nothing is free. I like FTP that lets me try a game like this before committing to it with a monthly sub.  The problem is, when I subbed, I had no idea what endgame was like, or that I'd basically be grinding for gear...
**************** The Ugly things – Not too many ugly things here... *******************
The Grind – Yes, I mentioned it before, but it really gets annoying past 30.  Even though more and more content opens up as you increase your level tier... All it really amounts to, is new instances to grind for marks.  There are no new levels, no new story arcs (not really).  If DCUO had proper content expansions for post 30, something to give you a REAL reason to level up (new story arcs, new levels etc), it would really be something special and give you a reason to grind.
No cross platform between PC and PS4, but you CAN play PS4 with PS3. - This sucks for people like me who are master race PC users, but whose friends and family are all Console limited.  My Son and Wife both wanted to play with me, but can't... but at least they can play together... without me! :(
********************* Final Verdict *********************
Totally worth playing till 30, and a little beyond. Totally worth a short sub to unlock all the powers etc, or buy them outright one by one to save some money. I subbed for 3 months, and will cancel before it renews. I got my fun out of it, and will sub again only if any major additions or changes warrant it.

A lot of discussions have been going on about Krater. While some players praise the fresh rpg setting and the challenging quests, others critisize the imbalanced powers of the monsters.
Here is what I experienced:
Pros:
- easy to get started, self-explanatory game mechanics, well-made learning curve
- a solid story about abusing power, elite leaders and supressing the masses, set in a post-nuclear Sweden, with a good sense of humour
- long-time motivation for those who love challenges, as there are perfect builds to find, the limbo (a 45-level-dungeon) to raid etc.
- Nice graphic style, clean and fitting sounds and soundtrack
Cons:
- Disastrous balancing: Some enemies are way too weak, others will bring your team down in no time. It takes a lot of time to find a good build for the final battle - but it does not depend on your own skill, but more on puzzling together different boosters (that improve strength, defense, stamina etc)
- Boring quests, standard rpg loot & collect tasks
- The coop mode is only three levels - well, for a game that calls itself a coop game, it's sparse, to put it mildly
In the first ten hours of playing, I was about to tell friends to try out the game, as it had this fresh setting and things went on pretty well, absolving quests and looting dungeons. But then I was stuck more often due to strong enemies, no money to buy upgrades, and misspent boosters. The final battle got pretty frustrating as I did not find a build good enough to beat the final boss. Also, until today, I never found a single player in the coop lounge to join a game.
Concerning that, I would not recommend to buy this game until one is going for a challenging rpg.

There are many things to like about this game, the shooting mechanics are decent and it looks reasonable graphically. As well, the vehicles handle nicely and aren't a pain to acquire like in some MMOs. However it suffers from a "monster closet" enemy spawning system which often spawns enemy npc's directly behind you with no sound cue to alert you of the imminent danger. As well, server lag causes many issues such as npc teleporting, aiming issues (due to teleporting), loot not picking up reliably, etc. PvE is very fun, and can be done solo. PvP is essentially pay to win since you can purchase lockboxes with rare gear/weapons with real cash. Worth the sale price (I got it for $5) but in no way is this game worth full price.
TLDR - On sale? Pick it up for a few days/weeks of fun. Regular price? Look elsewhere.

This program was exactly what I was looking for around the time it came out and I couldn't be more pleased. Controller companion allows you to use any driver supported controller to control your mouse cursor and keyboard. It is eternally useful for those who want to couch game or use their PCs as a media center with their TV but don't want to keep a wireless keyboard and mouse around for aesthetic or battery or whatever reasons.
The keyboard is accessed via a spiral menu - on a 360 controller the default is pressing the left stick. This also leads to the one and only problem I've encountered with the software. Some PC games do not work well and natively support controller, as we know, so for those games you need to launch controller companion. However, for those games that do, and you have CC running when you eventually press left stick as part of the games control scheme - or on accident if you're a dumbass like me - it opens up the keyboard menu in the background and then it will constantly switch your control input between keyboard and controller until you alt tab and close the text menu. I don't know if this has been fixed yet but I don't think. Resident Evil 6 is a prime example of this and it makes it quite difficult to play if it happens.
Mouse operation, again on Xbox pad, is handled by right stick and A to left click. I am not sure of right click. Other than that, there seems to be a bit of a dead zone when you first try to move the mouse but I'm not so sure that's the software's fault.
CC also supports custom schemes and the workshop has blown up with them since it released. So you no longer have to use dodgy crap like Pinnacle Game Profiler that costs like 5 times more than this and doesn't necessarily even work.
This is $2. You won't find a better solution for controllers. Trust me, I've looked - I've used Xpadder, Pinnacle Game Profiler, neither one of them compares.
11/10 would get frustrated with text menu again.
***Update as of 2017***
Valve has added native controller support to Steam so this utility now kind of deprecated, and will likely interfere with the built-in controller support. But, it is still useful if you are using your computer from a couch or bed and either don't own a wireless keyboard/mouse combo, or don't want to use one.

If you use your computer or laptop to play video for more than one viewer then this little program is absolutely great. I take my laptop, hook it up to a TV with an HDMI cable, and watch shows using the controller for playback, volume control, and pause. I find that controllers are better at being "remotes" for this purpose than actual remotes!
Workshop integration is well-done too, and there's a lot of room for customizing the bindings for a specific program even with downloaded profiles. The "typing" is a little iffy- I think something like Steam Big Picture's typing options works better than the spiral, but that's just my own opinion. In all other regards this is a stellar program for the price. If you could see yourself using it for anything then I highly recommend it.

This starts out as a great game.  Good graphics, good movement mechanics.  Things look and sound like they should and there is a terrific amount of area on a map to explore as well as a variety of ways to develop your heroes.  But then things start going south rapidly.
First there is the premium currency trap.  You earn credits in the game based on how long you are playing.  Not how well you do in a given match, not for doing things, just for time in a match.  These credits must later be spent on maintaining your soldier's gear or you can't use them.  You also have to maintain any weapon upgrades.  You also have to maintain any vehicles you used, if any, as well as their upgrades and of course ammunition.  Once all that is done, if you have any credits left over, then you can buy things that your XP has unlocked.
But Wait!  All this can be avoided if you just open up your wallet and buy premium currency.   Otherwise you are stuck grinding up credits while using the basic gear.  Not because you don't have better but because you can't afford to use better.
Secondly, there are ways to set things up so the following will happen.  Player A and Player B round a corner and run into each other.  Player A has an automatic weapon and reacting first immediately fires a burst into the body of Player B.  Player B has a single shot, non-sniper rifle and fires back, hitting Player A in a limb and killing him instantly.  Player B carries on, only lightly damaged by the automatic weapons fire he took.  Player B wins the encounter, not due to superior skill, but rather due to superior use of money to maximize the games badge and perk system.
Thirdly, there is the poor balance of the strength of sides in battle formats.  An example:  Side A is defending a point against Side B.  Side B must cross an obstacle and open ground to reach their objectives.   Side A will have fortified positions, pillboxes, AA guns, machine gun nests and armor.  Side B gets....infantry, bicycles, jeeps and if very, very lucky, an apc.  What usually happens is that Side B rushes forward in an attempt to seize positions before Side A can mobilize from spawn.  If they succeed, well and good.  Side B has a fighting chance.  But what usually happens is the Side B gets driven back as Side A rolls over the 'attacker' with armor and wins by capping Side b's spawn points in an irresistable tide.
H and G could have become a truly, truly great game loved by thousands if not millions.  But the continuous repetition of the above examples and things like them drove people away from what could have been a legendary franchise.

If you haven't played this yet, you must.
From the start, this is a gorgeous game.  Top-tier artwork and level design from beginning to end, with enough technical oomph to back it up.  The game looks pristine on my mid-range laptop (1.8ghz quadcore, 4gb RAM, Radeon 6520), and hardly skipped a beat performance-wise.
Then there's the gameplay.  It seems a daunting premise- controlling two characters at once.  But the simple control scheme of WASD and space for one brother and arrow keys and right Ctrl for the other makes  it work.  I didn't try it with a gamepad, but I imagine it's easier on the wrists, and might work better with some of the game's cinematic camera angles.  There are puzzles here that just wouldn't work in any other game, and some climbs to put Assassin's Creed to shame.
But the real gem here is the story.  Tho the "spoken" dialogue is but a few words of a made-up language, the "acting" tells the tale more than sufficiently- the gestures, the character interactions, the camera angles and music.  Despite them not saying a single legible word save their names, I found myself very attached to the brothers, as well as the folk they meet along the way.  This title holds a special place next to Half-Life 2: Episode 2 as one of the few games to actually hit me emotionally, and I'm man enough to admit I cried at the end of this one.
It is a short playthrough- I knocked it out in a single 3-hour session.  But like a good movie (BETTER even than some movies), it's well worth the price of admission, doubly so with the Steam Christmas sale going on.  This is well-worth the Top 10 mention Ars Technica gave it, and deserves many an award alongside that 90/100 MetaCritic rating.  And it definitely deserves your time, money, and attention.

The lovers of old Japanese animation “Galaxy Express 999”, such as I, are supposed to dream to own a train, custom the train, and travel the sea of the stars by the train.
The “Bounty Train” make a part of the dream come true. In the game, the locomotives in the game do not talk, do not fly to the space, and there is no mysterious attendant. But we can custom our own locomotive, employ and arm crews, and have great adventures across the Unites States in the middle of 19th. The purpose of our hero, Walter, is to gather the 50% of stocks of the railroad company built by his father. We must hurry up because the evil merchant Tiberius also hunts the stocks.
To get the stocks scattered across the US, we need to earn money by transporting passengers and cargos, delivering emergent letters, and solving some special missions. The transportations of VIPs, criminals, and contraband goods have a risk of arrest and suspicious attack, but bring higher incomes. Further, the trust from the Northern and Southern governments, from native Americans, and even from bandits are also required to get the stocks.
On our journey, we sometimes need to fight against armies, native Americans, and bandits. In the battle mode, our locomotive becomes a moving fortress. If we have enhanced the speed, toughness, and fire protection of the locomotive, our crew can take an advantage. And the skills of crews, such as rapid firing, sniping, hand-to-hand combat, and nursing, also helps our victory.
The thrilling fight using a locomotive is the unique point of this game. As far as I know, this is the only game we can fire the gatling guns and through massive dynamites from a running train. The problem is that the fighting situation only this game could construct is not rich in the early-access version. For example, train-based weapons other than gatling guns, additional maps including bridges or tunnels, and train vs train battles appear to enhance the charm of this game further.
Anyway, the current version of this game has enough quality to run through, and can bring us a new type of experience. I hope further development of this game, and the development of Galaxy Express version in the future.

A decent multiplayer third person shooter, somewhat reminiscent of Borderlands in terms of the skill system and loot. The MMO aspect isn't something you'll see a lot of, many missions are instanced and most competitive PvP stuff puts the players on separate maps.
The story is, somewhat surprisingly considering it's based on a TV show, not particularly intriguing, the mission get somewhat stale after a while, but the setting - the overgrown United States after a failed alien terraforming attempt, is interesting in concept. As game mechanics go, it's solid for the genre, and it does get pretty cool when you team up with a bunch of other players to take on the timed world events. The player base has started waning at this point though, and other than the major arkfall events you'll rarely come across any larger crowds. At this point I would not recommend the DLC, they just barely provide what was promised in the season pass description, mostly coming down to a few new weapon types and missions, all taking place at the already existing land mass from the core game. Unless the specific weapon types in the DLC description seem to suit your preferred play style (I did like the charge weapons added with the first DLC), you'll probably not get much out of them.
As for the game itself, it's not charging a subscription, and I haven't found the need to use any of the stuff available in the microtransaction store (which mostly boil down to limited time XP gains, random weapon packs - which are very easy to get with the in-game currency - and some costumes), it's pretty solid at what it tries to do, but not as ambitious as you would hope hearing the talk about an MMO third person shooter. At the asked price point I think the base game is definitely worth it, but I'd hold off on the DLC until a sale.

Well, if you're a fan of the LEGO series of games in general, you'll probably be wondering whether this game lives up to the standard set by the original LEGO Marvel Super Heroes game. The original is considered by many to be amongst the best, if not 'the' best LEGO game to date. So, does it live up to the original? In short, the answer is no.
I find my own opinion very divided on this game, so will try to summarise the Pros (+) and Cons (-)
+ Original plot-line is well written and keeps you interested throughout
+ Graphics are the best of any LEGO game yet
+ Excellent range of characters & vehicles available (the lack of X-Men / Fantastic 4 doesn't bother me)
+ Good range of character skills you'll use as you make your way through the story
+ World map free roam area is large and varied
+ Level design is mostly good, with each level being unique, i.e no two levels will feel 'samey'
- Voice acting, and i don't necessarily mean in the same way as some of the other reviewers have said. Yes it's true, some of the voice acting is weak, but some of it is also very good. Kang, Ms Marvel, and Rocket Racoon all stand out in my mind as being some of the good ones. It's not 'all' bad anyway. What i do take issue with, however is the production standard. Two characters can be having a conversation, and one voice is much louder than the other. In the current version of the game, this will happen in the very first level, and sets the tone for the rest of the game really.
- Instability. Oddly enough, this wouldn't have been on the list when I first downloaded the game. When the game was first released, i clocked ~40 hours in without a single crash. Then they released a 3GB update (and didn't even release any patch notes with it). Since this update, frequent, random crashes. Very frustrating. Still, i soldiered on to 100% which leads me to my next point...
- Gets stale for 100%. This game has introduced challenges in the open world. These challenges consist of 'find all the x', or 'destroy all the x' in chronopolis. The location of 'x' however, is not on the map, and with some of these you don't even get a clue as to where they may be. I appreciate that they just wanted to add more for the player to do, but these challenges seem like an unnecessary and frankly uninteresting hurdle to achieve the fabled 100%, and I did not have fun doing these.
In summary, i personally didn't enjoy this game anywhere near as much as the first. If I was to give this game a score out of 10, in it's current state it's a 6/10, therefore 'just' earning a recommended review. It's still a recommended review as overall i still had enough fun from it to play for 60 hours, and it is, overall, a good game. You can tell the developers put a lot of effort in, it's just a shame that the technical issues really take the 'shine' off it.
If they could just fix the 'fixable', such as crash issues and normalising the voice sound levels, then that would only leave the chronopolis challenges as my main criticism. This is minor compared to the others so would naturally lead to me increasing my score.

In my opinion, one of the best (if not the best) of Choice of Games' interactive novels. It was extremely well-written with tight, compelling prose. More than that, the characters each felt unique, vivid, and like actual people (maybe because they're based on real-life historical figures, though of course the story takes lots of liberties). The story, world, and characters just felt alive and authentic, unlike some interactive novels where the characters feel faceless and bland. Highly recommend, great read and experience! Replay value is high too: there are tons of divergent paths and decisions, and your choices make a real difference!
Recommended if you enjoy those choose your own adventure books and alternate history. The writing is decent, the story doesn't slow down, and lots of chance for replayability. 8/10.

If you can get it on sale it's decent enough for a playthrough. It's by no means one of the best that I've played but I enjoyed myself. Some comments:
- I think the steam punk setting is heavily underutilized. If you're going to make an alternate timeline where this is in the forefront of the marketting, it could have been more than just a side activity to the main plot and a mention here and there. Seems like it ultimately is a game about espionage, politics and discussion.
- On the other note, your traits and 'stats' seem like they are very much what determine what choice you make instead of adding more options. I chose to be a skilled duelist, and I can safely say that based off my choices I only possibly had like one chance at a duel. In the authors' attempt to give sensible options that a non-bloodthirsty individual would make, I was left with a meaningless skill. Choosing to focus on science in my studies, I had some unintended laughs with some of the options that seem like deus ex machina skills. It doesn't seem intended in tone either, so seems like a failure of the stats to explain what you are and what you know.
- It's a surprisingly tame choose your own adventure. I understand that there is a charm for everything going your way, but even when you choose something and it doesn't go your way it's quickly corrected in like the very next page making your decision obsolete in the long run. And when things go your way, they go your way a bit too perfectly which makes it a tad boring. 'Oh hey a bunch of enemies to my friend', 'let's talk to them about their goals', 'oh ok, maybe they aren't so bad'.
- The story ended before I thought it had a chance to start. It ends very abruptly with a very used mechanic that is used when the author doesn't want to write more and instead opts to show you the long term results of your choices. It was a shame as I would have been more than glad to continue with it. And considering the topic of romance came up in the trailer and in the game's description, I couldn't help but think 'that's it' at a moment in the story near the end. Seems like you must either deny the advances of a character from the start, or flirt with them awkwardly with no knowledge of their character beforehand. At the end of the novel the character I wanted to romance felt no interest towards me because apparently I wasn't an amazing dancer, so instead the novel throws me a pity romance from another character I hadn't romanced in the whole novel and who I didn't ever get to know.
Like I said it isn't without its faults, but if you enjoy fiction and can spare 2-3 hours of your time there are worst ways to pass the time. Particularly at the price I paid. I give it a 'Eh, why the heck not'

Works great with my wireless Xbox360 controller. It's easy to add new profiles for games (you can select both running programs and recently run programs) and remapping the sticks and buttons is easy and takes just a few minutes. The only (minor) downsides I've found so far is that remapping the Guide button doesn't work in any of the games I've tried and you can't remap the 'back' button, because it's used as a shift button which can be used to map an extra function to most buttons and axes.

Controller Companion offers plenty of options to control games that don't support gamepads and should be sufficient for most of what you want to do with it.

I started playing after the timoshenko update hit and I absolutely loved it. Great gameplay, lots of laughs, premium players have no advantages (except leveling/money bonusses and weapon skins) and the way it worked was good. Reto did a lot to improve the game, they added new guns, nerfed and buffed stuff to make it more fair. The thing i loved about this game was the different weapons for each faction, all with their own characteristics. The grinding part of the game is kinda bad, but when you have grinded long enough you can upgrade your gun. That is also something i loved about this game, since you can mod your guns the way you like them. A big disadvantage about the grinding and modding thing is that people you'll fight against as a beginning player will have better guns, but that is not that bad since its lots of fun to play.
It was huge fun to participate in a battle with tanks, planes, and lots of lil' infantry jimmy's. There was still a lot of work to do, since hits werent always counted and character movement was quite poor. Reto improved that and added lots of stuff to the game in the updates. A little bit to much probably. We have loads of camo to choose from now but we only have a few maps to fight in. They keep adding camo and and unnecessary stuff (like the third german pistol), but it seems like they dont care about adding new maps. In one of the last updates they added more vegetation, but all they did was copy paste the same bush all over the place. After 5 years of early access developing, the graphical part of the game is still very bad.
Something else i dont like about the game is the toxic community who wants reto to nerf everything they get killed with. Thats also because of the different types of players (e.g. tankers want to nerf anti tank stuff, infantry wants to nerf tanks). I used to play all classes and i think it is pretty balanced. Reto did a good job on balancing, allthough the russians are a little bit underpowered and germans a bit overpowered (e.g. MG42(1200 max rpm) and the heavily armored tanks).
Till this "Devyatayev" squad update hit i absolutely loved it. Sometimes the battles where a little unbalanced, e.g. when the enemys had lots of tanks and your team had none, but if u had a tanker u could easily switch and kick some♥♥♥♥♥ This is diffirent right now. You have to grind your squad ribbon to be able to switch to diffirent classes. I have quit a lot of characters, I need to grind em all up to be able to play normally again. Another thing about this squad system is that you can never play alone, you will always be in a squad with some random guys who are f*cking around.
They have done such a thing with the ribbon system in an earlier update, when they went through the ribbon system, but it wasnt that bad, since u could still use all of your characters. At that time, there were not that much experienced players with lots of characters, so it didnt matter that much. Right now, there are lots of player who have grinded their way up and have lots of characters. They will all have to grind that ribbon on their characters to be able to play normally again.
With this being said, i dont recommend this game to new players, since it is still in early acces and things like this will probably happen some more in the future. It will also take a long time before it can be released, because there is still a lot of work to do, especially the amount of maps(maps are all same scenery) and graphical part of the game is very poor. For someone who just starts, this new squad (ribbon) system wont be the problem, you'll just level ur squad ribbon up through playing while ur grinding for better equipment. But still, something like this might happen again in the future, so you'll be just as mad on reto as a big part of the community right now.
If Reto dont chance this squad system and refuse to add new maps and if they dont improve the graphical part of the game im gonna leave and play some battalion 1944 or Red orchestra, or even WW1 (Verdun, Battlefield 1) instead. I always liked Heroes and generals more than other ww2 games like battalion and red orchestra just because of the tank, plane and infantry gameplay all together and of course because of the generals part of the game. If not this is after Warthunder the second Free2play WW2 game im gonna quit because the developers are f*cking it up.

Krater for everything that it is, ends up far more lackluster then it should be. A lot of it's issues lay at it's most core foundation, and it will keep nagging you from start to finish. It's biggest issue is that right from the get go, your skills per charater are already desided for you. Each 'class' always has the same attacks no matter what, witch makes the next guy to replace your last not feel any different...because he's not. Yet here comes the next kicker, charater rarity.
You have a team of 3 you use at once to clear maps, and it is massivly encouraged on you to buy and collect new guys to use, including once you relise 'white and green' 'rarity' versions of these guys have far less stats overall then their 'blue and purple' versions you don't start finding till a bit later on, after you've dumped a ton of money and gear into these other versions, and now have to scrap for the 'better'. Of couse the people you hire are all at level 1, and there is a 'max growth' cap on the 'lesser' units that will indeed force your hand to swap out that group that got you half of the way with the game...for another who work exactly the same, need to be leveled up all over again, if only because they can level up 5 more times then your last set and have a few more points overall, because you will need that extra 'omph' as you go more and more forward.
What little this game does as nifty ( such as the team dynamic, the crafting, and the visurals ) are just knocked down by a lot of pegs because it's got such a basic core, that drags it's feet because you will waste more time buying and upgrading 'slightly better' versions of your guys for others, and you never really get different attacks, only slightly changing a few effects towards them.

This is actually a nice game to start off with for all RPG beginners as well as a simple game for major rpg players to play. It provides you with many different styles to play, multiple zodiacs to influence your character and more.
To start it gives you a nice choice of Wizard, Warrior or Phantom Warlock and as you continue, from there level 10, and 36 the classes Wizard and warrior branch off to more classes. Phantom however, does not. but provides unique skills for players who have played the game for some time. Overall it provides you with about 15 classes if you stick to the class you like and stick to the game.
Although the combat is sort of unusual it is still a work in-progress game. It also provides hard dungeons, thus needing you to gain teammates to take it on. The game also includes a nice Soulmate system, though it needs some work. It beats mosts games as it allows a ton of options with the soulmate. Animated interactions, boosts in experience, boosts in abilities. along with the fact that the animations supply you with amazing buffs.
To summarize, this game is good for those who wish to get started in online roleplaying games. It gives the most basic intro into how Rpgs should be. I recommend that you play this for a while at least to level 20 or so. then moving up to bigger games.
4/10 for Ultra experianced players who come from the High quality, High tech RPGs.
9/10 for those who wish for a good intro to RPGs.
Pros:
Multiple classes if you stick to the game (I personally love the Solar guardian, and the Dawn Prophet)
Multiple Zodiacs

If you like trains, wild west and light economic gameplay - buy it now. If not, wait for sale, but get it anyway :)

It's a bit of a guilty pleasure, but probably the main reason I'm into this game is it's surprising difficulty. Think if Banished was toned down maybe 10%, and you have the "normal" difficulty setting on this game.
Every day and dollar counts in Bounty Train, and while it feels like there is a genuine choice of how to play the game (passenger transport, bounty hunting, cargo transport, etc) you will feel like no matter how you specialize, you will be strategizing your routes and your wallet.
Advice I have for new players: don't bother with ironman mode yet, there are a few gamebreaking bugs still in the game that are easily fixed with a reload. Also, as other people suggest, the learning curve is a little steep, but if you mount it, it actually feels like you accomplished something.

Horrifically, murderously, hideously evil difficulty curve in the current Campaign (non-sandbox) mode. This game's campaign was apparently designed by people who hate you more than they love the idea of making a good game.
It's extremely difficult to judge this as a 'recommend' or not. But given the amount of unreasonable frustration the game has caused me since I bought it, I have to say, 'not recommended'- but this will almost certainly change in the future.
To be fair- it's just the campaign and it's early access, so difficulty rebalances are still ongoing. Sandbox mode is a lot more accessible. Playing the campaign in its current state is a lot like playing Russian roulette with one empty chamber, two 'go back to an earlier save' chambers and three 'start again or simply hurl your computer out the window' chambers.
Even if you build a spreadsheet and factor in every price fluctuation at every stop, taking 15 minutes to examine every possible variable and issue, you'd still only have a 50% chance of beating the campaign first try.
If you are a masochist with obsesssive-compulsive disorder and a passion for railways and/or civil war era American history, you'll love the campaign. All others- just play sandbox. Or go slam your various appendages in a car door for three hours. It'll hurt about the same but won't cost anywhere near as much.
For others who may be interested, I think the game is very fun, but only in sandbox mode.
Lastly- I hate to bring this up, but it needs to be mentioned. The devs need to stop stereotyping the Confederacy as a bunch of hate-filled racists going to war to preserve their right to brutalise the slaves. Slavery wasn't the primary cassus belli of the civil war, and the overwhelming majority of Southerners owned no slaves and weren't members of the KKK.
No doubt people from former Confederate states are as tired of the "Southerners were all racist slave owners" meme as Germans are of the "All Germans were nazis who wanted to kill jews, gypsies and gays" meme. A bit of nuance and fair treatment goes a long way.
